SQL Problem Patterns: A Practice Guide

224 problems classified into 12 SELECT recipe categories by input and output shape, plus a Procedures tab for procedural shapes (DO blocks, sequential UPDATE, RETURNS TABLE), with a diagnostic process, decision tree, step-by-step templates, full solutions, and technique reference.

Last updated: April 2026

Six-Step Diagnostic Process

A systematic process for solving SQL problems. Use the reference cards below to work through the six-step diagnostic, then copy the template into your IDE.

Process The Six Steps (expand each for detail and a worked example)

▼

Before writing any SQL, work through these six steps (2-3 minutes). They prevent the most common mistakes: wrong JOIN type, missing GROUP BY column, wrong window function. Expand each step for what it means, how to fill it, and a worked example using #1193 Monthly Transactions I.

PROBLEM — Rewrite the Prompt

▼

Force yourself to actually read the problem by restating it in your own words.

What to do: Rewrite the prompt in plain language. If you can’t restate it simply, you don’t understand it yet. This single step catches most misreads before you write any SQL.

Worked example (#1193):

For each month and country, count total transactions and
sum amount, plus count and sum of approved transactions only.

Step 1: Map the Inputs and the Output

▼

Identify input tables, output columns, and the grain (what makes each row unique).

What to do: List every input table and its columns. Then list the output columns the problem asks for. Determine the grain — what combination of columns gives you exactly one row. Finally, note the row count direction:

  • Fewer rows → filter or aggregate
  • Same rows → transform or compare
  • Single value → scalar extract

This immediately narrows the decision tree before you even think about SQL.

Worked example (#1193):

Input: Transactions(id, country, state, amount, trans_date)
  where state is 'approved' or 'declined'
Output: month, country, trans_count, trans_total_amount,
  approved_count, approved_total_amount
Grain: one row per (month, country)
Row count direction: fewer rows (grouped)

Step 2: Classify the Inputs

▼

Pick one of three source types: Single table, Join 2+ tables, or Reshape.

What to do: Decide how the data arrives. Watch for disguised multi-table problems: scalar subquery denominators and self-joins involve a virtual second table. Remember: after a join, the result is effectively one table, so any single-table shape recipe (filter, aggregate, scalar, rank, transform, compare, window, pair, dedup) still applies to the joined result.

Common self-join shapes — employee/manager (managerId → id), category/parent (parent_id → id), user/referrer (referee_id → id) — use the enrich-join recipe, not row-compare (row-compare is for sequential LAG/LEAD comparisons, not foreign-key lookups).

Worked example (#1193):

[x] Single table  [ ] Join 2+ tables  [ ] Reshape

The "approved only" counts might tempt you to think you
need a second table, but everything lives in one
Transactions table.

Step 3: Name the Shape

▼

Match signal words from the prompt to a recipe category and state the shape in one sentence.

What to do: Scan the prompt for verbs and phrases that map to a recipe. Use the Signal Words Reference table to match them. Then say the shape in one sentence: “This is a __________ because __________.”

The 14 recipe category IDs:

CORE SHAPE RECIPES:
  row-filter               Keep/exclude rows by WHERE condition
  group-aggregate          One summary row per group
  scalar-extract           Reduce table to single value
  rank-partition           Top-N per group via window ranking
  row-transform            Add/rewrite columns, keep row count
  row-compare              Compare each row to neighbor (LAG/LEAD)
  time-window              Rolling/cumulative aggregate
  normalize-bidirectional  Flatten symmetric pairs
  delete-duplicates        Remove duplicate rows in place

JOIN-SPECIFIC RECIPES:
  enrich-join              Look up columns from reference table
  enrich-aggregate         Join tables then aggregate

RESHAPE RECIPE:
  reshape                  Pivot, unpivot, or UNION independent queries

PROCEDURAL RECIPES:
  function-wrapped         SELECT inside CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURNS TABLE
  do-block-sequential      DO $$ ... END $$; with FOR loop + UPDATE

Composite problems: A problem is composite when your sentence has two or more verbs (“join tables THEN aggregate THEN rank”) or two branches survive Step 4 elimination. Intermediate prep steps (assigning row numbers, building a calendar) count as their own move.

Worked example (#1193):

Signal words: "for each month and country" -> GROUP BY
  "count... and sum" -> aggregate
  "approved transactions only" -> conditional aggregation

Named shape: "This is a group-aggregate because I need
  one summary row per (month, country) with conditional splits."

Recipe category: group-aggregate
Composite: No (single recipe)

Step 4: Walk the Decision Tree by Elimination

▼

Rule out every wrong branch with a reason. The last one standing is your answer.

Open the Decision Tree tab and make two taps: first the source (Single table / Join 2+ / Reshape), then the shape leaf inside it. That lands you on the recipe. If your Step 3 and Step 4 answers disagree, re-read the problem — one assumption is wrong.

What to do: Go through every recipe on your decision tree side and say why each one is wrong. The last one standing is your answer. If two survive, it is a composite problem. This feels slow at first but it catches mistakes.

Copy-paste elimination sentences:

SOURCE (pick one, rule out the other two):
  Not Single table because I need to match rows across two tables
  Not Join 2+ tables because all the data lives in one table
  Not Reshape because the tables share a key and need to be joined

SHAPE (rule out shapes you do not need):
  Not Filter because I need to group or transform, not just keep/exclude rows
  Not Aggregate because the output is not one summary row per group
  Not Scalar because the output has multiple rows, not a single number
  Not Rank because I need all rows, not just top or bottom N per group
  Not Transform because the output has fewer rows, not the same count
  Not Compare because I do not need to compare each row to its neighbor
  Not Window because I am not computing a running total or moving average
  Not Pair because the columns have distinct roles, not interchangeable
  Not Dedup because this is a SELECT, not a physical DELETE

Worked example (#1193):

Ruled out:
  Not Filter — I need to group, not just keep/exclude rows
  Not Scalar — output has multiple rows, not a single number
  Not Rank — I need all rows, not top-N per group
  Not Transform — output has fewer rows than input
  Not Compare — no row-to-row comparison needed
  Not Window — not a running total or moving average
  Not Pair — columns have distinct roles
  Not Dedup — this is a SELECT, not a DELETE

Remaining: Aggregate Per Group

Step 5: Grab the Recipe, Adapt from a Linked Problem

▼

Pull the template from the recipe card and adapt column names, conditions, and edge cases.

What to do: Open the recipe card for your surviving branch. Copy its SQL template. Find the most similar linked problem inside that recipe card and adapt: join keys, column names, filter conditions, output columns, and edge cases (nulls, duplicates, empty groups).

Each recipe card lists its signal words (confirm you picked right), the technique (the SQL pattern), and example problems (expand any for ranked solutions).

Worked example (#1193):

Recipe template:
  SELECT group_cols, AGG(value_cols)
  FROM table
  GROUP BY group_cols
  HAVING condition (optional)

Adaptations:
  Group columns: TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM'), country
  Aggregates: COUNT(*), SUM(amount) for totals
  Conditional splits: SUM(CASE WHEN state='approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
  Date formatting: TO_CHAR for month extraction

Step 6: Sanity Check

▼

Run verification checks against common failure modes before submitting.

What to do: Look up the failure mode for your recipe branch (listed on each recipe card). Then run through the checklist:

  • Row count matches Step 1 expectation
  • NULL handling covered (JOIN keys, WHERE, aggregates)
  • Integer division cast to NUMERIC
  • GROUP BY includes all non-aggregated SELECT columns
  • ORDER BY is deterministic (tiebreaker if using LIMIT)
  • Edge cases: empty table, single row, all NULLs, ties

Red flags (if any appear, go back to Step 4): row count wrong, output grain wrong, missing expected groups.

Common failure modes by recipe:

row-filter:             Off-by-one, unintended NULL exclusion
group-aggregate:        Wrong grain, missing GROUP BY column
scalar-extract:         NULL when no rows qualify
row-transform:          CASE WHEN missing ELSE clause
row-compare:            Wrong ORDER BY in LAG/LEAD
time-window:            Wrong frame spec (ROWS vs RANGE)
normalize-bidirectional: Double-counting after UNION ALL
delete-duplicates:      Deleting wrong row (keep MIN id)
enrich-join:            Wrong join type, NULL join keys
enrich-aggregate:       Row explosion from many-to-many
rank-partition:         RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER
reshape:                Column count/type mismatch in UNION

Worked example (#1193):

Failure mode: group-aggregate — wrong grain or missing GROUP BY column

Checks:
  [x] Row count: one row per (month, country) combo
  [x] NULL handling: country could be NULL (GROUP BY treats as one group)
  [x] Integer division: not applicable (counts and sums, not ratios)
  [x] GROUP BY: TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM'), country matches SELECT
  [x] CASE WHEN ELSE 0: prevents NULL in approved sums
  [ ] Edge case: month with zero approved transactions still appears

Reference Identify the Shape

▼

Three lookups for Steps 3 and 4: confirm your shape choice and rule out the alternatives. Expand each.

Single Table Shape Comparison: Why This Recipe and Not That One

▼

Use this table to confirm your shape choice in Step 3 and rule out alternatives in Step 4. Each row explains what makes a single table recipe different from the others.

Recipe When to Use How to Confirm Not This If...
Output: fewer rows than input
Filter Rows The output is a subset of original rows that pass a condition. This includes deduplication via SELECT DISTINCT or GROUP BY (the table itself is not modified) Output columns match the input. Rows are removed, not combined. The original table is unchanged after the query runs The output has "for each" or "per" grouping, adds new computed columns, or the problem asks you to physically delete rows from the table
Aggregate Per Group The output has one summary row per group with a count, sum, or average The output has fewer rows than the input, and every value is either a group key or an aggregate Every input row appears in the output, or the answer is a single number
Extract Single Value The entire answer is one number or one row: any aggregate (SUM, COUNT, AVG, MAX, MIN, etc.), an Nth value, or a percentage across the whole table with no grouping The output is exactly one row with one or two columns The output has multiple rows, or you need a value "for each" group
Rank Within Groups You need the top, bottom, or Nth row within each group from a single table using a window function to rank and then filter The output keeps only some rows per group based on position (top 1, top 3, most recent). A window function assigns the rank, then you filter on it You need all rows per group with a summary value (that is Aggregate Per Group), or the ranking requires data from multiple tables (that is Multi Table > Rank Within Groups)
Output: same row count, new or rewritten column
Add or Rewrite Columns Every row stays but gets a new label, category, or reformatted value Output row count equals input row count. The new column depends only on values in that same row The new column needs to reference the previous or next row, or requires a window function
Compare Row to Neighbor Each row needs to see the previous or next row to detect changes, streaks, or gaps Output row count equals input row count. The new column compares a value to the row before or after it The comparison is against a rolling window or running total, not just the immediate neighbor
Output: time-based aggregate over ordered rows
Rolling or Cumulative Window Each row needs an aggregate computed over a date range or a running total up to that point The problem mentions "rolling," "cumulative," "last N days," or "running total" You only need to compare to the immediate previous row (that is Compare Row to Neighbor)
Special: pair flattening or physical deletion
Normalize Bidirectional Rows like (Alice, Bob) and (Bob, Alice) represent the same relationship and need to be merged before counting The table has two ID columns where the roles are interchangeable (sender/receiver, requester/accepter) The two columns have distinct roles (manager/employee, buyer/seller) where direction matters
Remove Duplicate Rows The problem asks you to physically DELETE rows from the table, not just query it. After the query runs, the table itself has changed The expected output is a modified table, not a SELECT result. The word "delete" or "remove" appears in the prompt. If you ran the query twice, the second run would find nothing to delete You just need unique rows in your output but the table should stay unchanged (that is Filter Rows with SELECT DISTINCT or GROUP BY)

Multi Table Shape Comparison: Why This Recipe and Not That One

▼

Use this table to confirm your recipe choice when the problem gives you two or more tables. Each row explains what makes a multi table recipe different from the others.

Post-join reminder: after a JOIN the result is effectively one table. If your shape is not enrich-join or enrich-aggregate, use any single-table shape recipe (Filter, Scalar, Rank, Transform, Compare, Window, Pair, Dedup) on the joined output. The Decision Tree's Join 2+ panel lists those cross-references explicitly.

Recipe When to Use How to Confirm Not This If...
Look Up Columns You need to attach descriptive columns from a reference table (names, labels) to fact rows. Includes self-joins where one table plays two roles (employee/manager, parent/child, referrer/referee) After joining (or self-joining), the row count stays roughly the same and no aggregation is needed After joining, you still need to GROUP BY and SUM/COUNT (that is Join Then Aggregate)
Join Then Aggregate You need to combine tables and then produce summary statistics from the joined result The output has fewer rows than either input table, and values are aggregates (totals, counts, rates) The output keeps every row from one table and just adds columns from another (that is Look Up Columns)
Rank Within Groups You need the top N rows within each group after joining tables The output asks for "top," "highest," or "first" per group, and the ranking requires data from multiple tables You need all rows per group, not just the top N (that is Join Then Aggregate or Look Up Columns)
Reshape (Pivot / Unpivot / Combine) The output reshapes rows to columns, columns to rows, or stacks independent queries that share the same column structure The result pivots long to wide, unpivots wide to long, or has sections that could each be written as standalone queries with no JOIN between them The rows need to be merged on a shared key (that is a JOIN, not a reshape)

Signal Words → Shape → Recipe Lookup

▼

Scan the problem statement for these phrases, match them to a shape, and go straight to the recipe.

Signal Words in the Problem Shape (Output Pattern) Recipe
Core Shape Recipes (single table or post-join)
find where, exclude, valid, not null, matching, whose, not boring Fewer rows → filtered subset Filter Rows
for each, per, how many, total, average, count of, at least N Fewer rows → one row per group Aggregate Per Group
the single, second highest, the one, overall percentage Single scalar value Extract Single Value
top N per department, highest in each, first per group, most recent per Ranked → top-N per partition Rank Partition
fix, convert, classify, label each, if...then, concatenate, swap Same rows → new/rewritten column Row Transform
rising, consecutive, previous day, day over day, increasing, streak, gap Same rows → neighbor comparison Row Compare
rolling, running total, cumulative, last N days, moving average, most recent before Time → windowed aggregate Time Window
friends, connections, either side, requester/accepter, both directions Bidirectional → flatten then count Normalize Bidirectional
delete, remove duplicates, keep only, deduplicate In-place deletion Delete Duplicates
Join-Specific Recipes (when the join itself is the core move)
replace ID with, look up, show name, regardless of, include from, manager/employee, parent/child, referrer/referee Enrichment or self-join → fact + dimension lookup Enrich Join
for each... from another table, rate, percentage, weighted, all products Enrichment → join then aggregate Enrich Aggregate
Reshape Recipe (pivot, unpivot, combine)
report X and also Y, fixed buckets, combine, categorize into, pivot, unpivot, long to wide, wide to long Rows reshaped to columns, columns to rows, or queries stacked Reshape

-- SOLUTION

Reference SQL Execution Order (How the Engine Processes Your Query)

▼

Understanding this order helps you predict which clauses can reference which aliases and columns.

  1. FROM / JOIN — Tables are loaded and joined first
  2. WHERE — Row-level filtering (no aggregates allowed here)
  3. GROUP BY — Rows are grouped
  4. HAVING — Group-level filtering (aggregates allowed here)
  5. SELECT — Columns are computed (window functions run here)
  6. DISTINCT — Deduplication
  7. ORDER BY — Sorting (can reference SELECT aliases)
  8. LIMIT / OFFSET — Final row restriction

see problems ▾
Two approaches — choose by data shape:
Window function (ROW_NUMBER) — one pass, no self-join, generally more efficient. Best when you only need the latest row per entity.
GROUP BY + self-join — find max date per group, then join back to get the full row. Necessary when you also need a default value for entities with no history (use LEFT JOIN + COALESCE).
ROW_NUMBER() = 1
latest per entity, one pass
FIRST_VALUE()
grab value from first/last row in window
GROUP BY + MAX(date)
find latest date, then self-join
LEFT JOIN + COALESCE
default value when no history exists
WHERE date <= cutoff
filter to events before target date
Efficiency comparison:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY date DESC) = 1 — single table scan, no self-join. Preferred when no default value is needed.
GROUP BY id + MAX(date) + self-join — requires a second pass (the self-join). Use when you need COALESCE for a default value or when you need multiple columns from the matching row.
Pair
bidirectional symmetric — friends, both directions, either side, sender/receiver, A-to-B same as B-to-A

Single-Table Recipes

10 recipe categories aligned with the Decision Tree single-table shapes (Filter, Aggregate, Scalar, Rank, Transform, Compare, Window, Point in Time, Pair, Dedup). These are the core shape recipes — they apply when your input is a single table and they also apply to the result of a JOIN. The Decision Tree's Join 2+ panel cross-links to every recipe here, so post-join problems land on the same page. Rank Within Groups physically lives under Multi-Table Recipes since most ranking problems involve joins.

Reference Technique Quick Reference: When and Why Each Method Works

▼

A quick lookup for the SQL techniques used across all 10 single table recipe categories, with explanations of when each method applies.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
Filtering Techniques
WHERE Keeps or removes rows based on a condition before any grouping happens The condition can be evaluated row by row without needing an aggregate 
SELECT name
FROM Users
WHERE age > 18;
HAVING Filters groups after GROUP BY, using aggregate results The condition depends on a count, sum, or other aggregate (e.g., "groups with more than 1 row") 
SELECT dept, COUNT(*)
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
IN / NOT IN Checks whether a value appears in a list or subquery result You need to filter rows based on whether a value exists in another set of values 
SELECT *
FROM Orders
WHERE status IN ('paid','shipped');
DISTINCT Removes duplicate rows from the output You want unique values but do not need a count or other aggregate 
SELECT DISTINCT country
FROM Customers;
String Techniques (for filtering and transforming text)
LIKE / NOT LIKE Pattern matches using % (any characters) and _ (one character) You need to filter rows where a text column starts with, ends with, or contains a substring 
SELECT *
FROM Users
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com';
REGEXP / RLIKE / ~ Matches rows using a regular expression. MySQL uses REGEXP or RLIKE, PostgreSQL uses ~ (case sensitive) or ~* (case insensitive) LIKE is not powerful enough: you need anchoring, alternation, character classes, or other regex features 
SELECT *
FROM Users
WHERE phone REGEXP '^[0-9]{10}$';
POSITION / STRPOS / INSTR Returns the position of a substring inside a string (0 or NULL if not found). PostgreSQL: POSITION(sub IN col) or STRPOS(col, sub). MySQL: INSTR(col, sub) You need to check whether a substring exists and LIKE's wildcards aren't precise enough, or you need the position for slicing 
SELECT POSITION('@' IN email) AS at_pos
FROM Users;
CONCAT Joins strings together. The space trick CONCAT(' ', col) adds a leading space so every value starts at a word boundary You need to combine columns into one string, or prepend a space so LIKE '% prefix%' won't false match mid-word 
SELECT CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name
FROM Users;
SUBSTRING / LEFT / RIGHT Extracts part of a string by position. LEFT(col, 4) grabs the first 4 characters You need to pull a fixed length prefix, suffix, or slice from a text value 
SELECT LEFT(name, 4)         AS first_four,
       SUBSTRING(name, 2, 3)  AS slice
FROM Users;
UPPER / LOWER Converts text to all uppercase or all lowercase You need case insensitive matching or the output requires a specific casing 
SELECT UPPER(name) AS upper_name,
       LOWER(email) AS lower_email
FROM Users;
REPLACE / TRIM Swaps or removes characters. TRIM strips leading/trailing whitespace You need to clean up messy text data or swap out specific characters in a column 
SELECT REPLACE(phone, '-', '') AS digits,
       TRIM(name)              AS clean_name
FROM Users;
STRING_AGG / GROUP_CONCAT Concatenates values from multiple rows into one comma separated string. Use ORDER BY inside to control sort order The output needs a list of values collapsed into a single cell per group (PostgreSQL: STRING_AGG, MySQL: GROUP_CONCAT) 
SELECT dept,
       STRING_AGG(name, ', ' ORDER BY name) AS members
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept;
Aggregation Techniques
GROUP BY Collapses rows into one row per group so aggregates can be computed The output needs one summary row per group (per department, per month, per user) 
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept;
SUM / COUNT / AVG / MAX / MIN Computes a single summary value from multiple rows With GROUP BY: one value per group. Without GROUP BY: one value for the whole table (scalar extract) 
SELECT MAX(salary) AS top_pay,
       AVG(salary) AS mean_pay,
       COUNT(*)    AS headcount
FROM Emp;
LIMIT / OFFSET Restricts how many rows are returned or skips a number of rows from the top You need the top 1, the Nth value, or need to skip incomplete window rows 
SELECT name
FROM Emp
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;  -- 2nd highest
Row Transform Techniques
CASE WHEN Returns different values based on conditional logic, like an if/else per row You need to classify, label, or remap values based on conditions 
SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN age >= 18 THEN 'Adult'
            ELSE 'Minor' END AS group
FROM Users;
UPDATE Modifies existing column values in place The problem asks you to change a column's value for rows that meet a condition 
UPDATE Emp
SET salary = salary * 1.10
WHERE dept = 'Engineering';
COALESCE Returns the first non NULL value from a list of columns or expressions You need a fallback value when a column might be NULL 
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'Unknown') AS display_name
FROM Users;
Window Function Techniques
LAG / LEAD Accesses the value from the previous (LAG) or next (LEAD) row in order Each row needs to compare itself to its immediate neighbor to detect changes, streaks, or gaps 
SELECT day, sales,
       LAG(sales)  OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev_day,
       LEAD(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS next_day
FROM Daily;
ROWS BETWEEN Defines a sliding window frame (e.g., 6 preceding and current row) for a window aggregate You need a rolling average, running total, or cumulative sum over a fixed number of rows 
SELECT day,
       AVG(sales) OVER (
         ORDER BY day
         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS rolling_7d
FROM Daily;
SUM() OVER / AVG() OVER Computes an aggregate across a window without collapsing rows You need a running or rolling aggregate while keeping every row in the output 
SELECT day, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
         PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day
       ) AS running_total
FROM Trans;
ROW_NUMBER() Assigns a unique sequential number to each row within a partition You need to identify duplicates for deletion or pick one row per group 
SELECT *,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
         PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC
       ) AS rn
FROM Emp;
Structural Techniques
UNION ALL Stacks rows from two queries vertically into one result set Two column roles are interchangeable (sender/receiver) and both directions need to appear as one column 
SELECT name FROM Customers
UNION ALL
SELECT name FROM Vendors;
LEAST / GREATEST Returns the smaller or larger of two values, normalizing pair order You need to treat (A, B) and (B, A) as the same pair by sorting them into a consistent order 
SELECT LEAST(user1, user2)    AS person1,
       GREATEST(user1, user2) AS person2,
       COUNT(*)               AS calls
FROM Calls
GROUP BY person1, person2;
DELETE + CTE Removes rows from the table using a CTE to identify which rows to keep or remove The problem asks you to physically modify the table, not just query it 
WITH dups AS (
  SELECT id,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id
         ) AS rn
  FROM Users
)
DELETE FROM Users
WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM dups WHERE rn > 1);

Filter 28 problems

▼

A single table with all rows visible → a subset of rows matching WHERE conditions.

Signal words: "find all where," "which rows," "valid," "not null," "matching," "whose," "exclude," "not boring"

Technique: WHERE, IS NULL/IS NOT NULL, LIKE, REGEXP, MOD, DISTINCT, NOT IN subquery

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Comparison & boolean logic 7 problems

▼

Plain row-by-row WHERE: =, !=, <, >, BETWEEN, IN (a literal list), AND / OR / NOT, modulo, comparing one column to another, and date ranges.

Template Comparison & boolean logic template

▼

Use when: the keep / drop test reads only the current row.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. List each condition; join with AND (all must hold) or OR (any).
  2. Reach for BETWEEN for ranges, IN (...) for a fixed list, % for modulo, and col1 = col2 to compare two columns.
SELECT *
FROM t
WHERE price >= 100
  AND category IN ('A', 'B')
  AND id % 2 = 1;        -- AND = all hold, OR = any holds

Easy Recyclable and Low Fat Products

▼

Find product ids that are both low fat AND recyclable.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A retailer flags products that are both low fat and recyclable for an eco-friendly shelf label.
  • The Products table stores two yes/no flags per product.
  • Return the product_id of every product where low_fats = 'Y' AND recyclable = 'Y', ordered by product_id.

Schema — Products

ColumnType
product_idINTEGER
low_fatsCHAR(1)
recyclableCHAR(1)

Example input — Products

product_idlow_fatsrecyclable
0YN
1YY
2NY
3YY
4NN

Expected output

product_id
1
3

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Both flags must be 'Y', so the two checks are joined with AND. Nothing fancy -- a single
  WHERE over one table. ORDER BY makes the result deterministic.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT product_id
FROM Products
WHERE low_fats = 'Y'        -- low fat
  AND recyclable = 'Y'      -- AND recyclable (both must hold)
ORDER BY product_id;

Easy Big Countries

▼

Find countries that are big by area OR by population.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A geography tool labels a country as big if it has a large area OR a large population.
  • The World table has one row per country.
  • Return name, population, area for countries where area >= 3000000 OR population >= 25000000, ordered by name.

Schema — World

ColumnType
nameVARCHAR
continentVARCHAR
areaINTEGER
populationINTEGER
gdpBIGINT

Example input — World

namecontinentareapopulationgdp
AfghanistanAsia6522302550010020343000000
AndorraEurope468781153712000000
AustraliaOceania7692024230000001300000000000
BrazilSouth America85157672120000001500000000000

Expected output

namepopulationarea
Afghanistan25500100652230
Australia230000007692024
Brazil2120000008515767

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  "Big by area OR by population" is a literal OR of two thresholds. Afghanistan qualifies on
  population alone (small area), Australia on area alone (population under 25M), and Brazil on
  both. Andorra clears neither and drops out.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT name, population, area
FROM World
WHERE area >= 3000000          -- big by land area
   OR population >= 25000000   -- OR big by population (either is enough)
ORDER BY name;

Easy Article Views I

▼

Find authors who viewed at least one of their own articles. Return distinct ids, sorted.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A content platform flags self-views, where an author viewed their own article.
  • The Views table records each view with the article's author and the viewer.
  • Return the distinct author_id (aliased id) of every author who has a row where author_id = viewer_id, ordered by id.

Schema — Views

ColumnType
article_idINTEGER
author_idINTEGER
viewer_idINTEGER
view_dateDATE

Example input — Views

article_idauthor_idviewer_idview_date
1352019-08-01
1362019-08-02
2772019-08-01
3772019-08-01
4712019-07-22
3442019-07-21

Expected output

id
4
7

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A self-view is simply author_id = viewer_id on the same row. Author 7 viewed their own
  articles twice, so DISTINCT collapses them to one id. Author 4 self-viewed once.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT DISTINCT author_id AS id   -- DISTINCT so an author who self-viewed many times appears once
FROM Views
WHERE author_id = viewer_id       -- the author is also the viewer
ORDER BY id;

Problem Case study & test data

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A platform flags tweets whose content is too long.
  • The Tweets table holds the tweet id and its text.
  • Return the tweet_id of every tweet whose content length is strictly greater than 15 characters, ordered by tweet_id.

Expected output

tweet_id
2

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LENGTH counts characters. Tweet 1 is 14 characters (kept out by the strict >), tweet 2 is 32.

Medium Not Boring Movies

▼

Find odd-id movies that are not boring, sorted by rating descending.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A cinema lists movies with an odd id whose description is not boring.
  • The Cinema table has one row per movie with a description and a rating.
  • Return all columns for movies where id is odd AND description <> 'boring', ordered by rating descending.

Schema — Cinema

ColumnType
idINTEGER
movieVARCHAR
descriptionVARCHAR
ratingDECIMAL(3,1)

Example input — Cinema

idmoviedescriptionrating
1Wargreat 3D8.9
2Sciencefiction8.5
3irishboring6.2
4Ice songFantacy8.6
5House cardInteresting9.1

Expected output

idmoviedescriptionrating
5House cardInteresting9.1
1Wargreat 3D8.9

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Two filters: id is odd (id % 2 = 1) and the description is not the literal 'boring'. Then
  sort by rating high to low. Movie 3 is odd but boring, movies 2 and 4 are even -- all drop.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT id, movie, description, rating
FROM Cinema
WHERE id % 2 = 1                 -- odd id
  AND description <> 'boring'    -- AND not boring
ORDER BY rating DESC;

Easy Friendly Movies Streamed Last Month

▼

Return distinct family-friendly movie titles streamed in June 2020.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A streaming service lists kid-friendly movies that aired in June 2020.
  • TVProgram records which content aired on which date; Content describes each piece of content.
  • Return the distinct title of content that is a movie (content_type = 'Movies'), kid friendly (Kids_content = 'Y'), and aired in June 2020, ordered by title.

Schema — TVProgram

ColumnType
program_dateDATE
content_idINTEGER
channelVARCHAR

Example input — TVProgram

program_datecontent_idchannel
2020-06-101CH1
2020-06-151CH2
2020-07-013CH1
2020-06-202CH1
2020-06-253CH1

Schema — Content

ColumnType
content_idINTEGER
titleVARCHAR
Kids_contentCHAR(1)
content_typeVARCHAR

Example input — Content

content_idtitleKids_contentcontent_type
1MickeyYMovies
2NewsXNSeries
3FrozenYMovies

Expected output

title
Frozen
Mickey

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Join the airing log to the content dimension, then apply the three filters: kid friendly,
  movie, and aired within June 2020. Content 3 (Frozen) also aired in July, but its June 25
  airing qualifies; DISTINCT keeps one title. Content 2 is a series and drops.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT DISTINCT c.title
FROM TVProgram t
JOIN Content c ON c.content_id = t.content_id
WHERE c.Kids_content = 'Y'                                         -- kid friendly
  AND c.content_type = 'Movies'                                   -- a movie, not a series
  AND t.program_date BETWEEN DATE '2020-06-01' AND DATE '2020-06-30'   -- aired in June 2020
ORDER BY c.title;

Problem Case study & test data

Prompt

  • A practice site flags low quality problems, where dislikes outnumber likes.
  • The Problems table has like and dislike counts per problem.
  • Return the problem_id of every problem where likes < dislikes, ordered by problem_id descending.

Example input — Problems

problem_idlikesdislikes
612901290
1124
153
7820

Expected output

problem_id
11
7

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Strict less-than, so problem 6 (equal likes and dislikes) is not low quality. Problems 11
  and 7 have more dislikes than likes.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.

SELECT problem_id
FROM Problems

NULL-aware filters 1 problems

▼

IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, and the traps where != or NOT IN silently drop or keep NULL rows. Any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, never TRUE.

Template NULL-aware filter template

▼

Use when: the test hinges on a value being present or missing.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL — never = NULL (always UNKNOWN).
  2. col <> v silently drops NULL rows; add OR col IS NULL to keep them.
  3. NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery yields any NULL — use NOT EXISTS.
SELECT *
FROM t
WHERE status <> 'closed'   -- this alone drops NULLs
   OR status IS NULL;     -- ...so add this to keep them

Easy Find Customer Referee

▼

Find customers not referred by customer id 2 (including those with no referrer).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A loyalty team lists customers who were NOT referred by customer 2.
  • The Customer table has a referee_id that is NULL when the customer was not referred by anyone.
  • Return the name of every customer whose referee_id is NULL OR is not 2.
  • The NULL handling is the point: a comparison with NULL is itself NULL (not true), so referee_id <> 2 alone would silently drop the not-referred customers -- you must add referee_id IS NULL.

Schema — Customer

ColumnType
idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
referee_idINTEGER

Example input — Customer

idnamereferee_id
1WillNULL
2JaneNULL
3Alex2
4BillNULL
5Zack1
6Mark2

Expected output

name
Will
Jane
Bill
Zack

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The trap: referee_id <> 2 is NULL (not true) for the rows where referee_id IS NULL, so those
  customers would vanish even though they were not referred by 2. Adding the explicit
  referee_id IS NULL branch keeps them. Customers 3 and 6 (referred by 2) are the only ones
  excluded.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

SELECT name
FROM Customer
WHERE referee_id IS NULL        -- not referred by anyone (a <> 2 check would miss these)
   OR referee_id <> 2           -- OR referred, but not by customer 2
ORDER BY id;

Pattern matching (LIKE / regex) 4 problems

▼

Match text with LIKE (% and _) or a regular expression: starts-with, contains, or anchored formats like emails and phone numbers.

Decide LIKE or regex? Pick the pattern tool

▼

Match text by its shape. Start simple: use LIKE unless the rule needs regex power.

How complex is the shape you need to match?
Simple wildcard — starts-with, ends-with, contains, or a single-character _→LIKE / ILIKE Character classes, quantifiers, anchors, alternation, or word boundaries→Regular expressions

Rule of thumb: LIKE is the simplest and most portable — reach for a regex only when LIKE cannot express the rule. For case-insensitivity alone, ILIKE (or LOWER(col) LIKE LOWER(pattern)) is enough, no regex needed.

LIKE / ILIKE (wildcard match) 1 problem

▼

Simple wildcard matching with % (any run) and _ (one character); ILIKE for case-insensitive. Reach here first — only escalate to regex when the shape needs classes or anchors.

Template LIKE / ILIKE template

▼

Use when: match text by a simple wildcard shape.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. % matches any run of characters, _ matches exactly one.
  2. 'A%' starts-with, '%A' ends-with, '%A%' contains.
  3. Case-insensitive: Postgres ILIKE, or LOWER(col) LIKE LOWER(pattern) anywhere.
  4. To match a literal % or _, escape it: LIKE '100\%%' ESCAPE '\'.
SELECT * FROM t WHERE name LIKE 'A%';                 -- starts with A
SELECT * FROM t WHERE name LIKE '%report%';           -- contains report
SELECT * FROM t WHERE code LIKE 'A_C';                -- _ = exactly one character
SELECT * FROM t WHERE name ILIKE '%abc%';             -- case-insensitive (Postgres)
SELECT * FROM t WHERE note LIKE '%100\%%' ESCAPE '\';  -- match a literal %

Easy Patients With a Condition

▼

Find patients whose conditions include a Type I Diabetes code (DIAB1 prefix).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A clinic finds patients with Type I Diabetes, coded as a word starting with DIAB1.
  • The Patients table stores a space-separated list of condition codes in one column.
  • Return patient_id, patient_name, conditions for patients whose conditions contains a code starting with DIAB1.
  • The code can be the first word OR follow a space, so two LIKE patterns are needed; a bare %DIAB1% would wrongly match codes like SDIAB1 where DIAB1 is mid-word.

Schema — Patients

ColumnType
patient_idINTEGER
patient_nameVARCHAR
conditionsVARCHAR

Example input — Patients

patient_idpatient_nameconditions
1DanielYFEV COUGH
2Alice
3BobDIAB100 MYOP
4GeorgeACNE DIAB100
5AlainDIAB201

Expected output

patient_idpatient_nameconditions
3BobDIAB100 MYOP
4GeorgeACNE DIAB100

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A code "starts with DIAB1" if it is the very first word (LIKE 'DIAB1%') or it follows a space
  (LIKE '% DIAB1%'). Bob has it as the first code; George has it after a space. Alain's DIAB201
  is a different code (DIAB2) and is correctly skipped.

  Why not a single '%DIAB1%': that would also match codes where DIAB1 sits in the middle of a
  word (e.g. XDIAB1), which are not Type I Diabetes.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT patient_id, patient_name, conditions
FROM Patients
WHERE conditions LIKE 'DIAB1%'      -- DIAB1 is the first code
   OR conditions LIKE '% DIAB1%'    -- OR DIAB1 starts a code after a space
ORDER BY patient_id;

Regular expressions 3 problems

▼

When LIKE is not enough: character classes, quantifiers, anchors, alternation, and word boundaries. Two common jobs — validate a whole value, or find / count matches inside text.

Decide Which regex job?

▼

Two regex shapes show up the most: validating a whole value, and finding matches inside text.

Are you checking a whole value, or finding matches inside text?
The WHOLE value must match a format — email, product code, id→Validate an anchored format Match a sub-pattern anywhere — count files, whole words, extract pieces→Find / count / extract

Anchors decide it: ^...$ forces the entire string to match a shape (validation); an unanchored pattern matches if it appears anywhere (search, count, extract).

Validate an anchored format (^...$) 2 problems

▼

The whole value must match a shape: email, product code, id. Anchor with ^ and $ so a partial match cannot sneak through.

Template Anchored format template (^...$)

▼

Use when: the whole value must match a fixed shape.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Wrap the pattern in ^ and $ so the ENTIRE value must match, not just part.
  2. Build the shape from classes [A-Za-z0-9_.-], quantifiers * + {n}, and alternation (a|b).
  3. Escape regex metacharacters: a literal dot is \..
  4. Postgres uses ~ (~* for case-insensitive); RE2 engines (DuckDB) use regexp_matches / regexp_full_match.
-- Postgres operator form
SELECT * FROM t WHERE col ~ '^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*@example\.com$';
SELECT * FROM t WHERE sku ~ '_[A-Z]{2}$';   -- underscore + exactly two capitals at the end
-- RE2 / DuckDB equivalent
SELECT * FROM t WHERE regexp_matches(col, '^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*@example\.com$');

Easy Find Users With Valid E-Mails

▼

Find users whose email matches the valid pattern at @example.com.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A service validates email addresses against a fixed rule.
  • The Users table holds each user's email in mail.
  • A valid email's prefix starts with a letter and contains only letters, digits, underscore, period, or dash, followed by @example.com.
  • Return all columns for users whose mail matches that pattern, ordered by user_id.

Schema — Users

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
mailVARCHAR

Example input — Users

user_idnamemail
1Winstonwinston@example.com
2Jonathanjonathanisgreat
3Annabellebella-@example.com
4Sallysally.come@example.com
5Marwanquarz#2020@example.com
6Daviddavid69@gmail.com
7Shapiro.shapo@example.com

Expected output

user_idnamemail
1Winstonwinston@example.com
3Annabellebella-@example.com
4Sallysally.come@example.com

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The whole rule is one anchored regular expression:
    ^                  start of string
    [A-Za-z]           first character must be a letter
    [A-Za-z0-9_.-]*    then any run of letters, digits, underscore, period, or dash
    @example\.com$     literal @example.com at the end (the \. is a literal dot)

  Jonathan has no @example.com, Marwan has a '#', David is @gmail.com, and Shapiro starts with
  a dot -- all fail. The ^ and $ anchors force the WHOLE string to match, not just part of it.

  Note: this is the Postgres operator form (~). In a RE2 engine such as DuckDB the same check
  reads regexp_matches(mail, '^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*@example\.com$').

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT user_id, name, mail
FROM Users
WHERE mail ~ '^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*@example\.com$'   -- anchored pattern: whole string must match
ORDER BY user_id;

Easy Find SKUs with Size Variant Codes

▼

Anchored regex: keep rows whose code ends in an underscore plus exactly two uppercase letters.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A warehouse team finds SKUs that follow the size-variant naming rule.
  • A SKU qualifies if it contains an underscore followed by exactly two uppercase letters at the end (the size code), e.g. DRESS_SM, JACKET_XL, BLOUSE_MD.
  • inventory_items has one row per SKU.
  • Return sku, product_name, and stock_quantity for matching SKUs, ordered by sku.

Schema — inventory_items

ColumnType
skuVARCHAR (PK)
product_nameVARCHAR
stock_quantityINTEGER
last_restockedDATE

Example input — inventory_items

skuproduct_namestock_quantitylast_restocked
DRESS_SMFloral Midi Dress452024-01-15
JACKET_XLLeather Bomber Jacket122024-01-20
SCARF-REDSilk Red Scarf782024-02-01
BLOUSE_MDCotton White Blouse332024-01-25
HANDBAG_LARGETote Handbag222024-02-05
SHOES_10Running Sneakers562024-01-18
BELT_MCasual Brown Belt89NULL
SWEATER_LGWool Cardigan Sweater192024-01-30

Expected output

skuproduct_namestock_quantity
BLOUSE_MDCotton White Blouse33
DRESS_SMFloral Midi Dress45
JACKET_XLLeather Bomber Jacket12
SWEATER_LGWool Cardigan Sweater19

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The rule "underscore then exactly two uppercase letters at the end" is one anchored regular expression:
    _          a literal underscore
    [A-Z]{2}   exactly two uppercase letters
    $          end of string -- so the two letters are the last characters

  The $ anchor is what enforces "exactly two": SWEATER_LG and BLOUSE_MD end in _ plus two capitals, but
  HANDBAG_LARGE (five letters), BELT_M (one), SHOES_10 (digits), and SCARF-RED (a dash, not an underscore)
  all fail. An explicit alternation of known codes -- '(_XS|_SM|_MD|_LG|_XL|_OS)$' -- also works when the
  set of sizes is fixed, but the class form needs no list.

  Note: this is the Postgres operator form (~). In a RE2 engine such as DuckDB the same check reads
  regexp_matches(sku, '_[A-Z]{2}$').

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

SELECT sku, product_name, stock_quantity
FROM inventory_items
WHERE sku ~ '_[A-Z]{2}$'        -- underscore + exactly two uppercase letters, anchored to the end
ORDER BY sku;

Find / count / extract matches 1 problem

▼

Match a sub-pattern anywhere in the text — whole words via boundaries, counting files, or pulling out pieces. No end anchor; the pattern just has to appear.

Template Find / count / extract template

▼

Use when: match a sub-pattern anywhere in the text.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Word boundaries keep whole words exact: Postgres \y...\y, RE2 / DuckDB \b...\b — so bull does not match bullets.
  2. Count ROWS that contain a match: filter with ~ (or regexp_matches) then COUNT(*).
  3. Count or pull matches WITHIN one string: regexp_count, regexp_extract, or regexp_matches(col, pat, 'g').
-- whole word only (Postgres \y, RE2/DuckDB \b)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE content ~ '\ybull\y';
-- count occurrences inside each string
SELECT regexp_count(content, '[0-9]+') FROM t;

Medium Count Occurrences in Text

▼

Count how many files contain the whole word 'bull' and how many contain 'bear'.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A news team counts how many files mention bull and how many mention bear as whole words.
  • The Files table has one row per file with its text in content.
  • Return two rows: the word and the number of files whose content contains that whole word.
  • Whole word matters: bullets and bearings must NOT count, so a word-boundary regular expression is used instead of a plain substring search.

Schema — Files

ColumnType
file_nameVARCHAR
contentVARCHAR

Example input — Files

file_namecontent
draft1.txtThe bull market is strong
draft2.txtA bear attacked the bull
draft3.txtbullets and bearings
draft4.txtbull and bear together

Expected output

wordcount
bull3
bear2

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Word boundaries are the whole point. '\ybull\y' matches bull only as a standalone word, so
  "bullets" and "bearings" in draft3 do not count. Bull appears as a whole word in drafts 1, 2,
  and 4 (count 3); bear in drafts 2 and 4 (count 2). UNION ALL stacks the two counts into the
  two required rows.

  Note: \y is the Postgres word-boundary marker. A RE2 engine such as DuckDB writes it as \b:
  regexp_matches(content, '\bbull\b').

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT 'bull' AS word, COUNT(*) AS count
FROM Files
WHERE content ~ '\ybull\y'        -- whole word bull, not "bullets"
UNION ALL
SELECT 'bear', COUNT(*)
FROM Files
WHERE content ~ '\ybear\y';       -- whole word bear, not "bearings\"

Membership via subquery (IN / EXISTS) 5 problems

▼

Keep rows whose key appears in another set: IN (subquery), EXISTS, "bought both A and B", or a value above a subquery aggregate.

Template Membership via subquery template

▼

Use when: keep rows that DO appear in another set.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. IN (subquery) or EXISTS — EXISTS short-circuits and is NULL-safe.
  2. "Has both A and B": group the related table and gate with HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT needed) = 2.
SELECT *
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.cust_id = c.id
);

Easy Sales Analysis III

▼

Find products sold only within Q1 2019 and never outside it.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A merchandiser finds products that sold only during the first quarter of 2019.
  • Sales records each sale date per product; Product holds product names.
  • Return product_id and product_name for products whose every sale falls within Jan 1 to Mar 31, 2019.
  • The key idea: a product qualifies only if its earliest AND latest sale both sit inside the window, so check MIN and MAX of the sale date, not a per-row filter.

Schema — Product

ColumnType
product_idINTEGER
product_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Product

product_idproduct_name
1S8
2G4
3iPhone

Schema — Sales

ColumnType
product_idINTEGER
sale_dateDATE

Example input — Sales

product_idsale_date
12019-01-21
12019-02-17
22019-02-10
22019-05-21
32019-01-15

Expected output

product_idproduct_name
1S8
3iPhone

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  "Sold only in Q1" means the product never sold outside Q1, which is true exactly when both the
  earliest and latest sale fall inside the window. Group per product and check MIN and MAX of
  sale_date. Product 2 sold again in May, so its MAX falls outside and it drops.

  Why not a per-row WHERE sale_date BETWEEN ...: that keeps a product's Q1 rows while ignoring
  its May row, wrongly including product 2. The MIN/MAX-after-grouping check is what enforces
  "every sale is inside."

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM Sales s
JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = s.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
HAVING MIN(s.sale_date) >= DATE '2019-01-01'    -- earliest sale on/after Jan 1
   AND MAX(s.sale_date) <= DATE '2019-03-31'    -- latest sale on/before Mar 31
ORDER BY p.product_id;

Medium All People Report to the Given Manager

▼

Find every employee who reports directly or indirectly to manager id 1.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • HR needs everyone under the top manager (id 1), at any depth.
  • The Employees table is self-referencing: each row's manager_id points at another employee.
  • Return the employee_id of every employee who reports to manager 1 directly or through a chain, excluding manager 1 itself.
  • Walk the reporting tree with a recursive query, since the depth is not fixed.

Schema — Employees

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
employee_nameVARCHAR
manager_idINTEGER

Example input — Employees

employee_idemployee_namemanager_id
1Boss1
2Ann1
3Bo2
4Cy3
5Di1
6Ed9

Expected output

employee_id
2
3
4
5

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A recursive CTE walks down the org chart. The anchor grabs manager 1's direct reports (2 and
  5, excluding manager 1 itself, who points at himself). Each recursive step joins the next
  level: 2's report is 3, then 3's report is 4. Employee 6 reports to 9, who is not under
  manager 1, so 6 never enters the set.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH RECURSIVE Subordinates AS (
    SELECT employee_id, manager_id
    FROM Employees
    WHERE manager_id = 1 AND employee_id <> 1     -- anchor: direct reports of manager 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.employee_id, e.manager_id
    FROM Employees e
    JOIN Subordinates s ON e.manager_id = s.employee_id   -- step: reports of everyone found so far
)
SELECT employee_id
FROM Subordinates
ORDER BY employee_id;

Medium Customers Who Bought Products A and B but Not C

▼

Find customers who bought both A and B but never C.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Marketing wants customers who own products A and B but not C, to cross-sell C.
  • Orders records each purchased product per customer; Customers holds names.
  • Return customer_id and customer_name for customers who bought A AND B AND never bought C, ordered by customer_id.

Schema — Customers

ColumnType
customer_idINTEGER
customer_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Customers

customer_idcustomer_name
1Daniel
2Diana
3Elizabeth
4Jhon
5Bob

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
product_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Orders

order_idcustomer_idproduct_name
11A
21B
31C
42A
52B
63A
73B
83C
94A
105A
115B

Expected output

customer_idcustomer_name
2Diana
5Bob

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Group each customer's orders into one row, then use conditional SUMs as per-product counters.
  SUM(CASE WHEN product = 'A' ...) > 0 means "bought at least one A"; the C counter must equal 0
  for "never bought C". All three conditions ANDed in HAVING.

  Diana and Bob bought A and B but no C. Daniel and Elizabeth also bought C, so they drop; Jhon
  bought only A.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN o.product_name = 'A' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0    -- bought A
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN o.product_name = 'B' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0    -- AND bought B
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN o.product_name = 'C' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0    -- AND never bought C
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Easy Find Expensive Cities

▼

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A real estate portal highlights cities pricier than the national average.
  • The Listings table has one row per listing with its city and price.
  • Return each city whose average price is strictly greater than the average price across all listings, ordered by city.
  • The overall average is one number computed across the whole table, used as the bar in HAVING.

Schema — Listings

ColumnType
listing_idINTEGER
cityVARCHAR
priceINTEGER

Example input — Listings

listing_idcityprice
1Austin300
2Austin700
3Dallas200
4Dallas220
5Miami900

Expected output

city
Austin
Miami

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The bar is the average over ALL listings (here 464). The scalar subquery computes it once.
  Group by city, and HAVING keeps cities whose own average beats the overall one: Austin
  averages 500 and Miami 900, both above 464; Dallas averages 210 and drops.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT city
FROM Listings
GROUP BY city
HAVING AVG(price) > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM Listings)   -- city average beats the overall average
ORDER BY city;

Prompt

  • A lender finds users holding both a Refinance and a Mortgage loan.
  • The Loans table has one row per loan with its type.
  • Return the user_id of every user who has at least one Refinance AND at least one Mortgage, ordered by user_id.
  • Filter to the two types of interest, then require both appear via a distinct count of 2.

Schema — Loans

ColumnType
loan_idINTEGER
user_idINTEGER
loan_typeVARCHAR

Example input — Loans

loan_iduser_idloan_type
11Mortgage
21Refinance
32Refinance
43Mortgage
53Auto
64Refinance
74Mortgage

Expected output

user_id
1
4

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  First keep only the two loan types that matter. After grouping per user, COUNT(DISTINCT
  loan_type) = 2 means both showed up. User 1 and user 4 hold both; user 2 has only Refinance,
  and user 3's Auto is filtered out so only Mortgage remains.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT user_id
FROM Loans
WHERE loan_type IN ('Refinance', 'Mortgage')   -- only the two types we care about

Anti-join: never / did not / no match 11 problems

▼

Keep rows with NO matching row in another set: NOT IN, NOT EXISTS, or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right IS NULL. The "customers who never ordered" shape.

Decide Which anti-join method?

▼

All three keep rows with NO match. Choose by NULL safety, whether you need the other table's columns, and readability — then open the matching container below.

Could the right-side key you match on ever be NULL?
Yes, or not sure — the NULL-safe default that reads as “keep rows where none matches”→NOT EXISTS No — the column is guaranteed NOT NULL (e.g. a primary key) and you want the shortest read→NOT IN
Do you also need columns FROM the other table in the output, not just the keep / drop test?
Yes — you want matched values too, or it simply reads more naturally as a join→LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right IS NULL No — you only test existence and return the left row→NOT EXISTS

Rule of thumb: reach for NOT EXISTS first — correct with NULLs and states the intent directly. Use LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL when the same query already needs the other table's columns. Use NOT IN only when the subquery column cannot be NULL — a single stray NULL silently returns zero rows.

NOT EXISTS (NULL-safe default) 6 problems

▼

A correlated subquery with the link in its WHERE (never an ON); keep the row when no matching row exists. NULL-safe and the form to reach for first.

Template Anti-join template — NOT EXISTS (safe default)

▼

Use when: keep rows with NO match; the right-side key might be NULL.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. The subquery is CORRELATED — it has no JOIN, so the link to the outer row goes in its WHERE (o.cust_id = c.id), never an ON.
  2. NULL-safe: a NULL on the right does not break the test.
  3. This is the default for “never / did not / no match.”
SELECT c.*
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.cust_id = c.id   -- correlate in WHERE, not ON
);

Medium Students Who Never Improved Their Grades

▼

Combine a positive EXISTS (has at least one related row) with a negative NOT EXISTS (no related row of another kind).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A homework app wants students who have done work but never bettered a score on a resubmission.
  • students lists students; assignments logs every submission; grade_improvements logs each time a resubmission beat the first attempt.
  • Return the student_id and student_name of students who submitted at least one assignment AND never have an improvement row, ordered by student id.

Schema — students

ColumnType
student_idINTEGER (PK)
student_nameVARCHAR
grade_levelINTEGER

Example input — students

student_idstudent_namegrade_level
101Alice Chen7
102Bob Martinez8
103Carol White7
104David Kim9
105Emma Brown8

Schema — assignments

ColumnType
assignment_idINTEGER (PK)
student_idINTEGER
assignment_nameVARCHAR
scoreINTEGER
submitted_atTIMESTAMP

Example input — assignments

assignment_idstudent_idassignment_namescoresubmitted_at
1101Math Quiz 1752024-01-10 10:00:00
2101Math Quiz 1852024-01-12 14:00:00
3102Science Lab602024-01-11 09:00:00
4103History Essay802024-01-13 11:00:00
5104Math Quiz 1702024-01-10 10:30:00
6105Science Lab902024-01-14 15:00:00

Schema — grade_improvements

ColumnType
improvement_idINTEGER (PK)
student_idINTEGER
assignment_nameVARCHAR
old_scoreINTEGER
new_scoreINTEGER
improved_atTIMESTAMP

Example input — grade_improvements

improvement_idstudent_idassignment_nameold_scorenew_scoreimproved_at
1101Math Quiz 175852024-01-12 14:00:00
2104Math Quiz 170782024-01-15 16:00:00

Expected output

student_idstudent_name
102Bob Martinez
103Carol White
105Emma Brown

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Two membership tests on the same student. The positive EXISTS keeps only students who submitted at least
  one assignment; the negative NOT EXISTS drops any student who has an improvement row. Each is a CORRELATED
  subquery: it has no JOIN, so the link to the outer row lives in its WHERE (a.student_id = s.student_id),
  never an ON -- writing ON here is the syntax error, since there is nothing to join ON. Alice and David
  each improved, so they fall out; Bob, Carol, and Emma submitted work and never improved.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name
FROM students AS s
WHERE EXISTS (                                              -- has at least one submission
        SELECT 1 FROM assignments AS a
        WHERE a.student_id = s.student_id                  -- correlation in WHERE, not ON
      )
  AND NOT EXISTS (                                          -- never improved: the anti-join half
        SELECT 1 FROM grade_improvements AS g
        WHERE g.student_id = s.student_id
      )
ORDER BY s.student_id;

/* Same answer as a LEFT JOIN anti-join: keep students whose improvement side is missing.
   INNER JOIN to assignments enforces the "submitted at least one"; the LEFT JOIN + IS NULL is the anti-join.
SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name
FROM students AS s
JOIN assignments AS a            ON a.student_id = s.student_id   -- must have a submission
LEFT JOIN grade_improvements AS g ON g.student_id = s.student_id  -- look for an improvement
WHERE g.improvement_id IS NULL                                    -- ... and keep only those with none
GROUP BY s.student_id, s.student_name                             -- collapse multiple assignment rows
ORDER BY s.student_id;
*/

Easy Employees Whose Manager Left the Company

▼

Find low-paid employees whose manager id no longer exists in the table.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • After departures, HR audits for employees pointing at a manager who is gone.
  • The Employees table is self-referencing via manager_id.
  • Return the employee_id of employees where salary < 30000, manager_id is not NULL, and that manager_id is not an existing employee_id, ordered by employee_id.

Schema — Employees

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
manager_idINTEGER
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Employees

employee_idnamemanager_idsalary
3Mila960301
12AntonellaNULL31000
13EmeryNULL67084
1Kalel721241
9Mindy650937
2Mayer1265804
11HercyNULL64927
6AlexNULL28107

Expected output

employee_id
1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Three filters: low salary, a non-NULL manager, and that manager no longer in the table. The
  anti-join is NOT EXISTS: keep an employee only when NO row has an employee_id matching their
  manager_id -- the manager is gone. Kalel earns under 30000 and reports to manager 7, who is not
  an employee_id in the table, so Kalel is the orphaned row. Alex also earns under 30000 but his
  manager_id is NULL, so the IS NOT NULL guard drops him (a NULL manager did not "leave").

  NOT EXISTS over NOT IN: if the employee_id set could contain a NULL, NOT IN turns every row
  unknown and returns nothing; the correlated NOT EXISTS (or a LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL) is NULL-safe.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT e.employee_id
FROM Employees e
WHERE e.salary < 30000                  -- low salary band
  AND e.manager_id IS NOT NULL          -- actually has a manager
  AND NOT EXISTS (                      -- whose id is gone from the table (the anti-join)
        SELECT 1 FROM Employees m
        WHERE m.employee_id = e.manager_id
      )
ORDER BY e.employee_id;

Prompt

  • Customers holds the people; Orders records orders by customerId.

/*
  An anti-join: keep customers with no matching order. NOT EXISTS returns customers for whom the
  subquery finds nothing. Only customers 1 and 3 placed orders, so Henry (2) and Max (4) remain.

  NOT EXISTS is preferred over NOT IN here because it is NULL-safe: a NULL customerId in Orders
  would make NOT IN return no rows at all.

SELECT name AS customers
FROM Customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (                       -- no order belongs to this customer

ORDER BY id;

Medium Drop Type 1 Orders for Customers With Type 0 Orders

▼

If a customer has any Type 0 order keep only their Type 0 rows, otherwise keep their Type 1 rows.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A billing pipeline keeps a customer's primary order rows and drops the fallback.
  • The Orders table has an order_type of 0 or 1 per order.
  • For each customer who has any Type 0 order, keep only their Type 0 rows; for customers with no Type 0 order, keep their Type 1 rows.
  • Return all order columns, ordered by order_id.

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
order_typeINTEGER

Example input — Orders

order_idcustomer_idorder_type
110
211
321
421
530
630

Expected output

order_idcustomer_idorder_type
110
321
421
530
630

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Anti-join framing: keep every Type 0 row outright, and keep a Type 1 row only when its customer has
  NO Type 0 order -- a NOT EXISTS against the same table. The Type 1 rows that DO have a Type 0 sibling
  are exactly the ones the anti-join removes. Customer 1 has a zero, so their Type 1 order 2 is dropped;
  customer 2 has no zero, so both Type 1 rows survive; customer 3's two Type 0 rows are kept directly.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

SELECT o.*
FROM Orders o
WHERE o.order_type = 0                          -- always keep Type 0 rows
   OR NOT EXISTS (                              -- keep a Type 1 row only if the customer
        SELECT 1 FROM Orders z                  -- has no Type 0 order at all (the anti-join)
        WHERE z.customer_id = o.customer_id
          AND z.order_type = 0
      )
ORDER BY o.order_id;

episode_idINT
titleVARCHAR
duration_minutesINT
published_dateDATE

Schema — listening_sessions

ColumnType
session_idINT
episode_idINT
user_idINT
completedBOOLEAN
listened_minutesINT

Example input — episodes

episode_idtitleduration_minutespublished_date
101Introduction to PostgreSQL452024-01-15
102Advanced SQL Joins602024-01-22
103Database Indexing Basics502024-02-01
104Query Optimization Tips552024-02-10
105Transactions and ACID482024-02-20

Example input — listening_sessions

session_idepisode_iduser_idcompletedlistened_minutes
11011001true45
21011002false20
31021001false30
41021003NULL15
51031001false10
61041002true55

Expected output

episode_idtitleduration_minutes
102Advanced SQL Joins60
103Database Indexing Basics50
105Transactions and ACID48

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  "Never completed" means NO session with completed = true exists for that episode. Put that
  whole condition INSIDE one NOT EXISTS: the correlated subquery looks only for a finished
  session, and the episode is kept when none is found. This one shape covers all three cases at
  once -- partial-only sessions (102, 103), a NULL completed flag (102), and no sessions at all
  (105) -- so you do NOT need an OR of "no sessions" plus "all sessions unfinished".
  Why NOT EXISTS and not NOT IN: completed can be NULL, and `episode_id NOT IN (... WHERE
  completed = true)` would compare against a set and break on the NULL; NOT EXISTS just asks
  "does a finished row exist?" and is NULL-safe. The partial / NULL rows simply are not
  completed = true, so they never disqualify an episode.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT
    e.episode_id,
    e.title,
    e.duration_minutes
FROM episodes AS e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (                       -- keep episodes with NO finished session
    SELECT 1
    FROM listening_sessions AS l
    WHERE l.episode_id = e.episode_id    -- correlate to this episode
      AND l.completed = true             -- the gate lives INSIDE the subquery
)
ORDER BY e.episode_id;

LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right IS NULL 3 problems

▼

Attach the other table with a LEFT JOIN, then keep the rows whose right-side key came back NULL. Best when the query also needs columns from the other table, or when manufacturing a full spine and keeping the gaps.

Template Anti-join template — LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL

▼

Use when: you also want the other table's columns, or it reads better as a join.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. LEFT JOIN keeps every left row; unmatched rows get NULLs on the right side.
  2. Filtering WHERE right.key IS NULL keeps exactly the rows that did NOT match.
  3. If the join can fan out (many matches per left row), add DISTINCT or GROUP BY — though unmatched rows never fan out.
SELECT c.*
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id   -- attach matches; NULLs where none
WHERE o.cust_id IS NULL;                 -- keep only the unmatched left rows

Easy Sellers With No Sales

Prompt

  • Sales leadership reviews reps with zero sales in 2020.
  • Seller holds reps; Orders records each order with a date and seller; Customer is the buyer dimension.
  • Return the seller_name of every seller with no order dated in 2020, ordered by seller_name.
  • Filter the join to 2020 inside the ON clause so a seller who sold only in other years still counts as having no 2020 sales.

Schema — Customer

ColumnType
customer_idINTEGER
customer_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Customer

customer_idcustomer_name
1Aria
2Bert

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
sale_dateDATE
order_costINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
seller_idINTEGER

Example input — Orders

order_idsale_dateorder_costcustomer_idseller_id
12020-03-0110011
22019-12-015022
32020-07-158011

Schema — Seller

ColumnType
seller_idINTEGER
seller_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Seller

seller_idseller_name
1Daniel
2Elizabeth
3Frank

Expected output

seller_name
Elizabeth
Frank

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LEFT JOIN every seller to their 2020 orders, with the year filter in the ON clause. Keeping the
  year condition in ON (not WHERE) means a seller whose only orders are from other years still
  gets NULLs on the right and survives the IS NULL anti-filter. Elizabeth sold only in 2019 and
  Frank never sold, so both qualify; Daniel had 2020 orders and drops.

  Putting EXTRACT(YEAR ...) = 2020 in WHERE instead would turn the LEFT JOIN into an inner join
  and wrongly drop the no-2020 sellers.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT s.seller_name
FROM Seller s
LEFT JOIN Orders o
       ON o.seller_id = s.seller_id
      AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.sale_date) = 2020    -- year filter in ON, so no-2020 sellers stay
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL                           -- kept only sellers with no 2020 match
ORDER BY s.seller_name;

Hard Find the Subtasks That Did Not Execute

▼

For each task, list the subtask ids that are missing from the Executed log.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An orchestration platform finds subtasks that never ran.
  • Tasks says each task has subtasks numbered 1..subtasks_count; Executed logs which ran.
  • Return task_id and subtask_id for every expected subtask that has no matching row in Executed, ordered by task_id, subtask_id.
  • Manufacture the full set of expected subtask ids first, then anti-join the executed log.

Schema — Tasks

ColumnType
task_idINTEGER
subtasks_countINTEGER

Example input — Tasks

task_idsubtasks_count
13
22
31

Schema — Executed

ColumnType
task_idINTEGER
subtask_idINTEGER

Example input — Executed

task_idsubtask_id
12
31

Expected output

task_idsubtask_id
11
13
21
22

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  You can only find a missing subtask if you first build every subtask that SHOULD exist. A
  recursive CTE counts 1, 2, ... up to each task's subtasks_count, producing the full expected
  set. Then a LEFT JOIN to Executed plus an IS NULL filter returns the ones that never ran:
  task 1 ran only subtask 2 (1 and 3 missing), task 2 ran nothing (1 and 2 missing), task 3 ran
  its only subtask.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH RECURSIVE AllSubtasks AS (
    SELECT task_id, 1 AS subtask_id, subtasks_count FROM Tasks      -- start at subtask 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT task_id, subtask_id + 1, subtasks_count
    FROM AllSubtasks
    WHERE subtask_id < subtasks_count                              -- count up to subtasks_count
)
SELECT a.task_id, a.subtask_id
FROM AllSubtasks a
LEFT JOIN Executed e ON e.task_id = a.task_id AND e.subtask_id = a.subtask_id
WHERE e.subtask_id IS NULL                                         -- expected but never executed
ORDER BY a.task_id, a.subtask_id;

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A content PM lists playback sessions that served no ad.
  • Playback has each session's customer and time window; Ads logs ad impressions per customer at a timestamp.
  • Return the session_id of every session with no ad for that customer falling between its start_time and end_time, ordered by session_id.
  • Join on the customer plus the time-window overlap, then keep the sessions that found no match.

Schema — Playback

ColumnType
session_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
start_timeINTEGER
end_timeINTEGER

Example input — Playback

session_idcustomer_idstart_timeend_time
1115
2169
321115
422025

Schema — Ads

ColumnType
ad_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
timestampINTEGER

Example input — Ads

ad_idcustomer_idtimestamp
117
2212
325

Expected output

session_id
1
4

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LEFT JOIN each session to ads for the same customer whose timestamp falls inside the session
  window. Sessions that find no such ad come back with NULLs on the right, and the IS NULL filter
  keeps exactly those. Session 1's customer ad at t=7 is outside [1,5]; session 4's window [20,25]
  has no ad -- both are ad-free. Sessions 2 and 3 each contain an ad.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT p.session_id
FROM Playback p
LEFT JOIN Ads a
       ON a.customer_id = p.customer_id
      AND a.timestamp BETWEEN p.start_time AND p.end_time   -- ad fell inside the session window
WHERE a.ad_id IS NULL                                       -- no ad matched: session was ad-free
ORDER BY p.session_id;

NOT IN (only when the column is NOT NULL) 3 problems

▼

Shortest to write, but only safe when the subquery column cannot be NULL — one stray NULL makes NOT IN return nothing. Often the natural fit when anti-joining against a derived set built in the same query.

Template Anti-join template — NOT IN (only when the column is NOT NULL)

▼

Use when: the subquery column cannot be NULL and you want the shortest read.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Shortest to write, but fragile: if the subquery returns ANY NULL, NOT IN evaluates to unknown for every row and the query returns NOTHING.
  2. Only safe when the subquery column is guaranteed NOT NULL, or you filter the NULLs out as shown.
  3. When in doubt, prefer NOT EXISTS — same result, no NULL trap.
SELECT c.*
FROM customers c
WHERE c.id NOT IN (
  SELECT o.cust_id FROM orders o
  WHERE o.cust_id IS NOT NULL   -- guard: a single NULL here would return zero rows
);

  • Build the set of reps who DID sell to RED, then exclude them.

/*

  exclude those reps with NOT IN. Only Amy (sales_id 2) ordered to RED, so everyone else --
  John, Mark, Pam, Alex (the last two have no orders at all) -- is returned.
