Hard Find the Quiet Students in All Exams

▼

Return students who took at least one exam and never scored the min or max on any exam.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An advisor wants steady mid-pack students who never stood out, high or low.
  • Student holds names; Exam holds each student's score per exam.
  • Return student_id and student_name of students who took at least one exam and never had the minimum or maximum score on any exam they sat, ordered by student_id.
  • Mark every row that is its exam's min or max as loud, then anti-join those students away; also require the student to have taken at least one exam.

Schema — Student

ColumnType
student_idINTEGER
student_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Student

student_idstudent_name
1Daniel
2Jade
3Stella
4Jonathan
5Will
6Nina

Schema — Exam

ColumnType
exam_idINTEGER
student_idINTEGER
scoreINTEGER

Example input — Exam

exam_idstudent_idscore
10170
10280
10390
20460
20280
205100

Expected output

student_idstudent_name
2Jade

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Per exam, MIN(score) and MAX(score) OVER (PARTITION BY exam_id) put each exam's lowest and
  highest score on every row. A student is "loud" if any of their rows equals its exam's min or
  max. The anti-join (NOT IN that loud set) keeps only students who were never loud.

  The extra IN (SELECT student_id FROM Exam) guard enforces "took at least one exam," so Nina
  (in Student but with no exam rows) is excluded rather than slipping in as vacuously quiet.

  Here Jade scored 80 (the middle) in both exams, never a min or max, so she is the only quiet
  student.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT student_id, score,
           MIN(score) OVER (PARTITION BY exam_id) AS min_score,    -- this exam's low
           MAX(score) OVER (PARTITION BY exam_id) AS max_score     -- this exam's high
    FROM Exam
)
SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name
FROM Student s
WHERE s.student_id IN (SELECT student_id FROM Exam)        -- took at least one exam
  AND s.student_id NOT IN (                                -- never the min or max on any exam
        SELECT student_id FROM ranked
        WHERE score = min_score OR score = max_score
  )
ORDER BY s.student_id;

▼

Prompt

  • A service counts paid-but-idle accounts: active in 2021 but no 2021 streams.
  • Subscriptions has each account's active date range; Streams logs streaming sessions by date.
  • Count accounts whose subscription overlapped 2021 AND that have no stream dated in 2021.
  • Return a single column accounts_count.

Schema — Subscriptions

ColumnType
account_idINTEGER
start_dateDATE
end_dateDATE

Example input — Subscriptions

account_idstart_dateend_date
12021-01-012021-12-31
22021-06-012021-12-31
32020-01-012020-12-31
42021-03-012021-09-01

Schema — Streams

ColumnType
session_idINTEGER
account_idINTEGER
stream_dateDATE

Example input — Streams

session_idaccount_idstream_date
10012021-05-01
10142020-12-01

Expected output

accounts_count
2

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  An account is active in 2021 if its range overlaps the year: start on/before Dec 31 2021 AND
  end on/after Jan 1 2021. That keeps accounts 1, 2, and 4 (account 3 is 2020 only). Of those,
  NOT IN the set of 2021 streamers drops account 1 (streamed in May 2021). Account 4 streamed
  only in 2020, so it counts as idle; account 2 never streamed. COUNT returns 2.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT COUNT(*) AS accounts_count
FROM Subscriptions s
WHERE s.start_date <= DATE '2021-12-31'        -- subscription overlaps 2021 ...
  AND s.end_date   >= DATE '2021-01-01'        -- ... on both ends
  AND s.account_id NOT IN (                    -- and the account never streamed in 2021
        SELECT account_id FROM Streams
        WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM stream_date) = 2021
  );

Qualify on thresholds across distinct rows (GROUP BY + HAVING) 2 problems

▼

The keep / drop test needs several conditions that sit in different rows (per month, per category). Collapse the entity with GROUP BY, build one conditional SUM per condition, and AND the thresholds in HAVING.

Template Thresholds across distinct rows template

▼

Use when: an entity qualifies only if it meets two or more conditions that live in SEPARATE rows (spent ≥ X in June AND ≥ X in July, bought A AND bought B).

What this template does, step by step:

  1. GROUP BY the entity so all its rows collapse into one group.
  2. One SUM(CASE WHEN <slice> THEN value ELSE 0 END) per condition — each isolates the rows for that slice (a month, a category).
  3. AND the thresholds together in HAVING; the group passes only if every slice clears its bar.
  4. Do NOT put the slice column in GROUP BY — that splits the entity into one row per slice and the AND can never hold (a single row is only one month).
SELECT entity_id, entity_name
FROM t
GROUP BY entity_id, entity_name
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN slice = 'A' THEN value ELSE 0 END) >= threshold_a
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN slice = 'B' THEN value ELSE 0 END) >= threshold_b;
-- the broken instinct: GROUP BY entity, slice HAVING slice='A' AND slice='B' (impossible on one row)

Easy Customer Order Frequency

▼

Find customers who spent at least $100 in both June and July 2020.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A loyalty program rewards customers who spent $100+ in both June and July 2020.
  • Orders has quantities per product; Product has prices; Customers has names. Spend is quantity times price.
  • Return customer_id and name for customers whose June 2020 spend is >= 100 AND July 2020 spend is >= 100, ordered by customer_id.
  • Use one conditional SUM per month and AND both thresholds in HAVING; do not put the month in GROUP BY.

Schema — Customers

ColumnType
customer_idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
countryVARCHAR

Example input — Customers

customer_idnamecountry
1WinstonUSA
2JonathanPeru
3MoustafaEgypt

Schema — Product

ColumnType
product_idINTEGER
descriptionVARCHAR
priceINTEGER

Example input — Product

product_iddescriptionprice
1keyboard120
2mouse8

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
product_idINTEGER
order_dateDATE
quantityINTEGER

Example input — Orders

order_idcustomer_idproduct_idorder_datequantity
1112020-06-101
2112020-07-011
3222020-06-1510
4312020-06-201
5322020-07-102

Expected output

customer_idname
1Winston

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Join orders to product to get each line's spend (quantity * price), then group per customer.
  One conditional SUM isolates June 2020 spend, another isolates July 2020 spend, and both are
  required to clear 100 in HAVING. Winston spent 120 in each month. Jonathan's June spend is 80,
  and Moustafa's July spend is 16, so both fail one side.

  Keep the month OUT of GROUP BY: grouping by (customer, month) would split each customer into
  separate month rows, and one row can never satisfy both month thresholds at once.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = o.product_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2020 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM o.order_date) = 6
                THEN o.quantity * p.price ELSE 0 END) >= 100     -- June 2020 spend
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2020 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM o.order_date) = 7
                THEN o.quantity * p.price ELSE 0 END) >= 100     -- AND July 2020 spend
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Medium Identify Consistent Summer Subscribers

▼

Return customers who spent at least $150 in June 2024 AND at least $150 in July 2024.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A subscription box rewards customers who spent $150+ in both June and July 2024.
  • subscription_orders has each order's amount and date; customers holds names.
  • Return customer_id and customer_name for customers whose June 2024 spend is >= 150 AND July 2024 spend is >= 150, ordered by customer_id.
  • One conditional SUM per month, both ANDed in HAVING; spend in any other month must not count.

Schema — customers

ColumnType
customer_idINTEGER
customer_nameVARCHAR

Example input — customers

customer_idcustomer_name
1Ava
2Ben
3Cara
4Dan

Schema — subscription_orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
order_dateDATE
order_amountINTEGER

Example input — subscription_orders

order_idcustomer_idorder_dateorder_amount
112024-06-05100
212024-06-2060
312024-07-10150
422024-06-01200
522024-08-01200
632024-07-01300
742024-05-01500

Expected output

customer_idcustomer_name
1Ava

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  One conditional SUM isolates each month's spend per customer; DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
  buckets an order to the first of its month, so comparing to '2024-06-01' (or '2024-07-01')
  picks out that month and any other month contributes 0. Both thresholds are ANDed in HAVING,
  so a customer passes only if BOTH months clear 150. Ava spent 160 in June and 150 in July.
  Ben has no July spend, Cara no June, Dan only May -- all fail.

  Do NOT group by month: that splits each customer per month and no single row can satisfy both
  "June >= 150" and "July >= 150" together.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM subscription_orders AS s
JOIN customers AS c ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN DATE_TRUNC('month', s.order_date)::date = DATE '2024-06-01'
                THEN s.order_amount ELSE 0 END) >= 150      -- June 2024 spend
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN DATE_TRUNC('month', s.order_date)::date = DATE '2024-07-01'
                THEN s.order_amount ELSE 0 END) >= 150      -- AND July 2024 spend
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Aggregate 36 problems

▼

A single table of granular records → one summary row per group with aggregated values.

Signal words: "for each," "per," "how many," "total," "average," "count of," "at least N"

Technique: GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT DISTINCT, CASE WHEN inside aggregates, self-join + GROUP BY

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Count rows per group 5 problems

▼

A plain COUNT(*) or COUNT(col) tally per group — how many rows each group has.

Template Count per group template

▼

Use when: the output is how many rows each group has.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. GROUP BY the group key, then COUNT(*).
  2. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs in that column.
SELECT group_col, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM t
GROUP BY group_col;

Easy #1731 The Number of Employees Which Report to Each Employee

▼

For each manager, show id, name, count of direct reports, and rounded average age of reports.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An org tool reports each manager's team size and average team age.
  • The Employees table is self-referencing: reports_to points at a manager's employee_id.
  • Return employee_id, name, reports_count, and average_age (rounded to the nearest integer) for every employee who has at least one direct report, ordered by employee_id.

Schema — Employees

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
reports_toINTEGER
ageINTEGER

Example input — Employees

employee_idnamereports_toage
9HercyNULL43
6Alice941
4Bob936
2WinstonNULL37

Expected output

employee_idnamereports_countaverage_age
9Hercy239

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Self-join each manager (e1) to their direct reports (e2) on e1.employee_id = e2.reports_to.
  Because the inner join only keeps managers that actually have reports, the HAVING >= 1 is
  effectively automatic. COUNT and ROUND(AVG(age)) give team size and rounded mean age.
  Hercy manages Alice (41) and Bob (36): 2 reports, average age round((41+36)/2)=39.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT e1.employee_id,
       e1.name,
       COUNT(e2.employee_id)  AS reports_count,      -- team size
       ROUND(AVG(e2.age))     AS average_age         -- rounded mean age of the reports
FROM Employees e1
JOIN Employees e2 ON e1.employee_id = e2.reports_to  -- manager to direct report
GROUP BY e1.employee_id, e1.name
HAVING COUNT(e2.employee_id) >= 1                     -- has at least one report (implicit via the join)
ORDER BY e1.employee_id;

Example input — Traffic

user_idactivityactivity_date
1login2024-03-01
1login2024-03-10
2login2024-03-01
3login2024-03-15
4login2023-10-01
4login2024-03-20
5logout2024-03-02

Expected output

login_dateuser_count
2024-03-012
2024-03-151

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Two stages. The firsts CTE reduces each user to their earliest login (MIN over login rows).
  The outer query then counts first logins per day, keeping only days on or after the trailing
  90-day cutoff measured from the table's latest activity. User 4's first login (2023-10-01)
  falls before the cutoff and drops; on 2024-03-01 two users first logged in.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH firsts AS (
    SELECT user_id, MIN(activity_date) AS first_date    -- each user's first login
    FROM Traffic
    WHERE activity = 'login'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT first_date AS login_date, COUNT(*) AS user_count
FROM firsts
WHERE first_date >= (SELECT MAX(activity_date) - 90 FROM Traffic)   -- trailing 90-day window
GROUP BY first_date
ORDER BY first_date;

Easy Tasks Count in the Weekend

▼

Count tasks submitted on weekends versus weekdays, in one row.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An ops leader compares weekend versus weekday task load.
  • The Tasks table has one row per task with a submit date.
  • Return a single row with weekend_cnt (tasks submitted on Saturday or Sunday) and working_cnt (all other days).

Schema — Tasks

ColumnType
task_idINTEGER
assignee_idINTEGER
submit_dateDATE

Example input — Tasks

task_idassignee_idsubmit_date
1102024-06-01
2102024-06-02
3112024-06-03
4112024-06-04
5122024-06-05

Expected output

weekend_cntworking_cnt
23

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  EXTRACT(DOW FROM date) returns 0 for Sunday through 6 for Saturday, so weekend = 0 or 6. Two
  conditional SUMs over the same single scan produce both counts in one row. June 1 (Sat) and
  June 2 (Sun) are the weekend; the other three are weekdays.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT
    SUM(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(DOW FROM submit_date) IN (0, 6) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)     AS weekend_cnt,   -- Sat/Sun
    SUM(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(DOW FROM submit_date) NOT IN (0, 6) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS working_cnt    -- Mon-Fri
FROM Tasks;

Easy User Activity for the Past 30 Days I

▼

▼

Prompt

  • Product analytics reports Daily Active Users (DAU) over a 30-day window ending 2019-07-27.
  • The Activity table logs sessions; a user is active on a day if they have at least one row that day.
  • For each day in 2019-06-28 through 2019-07-27 that has activity, return day and active_users (distinct users), ordered by day.
  • Multiple sessions by one user on the same day count as one active user.

Schema — Activity

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
session_idINTEGER
activity_dateDATE
activity_typeVARCHAR

Example input — Activity

user_idsession_idactivity_dateactivity_type

dayactive_users
2019-07-202

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Filter to the inclusive 30-day window, then COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) per day so a user with two
  sessions the same day (user 1 on 2019-07-20) still counts once. The 2019-06-25 row falls before
  the window and drops.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT activity_date AS day,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users     -- a user with many sessions counts once
FROM Activity
WHERE activity_date BETWEEN DATE '2019-06-28' AND DATE '2019-07-27'   -- inclusive 30-day window
GROUP BY activity_date
ORDER BY activity_date;

/*

  • Return the distinct id (viewer id) of viewers who saw 2 or more distinct articles on some day, ordered by id.
  • Group at the (viewer, day) grain, count distinct articles, keep groups of 2+, then dedupe viewers who qualify on multiple days.

Schema — Views

ColumnType

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Group at the (viewer, day) grain and keep groups where the viewer saw 2+ distinct articles.
  Viewer 5 read articles 1 and 3 on 2019-08-01; viewer 6 read 4 and 5 on 2019-08-02. The outer
  DISTINCT collapses a viewer who qualifies on more than one day to a single id.

SELECT DISTINCT viewer_id AS id

Schema — Orders

/*
  Filter to high-value invoices first, bucket each order to its month with TO_CHAR, then COUNT(*)
  for orders and COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) for unique buyers. September keeps two orders from
  two customers (the $10 order drops); October keeps two orders, both from customer 3.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.

SELECT TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       COUNT(*)                    AS order_count,

/*

Schema — Sales

ColumnType

user_idspending
101125

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Join sales to product to price each line, then SUM(quantity * price) per user. User 101 spent
  10*10 + 1*25 = 125; user 102 spent 5*10 = 50.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT s.user_id, SUM(s.quantity * p.price) AS spending
FROM Sales s
JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = s.product_id

Medium Pizza Toppings Cost Analysis

▼

For every triple of distinct toppings, compute the combined cost.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A pizzeria prices every possible three-topping combination.
  • The Toppings table has one row per topping with its cost.
  • Return each distinct triple as pizza (the three names joined by commas in name order) and total_cost (their summed cost), ordered by total cost descending then pizza.
  • Each unordered triple appears once.

Schema — Toppings

ColumnType
topping_nameVARCHAR
costDECIMAL(5,2)

Example input — Toppings

topping_namecost
Beef5.5
Cheese3.0
Onion2.5
Pepper4.0

Expected output

pizzatotal_cost
Beef,Cheese,Pepper12.50
Beef,Onion,Pepper12.00
Beef,Cheese,Onion11.00
Cheese,Onion,Pepper9.50

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A three-way self-join builds every combination. The strict name-ordering predicates
  (t2.topping_name > t1.topping_name and t3 > t2) keep each unordered triple exactly once and
  avoid pairing a topping with itself. CONCAT joins the three names; the costs are summed.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

SELECT CONCAT(t1.topping_name, ',', t2.topping_name, ',', t3.topping_name) AS pizza,
       ROUND(t1.cost + t2.cost + t3.cost, 2) AS total_cost
FROM Toppings t1
JOIN Toppings t2 ON t2.topping_name > t1.topping_name      -- strict order: each triple once
JOIN Toppings t3 ON t3.topping_name > t2.topping_name
ORDER BY total_cost DESC, pizza;

▼

Keep only the groups whose count / sum / aggregate passes a test: at least N, more than one (duplicates), or above the average.

Template Filter groups (HAVING) template

▼

Use when: keep only groups whose aggregate passes a test.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping; HAVING filters groups AFTER, reading the aggregate.
  2. Duplicates = HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; "at least N" = HAVING COUNT(*) >= N.
SELECT group_col, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM t
GROUP BY group_col
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;

Prompt

  • A school keeps only classes that have at least 5 students enrolled.
  • The Courses table has one row per (student, class).
  • Return each class with 5 or more students, ordered by class.
  • Filtering on a group count needs HAVING (after grouping), not WHERE (before grouping).

Schema — Courses

ColumnType
studentVARCHAR
classVARCHAR

Example input — Courses

studentclass
AMath
BMath
CMath
DMath
EMath
FEnglish
GEnglish

Expected output

class
Math

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Group by class and keep groups whose student count is at least 5. HAVING runs after the GROUP
  BY, so it can see COUNT(*); a WHERE COUNT(*) would error because WHERE runs before grouping.
  Math has 5 students; English has 2.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.

SELECT class
FROM Courses
GROUP BY class
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5        -- filter the GROUP, not the rows
ORDER BY class;

Medium Managers with at Least 5 Direct Reports

▼

Prompt

  • HR lists managers with a large span of control (5 or more direct reports).
  • The Employee table is self-referencing via managerId.
  • Return the name of every manager who has at least 5 direct reports, ordered by name.

Schema — Employee

ColumnType
idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
departmentVARCHAR
managerIdINTEGER

Example input — Employee

idnamedepartmentmanagerId
101JohnANULL
102DanA101
103JamesA101
104AmyA101
105AnneA101
106RonB101

Expected output

name
John

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Self-join pairs each employee (e) with their manager (m) on e.managerId = m.id. Grouping by the
  manager and counting the employees gives each manager's report count; HAVING keeps those with
  5 or more. John manages five people (Dan, James, Amy, Anne, Ron).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT m.name
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m ON e.managerId = m.id        -- employee to their manager
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
HAVING COUNT(e.id) >= 5                       -- five or more direct reports
ORDER BY m.name;

  Group by email and keep groups whose row count exceeds 1. a@x.com appears twice.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT email
FROM Person
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1      -- email shared by more than one account
ORDER BY email;

Medium Unpopular Books

▼

Older books that sold fewer than 10 copies in the trailing year.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A bookseller flags older titles that sold poorly in the last year for delisting.
  • Books holds each title and when it became available; Orders logs each sale's quantity and dispatch date.
  • Keep books available before 2019-05-23, and return book_id and name for those whose total quantity dispatched between 2018-06-23 and 2019-06-23 is fewer than 10 (including books that never sold), ordered by book id.
  • Filter the join window in the ON clause and LEFT JOIN so never-sold books survive; COALESCE the missing sum to 0.

Schema — Books

ColumnType
book_idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
available_fromDATE

Example input — Books

book_idnameavailable_from
1B12019-01-01
2B22019-06-01
3B32018-01-01

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
book_idINTEGER
quantityINTEGER
dispatch_dateDATE

Example input — Orders

order_idbook_idquantitydispatch_date
1122018-08-01
2132018-09-01
33152018-12-01

Expected output

book_idname
1B1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  WHERE keeps only books old enough to have had a fair shot (available before 2019-05-23), which
  drops B2. LEFT JOIN with the trailing-year window in the ON clause preserves books with no sales;
  COALESCE(SUM(quantity), 0) treats those as 0. HAVING keeps books that sold fewer than 10: B1 sold
  5, B3 sold 15 (kept out).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT b.book_id, b.name
FROM Books b
LEFT JOIN Orders o
       ON o.book_id = b.book_id
      AND o.dispatch_date BETWEEN DATE '2018-06-23' AND DATE '2019-06-23'   -- trailing year, in ON
WHERE b.available_from < DATE '2019-05-23'                                  -- old enough to judge
GROUP BY b.book_id, b.name
HAVING COALESCE(SUM(o.quantity), 0) < 10;                                   -- never-sold counts as 0

Medium Active Businesses

▼

Businesses that beat the per-event-type average on more than one event type.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A marketplace flags businesses unusually active across multiple event types.
  • The Events table has one row per (business, event_type) with an occurrences count.
  • For each event type, compute its average occurrences across businesses. Return the business_id of businesses whose occurrences exceed that average on more than one event type, ordered by business id.

Schema — Events

ColumnType
business_idINTEGER
event_typeVARCHAR
occurencesINTEGER

Example input — Events

business_idevent_typeoccurences
1reviews7
3reviews3
1ads11
2ads7
3ads6
1page3
2page12

Expected output

business_id
1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The type_avg CTE computes each event type's average occurrences across businesses. Joining back
  and filtering to rows above their type's average finds each "exceedance"; grouping per business
  and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps businesses that beat the average on more than one type. Business 1
  beats the average on reviews (7 > 5) and ads (11 > 8).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH type_avg AS (
    SELECT event_type, AVG(occurences) AS avg_occ      -- average per event type
    FROM Events
    GROUP BY event_type
)
SELECT e.business_id
FROM Events e
JOIN type_avg t ON t.event_type = e.event_type
WHERE e.occurences > t.avg_occ                         -- this business beats its type's average
GROUP BY e.business_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1                                     -- on more than one event type
ORDER BY e.business_id;

Medium Activity Participants

Prompt

  • Friends assigns each person to one activity; Activities is the list of activities.
  • Count participants per activity, then return the activity whose count is neither the overall maximum nor the overall minimum.
  • The Activities table is just the catalog; the counts come from Friends.

Schema — Friends

ColumnType
idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
activityVARCHAR

Example input — Friends

idnameactivity
1AliceEating
2BobEating
3CaraEating
4DanSinging
5EveSinging
6FinnDancing

Schema — Activities

ColumnType
idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR

Example input — Activities

idname
1Eating
2Singing
3Dancing

Expected output

activity
Singing

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The counts CTE gives participants per activity. The outer query compares each count to the
  overall max and min (computed once each as scalar subqueries) and keeps only the middle ones.
  Eating has 3 (max), Dancing has 1 (min), Singing has 2 -- the only non-extreme.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH counts AS (
    SELECT activity, COUNT(*) AS c       -- participants per activity
    FROM Friends
    GROUP BY activity
)
SELECT activity
FROM counts
WHERE c <> (SELECT MAX(c) FROM counts)   -- not the most popular
  AND c <> (SELECT MIN(c) FROM counts);  -- not the least popular

Medium Products With Three or More Orders in Two Consecutive Years

▼

Products with at least three orders in each of two consecutive years.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A merch team finds evergreen products that sold steadily across consecutive years.
  • The Orders table logs each order with a product and a purchase date.
  • Return the product_id of products that had 3 or more orders in some year AND 3 or more orders in the very next year, ordered by product id.
  • Count orders per (product, year), keep the qualifying years, then self-join on consecutive years.

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
product_idINTEGER
quantityINTEGER
purchase_dateDATE

Example input — Orders

order_idproduct_idquantitypurchase_date
1112019-01-01
2112019-02-01
3112019-03-01
4112020-01-01
5112020-02-01
6112020-03-01
7212019-01-01
8212019-02-01
9212019-03-01
10212021-01-01
11212021-02-01
12212021-03-01

Expected output

product_id
1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The yearly CTE counts orders per (product, year) and keeps only years with 3 or more orders.
  Self-joining that on yr and yr+1 finds products that qualified in two consecutive years. Product
  1 qualified in 2019 and 2020 (consecutive); product 2 qualified in 2019 and 2021 (a gap), so it
  drops.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH yearly AS (
    SELECT product_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM purchase_date) AS yr, COUNT(*) AS cnt
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY product_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM purchase_date)
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3                 -- a year is "qualifying" only with 3+ orders
)
SELECT DISTINCT y1.product_id
FROM yearly y1
JOIN yearly y2 ON y2.product_id = y1.product_id
             AND y2.yr = y1.yr + 1        -- the next year also qualifies
ORDER BY y1.product_id;

Conditional aggregation (CASE inside the aggregate) 7 problems

▼

SUM / COUNT of a CASE: split one metric by category, pivot categories into columns, or net opposing signs (gain / loss, wins / losses).

Template Conditional aggregation template

▼

Use when: split one metric by category or pivot into columns.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Put CASE INSIDE the aggregate: SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN x ELSE 0 END).
  2. Use ELSE 0 for SUM; for a conditional COUNT, drop ELSE so non-matches are NULL and ignored.
SELECT month,
       SUM(CASE WHEN state='approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS approved_amt,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN state='declined' THEN 1 END)          AS declined_cnt
FROM tx
GROUP BY month;

Medium #1193 Monthly Transactions I

▼

Per month and country, count and sum all transactions plus approved-only.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Finance reports transaction volume and value by country and month, broken out for approved transactions.
  • The Transactions table has a state of 'approved' or 'declined'.
  • For each (month, country), return trans_count, trans_total_amount, approved_count, and approved_total_amount, ordered by month then country.
  • Approved-only metrics come from a CASE inside the aggregate, not a WHERE (which would drop the all-transaction totals).

Schema — Transactions

ColumnType
idINTEGER
countryVARCHAR
stateVARCHAR
amountINTEGER
trans_dateDATE

Example input — Transactions

idcountrystateamounttrans_date
121USapproved10002018-12-18
122USdeclined20002018-12-19
123USapproved20002019-01-01
124DEapproved20002019-01-07

Expected output

monthcountrytrans_counttrans_total_amountapproved_countapproved_total_amount
2018-12US2300011000
2019-01DE1200012000
2019-01US1200012000

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  One grouped pass over (month, country). COUNT(*) and SUM(amount) cover all transactions; the two
  CASE-inside-aggregate columns count and sum only the approved ones. Doing the approved filter
  inside the aggregate (not in WHERE) keeps the all-transaction totals intact in the same row.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       country,
       COUNT(*)                                              AS trans_count,
       SUM(amount)                                           AS trans_total_amount,
       SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)      AS approved_count,
       SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS approved_total_amount
FROM Transactions
GROUP BY TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM'), country
ORDER BY month, country;

Medium #1612 Monthly Transactions II

▼

Per month and country, report approved and chargeback counts and amounts (no all-zero rows).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Risk reporting combines approved transactions with chargebacks by month and country.
  • Transactions has state and amount; Chargebacks links a transaction id to the date the chargeback was filed.
  • For each (month, country), return approved_count, approved_amount, chargeback_count, chargeback_amount, ordered by month then country.
  • Chargebacks are bucketed by the chargeback date, not the original transaction date. Rows where all four values would be zero are excluded.
  • Pre-filter to approved transactions, stack approved and chargeback streams with UNION ALL, then pivot with conditional aggregation.

Schema — Transactions

ColumnType
idINTEGER
countryVARCHAR
stateVARCHAR
amountINTEGER
trans_dateDATE

Example input — Transactions

idcountrystateamounttrans_date
101USapproved10002019-05-18
102USdeclined20002019-05-19
103USapproved30002019-06-10
104DEapproved50002019-06-13

Schema — Chargebacks

ColumnType
trans_idINTEGER
trans_dateDATE

Example input — Chargebacks

trans_idtrans_date
1022019-05-29
1012019-06-30

Expected output

monthcountryapproved_countapproved_amountchargeback_countchargeback_amount
2019-05US1100012000
2019-06DE1500000
2019-06US1300011000

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Three CTEs, each one job. approved pre-filters to approved transactions, so declined rows never
  enter the pipeline and no all-zero output row can form. chargebacks joins back to the original
  transaction for country and amount, but buckets by the chargeback's own date. stacked unions the
  two streams with a type label, and the final SELECT pivots with conditional aggregation.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH approved AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', trans_date)::date AS month, country, amount
    FROM Transactions
    WHERE state = 'approved'                 -- declined rows never enter the pipeline
),
chargebacks AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', c.trans_date)::date AS month, t.country, t.amount
    FROM Chargebacks AS c
    JOIN Transactions AS t ON c.trans_id = t.id     -- chargeback bucketed by its own date
),
stacked AS (
    SELECT month, country, amount, 'approved'   AS type FROM approved
    UNION ALL
    SELECT month, country, amount, 'chargeback' AS type FROM chargebacks
)
SELECT TO_CHAR(month, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, country,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'approved'   THEN 1      ELSE 0 END) AS approved_count,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'approved'   THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS approved_amount,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'chargeback' THEN 1      ELSE 0 END) AS chargeback_count,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'chargeback' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS chargeback_amount
FROM stacked
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

Medium Monthly Transactions II

▼

Per month and country, report approved and chargeback counts and amounts via a UNION-stack.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A payments team reviews approved versus chargeback volume by country each month.
  • Transactions has state and amount; Chargebacks links a transaction id to the chargeback date.
  • For each (month, country), return approved_count, approved_amount, chargeback_count, chargeback_amount, ordered by month then country.
  • Stack the transaction and chargeback streams into a common shape, then group once, dropping rows where both counts are zero.

Schema — Transactions

ColumnType
idINTEGER
countryVARCHAR
stateVARCHAR
amountINTEGER
trans_dateDATE

Example input — Transactions

idcountrystateamounttrans_date
101USapproved10002019-05-18
102USdeclined20002019-05-19
103USapproved30002019-06-10
104DEapproved50002019-06-13

Schema — Chargebacks

ColumnType
trans_idINTEGER
trans_dateDATE

Example input — Chargebacks

trans_idtrans_date
1022019-05-29
1012019-06-30

Expected output

monthcountryapproved_countapproved_amountchargeback_countchargeback_amount
2019-05US1100012000
2019-06DE1500000
2019-06US1300011000

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Build a common shape from two sources: transactions contribute approved counts/amounts (and
  zeros for chargebacks), and the chargeback join contributes the other pair. UNION ALL stacks
  them, one GROUP BY rolls up per month and country, and the HAVING drops any month/country with
  neither an approved transaction nor a chargeback.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT month, country,
       SUM(approved_count)    AS approved_count,
       SUM(approved_amount)   AS approved_amount,
       SUM(chargeback_count)  AS chargeback_count,
       SUM(chargeback_amount) AS chargeback_amount
FROM (
    SELECT TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, country,
           CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END      AS approved_count,
           CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END AS approved_amount,
           0 AS chargeback_count, 0 AS chargeback_amount
    FROM Transactions
    UNION ALL
    SELECT TO_CHAR(c.trans_date, 'YYYY-MM'), t.country, 0, 0, 1, t.amount
    FROM Chargebacks c
    JOIN Transactions t ON t.id = c.trans_id
) u
GROUP BY month, country
HAVING SUM(approved_count) + SUM(chargeback_count) > 0     -- drop empty month/country rows
ORDER BY month, country;

  • The Stocks table logs each operation ('Buy' or 'Sell') with a price.

Schema — Stocks

ColumnType

Solution Annotated SQL

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*

  nets 1500 - 1000 = 500; stock B nets 300 - 500 = -200.

Medium League Statistics

▼

Per team: matches played, points, goals for/against, and goal difference.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A league builds a standings table from match results.
  • Teams lists teams; Matches has home and away teams with their goals.
  • For each team return matches_played, points (3 for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss), goal_for, goal_against, and goal_diff, ordered by points descending, then goal difference descending, then team name.
  • Normalize home and away rows into one per-team shape with UNION ALL so a single aggregate computes every metric.

Schema — Teams

ColumnType
team_idINTEGER
team_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Teams

team_idteam_name
1Alpha
2Beta
3Gamma

Schema — Matches

ColumnType
home_team_idINTEGER
away_team_idINTEGER
home_team_goalsINTEGER
away_team_goalsINTEGER

Example input — Matches

home_team_idaway_team_idhome_team_goalsaway_team_goals
1231
2322
3104

Expected output

team_namematches_playedpointsgoal_forgoal_againstgoal_diff
Alpha26716
Beta2135-2
Gamma2126-4

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The perteam CTE flattens each match into two rows -- one for the home side, one for the away side
  -- each carrying that team's goals for (gf) and against (ga). After that, a single GROUP BY does
  everything: COUNT(*) is matches played, a CASE-sum turns each result into points (3/1/0), and the
  goal columns are plain sums. LEFT JOIN from Teams would also keep teams that never played.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH perteam AS (
    SELECT home_team_id AS team_id, home_team_goals AS gf, away_team_goals AS ga FROM Matches
    UNION ALL
    SELECT away_team_id, away_team_goals, home_team_goals FROM Matches
)
SELECT t.team_name,
       COUNT(*)                                                AS matches_played,
       SUM(CASE WHEN gf > ga THEN 3 WHEN gf = ga THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS points,   -- 3 win / 1 draw / 0 loss
       SUM(gf)                                                 AS goal_for,
       SUM(ga)                                                 AS goal_against,
       SUM(gf) - SUM(ga)                                       AS goal_diff
FROM Teams t
LEFT JOIN perteam p ON p.team_id = t.team_id
GROUP BY t.team_id, t.team_name
ORDER BY points DESC, goal_diff DESC, t.team_name;

Medium Friday Purchases I

▼

For each Friday in November 2023 with sales, report total spend by week of the month.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A retail analyst studies Friday spend in November 2023 to plan promotions.
  • The Purchases table logs each purchase with a date and amount.
  • For each Friday in November 2023 that has purchases, return week_of_month (1 for days 1 to 7, and so on), purchase_date, and total_amount, ordered by week of month.
  • Only Fridays with sales appear (no zero-fill).

Schema — Purchases

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
purchase_dateDATE
amount_spendINTEGER

Example input — Purchases

user_idpurchase_dateamount_spend
12023-11-0350
22023-11-0330
12023-11-17100
32023-11-06999

Expected output

week_of_monthpurchase_datetotal_amount
12023-11-0380
32023-11-17100

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Filter to Fridays (EXTRACT(DOW) = 5) within November 2023, then total spend per Friday. The
  week-of-month formula floors (day - 1) / 7 and adds 1, so Nov 3 is week 1 and Nov 17 is week 3.
  Nov 6 is a Monday and drops. Unlike the zero-fill version, only Fridays that actually had sales
  appear.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT CAST(FLOOR((EXTRACT(DAY FROM purchase_date) - 1) / 7) + 1 AS INT) AS week_of_month,
       purchase_date,
       SUM(amount_spend) AS total_amount
FROM Purchases
WHERE EXTRACT(DOW FROM purchase_date) = 5                                  -- Fridays only
  AND purchase_date BETWEEN DATE '2023-11-01' AND DATE '2023-11-30'
GROUP BY week_of_month, purchase_date
ORDER BY week_of_month;

Ratio / percentage 3 problems

▼

A numerator over a denominator per group: rates, percentages, or the AVG of a 0 / 1 CASE flag.

Template Ratio / percentage template

▼

Use when: a numerator over a denominator per group.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Force numeric division (* 1.0 or ::numeric) so integers do not floor.
  2. Wrap the denominator in NULLIF(..., 0) to dodge divide-by-zero.
SELECT group_col,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN hit THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 2) AS rate
FROM t
GROUP BY group_col;

CatSphynx74

Expected output

query_namequalitypoor_query_percentage
Dog2.5033.33
Cat0.6633.33

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  quality is AVG(rating / position) -- rating::numeric forces real division so 1/200 is 0.005, not
  0. poor_query_percentage is the share of rows with rating below 3: the 100.0 literal forces the
  count ratio to numeric so it does not collapse under integer division (Postgres integer / integer
  truncates). Each query here has one poor result out of three, so 33.33 percent.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT query_name,
       ROUND(AVG(rating::numeric / position), 2) AS quality,                       -- numeric division
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN rating < 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2)
           AS poor_query_percentage                                                -- 100.0 forces numeric
FROM Queries
GROUP BY query_name
ORDER BY quality DESC, query_name;

Easy Ads Performance

▼

Compute click-through rate per ad as a percentage, ignoring non-click/view actions.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Marketing reports each ad's click-through rate (CTR) to decide which to keep.
  • The Ads table logs an action per (ad, user): 'Clicked', 'Viewed', or 'Ignored'.
  • CTR = clicks / (clicks + views) as a percentage rounded to 2 decimals; ads with no clicks or views report 0. Ignored actions do not count.
  • Return ad_id and ctr, ordered by ctr descending then ad id.

Schema — Ads

ColumnType
ad_idINTEGER
user_idINTEGER
actionVARCHAR

Example input — Ads

ad_iduser_idaction
11Clicked
12Viewed
13Viewed
21Viewed
22Viewed
31Clicked
32Clicked
51Ignored

Expected output

ad_idctr
3100.00
133.33
20.00
50.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Numerator is the count of clicks; denominator is clicks plus views. The CASE-sums build both;
  NULLIF turns a zero denominator into NULL so the division does not error, and COALESCE then reports
  0 CTR for an ad with no clicks or views (ad 5, only an Ignored row). The 1.0 keeps the division
  numeric. Ad 1 = 1/3 = 33.33, ad 3 = 2/2 = 100.00, ad 2 = 0/2 = 0.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

SELECT ad_id,
       ROUND(COALESCE(
           SUM(CASE WHEN action = 'Clicked' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN action IN ('Clicked','Viewed') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0)
             * 100, 0), 2) AS ctr
FROM Ads
GROUP BY ad_id
ORDER BY ctr DESC, ad_id;

Medium Immediate Food Delivery III

Per day, the percent of deliveries ordered for that same day.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An ops PM tracks each day's share of immediate (same-day) orders.
  • The Delivery table logs each order's order date and the customer's preferred delivery date.
  • An order is immediate when the preferred delivery date equals the order date. For each order_date, return immediate_percentage = percent of immediate orders rounded to 2 decimals, ordered by order date.

Schema — Delivery

ColumnType
delivery_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
order_dateDATE
customer_pref_delivery_dateDATE

Example input — Delivery

delivery_idcustomer_idorder_datecustomer_pref_delivery_date
112019-08-012019-08-01
222019-08-012019-08-02
312019-08-022019-08-02

Expected output

order_dateimmediate_percentage
2019-08-0150.00
2019-08-02100.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Average a 0/1 flag (1 when the order is for the same day) per order date and multiply by 100 to
  get the percentage. The 1.0 keeps the average numeric. On 2019-08-01 one of two orders is
  immediate (50 percent); on 2019-08-02 the single order is immediate (100 percent).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT order_date,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN order_date = customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) * 100, 2)
           AS immediate_percentage
FROM Delivery

Scalar 12 problems

▼

A single table (possibly grouped first) → one row, one column: a scalar result.

Signal words: "the single," "the highest," "second highest," "the one," "overall percentage"

Technique: MAX of filtered set, OFFSET for Nth value, MIN subquery + percentage

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Single aggregate over the whole table 3 problems

▼

One value from all rows: a single MAX / MIN / SUM / COUNT, or two aggregates combined (max minus min, totals across categories). No GROUP BY in the final answer.

Template Single aggregate template

▼

Use when: one value from all rows.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. No GROUP BY → the aggregate returns exactly one row.
  2. Combine aggregates in one SELECT (e.g. MAX(x) - MIN(x)).
SELECT MAX(salary) - MIN(salary) AS spread,
       COUNT(*)              AS n
FROM emp;

Easy #619 Biggest Single Number

▼

Find the largest number that appears exactly once; NULL if none.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A data-quality check finds the biggest value that occurs only once.
  • The MyNumbers table has one column of integers, with repeats.
  • Return the largest num that appears exactly once, aliased num. If no number is unique, return NULL.

Schema — MyNumbers

ColumnType
numINTEGER

Example input — MyNumbers

num
8
8
3
3
1
4
5
6

Expected output

num
6

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  First isolate the numbers that appear exactly once (GROUP BY num HAVING COUNT(*) = 1), then take
  the MAX of that set. Here the unique numbers are 1, 4, 5, 6, so the answer is 6. If there were no
  unique numbers, the subquery would be empty and MAX returns NULL.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT MAX(num) AS num
FROM (
    SELECT num
    FROM MyNumbers
    GROUP BY num
    HAVING COUNT(*) = 1        -- keep only numbers that occur once
) AS singles;

Medium Count Apples and Oranges

▼

Total apples and oranges across boxes and their nested chests, in one row.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A warehouse audit totals fruit across boxes and the chests some boxes contain.
  • Boxes may reference a chest via chest_id (NULL if the box has no chest); Chests holds each chest's own fruit counts.
  • Return a single row with total apple_count and orange_count = the box counts plus the counts of any chest inside the box.
  • Use a LEFT JOIN so boxes without a chest survive, and COALESCE the chest counts to 0.

Schema — Boxes

ColumnType
box_idINTEGER
chest_idINTEGER
apple_countINTEGER
orange_countINTEGER

Example input — Boxes

box_idchest_idapple_countorange_count
2NULL615
1814415
19399

Schema — Chests

ColumnType
chest_idINTEGER
apple_countINTEGER
orange_countINTEGER

Example input — Chests

chest_idapple_countorange_count
142010
355

Expected output

apple_countorange_count
4454

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LEFT JOIN each box to its chest (if any). For each box the fruit is the box's own count plus the
  chest's count; COALESCE turns a missing chest's NULL into 0 so box 2 (no chest) still contributes.
  SUM over all boxes collapses to one row. Apples: 6 + (4+20) + (9+5) = 44; oranges: 15 + (15+10) +
  (9+5) = 54.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT
    SUM(b.apple_count  + COALESCE(c.apple_count, 0))  AS apple_count,
    SUM(b.orange_count + COALESCE(c.orange_count, 0)) AS orange_count
FROM Boxes b
LEFT JOIN Chests c ON c.chest_id = b.chest_id;

Easy Highest Salaries Difference

▼

Absolute difference between the top Engineering and top Marketing salary.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • HR compares the salary ceilings of two departments.
  • The Salaries table has one row per employee with their department and salary.
  • Return salary_difference = the absolute difference between the highest Engineering salary and the highest Marketing salary.

Schema — Salaries

ColumnType
emp_nameVARCHAR
departmentVARCHAR
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Salaries

emp_namedepartmentsalary
AEngineering100
BEngineering120
CMarketing90
DMarketing150

Expected output

salary_difference
30

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A conditional MAX picks each department's top salary in the same single-row aggregate: the CASE
  returns the salary only for the matching department, so MAX ignores the NULLs from the other one.
  ABS wraps the difference. Engineering tops at 120, Marketing at 150, so |120 - 150| = 30.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT ABS(
    MAX(CASE WHEN department = 'Engineering' THEN salary END)    -- top Engineering salary
  - MAX(CASE WHEN department = 'Marketing'   THEN salary END)    -- top Marketing salary
) AS salary_difference
FROM Salaries;

Second / Nth highest value 2 problems

▼

The 2nd, 3rd, or Nth largest distinct value: DISTINCT + ORDER BY + LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1, or a subquery-in-SELECT so an empty result returns NULL instead of zero rows.

Template Nth highest value template

▼

Use when: the 2nd / 3rd / Nth largest distinct value.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. DISTINCT + ORDER BY ... DESC + LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1.
  2. Wrap it as a subquery inside SELECT so an empty result returns NULL, not zero rows.
SELECT (
  SELECT DISTINCT salary
  FROM emp
  ORDER BY salary DESC
  LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1        -- 2nd highest; OFFSET N-1 for the Nth
) AS second_highest;

Medium Second Highest Salary

▼

Return the second highest distinct salary, or NULL if fewer than two exist.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • HR wants the runner-up salary level for benchmarking.
  • The Employee table has one salary per employee, possibly with duplicate values.
  • Return the second highest distinct salary as SecondHighestSalary; if there is no second distinct value, return NULL.
  • Wrapping the lookup as a subquery in SELECT makes an empty result come back as NULL rather than zero rows.

Schema — Employee

ColumnType
idINTEGER
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Employee

idsalary
1100
2200
3300
4300

Expected output

SecondHighestSalary
200

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Sort distinct salaries high to low and skip the first with OFFSET 1, taking the next with LIMIT 1.
  DISTINCT matters: the two 300s count as one top value, so the second highest is 200. Wrapping it as
  a scalar subquery in SELECT means that if there were no second value, the result is NULL (one row
  with NULL) instead of an empty result set -- no IFNULL needed in Postgres.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT (
    SELECT DISTINCT salary
    FROM Employee
    ORDER BY salary DESC
    LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1            -- skip the highest, take the next distinct salary
) AS SecondHighestSalary;

Medium Nth Highest Salary

▼

Return the N-th highest distinct salary (shown for N = 3), or NULL if fewer than N exist.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • HR asks for the rank-N salary benchmark; this example uses N = 3.
  • The Employee table has one salary per employee, possibly duplicated.
  • Return the N-th highest distinct salary as getNthHighestSalary; NULL if fewer than N distinct values exist.
  • DENSE_RANK numbers distinct values (ties share a rank); pick the rows where the rank equals N.

Schema — Employee

ColumnType
idINTEGER
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Employee

idsalary
1100
2200
3300
4300

Expected output

getNthHighestSalary
100

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  DENSE_RANK orders the salaries high to low and gives tied salaries the same rank, so the two 300s
  both rank 1, 200 ranks 2, and 100 ranks 3. Selecting the rows where the rank equals N (3 here) and
  taking the distinct value yields the N-th highest. As a scalar subquery it returns NULL when no
  row has rank N. Replace the literal 3 with your N.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT (
    SELECT DISTINCT salary
    FROM (
        SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk   -- ties share a rank
        FROM Employee
    ) t
    WHERE rnk = 3                -- the N-th highest distinct salary (N = 3)
) AS getNthHighestSalary;

What this template does, step by step:

  1. GROUP BY + ORDER BY metric DESC + LIMIT 1.
  2. If ties should all win, instead keep rows whose metric = (SELECT MAX(...)).
SELECT group_col
FROM t
GROUP BY group_col
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC
LIMIT 1;

Easy The Winner University

▼

Return the university with more students scoring 90 or above.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Two universities are compared on how many students scored 90 or above.
  • NewYork and California each list their students' scores.
  • Return winner: 'New York University' if it has strictly more 90+ scorers, 'California University' if California does, else 'No Winner'.

Schema — NewYork

ColumnType
student_idINTEGER
scoreINTEGER

Example input — NewYork

student_idscore
190
295
380

Schema — California

ColumnType
student_idINTEGER
scoreINTEGER

Example input — California

student_idscore
191
289

Expected output

winner
New York University

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Each scalar subquery counts the 90-or-above students in one school; the subqueries run once. CASE
  compares the two counts and labels the winner, with a tie returning 'No Winner'. New York has two
  qualifying students (90 and 95) versus California's one (91).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT CASE
    WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM NewYork WHERE score >= 90)
       > (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM California WHERE score >= 90) THEN 'New York University'
    WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM NewYork WHERE score >= 90)
       < (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM California WHERE score >= 90) THEN 'California University'
    ELSE 'No Winner'
END AS winner;

Template Ratio / weighted average template

▼

Use when: one rate over the whole table.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Divide two whole-table aggregates; force numeric and NULLIF the denominator.
  2. A count-weighted mean is SUM(weight * value) / SUM(weight).
SELECT ROUND(SUM(weight * value) * 1.0
             / NULLIF(SUM(weight), 0), 2) AS weighted_mean
FROM t;

Medium Immediate Food Delivery II

▼

Percent of customers whose FIRST order was immediate (same-day).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A delivery platform measures onboarding by whether each customer's first order was same-day.
  • The Delivery table logs each order's order date and the customer's preferred delivery date; an order is immediate when they match.
  • Consider only each customer's first order (earliest order date). Return immediate_percentage = percent of those first orders that were immediate, rounded to 2 decimals.
  • Find the first order per customer, then average the immediate flag over just those rows.

Schema — Delivery

ColumnType
delivery_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
order_dateDATE
customer_pref_delivery_dateDATE

Example input — Delivery

delivery_idcustomer_idorder_datecustomer_pref_delivery_date
112019-08-012019-08-02
222019-08-022019-08-02
312019-08-112019-08-11
432019-08-242019-08-26
532019-08-212019-08-22
622019-04-212019-04-21

Expected output

immediate_percentage
33.33

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The FirstOrders CTE finds each customer's earliest order date. The join keeps only those first
  orders, and the conditional average reports the share that were immediate (order date equals the
  preferred date). The 100.0 forces numeric division so the percentage does not truncate. Customer
  2's first order (2019-04-21) was immediate; customers 1 and 3's first orders were not -- 1 of 3 =
  33.33 percent.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH FirstOrders AS (
    SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_order_date   -- each customer's first order
    FROM Delivery
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT ROUND(
    100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN d.order_date = d.customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
    / COUNT(*), 2
) AS immediate_percentage
FROM Delivery d
JOIN FirstOrders f ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id
WHERE d.order_date = f.first_order_date;

Prompt

  • FriendRequest logs each request (sender, recipient); RequestAccepted logs each acceptance (requester, accepter). Both can contain duplicate pairs.
  • Return accept_rate = distinct accepted pairs divided by distinct requested pairs, rounded to 2 decimals.
  • Count DISTINCT pairs so duplicate rows do not inflate either side, and guard the denominator with NULLIF.

Schema — FriendRequest

ColumnType
sender_idINTEGER
send_to_idINTEGER
request_dateDATE

Example input — FriendRequest

sender_idsend_to_idrequest_date

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The rate is distinct accepted pairs over distinct requested pairs. Counting DISTINCT pairs (via a
  derived table that dedupes each source first) keeps a duplicate accepted row -- the second (1,2) --
  from inflating the numerator. The ::numeric cast forces real division and NULLIF guards against a
  zero denominator. Accepted distinct pairs = 3, requested = 4, so 0.75.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT ROUND(
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT requester_id, accepter_id FROM RequestAccepted) a)::numeric
    / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT sender_id, send_to_id FROM FriendRequest) r), 0),
    2
) AS accept_rate;

Easy User Activity for the Past 30 Days II

▼

Average sessions per active user over a fixed 30-day window.

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A growth PM tracks average sessions per active user over the 30 days ending 2019-07-27.
  • The Activity table logs one row per session.
  • Return average_sessions_per_user = distinct sessions divided by distinct active users in the window, rounded to 2 decimals (0 if there is no activity).
  • Force numeric division so the ratio does not truncate, and guard the denominator with NULLIF.

Schema — Activity

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
session_idINTEGER
activity_dateDATE
activity_typeVARCHAR

Example input — Activity

user_idsession_idactivity_dateactivity_type
112019-07-01open

average_sessions_per_user
1.50

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Filter to the 30-day window, then divide distinct sessions by distinct users. The ::numeric cast
  forces real division (otherwise integer division would floor 3/2 to 1); NULLIF guards a zero
  denominator and COALESCE reports 0 when the window is empty. In the window there are 3 sessions
  across 2 users, so 1.50. The 2019-06-25 row is outside the window and drops.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT COALESCE(
    ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT session_id)::numeric / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT user_id), 0), 2),
    0
) AS average_sessions_per_user
FROM Activity
WHERE activity_date BETWEEN DATE '2019-06-28' AND DATE '2019-07-27';

  50.00. (Contrast with Immediate Food Delivery II, which restricts to each customer's first order.)

  • Force numeric division so integer division does not truncate.

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER

order_occurrencesINTEGER

Example input — Orders

order_iditem_countorder_occurrences

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A weighted mean: each basket size is weighted by how many times it occurred, so the numerator is
  SUM(item_count * order_occurrences) and the denominator is SUM(order_occurrences). The ::numeric
  cast forces real division (otherwise integer / integer would floor); NULLIF guards an empty table.
  Here (2*3 + 5*1 + 3*2) / (3+1+2) = 17 / 6 = 2.83.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT ROUND(
    SUM(item_count * order_occurrences)::numeric
    / NULLIF(SUM(order_occurrences), 0), 2
) AS average_items_per_order
FROM Orders;

Rank & Percentile 20 problems

▼

A single table with a group key → score each row's position in the group, then either annotate every row with a rank or percentile, or filter to the top-N rows per group.

Signal words: "top N per," "Nth highest," "highest in each," "most recent per," "median," "P50 / P90," "percentile," "quartile," "decile," "top X%"

Technique: ROW_NUMBER / RANK / DENSE_RANK / NTILE / PERCENT_RANK / PERCENTILE_CONT / PERCENTILE_DISC OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric) — then either keep every row (annotate) or filter on the score (top N, top X%).

Cross-link: The multi-table version (top customer per region, etc.) lives at Rank Within Groups (Multi-Table). LAG / LEAD neighbour comparison lives at Compare. Rolling and running aggregates live at Window.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

ROW_NUMBER for top-N per group 1 problem

▼

nb01 qtype: window_top_n_per_group — ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY rank_col) wrapped in a CTE and filtered to rn ≤ N. The canonical way to pick the latest, highest, or first N rows per group. Pick ROW_NUMBER (not RANK / DENSE_RANK) when you want EXACTLY N rows per group with deterministic tiebreaking.

ROW_NUMBER + filter rn ≤ N (back to tree)

▼

Use when: keep the highest, latest, or first N rows per group, with deterministic tiebreaking.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Apply ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) inside a CTE so every row in each group is numbered 1, 2, 3 ...
  2. Add a tiebreaker column to the ORDER BY so numbering is deterministic when two rows tie on the main metric.
  3. Outer SELECT filters rn ≤ N to keep exactly N rows per group.
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT t.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_col
                            ORDER BY rank_col DESC, tiebreak_col) AS rn
  FROM t
)
SELECT group_col, rank_col, ...
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= N;

Medium Product Price at a Given Date

▼

The price of each product as of a target date, defaulting to 10 before any change.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • E-commerce shows the price a customer was charged on a historical date (here 2019-08-16).
  • The Products table logs each price change with its date; a product with no change on or before the date is priced at the default 10.
  • Return product_id and price as of 2019-08-16, ordered by product id.

Schema — Products

ColumnType
product_idINTEGER
new_priceINTEGER
change_dateDATE

Example input — Products

product_idnew_pricechange_date
1202019-08-14
1302019-08-15
2502019-08-17
3252019-08-10

Expected output

product_idprice
130
210
325

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Keep only changes on or before the target date, then ROW_NUMBER per product ordered by date
  DESC so rn = 1 is the most recent price. LEFT JOIN from the distinct product list so a product
  with no qualifying change still appears, and COALESCE supplies the default 10. Product 2's only
  change is after the date, so it falls back to 10.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH latest_prices AS (
    SELECT product_id, new_price,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY change_date DESC) AS rn   -- newest change first
    FROM Products
    WHERE change_date <= DATE '2019-08-16'
)
SELECT p.product_id, COALESCE(lp.new_price, 10) AS price          -- default 10 when no change applies
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM Products) p
LEFT JOIN latest_prices lp ON p.product_id = lp.product_id AND lp.rn = 1
ORDER BY p.product_id;

RANK for Nth highest, ties tied no problems yet

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics (rank flavor coming) — RANK() OVER (...) returns the same rank to tied rows and SKIPS the next rank. Use this when the prompt says "Nth highest" and ties should share the position; if the prompt says "Nth distinct value," use DENSE_RANK instead. Worked example to be added.

RANK (ties tied, ranks skip)

▼

Use when: "Nth highest" where rows with the same value should share that rank.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Apply RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) — ties share the same rank, the next rank skips.
  2. Filter rk = N in the outer query to keep the Nth-highest tier; multiple rows can come back when there are ties at that rank.
SELECT
  metric_col,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY group_col ORDER BY metric_col DESC) AS rk
FROM t;
-- Then filter on rk = N. Multiple rows can share rk = N.

No worked card in this leaf yet. See the generic template above and the DENSE_RANK leaf for the contrast on ties.

Medium Rank Scores

▼

Rank every score with no gaps after ties (dense rank).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A leaderboard shows each score with its rank; tied scores share a rank and no gaps appear behind them.
  • The Scores table has one row per score.
  • Return score and its rank, ordered by score descending.

Schema — Scores

ColumnType
idINTEGER
scoreDECIMAL(3,2)

Example input — Scores

idscore
13.5
23.65
34.0
43.85
54.0
63.65

Expected output

scorerank
4.001
4.001
3.852
3.653
3.653
3.504

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  DENSE_RANK gives tied scores the same rank and never skips the next rank (so after a pair at
  rank 1 the next distinct score is rank 2, not 3). That "no gaps" behavior is the whole point --
  RANK would leave holes. The alias is quoted because rank is a reserved word.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 6 expected rows.
*/

SELECT score,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS "rank"    -- ties tied, no gaps
FROM Scores
ORDER BY score DESC;

DENSE_RANK for Nth distinct value no problems yet

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics (dense_rank flavor coming) — DENSE_RANK() OVER (...) returns the same rank to tied rows but does NOT skip after a tie. Use this when the prompt says "Nth distinct" (the 3rd highest distinct salary). Worked example to be added.

DENSE_RANK (Nth distinct)

▼

Use when: "the 3rd highest distinct salary" — ties share the rank, but ranks do NOT skip.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Apply DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY metric DESC) — ties share the rank but ranks do NOT skip.
  2. Wrap in a subquery, then SELECT DISTINCT on the metric column to drop the duplicate "Nth-distinct" rows.
  3. Filter dr = N in the outer query to return the Nth distinct value.
SELECT DISTINCT metric_col
FROM (
  SELECT metric_col,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY metric_col DESC) AS dr
  FROM t
) x
WHERE dr = N;

Easy Group Employees of the Same Salary

▼

Keep employees whose salary is shared, with a dense team id per salary band.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A pay-parity report keeps only employees whose salary is shared by someone else, grouped into bands.
  • The Employees table has one row per employee with a salary.
  • Return employee_id, name, salary, and a team_id that is the same for equal salaries and consecutive across bands, ordered by team id then employee id.

Schema — Employees

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Employees

employee_idnamesalary
1A1000
2B2000
3C1000
4D3000
5E2000

Expected output

employee_idnamesalaryteam_id
1A10001
3C10001
2B20002
5E20002

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  First keep only salaries shared by two or more employees (the HAVING COUNT > 1 subquery). Then
  DENSE_RANK over the filtered rows ordered by salary makes consecutive team ids that are equal for
  equal salaries. The lone 3000 earner is filtered out before ranking.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

SELECT employee_id, name, salary,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS team_id     -- same id per salary band, consecutive
FROM Employees
WHERE salary IN (
    SELECT salary FROM Employees GROUP BY salary HAVING COUNT(*) > 1   -- only shared salaries
)
ORDER BY team_id, employee_id;

NTILE(n) for quartile / decile buckets 2 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics (ntile_buckets flavor) — NTILE(n) OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) bucketizes rows into n even-ish groups. DESC puts the best in bucket 1; ASC puts the worst in bucket 1. NTILE only accepts a LITERAL integer.

NTILE(n) (quartile / decile buckets)

▼

Use when: "which bucket each row falls in" with even-ish bucket sizes. ORDER BY metric DESC puts the best in bucket 1; ASC puts the worst in bucket 1.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Apply NTILE(n) OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric) — bucketizes rows into n even-ish groups.
  2. Use DESC for "bucket 1 = best", ASC for "bucket 1 = worst".
  3. Each row carries its bucket number directly; no further filter unless you only want a specific bucket.
SELECT
  entity_col, metric_col,
  NTILE(4) OVER (PARTITION BY group_col ORDER BY metric_col DESC) AS quartile
FROM t;

Medium Tutor Quartile Ranking by Completion Rate

▼

Bucket tutors into quartiles by completion rate, best in bucket 1, excluding zero-session tutors.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A tutoring marketplace sorts tutors into 4 quartiles by completion rate (completed / total), with the highest rates in quartile 1.
  • The tutors table has completed and total session counts; exclude tutors with zero total sessions.
  • Return tutor_name, completion_rate (2 decimals), and quartile, ordered by quartile then completion rate descending.

Schema — tutors

ColumnType
tutor_idINTEGER
tutor_nameVARCHAR
completed_sessionsINTEGER
total_sessionsINTEGER

Example input — tutors

tutor_idtutor_namecompleted_sessionstotal_sessions
1Alice Chen95100
2David Park4550
3Bob Martinez7890
4Carol Kim6080
5Emma Wilson3060
6Grace Taylor1630
7Frank Lee1840
8Henry Zhang525
9Zoe Null00

Expected output

tutor_namecompletion_ratequartile
Alice Chen0.951
David Park0.901
Bob Martinez0.872
Carol Kim0.752
Grace Taylor0.533
Emma Wilson0.503
Frank Lee0.454
Henry Zhang0.204

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The CTE computes completion_rate once (cast the numerator to numeric so the division stays
  decimal, not integer-floored to 0), filtering out zero-session tutors. NTILE(4) over the rate
  DESC splits the 8 tutors into 4 even buckets with the best rates in bucket 1.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 8 expected rows.
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT tutor_name, completed_sessions, total_sessions,
           COALESCE(ROUND(completed_sessions::numeric / total_sessions, 2), 0.00) AS completion_rate
    FROM tutors
    WHERE total_sessions > 0
)
SELECT tutor_name, completion_rate,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY completion_rate DESC) AS quartile    -- DESC -> best in bucket 1
FROM base
ORDER BY quartile, completion_rate DESC;

Medium Quartile Segmentation of Customer Basket Spend (NULL handling with NULLS LAST)

▼

Bucket customers into quartiles by basket spend, best in quartile 1, with NULL spenders forced to the bottom.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A grocery team segments customers into 4 spend quartiles, quartile 1 = highest spend.
  • The customer_metrics table has a pre-computed avg_basket_value that is NULL for customers with no orders.
  • Include NULL-spend customers but place them at the BOTTOM (not the top). Return customer_id, avg_basket_value, spend_quartile, ordered by quartile then basket value descending.
  • The whole lesson: DESC defaults to NULLS FIRST in Postgres, so add NULLS LAST inside the NTILE's ORDER BY.

Schema — customer_metrics

ColumnType
customer_idINTEGER
customer_nameVARCHAR
avg_basket_valueDECIMAL(10,2)
total_ordersINTEGER
last_order_dateDATE

Example input — customer_metrics

customer_idcustomer_nameavg_basket_valuetotal_orderslast_order_date
101Alice142.552024-03-01
102Bob87.332024-03-02
103Carol215.892024-03-03
104David63.222024-03-04
105Emma198.472024-03-05
106Frank45.912024-03-06
107GraceNULL0NULL
108Henry125.642024-03-08

Expected output

customer_idavg_basket_valuespend_quartile
103215.801
105198.401
101142.502
108125.602
10287.303
10463.203
107NULL4
10645.904

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  NTILE(4) over avg_basket_value DESC NULLS LAST is the fix. In Postgres, DESC defaults to NULLS
  FIRST, which would rank Grace's NULL above the highest real value and drop her into quartile 1;
  NULLS LAST sorts NULL below every real value so she lands in quartile 4. The NULLS keyword belongs
  inside the OVER (it drives the bucket), not in the outer display sort.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 8 expected rows.
*/

SELECT customer_id, avg_basket_value,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY avg_basket_value DESC NULLS LAST) AS spend_quartile   -- NULLs to the bottom
FROM customer_metrics
ORDER BY spend_quartile, avg_basket_value DESC;
