PERCENT_RANK for top X% of rows 1 problem

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics (top_n_percent flavor) — PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) returns a fraction from 0 to 1 measuring row position. Order so the best row sits at pr = 0 and filter pr ≤ X / 100. Beware "top 10%" by VALUE band — that is PERCENTILE_DISC, not PERCENT_RANK.

PERCENT_RANK ≤ X / 100 (top X% of rows)

▼

Use when: "top X% per group" measured as a fraction of ROW COUNT. Order DESC so the best row sits at pr = 0; filter pr <= X/100.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Apply PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) inside a CTE — returns 0..1 where 0 = best.
  2. Order DESC so the best row sits at pr = 0.
  3. Filter pr ≤ X / 100 in the outer query to keep the top X% of rows per group.
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT t.*,
         PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY group_col ORDER BY metric_col DESC) AS pr
  FROM t
)
SELECT group_col, entity_col, metric_col
FROM ranked
WHERE pr <= 0.10;   -- top 10% of rows per group

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A music team surfaces the top 15% most-curated playlists by track count across the whole catalog.
  • playlists lists each playlist; playlist_tracks has one row per track in a playlist (empty playlists count 0).
  • A playlist qualifies if its PERCENT_RANK (ordered by track count descending) is at most 0.15; boundary ties are included.
  • Return playlist_id, playlist_name, track_count, percent_rank (4 decimals), ordered by track count descending then playlist id.

Schema — playlists

ColumnType
playlist_idINTEGER
user_idINTEGER
playlist_nameVARCHAR
created_atDATE

Example input — playlists

playlist_iduser_idplaylist_namecreated_at
11Rock2024-01-01
21Pop2024-01-02
32Jazz2024-01-03
42Indie2024-01-04
53Folk2024-01-05
63Metal2024-01-06
74Soul2024-01-07
84Empty2024-01-08

Schema — playlist_tracks

ColumnType
playlist_idINTEGER
track_idINTEGER
added_atDATE

Example input — playlist_tracks

playlist_idtrack_idadded_at
112024-01-01
122024-01-01
132024-01-01
142024-01-01
252024-01-02
262024-01-02
272024-01-02
382024-01-03
392024-01-03
4102024-01-04
4112024-01-04
5122024-01-05
6132024-01-06
7142024-01-07

Expected output

playlist_idplaylist_nametrack_countpercent_rank
1Rock40.0000

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The inner query counts tracks per playlist (LEFT JOIN so the empty playlist still counts 0), then
  PERCENT_RANK ranks across ALL playlists -- no PARTITION BY, because "top X% overall" means one
  global ranking. Ordering DESC puts the busiest playlist at pr = 0, so pr <= 0.15 keeps the top
  slice; a window function can't sit in WHERE, so the rank is filtered in the outer query.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT playlist_id, playlist_name, track_count, percent_rank
FROM (
    SELECT p.playlist_id, p.playlist_name,
           COUNT(t.track_id) AS track_count,
           ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(t.track_id) DESC)::numeric, 4) AS percent_rank   -- 0 = busiest
    FROM playlists AS p
    LEFT JOIN playlist_tracks AS t ON p.playlist_id = t.playlist_id
    GROUP BY p.playlist_id, p.playlist_name
) ranked
WHERE percent_rank <= 0.15
ORDER BY track_count DESC, playlist_id;

Medium Compute the Rank as a Percentage

▼

Each student's percentile rank within their department, handling single-student departments.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An education dashboard shows each student their percentile rank within their department.
  • The Students table has each student's mark and department.
  • Return student_id, department_id, and percentage = (rank - 1) * 100 / (department size - 1), rounded to 2 decimals; a department with one student is 0.
  • Build the percent rank from RANK and COUNT so single-student departments do not divide by zero.

Schema — Students

ColumnType
student_idINTEGER
department_idINTEGER
markINTEGER

Example input — Students

student_iddepartment_idmark
1190
2180
3170
4250

Expected output

student_iddepartment_idpercentage
110.00
2150.00
31100.00
420.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  PERCENT_RANK by hand: (RANK - 1) * 100 / (group size - 1). RANK and COUNT are both windowed over
  the department. The CASE guards the single-student department (size 1 would divide by zero) by
  returning 0. The 100.0 forces numeric division. Department 1's top student is 0%, the middle 50%,
  the lowest 100%.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

SELECT student_id, department_id,
       ROUND(
         CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) = 1 THEN 0
              ELSE (RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY mark DESC) - 1) * 100.0
                   / (COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) - 1)
         END, 2) AS percentage
FROM Students;

Medium Top 10% Trial Sites by Enrollment Rate (PERCENT_RANK + ratio output)

▼

Top 10% of sites by enrollment rate (a row-fraction PERCENT_RANK shape), ratio shown in the output.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A clinical ops team flags the top 10% of trial sites by enrollment rate (enrolled / target), including ties at the boundary.
  • The trial_sites table has enrolled and target counts per site.
  • Here 'top 10%' means the top 10% of ROWS, so PERCENT_RANK <= 0.10 (ordered by rate descending) is the right shape.
  • Return site_id, site_name, enrolled_participants, target_enrollment, enrollment_rate (4 decimals), ordered by rate descending then site id.

Schema — trial_sites

ColumnType
site_idINTEGER
site_nameVARCHAR
trial_phaseVARCHAR
enrolled_participantsINTEGER
target_enrollmentINTEGER
principal_investigatorVARCHAR

Example input — trial_sites

site_idsite_nametrial_phaseenrolled_participantstarget_enrollmentprincipal_investigator
101Site AII4550Dr X
102Site BII3840Dr Y
103Site CIII7280Dr Z
104Site DI2835Dr W
105Site EII5460Dr V
106Site FIII4250Dr U
107Site GI3340Dr T
108Site HII2530Dr S

Expected output

site_idsite_nameenrolled_participantstarget_enrollmentenrollment_rate
102Site B38400.9500

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Two CTEs: base computes the ratio (cast to numeric so it isn't integer-floored, NULLIF guards a
  zero target), ranked attaches PERCENT_RANK ordered DESC so the best site sits at pr = 0. The
  filter uses the unrounded pr so boundary ties are kept; the SELECT rounds only the displayed
  ratio. Site B (0.95) is the sole site at pr <= 0.10; the three sites tied at 0.90 land at pr 0.143.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT site_id, site_name, enrolled_participants, target_enrollment,
           enrolled_participants::numeric / NULLIF(target_enrollment, 0) AS enrollment_rate
    FROM trial_sites
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT *, PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY enrollment_rate DESC) AS pr    -- best at pr = 0
    FROM base
)
SELECT site_id, site_name, enrolled_participants, target_enrollment,
       ROUND(enrollment_rate, 4) AS enrollment_rate
FROM ranked
WHERE pr <= 0.10                 -- top 10% of rows, ties at the boundary included
ORDER BY enrollment_rate DESC, site_id;

PERCENTILE_CONT / DISC for one value per group migrate next

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics (percentile_aggregate flavor) — PERCENTILE_CONT(p) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY metric) returns ONE interpolated value at percentile p; PERCENTILE_DISC(p) returns a real data value. Aggregate, not per-row. Use CONT for medians and reported percentiles; DISC + >= for "top X% by value band" where boundary ties must be kept.

PERCENTILE_CONT / PERCENTILE_DISC (one value per group)

▼

Use when: you need a single value — the median, P90, top X% by value band. CONT interpolates; DISC returns a real data value (use DISC with >= to catch ties at the boundary).

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Use PERCENTILE_CONT(p) (interpolated) or PERCENTILE_DISC(p) (real data value) as an aggregate.
  2. WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY metric) sets the sort axis for the percentile.
  3. GROUP BY the entity column to get ONE percentile value per group.
-- One median per region (aggregate)
SELECT region,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency) AS median_latency
FROM t
GROUP BY region;

-- Top 10% by value band: every row at or above the P90 cutoff
WITH cutoff AS (
  SELECT PERCENTILE_DISC(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY rate) AS p90
  FROM t
)
SELECT t.* FROM t, cutoff WHERE t.rate >= cutoff.p90;

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  "Top 10% by value" means rate at or above the 90th percentile VALUE. PERCENTILE_DISC(0.9) returns
  an actual data value (0.95 here), and keeping every worker with rate >= that cutoff pulls in the
  whole tie cluster for free -- five workers, far more than 10% of the rows, which is the signature
  of the value-band reading. PERCENT_RANK <= 0.10 would cut the cluster and return too few. (DISC,
  not CONT: CONT would interpolate to a value just above 0.95 and drop the ties.)

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

WITH rated AS (
    SELECT worker_id, worker_name,
           ROUND(completed_jobs::numeric / NULLIF(total_jobs_accepted, 0), 2) AS completion_rate
    FROM gig_workers
)
SELECT worker_id, worker_name, completion_rate
FROM rated
WHERE completion_rate >= (
    SELECT PERCENTILE_DISC(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY completion_rate) FROM rated   -- 90th percentile value
)
ORDER BY completion_rate DESC, worker_id;

Easy Trial Duration Percentiles by Plan Tier (PERCENTILE_CONT per group)

▼

The median, 75th, and 90th percentile of trial duration per plan tier, interpolated.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A SaaS team reports trial-duration percentiles per plan tier.
  • The trial_signups table has each signup's plan tier and trial duration in days.
  • Using PERCENTILE_CONT (interpolated), return plan_tier, p50_duration, p75_duration, p90_duration, ordered by plan tier.
  • PERCENTILE_CONT is an ordered-set aggregate that pairs with GROUP BY via WITHIN GROUP.

Schema — trial_signups

ColumnType
signup_idINTEGER
company_nameVARCHAR
plan_tierVARCHAR
trial_duration_daysINTEGER
converted_to_paidBOOLEAN
signup_dateDATE

Example input — trial_signups

signup_idcompany_nameplan_tiertrial_duration_daysconverted_to_paidsignup_date
1Astarter7True2024-01-01
2Bstarter10False2024-01-02
3Cstarter14True2024-01-03
4Dstarter21False2024-01-04
5Eenterprise45True2024-01-05

Expected output

plan_tierp50_durationp75_durationp90_duration
enterprise45.045.045.0
starter12.015.7518.9

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  PERCENTILE_CONT(p) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY value) is an ordered-set aggregate: one pass, three
  percentiles per group, interpolating between the two neighbours when the target position falls
  between rows. The starter tier (7, 10, 14, 21) gives p50 = 12, p75 = 15.75, p90 = 18.9; the
  single-value enterprise group returns 45 at every percentile.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT plan_tier,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5)  WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY trial_duration_days) AS p50_duration,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY trial_duration_days) AS p75_duration,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9)  WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY trial_duration_days) AS p90_duration
FROM trial_signups
GROUP BY plan_tier
ORDER BY plan_tier;

Median fallback (frequency-based, expand-then-rank) no problems yet

▼

For dialects without PERCENTILE_CONT (e.g. MySQL), or for #571-style frequency-table prompts, EXPAND the frequency table into one row per occurrence, ROW_NUMBER over the expanded set, and pick the middle one (or two for even N, then AVG). Skip if PERCENTILE_CONT is available.

Template Median template

▼

Use when: the middle value per group (or overall).

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Postgres has it built in: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x) as an aggregate per group.
  2. Portable trick: rank each row ASC and DESC; the median rows are where ABS(rn_asc - rn_desc) <= 1, then average them.
SELECT group_col,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x) AS median_x
FROM t
GROUP BY group_col;

Worked example to be added. Use this leaf for problems where PERCENTILE_CONT is unavailable or the input is a frequency table that needs expansion first.

Medium Highest Grade For Each Student

▼

Each student's best course, ties broken by smallest course id.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A transcript highlights each student's best course.
  • The Enrollments table has one row per (student, course) with a grade.
  • Return student_id, course_id, grade for each student's highest grade, breaking ties by the smallest course id, ordered by student id.

Schema — Enrollments

ColumnType
student_idINTEGER
course_idINTEGER
gradeINTEGER

Example input — Enrollments

student_idcourse_idgrade
110190
110290
110385
210180
210275

Expected output

student_idcourse_idgrade
110190
210180

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  ROW_NUMBER per student ordered by grade DESC then course_id picks exactly one winner and encodes
  the tie-break in the same ORDER BY. Student 1 ties at grade 90 on courses 101 and 102, so the
  smaller course id 101 wins. Filter rn = 1.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT student_id, course_id, grade
FROM (
    SELECT student_id, course_id, grade,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY student_id ORDER BY grade DESC, course_id) AS rn   -- best grade, then smallest course
    FROM Enrollments
) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY student_id;

Medium Maximum Transaction Each Day

Prompt

  • A fraud team reviews each day's largest transaction.
  • The Transactions table has one row per transaction with a day and amount.
  • Return the transaction_id of the maximum-amount transaction per day; if several tie for the max, return all of them, ordered by transaction id.

Schema — Transactions

ColumnType
transaction_idINTEGER
dayDATE
amountINTEGER

Example input — Transactions

transaction_iddayamount
12024-01-01100
22024-01-01200
32024-01-0250
42024-01-0250

Expected output

transaction_id
2

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  RANK per day ordered by amount DESC; rk = 1 is the day's largest. RANK (not ROW_NUMBER) keeps
  ties, so when two transactions share the day's max (the 50s on Jan 2) both come back.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT transaction_id
FROM (
    SELECT transaction_id,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY day ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rk   -- ties share rank 1
    FROM Transactions
) t
WHERE rk = 1
ORDER BY transaction_id;

Medium The Airport With the Most Traffic

▼

The airport(s) with the highest total traffic counting both arrivals and departures.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A network planner finds the busiest airport by total traffic in either direction.
  • The Flights table has a departure airport, an arrival airport, and a flight count per row.
  • Sum each airport's traffic as a departure plus as an arrival, then return the airport_id with the maximum total (ties kept).

Schema — Flights

ColumnType
departure_airportINTEGER
arrival_airportINTEGER
flights_countINTEGER

Example input — Flights

departure_airportarrival_airportflights_count
1210
235
318

Expected output

airport_id
1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Normalize each flight row into two rows -- one crediting the departure airport, one the arrival --
  with UNION ALL, then sum per airport so traffic in both directions counts. RANK over the totals
  and keep rk = 1. Airport 1 totals 10 (departures) + 8 (arrivals) = 18, the most.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH n AS (
    SELECT departure_airport AS airport_id, flights_count FROM Flights
    UNION ALL
    SELECT arrival_airport,   flights_count FROM Flights
),
totals AS (SELECT airport_id, SUM(flights_count) AS total FROM n GROUP BY airport_id)
SELECT airport_id
FROM (SELECT airport_id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total DESC) AS rk FROM totals) t
WHERE rk = 1;

Medium Election Results

▼

The winning candidate(s), splitting each voter's single vote across the candidates they picked.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A ranked-choice tally splits each voter's vote equally across the candidates they selected.
  • The Votes table has one row per (voter, candidate); a NULL candidate means the voter abstained.
  • Give each voter's pick a share of 1 / (their number of valid picks), sum per candidate, and return the candidate with the most total votes (ties kept).
  • Exclude NULL candidates before computing the share.

Schema — Votes

ColumnType
voterINTEGER
candidateVARCHAR

Example input — Votes

votercandidate
1A
1B
2A
3B
4A
5NULL

Expected output

candidate
A

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Each valid vote is worth 1 / (the voter's count of valid picks): a voter who named two candidates
  gives each 0.5. The WHERE drops abstentions (NULL) before the per-voter count, so voter 5
  contributes nothing. Sum the shares per candidate, RANK, and keep rk = 1. Candidate A totals
  0.5 + 1 + 1 = 2.5, beating B's 1.5.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH w AS (
    SELECT candidate, 1.0 / COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY voter) AS share   -- split the voter's vote
    FROM Votes
    WHERE candidate IS NOT NULL
),
totals AS (SELECT candidate, SUM(share) AS s FROM w GROUP BY candidate)
SELECT candidate
FROM (SELECT candidate, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY s DESC) AS rk FROM totals) t
WHERE rk = 1
ORDER BY candidate;

Medium Find Peak Calling Hours for Each City

▼

The hour(s) with the most calls in each city.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A telco planner finds each city's busiest calling hour.
  • The Calls table logs each call with a timestamp and city.
  • Count calls per (city, hour), then return the city, peak_calling_hour, and number_of_calls for the hour(s) with the maximum count per city (ties kept), ordered by city descending then hour descending.

Schema — Calls

ColumnType
caller_idINTEGER
recipient_idINTEGER
call_timeTIMESTAMP
cityVARCHAR

Example input — Calls

caller_idrecipient_idcall_timecity
122024-01-01 09:00:00LA
342024-01-01 09:30:00LA
562024-01-01 10:00:00LA
782024-01-01 14:00:00NY
9102024-01-01 15:00:00NY

Expected output

citypeak_calling_hournumber_of_calls
NY151
NY141
LA92

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Count calls per (city, hour) using EXTRACT(HOUR FROM call_time), then RANK those counts per city
  and keep rk = 1. RANK keeps ties, so NY's two single-call hours (14 and 15) both come back as
  peaks; LA's hour 9 has two calls and wins outright.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH counts AS (
    SELECT city, EXTRACT(HOUR FROM call_time) AS h, COUNT(*) AS cnt
    FROM Calls
    GROUP BY city, EXTRACT(HOUR FROM call_time)
)
SELECT city, h AS peak_calling_hour, cnt AS number_of_calls
FROM (SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY cnt DESC) AS rk FROM counts) t
WHERE rk = 1
ORDER BY city DESC, peak_calling_hour DESC;

Medium Manager of the Largest Department

▼

The manager(s) of the department with the most employees.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • HR highlights the leader of the biggest team.
  • The Employees table has each employee's department and position.
  • Find the department with the most employees, then return the manager_name and dept_id of its manager (the employee whose position is 'Manager').

Schema — Employees

ColumnType
emp_idINTEGER
emp_nameVARCHAR
dept_idINTEGER
positionVARCHAR

Example input — Employees

emp_idemp_namedept_idposition
1Alice1Manager
2Bob1Engineer
3Cara1Engineer
4Dan2Manager
5Eve2Engineer

Expected output

manager_namedept_id
Alice1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Count employees per department, RANK the departments by size, and keep rk = 1 (the largest). Join
  back to the employee rows and pick the one whose position is 'Manager'. Department 1 has three
  employees, so its manager Alice is returned.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH sizes AS (SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS c FROM Employees GROUP BY dept_id)
SELECT e.emp_name AS manager_name, e.dept_id
FROM Employees e
JOIN sizes s ON s.dept_id = e.dept_id
JOIN (SELECT dept_id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY c DESC) AS rk FROM sizes) r ON r.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.position = 'Manager' AND r.rk = 1;

Medium All the Pairs With the Maximum Number of Common Followers

▼

The user pair(s) sharing the most common followers.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A social team finds the most-overlapping audience pairs.
  • The Relations table has one row per (user, follower).
  • For each unordered user pair, count shared followers, then return the user1_id, user2_id pairs whose count equals the maximum across all pairs.

Schema — Relations

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
follower_idINTEGER

Example input — Relations

user_idfollower_id
110
111
210
211
310

Expected output

user1_iduser2_id
12

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Self-join on a shared follower with a.user_id < b.user_id (so each unordered pair appears once and
  no user pairs with itself), count shared followers per pair, then RANK and keep rk = 1. Users 1
  and 2 share two followers (10 and 11), the most.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH pairs AS (
    SELECT a.user_id AS user1_id, b.user_id AS user2_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt
    FROM Relations a
    JOIN Relations b ON a.follower_id = b.follower_id AND a.user_id < b.user_id   -- each pair once
    GROUP BY a.user_id, b.user_id
)
SELECT user1_id, user2_id
FROM (SELECT *, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY cnt DESC) AS rk FROM pairs) r
WHERE rk = 1;

Medium Get Highest Answer Rate Question

▼

The question with the highest answer rate (answers / shows), ties broken by smallest id.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A survey tool ranks questions by answer rate (answers divided by shows).
  • The SurveyLog table logs an action ('show' or 'answer') per question per event.
  • Return the question_id (aliased survey_log) with the highest answer rate, breaking ties by the smallest question id.

Schema — SurveyLog

ColumnType
idINTEGER
actionVARCHAR
question_idINTEGER
answer_idINTEGER
q_numINTEGER
timestampTIMESTAMP

Example input — SurveyLog

idactionquestion_idanswer_idq_numtimestamp
1show1NULL12024-01-01 10:00:00
2answer11112024-01-01 10:01:00
3show1NULL22024-01-01 10:02:00
4show2NULL12024-01-01 10:03:00
5answer22212024-01-01 10:04:00

Expected output

survey_log
2

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Per question, answer rate is the count of 'answer' actions over the count of 'show' actions. The
  conditional SUMs build both; cast to numeric so the division is decimal and NULLIF guards a zero
  denominator. Order by that rate descending, then question id for ties, and take the top one.
  Question 1 has rate 1/2 = 0.5; question 2 has 1/1 = 1.0, so question 2 wins.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT question_id AS survey_log
FROM SurveyLog
GROUP BY question_id
ORDER BY SUM(CASE WHEN action = 'answer' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)::numeric
         / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN action = 'show' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0) DESC,
         question_id
LIMIT 1;

  150 row and employee 2's 200 row.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.

Hard Customers with Maximum Number of Transactions on Consecutive Days

▼

Customers whose longest run of consecutive transaction days ties the overall maximum.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A loyalty program rewards the longest daily purchase streak.
  • The Transactions table has one row per transaction with a customer and a date.
  • Find each customer's longest run of consecutive calendar days with a transaction, then return the customer_id(s) whose longest run equals the maximum across all customers, ordered by customer id.

Schema — Transactions

ColumnType
transaction_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
transaction_dateDATE

Example input — Transactions

transaction_idcustomer_idtransaction_date
112024-01-01
212024-01-02
312024-01-03
422024-01-01
522024-01-02
622024-01-05

Expected output

customer_id
1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A gaps-and-islands streak. Dedupe to one row per (customer, day), then subtract a per-customer
  ROW_NUMBER from the date: consecutive days share the same (date - row number) value, so that
  grp labels each streak. COUNT per grp is the streak length; take each customer's MAX, then keep
  customers whose max equals the global max. Customer 1's 3-day streak beats customer 2's best of 2.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH d AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, transaction_date FROM Transactions
),
g AS (
    SELECT customer_id, transaction_date,
           transaction_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date))::int AS grp  -- consecutive days share grp
    FROM d
),
runs AS (SELECT customer_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS run_len FROM g GROUP BY customer_id, grp),
max_run AS (SELECT customer_id, MAX(run_len) AS maxlen FROM runs GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT customer_id
FROM max_run
WHERE maxlen = (SELECT MAX(maxlen) FROM max_run)
ORDER BY customer_id;

nb01 qtype: window_top_n_per_group — ROW_NUMBER PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC, rn ≤ N. Use ROW_NUMBER for exactly N per group; switch to RANK / DENSE_RANK if the prompt says ties share the rank.

Hard Top Three Wineries

▼

Each country's top three wineries by points, with fallback labels when fewer than three exist.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A wine app lists each country's top three wineries by total points.
  • The Wineries table has one row per winery entry with its country and points.
  • Return one row per country with top_winery, second_winery, third_winery, each formatted 'name (points)'; use 'No second winery' / 'No third winery' when a country has fewer than three.
  • Order by country.

Schema — Wineries

ColumnType
idINTEGER
countryVARCHAR
pointsINTEGER
wineryVARCHAR

Example input — Wineries

idcountrypointswinery
1US90A
2US80B
3US70C
4FR50X

Expected output

countrytop_winerysecond_winerythird_winery
FRX (50)No second wineryNo third winery
USA (90)B (80)C (70)

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Total points per (country, winery), then ROW_NUMBER per country ordered by points DESC (winery
  name breaks ties). A conditional MAX pivots the top three ranks into three columns on one row per
  country, and COALESCE supplies the fallback label when a rank is missing -- France has only one
  winery, so its second and third are placeholders.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH totals AS (
    SELECT country, winery, SUM(points) AS pts FROM Wineries GROUP BY country, winery
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT country, winery, pts,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY pts DESC, winery) AS rn   -- 1 = top winery
    FROM totals
)
SELECT country,
       MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 1 THEN CONCAT(winery, ' (', pts, ')') END) AS top_winery,
       COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 2 THEN CONCAT(winery, ' (', pts, ')') END), 'No second winery') AS second_winery,
       COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 3 THEN CONCAT(winery, ' (', pts, ')') END), 'No third winery')  AS third_winery
FROM ranked
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY country;

Hard Get the Second Most Recent Activity

▼

Each user's second most recent activity, or their only one if they have just one.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A profile page shows the activity behind the most recent one, falling back to the only activity for new users.
  • The UserActivity table has one row per activity with start and end dates.
  • Return username, activity, startDate, endDate for each user's second most recent activity (by start date); if a user has only one activity, return that one.
  • Order by username.

Schema — UserActivity

ColumnType
usernameVARCHAR
activityVARCHAR
startDateDATE
endDateDATE

Example input — UserActivity

usernameactivitystartDateendDate
AliceTravel2020-02-122020-02-20
AliceDancing2020-02-212020-02-23
BobTravel2020-02-112020-02-18

Expected output

usernameactivitystartDateendDate
AliceTravel2020-02-122020-02-20
BobTravel2020-02-112020-02-18

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Number each user's activities most-recent-first (rn) and also carry the per-user count. The filter
  keeps rn = 2 when the user has more than one activity, but falls back to rn = 1 (the only row) when
  they have exactly one. Alice's second-most-recent is her Travel row; Bob has just one, so it stays.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY username ORDER BY startDate DESC) AS rn,   -- most recent = 1
           COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY username)                         AS cnt
    FROM UserActivity
)
SELECT username, activity, startDate, endDate
FROM ranked
WHERE (cnt > 1 AND rn = 2) OR (cnt = 1 AND rn = 1)
ORDER BY username;

Medium Find Third Transaction

▼

Each user's third transaction, but only if it out-spends both prior ones.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A product analyst flags users whose third purchase escalates spend over the first two.
  • The Transactions table has one row per transaction with a user, spend, and date.
  • Return user_id, third_transaction_spend, third_transaction_date for the third transaction (by date) whose spend is greater than BOTH the first and second transactions.

Schema — Transactions

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
spendINTEGER
transaction_dateDATE

Example input — Transactions

user_idspendtransaction_date
11002024-01-01
11502024-01-02
12002024-01-03
21002024-01-01
22002024-01-02
21502024-01-03

Expected output

user_idthird_transaction_spendthird_transaction_date
12002024-01-03

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Number each user's transactions by date and pull the two previous spends with LAG(1) and LAG(2).
  Keep rn = 3 only when its spend beats both prior values. User 1's third (200) tops 150 and 100, so
  it qualifies; user 2's third (150) does not beat its second (200), so it drops.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT user_id, spend, transaction_date,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS rn,
           LAG(spend, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS p1,   -- previous spend
           LAG(spend, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS p2    -- one before that
    FROM Transactions
)
SELECT user_id, spend AS third_transaction_spend, transaction_date AS third_transaction_date
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 3 AND spend > p1 AND spend > p2;

Median, threshold, rank deltas (single-table) 2 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics — rank-shaped problems that don't fit a "top N" mold: median per group, threshold cutoffs, and rank deltas across snapshots.

Hard Median Employee Salary

▼

The median salary row(s) per company, handling odd and even group sizes.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Finance reports the median salary row per company.
  • The Employee table has one row per employee with a company and salary.
  • Return id, company, salary for the median row(s): one row for odd-sized companies, two for even-sized ones.
  • The trick: median rows have |ascending position - descending position| at most 1.

Schema — Employee

ColumnType
idINTEGER
companyVARCHAR
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Employee

idcompanysalary
1A100
2A200
3A300
4B100
5B200

Expected output

idcompanysalary
2A200
4B100
5B200

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Number each company's rows from both ends by salary. A row is a median exactly when its ascending
  and descending positions are within 1 of each other -- that catches the single middle row of an
  odd group and the two middle rows of an even group. Company A (3 rows) yields the 200; company B
  (2 rows) yields both 100 and 200.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT id, company, salary
FROM (
    SELECT id, company, salary,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY company ORDER BY salary, id)      AS asc_n,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY company ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS desc_n
    FROM Employee
) t
WHERE ABS(asc_n - desc_n) <= 1
ORDER BY company, salary;

Medium Orders With Maximum Quantity Above Average

▼

Orders whose largest line-item quantity exceeds the average of all orders' maximums.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An inventory audit spotlights orders with an unusually large line item.
  • The OrdersDetails table has one row per (order, product) with a quantity.
  • Compute each order's maximum quantity, then return the order_id of orders whose maximum exceeds the average of those per-order maximums, ordered by order id.

Schema — OrdersDetails

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
product_idINTEGER
quantityINTEGER

Example input — OrdersDetails

order_idproduct_idquantity
1110
1220
215
225
3130

Expected output

order_id
1
3

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  First reduce to one row per order carrying its largest line item (per_order). Then compare each
  order's max to the average of all those maxes. Maxes are 20, 5, 30, averaging ~18.33; orders 1
  (20) and 3 (30) clear it.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH per_order AS (
    SELECT order_id, MAX(quantity) AS max_q FROM OrdersDetails GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT order_id
FROM per_order
WHERE max_q > (SELECT AVG(max_q) FROM per_order)
ORDER BY order_id;

Easy Triangle Judgement

▼

Label each row of three lengths as a valid triangle or not.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A QA check decides whether three measured lengths can form a triangle.
  • The Triangle table has one row of three side lengths x, y, z.
  • Return x, y, z, and triangle = 'Yes' if every pair of sides sums to more than the third, else 'No'.

Schema — Triangle

ColumnType
xINTEGER
yINTEGER
zINTEGER

Example input — Triangle

xyz
131530
102015

Expected output

xyztriangle
102015Yes
131530No

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The triangle inequality: each pair of sides must sum to strictly more than the third. All three
  checks ANDed give 'Yes'. The ELSE 'No' matters -- without it, false rows would return NULL, not
  'No'. (13, 15, 30) fails because 13 + 15 = 28 is not greater than 30.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT x, y, z,
       CASE
         WHEN x + y > z AND x + z > y AND y + z > x THEN 'Yes'   -- all three pairs clear the third side
         ELSE 'No'
       END AS triangle
FROM Triangle;

Easy Primary Department for Each Employee

▼

Each employee's primary department, falling back to their only department.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • HR resolves each employee's primary department.
  • The Employee table has one row per (employee, department) with a primary_flag of 'Y' or 'N'.
  • Return employee_id and department_id: the row flagged 'Y' for multi-department employees, or the single department for employees with just one (even if its flag is 'N'), ordered by employee id.

Schema — Employee

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
department_idINTEGER
primary_flagCHAR(1)

Example input — Employee

employee_iddepartment_idprimary_flag
11N
21Y
22N
33N
42N
43Y

Expected output

employee_iddepartment_id
11
21
33
43

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Rank each employee's rows so the primary one comes first: ORDER BY primary_flag DESC puts 'Y'
  ahead of 'N'. For a single-department employee there is only one row, so it is rn = 1 regardless
  of its flag -- that is the fallback. Keep rn = 1.

  Why not a window function in WHERE: Postgres does not allow window functions in WHERE, so the rank
  is computed in a CTE and filtered in the outer query.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT employee_id, department_id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY primary_flag DESC, department_id) AS rn  -- 'Y' first
    FROM Employee
)
SELECT employee_id, department_id
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY employee_id;

Medium Exchange Seats

▼

Swap each adjacent pair of seats, leaving a lone last seat in place.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Swap students in adjacent seat pairs: (1,2) become (2,1), (3,4) become (4,3), and so on.
  • The Seat table has one row per seat id with a student.
  • Return id and the swapped student, ordered by id. If the last seat has an odd id with no partner, it keeps its student.

Schema — Seat

ColumnType
idINTEGER
studentVARCHAR

Example input — Seat

idstudent
1Abbot
2Doris
3Emerson
4Green
5Jeames

Expected output

idstudent
1Doris
2Abbot
3Green
4Emerson
5Jeames

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  An odd seat takes the student from the NEXT seat (LEAD); an even seat takes the PREVIOUS one (LAG).
  MOD(id, 2) picks which. COALESCE handles the lone last odd seat (id 5) -- LEAD is NULL there, so it
  keeps its own student. No loop, no self-join.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

SELECT id,
       CASE
         WHEN MOD(id, 2) = 1 THEN COALESCE(LEAD(student) OVER (ORDER BY id), student)   -- odd: take next (or stay)
         ELSE LAG(student) OVER (ORDER BY id)                                           -- even: take previous
       END AS student
FROM Seat
ORDER BY id;

Medium Calculate Salaries

▼

Apply a per-company tax bracket (0/24/49%) and return each employee's post-tax salary.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A payroll processor taxes each company by a bracket set by its highest salary: 0% if under 1000, 24% if at most 10000, else 49%.
  • The Salaries table has one row per employee with their company and salary.
  • Return company_id, employee_id, employee_name, and the rounded post-tax salary, ordered by company then employee.

Schema — Salaries

ColumnType
company_idINTEGER
employee_idINTEGER
employee_nameVARCHAR
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Salaries

company_idemployee_idemployee_namesalary
11A500
12B800
23C5000
24D9000
35E15000
36F20000

Expected output

company_idemployee_idemployee_namesalary
11A500
12B800
23C3800
24D6840
35E7650
36F10200

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Compute each company's tax bracket once from its MAX salary, then apply it per employee. Company 1
  tops out at 800 (under 1000) so 0% tax; company 2 at 9000 so 24%; company 3 at 20000 so 49%.
  ROUND gives whole-dollar post-tax pay.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 6 expected rows.
*/

WITH brackets AS (
    SELECT company_id,
           CASE WHEN MAX(salary) < 1000  THEN 0.00
                WHEN MAX(salary) <= 10000 THEN 0.24
                ELSE 0.49 END AS tax        -- bracket set by the company's top salary
    FROM Salaries
    GROUP BY company_id
)
SELECT s.company_id, s.employee_id, s.employee_name,
       ROUND(s.salary * (1 - b.tax)) AS salary
FROM Salaries s
JOIN brackets b ON b.company_id = s.company_id
ORDER BY s.company_id, s.employee_id;

Easy Calculate Special Bonus

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A legacy bonus policy pays full salary only to employees whose id is odd AND whose name does not start with 'M'.
  • The Employees table has each employee's id, name, and salary.
  • Return employee_id and bonus (salary if the rule holds, else 0), ordered by employee id.

Schema — Employees

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Employees

employee_idnamesalary
2Meir3000
3Michael3800
7Addilyn7400
8Juan6100
9Kannon7700

Expected output

employee_idbonus
20
30
77400
80
97700

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  One CASE encodes both rules: odd id (id % 2 = 1) AND name not starting with 'M' (NOT LIKE 'M%')
  pays the salary, everything else 0. Id 3 is odd but 'Michael' starts with M, so it gets 0.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

SELECT employee_id,
       CASE
         WHEN employee_id % 2 = 1 AND name NOT LIKE 'M%' THEN salary   -- odd id AND not an M-name
         ELSE 0
       END AS bonus
FROM Employees
ORDER BY employee_id;

Hard The Number of Seniors and Juniors to Join the Company II

▼

The specific candidates hired under the greedy budget (seniors first, then juniors).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A recruiter hires within a $70,000 budget: take the cheapest seniors that fit, then spend the remainder on the cheapest juniors.
  • The Candidates table has each candidate's experience ('Senior' or 'Junior') and salary.
  • Return the employee_id of every candidate hired, ordered by employee id.

Schema — Candidates

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
experienceVARCHAR
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Candidates

employee_idexperiencesalary
1Senior20000
2Senior30000
3Junior10000
4Junior15000

Expected output

employee_id
1
2
3

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A running total of salary per experience (cheapest first) is the greedy spend order. Seniors whose
  running total stays within 70000 are hired; their summed cost reduces the budget for juniors, who
  are filtered the same way against the remainder. This returns the ids (the sibling card returns the
  counts). Seniors 1 and 2 cost 50000; junior 3 (10000) fits the remaining 20000, junior 4 does not.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH running AS (
    SELECT employee_id, experience, salary,
           SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY experience ORDER BY salary) AS run_total   -- cumulative cost, cheapest first
    FROM Candidates
),
seniors AS (SELECT * FROM running WHERE experience = 'Senior' AND run_total <= 70000),
senior_cost AS (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(salary), 0) AS cost FROM seniors)
SELECT employee_id FROM seniors
UNION ALL
SELECT r.employee_id
FROM running r
CROSS JOIN senior_cost sc
WHERE r.experience = 'Junior' AND r.run_total <= 70000 - sc.cost   -- juniors within the leftover budget
ORDER BY employee_id;

Hard The Number of Seniors and Juniors to Join the Company

▼

The count of seniors and juniors hired under the greedy budget.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A recruiter hires within a $70,000 budget: take the cheapest seniors that fit, then spend the remainder on the cheapest juniors.
  • The Candidates table has each candidate's experience ('Senior' or 'Junior') and salary.
  • Return experience and accepted_candidates (how many of each were hired); both groups must appear even if zero are hired.
  • Order by experience.

Schema — Candidates

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
experienceVARCHAR
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Candidates

employee_idexperiencesalary
1Senior20000
2Senior30000
3Junior10000
4Junior15000

Expected output

experienceaccepted_candidates
Junior1
Senior2

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Same greedy running-total logic as the sibling card, but counted. Seniors within budget are hired;
  their cost shrinks the budget for juniors. The RIGHT JOIN to a two-row base ('Senior','Junior')
  guarantees both experience levels appear even when zero are hired. Here 2 seniors and 1 junior fit.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH running AS (
    SELECT employee_id, experience, salary,
           SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY experience ORDER BY salary) AS run_total
    FROM Candidates
),
seniors AS (SELECT * FROM running WHERE experience = 'Senior' AND run_total <= 70000),
senior_cost AS (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(salary), 0) AS cost FROM seniors)
SELECT experience, COUNT(*) AS accepted_candidates
FROM (
    SELECT 'Senior' AS experience, employee_id FROM seniors
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'Junior', r.employee_id
    FROM running r CROSS JOIN senior_cost sc
    WHERE r.experience = 'Junior' AND r.run_total <= 70000 - sc.cost
) t
RIGHT JOIN (SELECT 'Senior' AS experience UNION ALL SELECT 'Junior') base USING (experience)  -- keep both levels
GROUP BY experience;

Medium The Category of Each Member in the Store

▼

Tier each member Diamond/Gold/Silver/Bronze by how often visits convert to purchases.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A loyalty program tiers members by purchase rate (purchases per visit).
  • Members lists members; Visits logs visits; Purchases links a visit to a charge.
  • Diamond if purchases are at least 80% of visits, Gold if at least 50%, else Silver; a member with no visits is Bronze.
  • Return member_id, name, category, ordered by member id.

Schema — Members

ColumnType
member_idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR

Example input — Members

member_idname
1A
2B
3C

Schema — Visits

ColumnType
visit_idINTEGER
member_idINTEGER
visit_dateDATE

Example input — Visits

visit_idmember_idvisit_date
112024-01-01
212024-01-02
322024-01-01

Schema — Purchases

ColumnType
visit_idINTEGER
charged_amountINTEGER

Example input — Purchases

visit_idcharged_amount
1100

Expected output

member_idnamecategory
1AGold
2BSilver
3CBronze

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Count visits and purchases per member with LEFT JOINs (so a member with no visits survives with 0).
  The CASE checks zero visits first (Bronze), then compares purchases to 80% and 50% of visits using
  cross-multiplication to avoid fractions. Member 1 made 1 purchase in 2 visits (50%) = Gold; member
  2 made 0 of 1 = Silver; member 3 never visited = Bronze.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT m.member_id, m.name,
           COUNT(v.visit_id) AS visits,
           COUNT(p.visit_id) AS purchases
    FROM Members m
    LEFT JOIN Visits v    ON v.member_id = m.member_id
    LEFT JOIN Purchases p ON p.visit_id  = v.visit_id
    GROUP BY m.member_id, m.name
)
SELECT member_id, name,
       CASE
         WHEN visits = 0                     THEN 'Bronze'
         WHEN purchases * 100 >= visits * 80 THEN 'Diamond'
         WHEN purchases * 100 >= visits * 50 THEN 'Gold'
         ELSE 'Silver'
       END AS category
FROM base
ORDER BY member_id;

Hard Total Sales Amount by Year

▼

Split each multi-year sales period into calendar-year buckets and total per year.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Finance splits multi-year sales contracts into calendar-year revenue buckets.
  • Sales has each contract's period (start to end) and average daily sales; Product holds names.
  • For each contract and each year it overlaps, clip the period to that year, multiply the number of days (inclusive) by the daily rate, and report it.
  • Return product_id, product_name, report_year, total_amount, ordered by product id then year.

Schema — Product

ColumnType
product_idINTEGER
product_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Product

product_idproduct_name
1A
2B

Schema — Sales

ColumnType
product_idINTEGER
period_startDATE
period_endDATE
average_daily_salesINTEGER

Example input — Sales

product_idperiod_startperiod_endaverage_daily_sales
12019-01-252019-02-28100
22018-12-012020-01-0150

Expected output

product_idproduct_namereport_yeartotal_amount
1A20193500
2B20181550
2B201918250
2B202050

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A small year spine (2018-2020) joined to each contract on the years it spans. For each year, clip
  the contract: GREATEST(start, Jan 1) and LEAST(end, Dec 31) give the overlap; subtracting the dates
  and adding 1 is the inclusive day count, times the daily rate is that year's revenue. Contract 2
  spans three years (31 days in 2018, 365 in 2019, 1 in 2020).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH years AS (
    SELECT 2018 AS yr UNION ALL SELECT 2019 UNION ALL SELECT 2020
)
SELECT s.product_id, p.product_name, y.yr AS report_year,
       (LEAST(s.period_end, MAKE_DATE(y.yr, 12, 31))
      - GREATEST(s.period_start, MAKE_DATE(y.yr, 1, 1)) + 1) * s.average_daily_sales AS total_amount  -- clipped days * rate
FROM Sales s
JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = s.product_id
JOIN years y ON y.yr BETWEEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM s.period_start) AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM s.period_end)
ORDER BY s.product_id, y.yr;

Prompt

  • A newsroom renders the Olympic medal table in standard order.
  • The Olympic table has one row per country with gold, silver, and bronze counts.
  • Return all columns sorted by gold descending, then silver descending, then bronze descending, then country ascending.

Schema — Olympic

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A pure multi-key sort: gold first, then silver, then bronze as tie-breakers, then country name. US
  and China both have 10 gold, so silver decides (5 beats 4).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.

SELECT country, gold_medals, silver_medals, bronze_medals
FROM Olympic

Medium Tree Node

▼

Label each node Root, Inner, or Leaf from the parent pointers.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Classify each node of a tree as Root (no parent), Inner (has a parent and children), or Leaf (has a parent, no children).
  • The Tree table has each node's id and its parent p_id (NULL for the root).
  • Return id and type, ordered by id.

Schema — Tree

ColumnType
idINTEGER
p_idINTEGER

Example input — Tree

idp_id
1NULL
21
31
42
52

Expected output

idtype
1Root
2Inner
3Leaf
4Leaf
5Leaf

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  CASE evaluates top to bottom, so each branch assumes the ones above failed. A NULL parent is the
  Root. Otherwise, if the id appears as some other row's p_id it has children, so it is Inner; if not,
  it is a Leaf. Node 2 is a parent of 4 and 5 (Inner); node 3 has a parent but no children (Leaf).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

SELECT id,
       CASE
         WHEN p_id IS NULL                  THEN 'Root'    -- no parent
         WHEN id IN (SELECT p_id FROM Tree) THEN 'Inner'   -- appears as someone's parent
         ELSE                                    'Leaf'
       END AS type
FROM Tree
ORDER BY id;

Medium Employees With Deductions

▼

Employees whose logged hours fall short of their monthly requirement.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Payroll deducts pay from employees whose total logged time is below their required hours.
  • Employees has each employee's needed hours; Logs has clock-in/out pairs.
  • Sum each employee's worked time, round UP to whole hours, and return the employee_id of those below their needed hours (an employee with no logs counts as 0), ordered by employee id.

Schema — Employees

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
needed_hoursINTEGER

Example input — Employees

employee_idneeded_hours
12
22
33

Schema — Logs

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
in_timeTIMESTAMP
out_timeTIMESTAMP

Example input — Logs

employee_idin_timeout_time
12024-01-01 09:00:002024-01-01 10:30:00
22024-01-01 09:00:002024-01-01 09:30:00

Expected output

employee_id
2
3

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LEFT JOIN so employees with no logs survive. Sum each employee's worked seconds, divide by 3600 for
  hours, and CEIL rounds up. COALESCE turns a no-logs NULL into 0. HAVING keeps those below their
  requirement: employee 1 worked 1.5h (rounds to 2, meets the 2-hour need); employee 2 worked 0.5h
  (rounds to 1, short of 2); employee 3 has no logs (0, short of 3).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT e.employee_id
FROM Employees e
LEFT JOIN Logs l ON l.employee_id = e.employee_id
GROUP BY e.employee_id, e.needed_hours
HAVING CEIL(COALESCE(SUM(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (l.out_time - l.in_time))) / 3600.0, 0)) < e.needed_hours
ORDER BY e.employee_id;

Easy Group Sold Products By The Date

▼

Per date, count distinct products and list them sorted, comma-separated.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A warehouse builds a daily manifest of products sold.
  • The Activities table has one row per (date, product) sale, with possible duplicates.
  • For each sell_date, return num_sold (distinct products) and products (those names, sorted, comma-separated), ordered by date.

Schema — Activities

ColumnType
sell_dateDATE
productVARCHAR

Example input — Activities

sell_dateproduct
2020-05-30Headphone
2020-06-01Pencil
2020-06-02Mask
2020-05-30Basketball
2020-06-01Bible
2020-06-02Mask
2020-05-30T-Shirt

Expected output

sell_datenum_soldproducts
2020-05-303Basketball,Headphone,T-Shirt
2020-06-012Bible,Pencil
2020-06-021Mask

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Group per day. COUNT(DISTINCT product) is the distinct-product count, and STRING_AGG with DISTINCT
  plus an internal ORDER BY concatenates the unique names in sorted order. June 2 has Mask listed
  twice, so DISTINCT collapses it to one.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT sell_date,
       COUNT(DISTINCT product) AS num_sold,
       STRING_AGG(DISTINCT product, ',' ORDER BY product) AS products   -- unique names, sorted
FROM Activities
GROUP BY sell_date
ORDER BY sell_date;

Easy Swap Sex of Employees

▼

Swap 'm' and 'f' in the sex column with a single UPDATE.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A migration script flips the binary sex code in place: every 'm' becomes 'f' and every 'f' becomes 'm'.
  • The Salary table has a sex column holding 'm' or 'f'.
  • Write one UPDATE (no SELECT, no temp column) that swaps the values. The expected output shows the table after the update.

Schema — Salary

ColumnType
idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
sexCHAR(1)
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Salary

idnamesexsalary
1Am2500
2Bf1500
3Cm5500
4Df500

Expected output (table after the UPDATE)

idnamesexsalary
1Af2500
2Bm1500
3Cf5500
4Dm500

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A single conditional UPDATE flips every value: CASE returns 'f' when the value is 'm' and 'm'
  otherwise, so the whole column swaps in one pass -- no temp column or two-step swap needed.

  Verified against the example data -- the table after the update matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

UPDATE Salary
SET sex = CASE sex WHEN 'm' THEN 'f' ELSE 'm' END;

Easy Convert Date Format

▼

Format each date as a long weekday-month-day-year string.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A report exports human-readable dates like 'Wednesday, October 25, 2017'.
  • The Days table has one DATE column.
  • Return day formatted as the full weekday name, full month name, day of month, and four-digit year.

Schema — Days

ColumnType
dayDATE

Example input — Days

day
2017-10-25
2019-05-16

Expected output

day
Wednesday, October 25, 2017
Thursday, May 16, 2019

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  TO_CHAR with the right format mask builds the string in one step: Day = full weekday name, Month =
  full month name, DD = day of month, YYYY = year. The FM prefix strips the padding TO_CHAR would
  otherwise add to the weekday and month names. (In a strftime engine such as DuckDB this is
  strftime(day, '%A, %B %d, %Y').)

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT TO_CHAR(day, 'FMDay, FMMonth DD, YYYY') AS day
FROM Days;

Easy Fix Names in a Table

▼

Standardize each name to a capital first letter and lowercase rest.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A CRM cleanup standardizes inconsistently cased names.
  • The Users table has each user's id and name.
  • Return user_id and name with the first letter uppercased and the remaining letters lowercased, ordered by user id.

Schema — Users

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR

Example input — Users

user_idname
1aLice
2bOB

Expected output

user_idname
1Alice
2Bob

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Take the first character uppercased and glue it to the rest of the name lowercased. LEFT(name, 1)
  is the first letter; SUBSTRING(name, 2) is everything after it. CONCAT joins them, so 'aLice'
  becomes 'Alice'.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT user_id,
       CONCAT(UPPER(LEFT(name, 1)), LOWER(SUBSTRING(name, 2))) AS name   -- Cap first, lower the rest
FROM Users
ORDER BY user_id;
