Date Operations 5 patterns

▼

Single-table date and timestamp math: bucket rows into periods, pull out date parts, add or subtract days, and measure durations — no joins, no reshape.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

DATE_TRUNC cohort buckets (month / week / quarter) 1 problem

▼

Collapse each date to the start of its period with DATE_TRUNC('month', d)::date, then GROUP BY that bucket. Optionally a HAVING on the per-bucket aggregate.

Template DATE_TRUNC cohort bucket

▼

The generic shape with placeholder names — swap in your tables and columns.

SELECT user_id,
       DATE_TRUNC('month', d)::date AS bucket,
       COUNT(DISTINCT d) AS n_days
FROM tbl
GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', d)
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT d) >= 5;   -- optional per-bucket gate

Medium Monthly Writing Streak Days by User

▼

Bucket sessions into months with DATE_TRUNC, count distinct active days, keep months with 5+.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A note-taking app logs one row per user per day they wrote. Group sessions into monthly cohorts and count the distinct days each user wrote that month.
  • Only keep month-user combinations with at least 5 distinct days.
  • Return user_id, writing_month (first day of the month as a DATE), days_written, ordered by user_id then writing_month.

Schema — users

ColumnType
user_idINT
usernameVARCHAR
signup_dateDATE

Schema — writing_sessions

ColumnType
session_idINT
user_idINT
session_dateDATE
notes_writtenINT

Example input — users

user_idusernamesignup_date
1alice2024-01-05
2bob2024-01-10
3charlie2024-02-01

Example input — writing_sessions

session_iduser_idsession_datenotes_written
10112024-01-103
10212024-01-122
10312024-01-151
10412024-01-204
10512024-01-252
10612024-02-031
10722024-01-115
10822024-01-123
10922024-01-182
11032024-02-051

Expected output

user_idwriting_monthdays_written
12024-01-015

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
DATE_TRUNC('month', session_date) collapses every date to the first of its month, so GROUP BY that bucket forms monthly cohorts. COUNT(DISTINCT session_date) counts active days (not sessions). The HAVING runs after grouping to keep only buckets with 5+ days -- only alice's January (5 days) qualifies; bob has 3, charlie has 1. Cast the bucket to ::date so it prints as a plain date.
*/

SELECT
    user_id,
    DATE_TRUNC('month', session_date)::date AS writing_month,   -- month bucket
    COUNT(DISTINCT session_date) AS days_written                -- active days, not sessions
FROM writing_sessions
GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', session_date)
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT session_date) >= 5                        -- keep 5+ day months
ORDER BY user_id, writing_month;

EXTRACT a date component (year, day-of-week, hour) 1 problem

▼

Pull one part out of a date with EXTRACT(DOW FROM d) / YEAR / HOUR and GROUP BY or filter on it.

Template EXTRACT a component

▼

The generic shape with placeholder names — swap in your tables and columns.

SELECT EXTRACT(DOW FROM d)::int AS dow, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM tbl
GROUP BY EXTRACT(DOW FROM d)
ORDER BY dow;

Reference EXTRACT field cheatsheet — tap a part to see its template

▼

Each row expands to a copy-ready snippet for that date part (year, month, week, day, weekday, hour, seconds/epoch).

EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)

▼

Calendar year, e.g. 2024

SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)::int AS yr, COUNT(*)
FROM tbl GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM d)

▼

Quarter 1-4

SELECT EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM d)::int AS q, COUNT(*)
FROM tbl GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

EXTRACT(MONTH FROM d)

▼

Month NUMBER 1-12 (for a month BUCKET use DATE_TRUNC)

SELECT EXTRACT(MONTH FROM d)::int AS mon, COUNT(*)
FROM tbl GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

EXTRACT(WEEK FROM d)

▼

ISO week of year 1-53

SELECT EXTRACT(WEEK FROM d)::int AS wk, COUNT(*)
FROM tbl GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

EXTRACT(DAY FROM d)

▼

Day of the MONTH 1-31

SELECT EXTRACT(DAY FROM d)::int AS dom, COUNT(*)
FROM tbl GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

EXTRACT(DOW FROM d)

▼

Day of WEEK 0=Sun .. 6=Sat

SELECT EXTRACT(DOW FROM d)::int AS dow, COUNT(*)
FROM tbl GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

EXTRACT(DOY FROM d)

▼

Day of YEAR 1-366

SELECT EXTRACT(DOY FROM d)::int AS doy, COUNT(*)
FROM tbl GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

EXTRACT(HOUR FROM ts)

▼

Hour of day 0-23 (needs a TIMESTAMP)

SELECT EXTRACT(HOUR FROM ts)::int AS hr, COUNT(*)
FROM tbl GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

EXTRACT(MINUTE FROM ts)

▼

Minute 0-59

SELECT EXTRACT(MINUTE FROM ts)::int AS mn, COUNT(*)
FROM tbl GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

EXTRACT(SECOND FROM ts)

▼

Second 0-59

SELECT EXTRACT(SECOND FROM ts)::int AS sec
FROM tbl;

EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM ts)

▼

Seconds since 1970 — subtract two to get a DURATION

-- raw epoch seconds of one timestamp:
SELECT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM ts) AS epoch_secs FROM tbl;
-- duration between two (see the Duration leaf):
SELECT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (b_ts - a_ts)) / 3600 AS hours FROM tbl;

Easy Orders by Day of Week

▼

Pull the weekday out of each date with EXTRACT(DOW ...) and group on it.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Count how many orders fall on each day of week (0 = Sunday … 6 = Saturday).
  • Return dow and orders, ordered by dow. Only days that occur appear.

Schema — orders

ColumnType
order_idINT
order_dateDATE

Example input — orders

order_idorder_date
12024-01-07
22024-01-08
32024-01-15
42024-01-13

Expected output

doworders
01
12
61

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
EXTRACT(DOW FROM order_date) returns the weekday as a number (0 = Sunday). Grouping on that same expression buckets the orders by weekday. Jan 7 is a Sunday (0), Jan 8 and Jan 15 are Mondays (1), Jan 13 is a Saturday (6). Cast to ::int for a clean integer column.
*/

SELECT
    EXTRACT(DOW FROM order_date)::int AS dow,   -- 0 = Sunday .. 6 = Saturday
    COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY EXTRACT(DOW FROM order_date)
ORDER BY dow;

Date arithmetic (DATE +/- days / INTERVAL, cutoffs) 1 problem

▼

Move a date by whole days (d + n) or an INTERVAL, or filter against a LITERAL / data-derived cutoff. Never CURRENT_DATE.

Template Date arithmetic

▼

The generic shape with placeholder names — swap in your tables and columns.

SELECT id, start_date + term_days AS end_date   -- DATE + INT moves N days
FROM tbl
WHERE start_date + term_days <= DATE '2024-02-01';  -- literal cutoff

Template “Before / within N days” cutoff (WHERE or ON)

▼

The pattern for “event older than N days” without CURRENT_DATE — anchor to a literal or the data’s MAX date, then subtract.

-- "happened more than N days before" WITHOUT CURRENT_DATE.
-- Anchor to the latest date in the data (or a literal), then subtract N.
WITH ref AS (SELECT MAX(event_date) AS anchor FROM events)
SELECT e.*
FROM events e CROSS JOIN ref
WHERE e.event_date <  ref.anchor - 90      -- older than 90 days
  -- e.event_date >= ref.anchor - 90       -- within the LAST 90 days
  -- e.event_date <  DATE '2024-01-01'     -- or a fixed literal cutoff
;
-- Same test inside a JOIN ON when the date lives on the JOINED table:
--   LEFT JOIN events e ON e.user_id = u.id AND e.event_date >= ref.anchor - 90

Medium Subscriptions Ending by a Cutoff

▼

Add a day count to a date (start_date + term_days), then filter against a literal cutoff.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Each subscription runs term_days from its start_date. Its end date is start_date + term_days.
  • Return sub_id and end_date for subscriptions ending on or before 2024-02-01, ordered by sub_id.

Schema — subscriptions

ColumnType
sub_idINT
start_dateDATE
term_daysINT

Example input — subscriptions

sub_idstart_dateterm_days
12024-01-0130
22024-02-157
32024-01-105

Expected output

sub_idend_date
12024-01-31
32024-01-15

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
Adding an integer to a DATE moves it forward that many days, so start_date + term_days is the end date -- no INTERVAL needed for whole days. The same expression in WHERE keeps only subscriptions ending by the LITERAL cutoff (never CURRENT_DATE, so the result is reproducible). Sub 2 ends Feb 22 and is dropped.
*/

SELECT
    sub_id,
    start_date + term_days AS end_date          -- DATE + INT moves forward N days
FROM subscriptions
WHERE start_date + term_days <= DATE '2024-02-01'   -- literal cutoff, not CURRENT_DATE
ORDER BY sub_id;

Duration between two timestamps (EXTRACT EPOCH) 1 problem

▼

Subtract two timestamps and convert the interval with EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (b - a)) / 3600 for hours (/ 86400 for days).

Template Duration via EXTRACT EPOCH

▼

The generic shape with placeholder names — swap in your tables and columns.

SELECT id,
  EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_ts - start_ts)) / 3600 AS hours   -- /86400 for days
FROM tbl;

Reference EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (b - a)) / N — tap a unit to see the divisor

▼

Subtract two timestamps, take the epoch (seconds), then divide by the unit you want. Each row expands to a copy-ready snippet.

Seconds

▼

Raw elapsed seconds — no divisor

SELECT id,
  EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_ts - start_ts)) AS seconds
FROM tbl;

/ 60 → minutes

▼

Seconds to minutes

SELECT id,
  EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_ts - start_ts)) / 60 AS minutes
FROM tbl;

/ 3600 → hours

▼

Seconds to hours (the common one)

SELECT id,
  EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_ts - start_ts)) / 3600 AS hours
FROM tbl;

/ 86400 → days

▼

Seconds to days

SELECT id,
  EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_ts - start_ts)) / 86400 AS days
FROM tbl;

/ 604800 → weeks

▼

Seconds to weeks

SELECT id,
  EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_ts - start_ts)) / 604800 AS weeks
FROM tbl;

ROUND(... , 1)

▼

Tidy the result to one decimal

SELECT id,
  ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_ts - start_ts)) / 3600, 1) AS hours
FROM tbl;

AVG(...) per group

▼

Average the per-row durations

SELECT grp,
  AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_ts - start_ts)) / 3600) AS avg_hours
FROM tbl
GROUP BY grp;

Keep it as an INTERVAL (no EPOCH)

▼

Subtraction alone is an INTERVAL; AGE() too

SELECT id,
  end_ts - start_ts      AS span,      -- INTERVAL
  AGE(end_ts, start_ts)  AS age_span
FROM tbl;

Medium Ticket Resolution Time in Hours

▼

Subtract two timestamps and convert the interval to hours with EXTRACT(EPOCH ...).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • For each ticket, compute how long it took to resolve, in hours.
  • Return ticket_id and hours, ordered by ticket_id.

Schema — tickets

ColumnType
ticket_idINT
opened_atTIMESTAMP
resolved_atTIMESTAMP

Example input — tickets

ticket_idopened_atresolved_at
12024-01-01 09:00:002024-01-01 12:00:00
22024-01-02 08:00:002024-01-03 08:00:00

Expected output

ticket_idhours
13.0
224.0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
Subtracting two timestamps yields an INTERVAL, which is awkward to compare. EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (resolved_at - opened_at)) turns it into total seconds; dividing by 3600 gives hours (use 86400 for days). Ticket 1 took 3 hours, ticket 2 a full 24.
*/

SELECT
    ticket_id,
    EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (resolved_at - opened_at)) / 3600 AS hours   -- seconds -> hours
FROM tickets
ORDER BY ticket_id;

Inclusive vs exclusive day counts 1 problem

▼

The off-by-one: end - start counts the nights between; an inclusive span is (end - start) + 1 days.

Template Inclusive day count

▼

The generic shape with placeholder names — swap in your tables and columns.

SELECT id, (end_date - start_date) + 1 AS days_inclusive   -- +1 = inclusive
FROM tbl;

Easy Inclusive Trial Length in Days

▼

The off-by-one: an inclusive span is (end - start) + 1 days.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Each trial runs from start_date to end_date inclusive (both days count).
  • Return trial_id and days_inclusive, ordered by trial_id.

Schema — trials

ColumnType
trial_idINT
start_dateDATE
end_dateDATE

Example input — trials

trial_idstart_dateend_date
12024-01-012024-01-10
22024-03-012024-03-01

Expected output

trial_iddays_inclusive
110
21

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
Subtracting two dates gives the number of nights BETWEEN them: Jan 10 - Jan 1 = 9. But a trial that runs Jan 1 through Jan 10 inclusive lasts 10 days, so add 1. A single-day trial (start = end) is 0 + 1 = 1. The + 1 is the whole point of this shape.
*/

SELECT
    trial_id,
    (end_date - start_date) + 1 AS days_inclusive   -- +1 makes the span inclusive
FROM trials
ORDER BY trial_id;

Compare 18 problems

▼

A single table with an ordering column → rows satisfying a comparison to the prior or next row in that order.

Signal words: "compared to previous," "rising," "consecutive," "increasing," "day over day," "streak," "gap"

Technique: LAG(), LEAD(), self-join on id+1 / date+1, date arithmetic

Reference Techniques used in Row Compare

▼

The 2 core neighbour-comparison techniques for this recipe. The third pattern, gaps-and-islands, has its own dedicated section below with a decision tree and worked traces, so it is not repeated here.

Compare to the previous or next row 5 problems

▼

LAG / LEAD / self-join — each row looks at the row immediately before or after it in ORDER BY order. Open the decision tree first, then the matching worked problem below.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Compare a row to its neighbour's value 1 problem

▼

LAG / LEAD then compare — pull the previous or next row's value onto the current row, then test bigger / smaller / equal.

Template — LAG / LEAD, then compare

▼

Use when the prompt says: "rising", "higher than the day before", "increasing", "day over day"

Core snippet

SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT t.*,
    LAG(val) OVER (PARTITION BY k
                   ORDER BY t) AS prev
  FROM tbl
) s
WHERE val > prev;

Edge & NULL handling

First row's LAG is NULL, so the comparison is NULL and the row drops from the WHERE.

Key pitfall

Forgetting PARTITION BY, so one group's last row is compared against the next group's first row.

Trace example

LAG compare: daily temperatures 12, 15, 14 — keep days warmer than the day before

date temp prev = LAG(temp) temp > prev?
Jan 112NULL— (dropped)
Jan 21512yes ✓
Jan 31415no

Easy Rising Temperature

▼

Find days warmer than the day before. LAG the temperature by date, then compare; the first day has no previous so it drops.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Return the id of each day whose temperature was higher than the PREVIOUS day's.
  • "Previous" = the immediately preceding calendar day (recordDate - 1), not just the previous row.
  • Order by id.

Schema — weather

ColumnType
idINTEGER
recordDateDATE
temperatureINTEGER

Example input — weather

idrecordDatetemperature
12015-01-0110
22015-01-0225
32015-01-0320
42015-01-0430

Expected output

id
2
4

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LAG pulls the previous row's temperature (and date) onto the current row, ordered by date. Keep
  rows that are warmer than the previous reading AND exactly one calendar day later, so a missing
  day never counts as 'yesterday'. Day 1's LAG is NULL, so it drops from the WHERE.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT id
FROM (
    SELECT id, recordDate, temperature,
           LAG(temperature) OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_temp,
           LAG(recordDate)  OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_date
    FROM weather
) t
WHERE temperature > prev_temp              -- warmer than the previous reading
  AND recordDate = prev_date + 1           -- and it was literally yesterday
ORDER BY id;

Measure the gap or delta to the previous or next row 2 problems

▼

LAG / LEAD then subtract — once the neighbour's value sits on the row, do arithmetic on it: days between dates, change in amount. The first row of each group has no neighbour, so its result stays NULL.

Template — LAG / LEAD, then subtract

▼

Use when the prompt says: "days since last", "time between", "gap between visits", "change from prior"

Core snippet

t - LAG(t) OVER (
    PARTITION BY k
    ORDER BY t
) AS gap   -- first row = NULL

Edge & NULL handling

First row's gap is NULL — leave it NULL. Do not COALESCE to 0; that fakes a zero-day gap that did not happen.

Key pitfall

Ordering on the wrong column, or mixing a DATE with a TIMESTAMP so the subtraction unit is off.

Trace example

LAG delta: one patient's visits — days since the previous visit

visit_date prev = LAG(visit_date) gap = date − prev
2024-01-15NULLNULL (first visit)
2024-02-202024-01-1536
2024-05-102024-02-2080 (> 60 → flag)

Reference Elapsed time by unit — EXTRACT(EPOCH) denominators

▼

Subtracting two timestamps gives an interval. EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM …) turns it into seconds; divide by the constant below to get any other unit. Wrap in FLOOR, ROUND, or ::int as the prompt needs.

Let diff = end_ts - start_ts (an interval). Then:

Unit Divide seconds by Expression Notes
Seconds 1 EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM diff) The epoch value is already in seconds.
Minutes 60 EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM diff) / 60 60 seconds.
Hours 3600 EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM diff) / 3600 60 × 60.
Days 86400 EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM diff) / 86400 24 × 3600. Elapsed 24 hour days, not calendar days.
Weeks 604800 EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM diff) / 604800 7 × 86400.
Months (approx) 2629800 EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM diff) / 2629800 30.4375 days average. Approximate — months vary in length.
Years (approx) 31557600 EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM diff) / 31557600 365.25 days. Approximate — ignores leap year placement.

Use epoch math only for fixed-length units (seconds through weeks). Months and years are not constant, so dividing seconds is an approximation. For exact calendar differences, subtract the dates as dates for whole days, or use AGE(end_ts, start_ts) with EXTRACT(YEAR FROM …) / EXTRACT(MONTH FROM …) for true calendar years and months.

Medium Track Days Between Follow-Up Visits per Patient

▼

For each visit, the number of days since that patient's previous visit (NULL for the first).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Care teams want the gap in days between each patient's consecutive visits.
  • The patient_visits table has one row per visit with a date.
  • Return patient_id, visit_date, visit_type, and days_since_last_visit (NULL for a patient's first visit), ordered by patient then date.
  • Do not COALESCE the first-visit NULL to 0 -- a 0 would read as a same-day repeat that never happened.

Schema — patient_visits

ColumnType
visit_idINTEGER
patient_idINTEGER
visit_dateDATE
visit_typeVARCHAR
diagnosis_codeVARCHAR

Example input — patient_visits

visit_idpatient_idvisit_datevisit_typediagnosis_code
112024-01-01NewD1
212024-01-10FollowUpD1
322024-02-01NewD2

Expected output

patient_idvisit_datevisit_typedays_since_last_visit
12024-01-01NewNULL
12024-01-10FollowUp9
22024-02-01NewNULL

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LAG, partitioned by patient and ordered by date, puts the previous visit_date on each row;
  subtracting gives the day gap. PARTITION BY patient_id keeps one patient's last visit from being
  compared to the next patient's first. Each patient's first visit has no prior row, so LAG is NULL
  and the gap stays NULL.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT patient_id, visit_date, visit_type,
       visit_date - LAG(visit_date) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS days_since_last_visit  -- gap to prior visit
FROM patient_visits
ORDER BY patient_id, visit_date;

▼

Days since the previous COMPLETED visit, from a timestamp (full 24-hour days, not calendar days).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A telehealth platform measures the gap between a patient's consecutive completed visits.
  • The telehealth_visits table has a completion timestamp and a status; cancelled visits must not count as the 'previous' visit.
  • For each completed visit, return patient_id, visit_id, visit_completed_at, and days_since_previous_visit (NULL for the first), ordered by patient then completion time.
  • The column is a timestamp, so count full elapsed 24-hour days, not calendar dates.

Schema — telehealth_visits

ColumnType
visit_idINTEGER
patient_idINTEGER
provider_idINTEGER
visit_scheduled_atTIMESTAMP
visit_completed_atTIMESTAMP
statusVARCHAR

Example input — telehealth_visits

visit_idpatient_idprovider_idvisit_scheduled_atvisit_completed_atstatus
104292024-01-08 11:00:002024-01-08 11:20:00completed
105292024-01-15 10:00:00NULLcancelled
107292024-01-22 09:00:002024-01-22 09:30:00completed

Expected output

patient_idvisit_idvisit_completed_atdays_since_previous_visit
21042024-01-08 11:20:00NULL
21072024-01-22 09:30:0013

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  WHERE status = 'completed' runs BEFORE the window functions, so LAG only sees completed visits and
  the cancelled Jan 15 visit is skipped -- visit 107's previous is visit 104. Subtracting two
  timestamps gives an interval; EXTRACT(EPOCH ...) turns it into seconds, / 86400 into fractional
  days, and FLOOR into whole 24-hour days. Jan 8 11:20 to Jan 22 09:30 is 13 full days elapsed (the
  second visit is earlier in the day), where a date-cast subtraction would wrongly count 14.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT patient_id, visit_id, visit_completed_at,
       FLOOR(
           EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (
               visit_completed_at
               - LAG(visit_completed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_completed_at)
           )) / 86400
       )::int AS days_since_previous_visit       -- full elapsed days
FROM telehealth_visits
WHERE status = 'completed'                       -- "previous" means previous COMPLETED visit
ORDER BY patient_id, visit_completed_at;
/*
  WHERE status = 'completed' runs BEFORE the window functions, so LAG only sees completed visits and
  the cancelled Jan 15 visit is skipped -- visit 107's previous is visit 104. Subtracting two
  timestamps gives an interval; EXTRACT(EPOCH ...) turns it into seconds, / 86400 into fractional
  days, and FLOOR into whole 24-hour days. Jan 8 11:20 to Jan 22 09:30 is 13 full days elapsed (the
  second visit is earlier in the day), where a date-cast subtraction would wrongly count 14.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT patient_id, visit_id, visit_completed_at,
       FLOOR(
           EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (
               visit_completed_at
               - LAG(visit_completed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_completed_at)
           )) / 86400
       )::int AS days_since_previous_visit       -- full elapsed days
FROM telehealth_visits
WHERE status = 'completed'                       -- "previous" means previous COMPLETED visit
ORDER BY patient_id, visit_completed_at;
/*
  Put both neighbours on each row: LAG is the row before, LEAD the row after. A value sits in a run
  of three when it equals BOTH its neighbours. DISTINCT collapses a longer run to one value. Checking
  both sides (not just one) is what makes it a run of three, not a pair.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM (
    SELECT num,
           LAG(num)  OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_num,   -- row before
           LEAD(num) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_num    -- row after
    FROM Logs
) t
WHERE num = prev_num AND num = next_num;

Gaps-and-Islands: Pick the Right Form by Data Shape 18 problems

▼

Find unbroken runs (islands) in ordered data. The formula and GROUP BY change with the data shape; open the decision tree first, then the tables, then the matching set of worked problems below.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Consecutive integer ids 6 problems

▼

id − ROW_NUMBER — The thing you are chaining is an integer id (seat numbers, customer ids). Subtract a row number from the id itself: consecutive ids land on the same anchor, a gap shifts it.

Consecutive integer ids (id − rn) ↑ tree

▼

Use when: the run column is a counting id (seat numbers, log ids, message ids).

What this template does, step by step:

  1. CTE: subtract a row number from the id. Order the row number by the same id you subtract — consecutive ids share one grp anchor, a gap bumps it.
  2. Only if a status label splits the runs, add PARTITION BY status inside the window and GROUP BY that label too. No status → leave it out.
  3. Output A — collapse to ranges: MIN(id) as start, MAX(id) as end, GROUP BY grp. A lone id falls out as start = end on its own.
  4. Output B — keep only streaks of N+: filter to grp values whose count is ≥ N.
WITH base AS (
  SELECT id,
         id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp  -- add PARTITION BY status only if it splits runs
  FROM tbl
)
SELECT MIN(id) AS start_id, MAX(id) AS end_id          -- output A: collapse to ranges
FROM base
GROUP BY grp
ORDER BY start_id;
-- output B (streaks of N+): WHERE grp IN (SELECT grp FROM base GROUP BY grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= N)

GROUP BY in the final SELECT

status, grp (drop status if there is no status column)

Key pitfall

Reaching for the rn − rn formula instead of id − rn; both work but id − rn is one less window function.

Trace example

Integer ids: seats 101, 102, 103, 105 all active

seat_id rn (per status) grp = id − rn Island
1011100A
1022100A
1033100A
1054101B (gap at 104)

Easy Consecutive Available Seats

▼

Free seats that have a free neighbour.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A ticketing UI offers seats that sit next to another free seat.
  • The Cinema table has one row per seat with free = 1 (free) or 0 (taken).
  • Return the seat_id of every free seat whose neighbour (seat_id +/- 1) is also free, ordered by seat id.

Schema — Cinema

ColumnType
seat_idINTEGER
freeINTEGER

Example input — Cinema

seat_idfree
11
20
31
41
51

Expected output

seat_id
3
4
5

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A self-join on adjacency: two seats are neighbours when their ids differ by exactly 1. Keeping pairs
  where both are free and DISTINCT-ing the left seat gives the free seats with a free neighbour. Seat 1
  is free but its only neighbour (seat 2) is taken, so it drops.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT DISTINCT c1.seat_id
FROM Cinema c1
JOIN Cinema c2
  ON ABS(c1.seat_id - c2.seat_id) = 1     -- adjacent seats
 AND c1.free = 1
 AND c2.free = 1
ORDER BY c1.seat_id;

Medium Find the Start and End Number of Continuous Ranges

▼

Collapse a sorted id list into [start, end] ranges of consecutive integers.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An export compresses a discrete id log into tidy consecutive ranges.
  • The Logs table has one column of ids with gaps.
  • Return start_id and end_id for each run of consecutive integers, ordered by start_id.

Schema — Logs

ColumnType
log_idINTEGER

Example input — Logs

log_id
1
2
3
7
8
10

Expected output

start_idend_id
13
78
1010

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The integer gaps-and-islands trick: subtract a row number from the id. Across a consecutive run both
  climb by 1, so id - rn stays constant; a gap bumps it, starting a new group. MIN and MAX per group
  are the range ends. 1,2,3 share an anchor; the gap to 7 starts a new one; 10 stands alone.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH grouped AS (
    SELECT log_id, log_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY log_id) AS grp   -- constant within a run
    FROM Logs
)
SELECT MIN(log_id) AS start_id, MAX(log_id) AS end_id
FROM grouped
GROUP BY grp
ORDER BY start_id;

Medium Find the Missing IDs

▼

Return ids from 1 to the max that are absent from the table.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A data-quality audit surfaces holes in a sequence of customer ids.
  • The Customers table has customer ids with possible gaps.
  • Return every ids from 1 through the maximum customer id that does not appear in the table, ordered by id.

Schema — Customers

ColumnType
customer_idINTEGER
customer_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Customers

customer_idcustomer_name
1A
2B
5C

Expected output

ids
3
4

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Manufacture the complete expected range 1..MAX with a recursive CTE, then anti-join: a LEFT JOIN to
  Customers plus IS NULL returns the ids that have no matching customer. Here 3 and 4 are the holes.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH RECURSIVE seq AS (
    SELECT 1 AS id
    UNION ALL
    SELECT id + 1 FROM seq WHERE id < (SELECT MAX(customer_id) FROM Customers)   -- build 1..MAX
)
SELECT s.id AS ids
FROM seq s
LEFT JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = s.id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;

Hard Human Traffic of Stadium

▼

High-attendance days that fall in a run of three or more consecutive qualifying days.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A facilities team flags streaks of busy days.
  • The Stadium table has a sequential id, a date, and a visitor count.
  • Keep only days with 100+ people, then return id, visit_date, people for days that belong to a run of three or more consecutive (by id) qualifying days, ordered by date.

Schema — Stadium

ColumnType
idINTEGER
visit_dateDATE
peopleINTEGER

Example input — Stadium

idvisit_datepeople
12017-01-0110
22017-01-02109
32017-01-03150
42017-01-0499
52017-01-05145
62017-01-061455
72017-01-07199
82017-01-08188

Expected output

idvisit_datepeople
52017-01-05145
62017-01-061455
72017-01-07199
82017-01-08188

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Filter to busy days first, then apply the integer gaps-and-islands trick on the surviving ids: within
  the filtered set, consecutive ids share id - ROW_NUMBER. Groups with 3+ rows are the qualifying
  streaks. Ids 2,3 form a run of 2 (dropped); ids 5,6,7,8 form a run of 4 (kept).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH hi AS (
    SELECT id, visit_date, people,
           id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp   -- anchor over the filtered busy days
    FROM Stadium
    WHERE people >= 100
)
SELECT id, visit_date, people
FROM hi
WHERE grp IN (SELECT grp FROM hi GROUP BY grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3)   -- streaks of 3+
ORDER BY visit_date;

Prompt

  • A robo-advisor compresses each strategy's portfolio ids into tidy ranges.
  • The portfolios table has a portfolio id and a rebalance strategy.
  • Within each rebalance_strategy, collapse consecutive portfolio_id values into [start_id, end_id] ranges (a lone id gives start = end), ordered by start id.
  • PARTITION BY the strategy on the row number, and GROUP BY both strategy and the id - rn anchor (the anchor is not unique across strategies).

Schema — portfolios

ColumnType
portfolio_idINTEGER
rebalance_strategyVARCHAR
current_aumINTEGER

Example input — portfolios

portfolio_idrebalance_strategycurrent_aum
101conservative1000

conservative101103
conservative105105
aggressive107108

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Same id - rn collapse, but the row number restarts per strategy (PARTITION BY rebalance_strategy) so
  one strategy's run never bleeds into another's. The GROUP BY must include the strategy as well as the
  anchor, because conservative and aggressive can produce the same anchor value. Conservative's 101-103
  collapse; the 103->105 gap isolates 105; each other strategy forms its own range.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT *,
           portfolio_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY rebalance_strategy ORDER BY portfolio_id) AS grp  -- per-strategy anchor
    FROM portfolios
)

       MIN(portfolio_id) AS start_id,
       MAX(portfolio_id) AS end_id
FROM base
GROUP BY rebalance_strategy, grp           -- strategy AND anchor; anchor alone is not unique
ORDER BY MIN(portfolio_id);

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*

  ordered by message_id (the column being subtracted). Ordering by sent_at would only happen to work
  when ids arrive in id order, and would shatter into singletons the moment a later id was sent earlier.

Consecutive calendar dates, no gaps in data 1 problem

▼

date − ROW_NUMBER — Every relevant day has a row (no missing days). Subtract the row number (in days) from the date: consecutive dates collapse to one anchor. Switch to the rn − rn form below if days can be missing.

Consecutive calendar dates, no gaps (date − rn) ↑ tree

▼

Use when: the run column is a date and every relevant day has a row.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. If the source can hold more than one row per day, dedupe to one row per (entity, day) FIRST — each extra row bumps the row number and inflates the streak.
  2. CTE: date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY date))::INT AS grp. Consecutive dates land on one anchor.
  3. GROUP BY grp (plus status if present); MIN / MAX for the span, COUNT for streak length.
WITH base AS (
  SELECT day,
         day - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY day))::INT AS grp
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT entity, day FROM tbl) d   -- dedupe to one row per day first
)
SELECT MIN(day) AS start_day, MAX(day) AS end_day, COUNT(*) AS streak_len
FROM base
GROUP BY grp
ORDER BY start_day;

GROUP BY in the final SELECT

status, grp

Key pitfall

Breaks on a missing day (e.g. Feb 29 absent). Switch to the rn − rn form if the data could have gaps.

Trace example

Hard Monthly Writing Streak Analysis by Cohort

▼

Per user: signup-month cohort, distinct active months, and longest consecutive-day writing streak.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A growth team segments users by signup cohort and measures monthly reach plus their longest daily writing streak.
  • users has signup dates; notebooks link to users; notes have a written date. A user can write in two notebooks on the same day -- that is still one streak day.
  • For users who signed up on or after 2024-01-01, return user_id, signup_cohort (YYYY-MM), active_months (distinct months with a note), and longest_streak_days, ordered by user id.
  • Dedupe to one row per (user, day) BEFORE the gaps-and-islands trick, or same-day multi-notebook writes inflate the streak.

Schema — users

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
usernameVARCHAR
signup_dateDATE

Example input — users

user_idusernamesignup_date
1alice2024-01-15
2bob2024-02-10
3cara2023-12-01

Schema — notebooks

ColumnType
notebook_idINTEGER
user_idINTEGER

Example input — notebooks

notebook_iduser_id
101
111
202

Schema — notes

ColumnType
note_idINTEGER
notebook_idINTEGER
written_dateDATE

Example input — notes

note_idnotebook_idwritten_date
1102024-04-10
2112024-04-10
3102024-04-11
4102024-04-12
5102024-06-01
6202024-05-01
7202024-05-02

Expected output

user_idsignup_cohortactive_monthslongest_streak_days
12024-0123
22024-0212

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The dedupe step leads: user_days collapses to one row per (user, written_date) so a day written in
  two notebooks counts once. streaks then applies date - rn per user (cast rn to INT; Postgres DATE
  minus BIGINT errors); consecutive days share grp. per_day uses COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user, grp)
  so every row carries its OWN streak length without collapsing. The final pass per user computes both
  metrics. Alice's Apr 10-12 (the duplicate Apr 10 collapsed) is a 3-day streak across two months.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH user_days AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT
        u.user_id,
        TO_CHAR(u.signup_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS signup_cohort,
        n.written_date
    FROM users u
    JOIN notebooks nb ON nb.user_id = u.user_id
    JOIN notes     n  ON n.notebook_id = nb.notebook_id
    WHERE u.signup_date >= DATE '2024-01-01'
),
streaks AS (
    SELECT user_id, signup_cohort, written_date,
           written_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY written_date))::INT AS grp  -- date - rn anchor
    FROM user_days
),
per_day AS (
    SELECT user_id, signup_cohort, written_date,
           COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, grp) AS streak_len   -- each row carries its run length
    FROM streaks
)
SELECT user_id, signup_cohort,
       COUNT(DISTINCT TO_CHAR(written_date, 'YYYY-MM')) AS active_months,
       MAX(streak_len)                                  AS longest_streak_days
FROM per_day
GROUP BY user_id, signup_cohort
ORDER BY user_id;

Consecutive dates with gaps / merged states 2 problems

▼

rn_overall − rn_per_status — One timeline where days can be missing, often built by UNION of two source tables and labelled with a state. Two row numbers, one overall and one per state; their difference is constant across a run.

Consecutive dates with gaps (rn − rn) ↑ tree

▼

Use when: inactive days have no row, or two tables are UNION'd — "consecutive in the data," not "every calendar day."

What this template does, step by step:

  1. One row number overall ordered by date; one row number per status ordered by date.
  2. grp = overall row number − per-status row number. Both windows must ORDER BY date or the math is undefined.
  3. GROUP BY status, grp. This form ignores missing days, so it does not need every calendar day present.
WITH base AS (
  SELECT status, day,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY day)
       - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY status ORDER BY day) AS grp
  FROM tbl
)
SELECT status, MIN(day) AS start_day, MAX(day) AS end_day
FROM base
GROUP BY status, grp
ORDER BY start_day;

GROUP BY in the final SELECT

status, grp

Key pitfall

Both windows must ORDER BY date or the math is undefined.

Dates, possible missing days: Feb 28 active, Feb 29 missing from data, Mar 1 active, Mar 2 active

Hard Report Contiguous Dates

▼

Summarize consecutive-day ranges of the same state (failed/succeeded) from two tables.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An uptime ledger shows contiguous spans of failed vs succeeded days.
  • Failed has fail dates; Succeeded has success dates (each date in one table).
  • Combine both into one labelled timeline and collapse consecutive same-state days into [start_date, end_date] ranges, ordered by start date.
  • Use the rn_overall - rn_per_state form so the difference of two row numbers groups same-state contiguous rows.

Schema — Failed

ColumnType
fail_dateDATE

Example input — Failed

fail_date
2019-01-01
2019-01-02
2019-01-04
2019-01-05
2019-01-06

Schema — Succeeded

ColumnType
success_dateDATE

Example input — Succeeded

success_date
2019-01-03

Expected output

period_statestart_dateend_date
failed2019-01-012019-01-02
succeeded2019-01-032019-01-03
failed2019-01-042019-01-06

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  UNION the two tables into one timeline with a state label. The difference of two row numbers -- one
  over the whole timeline, one per state -- stays constant across rows that are both the same state and
  consecutive in the ordering; it shifts when either changes. Grouping by (state, grp) and taking MIN
  and MAX gives each contiguous span.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH all_days AS (
    SELECT fail_date AS d, 'failed'    AS state FROM Failed    WHERE fail_date    BETWEEN DATE '2019-01-01' AND DATE '2019-12-31'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT success_date,   'succeeded'          FROM Succeeded WHERE success_date BETWEEN DATE '2019-01-01' AND DATE '2019-12-31'
),
numbered AS (
    SELECT d, state,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY d)
         - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY d) AS grp   -- constant across a same-state run
    FROM all_days
)
SELECT state AS period_state, MIN(d) AS start_date, MAX(d) AS end_date
FROM numbered
GROUP BY state, grp
ORDER BY start_date;

Hard Member Workout vs Skip Streaks (UNION + Gaps-and-Islands variant)

▼

Collapse consecutive active (workout) and inactive (skip) days into ranges, handling missing days.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A fitness app reports each member's continuous workout and skip streaks.
  • completed_workouts has workout dates; skipped_days has skip dates.
  • Combine both into one labelled timeline and collapse consecutive same-state days into [period_start, period_end] ranges, ordered by period start.
  • Use the rn_overall - rn_per_state form so a calendar day missing from both tables does not break a run.

Schema — completed_workouts

ColumnType
workout_dateDATE

Example input — completed_workouts

workout_date
2024-01-01
2024-01-02
2024-01-05

Schema — skipped_days

ColumnType
skip_dateDATE

Example input — skipped_days

skip_date
2024-01-03
2024-01-04

Expected output

activity_stateperiod_startperiod_end
active2024-01-012024-01-02
inactive2024-01-032024-01-04
active2024-01-052024-01-05

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Same UNION + two-row-number form as Report Contiguous Dates, in a workout/skip domain. The
  rn_overall - rn_per_state difference groups by data-sequence consecutiveness, so it tolerates a
  calendar day missing from both tables (the more permissive form than date - rn). Active Jan 1-2 form
  one run; the two skip days another; the lone active Jan 5 its own.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT 'active' AS activity_state, workout_date AS activity_date
    FROM completed_workouts
    WHERE workout_date BETWEEN DATE '2024-01-01' AND DATE '2024-03-31'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'inactive', skip_date
    FROM skipped_days
    WHERE skip_date BETWEEN DATE '2024-01-01' AND DATE '2024-03-31'
),
grouping AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY activity_date::date)
         - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY activity_state ORDER BY activity_date::date) AS grp
    FROM base
)
SELECT activity_state, MIN(activity_date) AS period_start, MAX(activity_date) AS period_end
FROM grouping
GROUP BY activity_state, grp
ORDER BY period_start;

Per-entity island timelines 3 problems

▼

PARTITION BY entity — One independent timeline per entity (user, order, customer). Every window must PARTITION BY the entity so one entity's rows never split another's runs. Islands form via grp or the LAG → flag → cumulative SUM recipe.

Per-entity island timelines (rn − rn, partitioned) ↑ tree

▼

Use when: each entity (order_id, user_id, ticket_id) has its own timeline.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Both row numbers PARTITION BY the entity; the second one also partitions by status.
  2. grp = per-entity row number − per-entity-and-status row number.
  3. GROUP BY entity, status, grp. Never substitute the status column for the entity — that collapses every same-status row into one giant island.
WITH base AS (
  SELECT entity_id, status, day,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id ORDER BY day)
       - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id, status ORDER BY day) AS grp
  FROM tbl
)
SELECT entity_id, status, MIN(day) AS start_day, MAX(day) AS end_day
FROM base
GROUP BY entity_id, status, grp
ORDER BY entity_id, start_day;

GROUP BY in the final SELECT

entity, status, grp

Key pitfall

Both windows must PARTITION BY entity or other entities' rows split the runs. Never substitute the status column for the entity — that collapses every same-status row into one giant island.

Trace example

Per-entity timelines: order 101 has processing then shipped, order 103 has processing in between

order_id status date rn (per entity) rn (per entity, status) grp Island
101processing2024-01-01110A (101 processing)
101processing2024-01-02220A
101shipped2024-01-04312B (101 shipped)
103processing2024-01-05110C (103 processing, separate from order 101's runs)

Telling the entity apart from the state. These problems often have two label columns — an entity (like user_id) and a state (like 'streaming' / 'offline'). They look similar but do different jobs:

  • Entity = who the timeline belongs to. The thing you handle "separately for each." You would never merge two entities' rows into one run. Test: whatever fills the blank in "for each ___" is the entity. Here, user_id — user 101's days never join user 102's.
  • State = what the row is, the value that must stay the same across a run. A run breaks the moment the state changes, even if the dates are still back to back. Example: streaming Jan 2–Jan 3, then offline Jan 4 — Jan 3 and Jan 4 are consecutive days, but the run still ends at Jan 3 because the activity flipped.

That is why entity and state sit in different places in the query:

  • entity goes in every window's PARTITION BY — it keeps entities from bleeding into each other.
  • state goes only in the second window's partition (PARTITION BY entity, state) — that is what makes the run break when the activity changes.
  • the final GROUP BY is entity, state, grp, then MIN(date) / MAX(date) give the start and end of each run.

Mental model: entity = who, state = what, dates = the run. You collapse consecutive dates where both who and what stay the same.

Medium Active Users (dedupe same day + per entity streak + membership semantics)

▼

Users with a 5+ consecutive-day login streak, deduping same-day logins and using membership semantics.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A growth team finds users with a login streak of 5 or more consecutive days.
  • Accounts lists users; Logins logs logins and can have duplicate (user, day) rows.
  • Return id and name of users with at least one 5+ day streak, ordered by id.
  • Dedupe to one row per (user, day) FIRST, then detect streaks per user, then use a membership check (EXISTS/IN) so a user with several streaks appears once.

Schema — Accounts

ColumnType
idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR

Example input — Accounts

idname
1Winston
7Jonathan

Schema — Logins

ColumnType
idINTEGER
login_dateDATE

Example input — Logins

idlogin_date
72024-05-30
72024-05-31
72024-06-01
72024-06-02
72024-06-02
72024-06-03
72024-06-10
12024-05-01
12024-05-03

Expected output

idname
7Jonathan

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Three traps, handled in order. (1) base dedupes same-day duplicates with DISTINCT -- without it the
  duplicate day advances the row number without advancing the date and the date - rn anchor lands wrong.
  (2) date_groups applies date - rn per user (PARTITION BY id is mandatory). (3) streaks keeps groups of
  5+. The final SELECT uses EXISTS against Accounts, so a user with multiple streaks collapses to one row
  -- membership semantics, not a cosmetic DISTINCT. Jonathan's 5 consecutive days (after dedupe) qualify;
  Winston's 2 days do not.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT id, login_date FROM Logins                       -- 1. dedupe same-day first
),
date_groups AS (
    SELECT id,
           login_date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY login_date)::int AS grp   -- 2. per-user anchor
    FROM base
),
streaks AS (
    SELECT id FROM date_groups GROUP BY id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5   -- 3. one row per 5+ day streak
)
SELECT a.id, a.name
FROM Accounts AS a
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM streaks s WHERE s.id = a.id)               -- 4. membership: user appears in any streak
ORDER BY a.id;

Hard Collapse Order Status Periods (UNION + per-entity partition)

▼

One row per order per status period, partitioning the window functions by the entity.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An ops team builds an order timeline: one row per status period per order.
  • processing_orders has processing dates; shipped_orders has ship dates, both keyed by order_id.
  • Combine into one labelled timeline and collapse consecutive same-status days into [start_date, end_date] ranges PER order, ordered by start date then order id.
  • Both window functions must PARTITION BY order_id, and the GROUP BY uses order_id, status, and the anchor.

Schema — processing_orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
process_dateDATE

Example input — processing_orders

order_idprocess_date
1012024-01-01
1012024-01-02
1012024-01-03
1032024-01-05

Schema — shipped_orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
ship_dateDATE

Example input — shipped_orders

order_idship_date
1012024-01-04
1012024-01-05
1012024-01-06

Expected output

order_idstatusstart_dateend_date
101processing2024-01-012024-01-03
101shipped2024-01-042024-01-06
103processing2024-01-052024-01-05

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Each order has its own timeline, so BOTH row numbers PARTITION BY order_id (the inner one also adds
  status). The difference is constant across an order's consecutive same-status run. Without order_id on
  the outer window, another order's row sitting between two of order 101's shipped rows would inflate the
  global row number and split 101's shipped run. The GROUP BY needs all three keys because the anchor is
  only local to one (order, status) pair.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT 'processing' AS status, order_id, process_date AS status_date FROM processing_orders
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'shipped',    order_id, ship_date              FROM shipped_orders
),
date_grouping AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY status_date)
         - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, status ORDER BY status_date) AS grp   -- per-order, per-status
    FROM base
)
SELECT order_id, status, MIN(status_date) AS start_date, MAX(status_date) AS end_date
FROM date_grouping
GROUP BY order_id, status, grp
ORDER BY MIN(status_date), order_id;

Hard Consecutive Transactions with Increasing Amounts

▼

Per customer, runs of three or more consecutive-day transactions with strictly increasing amounts.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A fraud-watch team finds runs of climbing daily transactions.
  • The Transactions table has each transaction's customer, date, and amount.
  • For each customer, find runs where each day is exactly one day after the previous AND its amount is strictly higher; return runs of length 3 or more as customer_id, consecutive_start, consecutive_end, ordered by customer.
  • Flag a row as a new island when the gap is not 1 day or the amount did not increase, then cumulative-sum the flags into a group id.

Schema — Transactions

ColumnType
transaction_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
transaction_dateDATE
amountINTEGER

Example input — Transactions

transaction_idcustomer_idtransaction_dateamount
112024-01-0110
212024-01-0220
312024-01-0330
412024-01-055
522024-01-01100
622024-01-0250

Expected output

customer_idconsecutive_startconsecutive_end
12024-01-012024-01-03

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Bring the previous day and amount onto each row with LAG. A row STARTS a new island when the gap is not
  exactly one day OR the amount did not strictly increase (flag 1, else 0). A cumulative SUM of that flag
  is the group id: rows that continue a run share it. Group, take MIN/MAX dates, and keep runs of 3+.
  Customer 1's Jan 1-3 climb qualifies; the Jan 5 gap-and-drop breaks it; customer 2 never increases.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH t AS (
    SELECT customer_id, transaction_date, amount,
           LAG(transaction_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS prev_date,
           LAG(amount)           OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS prev_amt
    FROM Transactions
),
flags AS (
    SELECT customer_id, transaction_date, amount,
           CASE WHEN transaction_date - prev_date = 1 AND amount > prev_amt THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS new_island  -- 1 = run breaks
    FROM t
),
grouped AS (
    SELECT customer_id, transaction_date,
           SUM(new_island) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS grp   -- running sum = group id
    FROM flags
)
SELECT customer_id, MIN(transaction_date) AS consecutive_start, MAX(transaction_date) AS consecutive_end
FROM grouped
GROUP BY customer_id, grp
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY customer_id;

Adjacency & gap checks (not full island collapsing) 6 problems

▼

LAG / LEAD / self-join — These look like gaps-and-islands but only compare each row to its neighbour (or find the gap), without collapsing whole runs. Reach for LAG/LEAD or a self-join on adjacent rows rather than the grp machinery.

Medium Biggest Window Between Visits

▼

Per user, the largest gap in days between visits (or to a fixed end date).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A lifecycle analyst finds each user's longest dormancy.
  • The UserVisits table has each user's visit dates.
  • For each user_id, return the largest gap in days between consecutive visits, counting the gap from the last visit to 2021-01-01.
  • LEAD with a default of 2021-01-01 supplies the trailing window for the final visit.

Schema — UserVisits

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
visit_dateDATE

Example input — UserVisits

user_idvisit_date
12020-11-28
12020-10-20
12020-12-03
22020-01-01

Expected output

user_idbiggest_window
139
2366

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LEAD gives the next visit per user; its third argument supplies a default (2021-01-01) for the last
  visit, so the trailing window is measured to that fixed end date. Subtract to get each gap and take the
  MAX per user. User 1's biggest gap is Oct 20 -> Nov 28 (39 days); user 2's single visit to 2021-01-01 is
  366 days (2020 is a leap year).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT user_id, MAX(next_visit - visit_date) AS biggest_window
FROM (
    SELECT user_id, visit_date,
           LEAD(visit_date, 1, DATE '2021-01-01') OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS next_visit  -- next visit, or the end date
    FROM UserVisits
) t
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id;

Medium Suspicious Bank Accounts

▼

Accounts whose monthly credit exceeds the income cap in two or more consecutive months.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An AML team flags accounts with large deposits across consecutive months.
  • Accounts has each account's income cap; Transactions logs credits with a date.
  • Sum each account's monthly credits, flag months over the cap, and return the account_id of accounts with two or more consecutive over-cap months, ordered by account id.
  • Self-join the flagged months on month + 1 to detect consecutiveness.

Schema — Accounts

ColumnType
account_idINTEGER
max_incomeINTEGER

Example input — Accounts

account_idmax_income
12000
25000

Schema — Transactions

ColumnType
trans_idINTEGER
account_idINTEGER
typeVARCHAR
amountINTEGER
dayDATE

Example input — Transactions

trans_idaccount_idtypeamountday
11Creditor30002024-01-15
21Creditor25002024-02-15
32Creditor60002024-01-10
42Creditor70002024-03-10

Expected output

account_id
1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Roll credits up to one total per (account, month) using DATE_TRUNC, then flag months whose credit beats
  the account's cap. A self-join of the flagged months on "this month + 1 = that month" finds two
  consecutive over-cap months. Account 1 is over in Jan AND Feb (consecutive); account 2 is over in Jan and
  March (a gap), so it is not flagged.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT account_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', day)::date AS ym, SUM(amount) AS credit
    FROM Transactions
    WHERE type = 'Creditor'
    GROUP BY account_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', day)
),
flagged AS (
    SELECT m.account_id, m.ym
    FROM monthly m JOIN Accounts a ON a.account_id = m.account_id
    WHERE m.credit > a.max_income          -- a month over the income cap
)
SELECT DISTINCT f1.account_id
FROM flagged f1
JOIN flagged f2
  ON f2.account_id = f1.account_id
 AND f2.ym = f1.ym + INTERVAL '1 month'    -- the next month is also over the cap
ORDER BY f1.account_id;

Medium Users With Two Purchases Within Seven Days

▼

Users whose two consecutive purchases are within seven days of each other.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A retention team finds quick repeat buyers.
  • The Purchases table has each user's purchase dates.
  • Return the distinct user_id of users with any two consecutive purchases at most 7 days apart, ordered by user id.

Schema — Purchases

ColumnType
purchase_idINTEGER
user_idINTEGER
purchase_dateDATE

Example input — Purchases

purchase_iduser_idpurchase_date
112024-01-01
212024-01-05
322024-01-01
422024-01-20

Expected output

user_id
1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LAG gives each purchase the user's previous purchase date; subtracting yields the gap. Keep users where
  some gap is 7 days or fewer. The first purchase per user has a NULL previous date (NULL <= 7 is unknown),
  so it never qualifies on its own. User 1's purchases are 4 days apart; user 2's are 19.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH lagged AS (
    SELECT user_id, purchase_date,
           LAG(purchase_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchase_date) AS prev_date
    FROM Purchases
)
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM lagged
WHERE purchase_date - prev_date <= 7     -- consecutive purchases within a week
ORDER BY user_id;

Prompt

Example input — Users

22024-01-01
22024-01-15

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Same LAG-and-subtract shape: bring the previous purchase date onto each row and keep gaps between 1 and 7
  days (the lower bound 1 excludes same-day repeats). User 1's purchases are 2 days apart; user 2's are 14.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM (
    SELECT user_id, purchase_date,
           LAG(purchase_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchase_date) AS prev_date
    FROM Users
) t
WHERE purchase_date - prev_date BETWEEN 1 AND 7   -- a rapid sequential buy
ORDER BY user_id;

Hard First and Last Call On the Same Day

▼

Users whose first and last call on a day were with different people.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A spam investigator finds users whose daily first and last contact differed.
  • The Calls table has a caller, a recipient, and a time. Either party counts as the user.
  • Return the distinct user_id of users for whom, on some day, the first and last call were with two different people.
  • Normalize each call into both directions, rank first/last per (user, day), then check that exactly two distinct partners appear among the day's first and last.

Schema — Calls

ColumnType
caller_idINTEGER
recipient_idINTEGER
call_timeTIMESTAMP

Example input — Calls

caller_idrecipient_idcall_time
122024-01-01 09:00:00
132024-01-01 18:00:00
452024-01-01 08:00:00
452024-01-01 20:00:00

Expected output

user_id
1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Either party can be "the user," so norm unions each call into both directions (u, other). Per (user, day),
  rank calls earliest-first and latest-first; the rows with rn_asc = 1 or rn_desc = 1 are the day's first and
  last call. Grouping per (user, day) and keeping those with two DISTINCT partners finds days whose first and
  last contact differed. User 1 called person 2 first and person 3 last; user 4's first and last were both
  person 5.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH norm AS (
    SELECT caller_id AS u, recipient_id AS other, call_time FROM Calls
    UNION ALL
    SELECT recipient_id, caller_id, call_time FROM Calls          -- both directions
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT u, other, call_time,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u, call_time::date ORDER BY call_time)      AS rn_asc,   -- first of the day
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u, call_time::date ORDER BY call_time DESC) AS rn_desc   -- last of the day
    FROM norm
)
SELECT DISTINCT u AS user_id
FROM ranked
WHERE rn_asc = 1 OR rn_desc = 1
GROUP BY u, call_time::date
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT other) = 2;

Hard Customers With Strictly Increasing Purchases

▼

Customers whose yearly spend strictly increases every consecutive year present.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Account management finds accounts that grow year over year with no dips.
  • The Orders table has each order's customer, date, and price.
  • Total spend per customer per year, then return the customer_id of customers whose yearly total strictly increases across consecutive years (and who have more than one year), ordered by customer id.
  • LAG the previous year's total and flag any year that did not strictly increase or skipped a year.

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
order_dateDATE
priceINTEGER

Example input — Orders

order_idcustomer_idorder_dateprice
112019-06-01100
212020-06-01200
312021-06-01300
422019-06-01100
522020-06-0150

Expected output

customer_id
1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Total spend per (customer, year), then LAG the previous year's total and year. A "violation" is any year
  whose total did not strictly exceed the prior year OR that skipped a year (yr <> prev_yr + 1). A customer
  qualifies when they have more than one year and zero violations. Customer 1 climbs 100 -> 200 -> 300 across
  consecutive years; customer 2 drops from 100 to 50.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 1 expected row.
*/

WITH yearly AS (
    SELECT customer_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS yr, SUM(price) AS total
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY customer_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)
),
lagged AS (
    SELECT customer_id, yr, total,
           LAG(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY yr) AS prev_total,
           LAG(yr)    OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY yr) AS prev_yr
    FROM yearly
)
SELECT customer_id
FROM lagged
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN prev_total IS NOT NULL AND (total <= prev_total OR yr <> prev_yr + 1) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0
   AND COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY customer_id;

Window 15 problems

▼

A single table with a date or sequence column → each row annotated with a rolling or running aggregate.

Signal words: "rolling," "running total," "last N days," "cumulative," "moving average," "most recent before"

Technique: SUM/AVG OVER (ROWS BETWEEN), running SUM with threshold, subquery for last value before date

The SQL techniques this recipe uses plus a frame clause cheat sheet. The cheat sheet applies to any window function (running aggregates, rolling windows, LAST_VALUE/FIRST_VALUE, sessionization), not just time-based queries.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
SUM() OVER / AVG() OVER Computes an aggregate across a window without collapsing rows You need a running or rolling aggregate while keeping every row in the output 
SELECT day, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
         PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day
       ) AS running_total
FROM Trans;
ROWS BETWEEN Defines a sliding window frame (e.g., 6 preceding and current row) for a window aggregate You need a rolling average, running total, or cumulative sum over a fixed number of rows 
SELECT day,
       AVG(sales) OVER (
         ORDER BY day
         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS rolling_7d
FROM Daily;

Frame Clause Cheat Sheet

The frame clause defines which rows in the partition a window function actually looks at. Every aggregate, FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE / NTH_VALUE, and even some ranking calls respect the frame — so getting the frame right is the difference between a correct answer and a silently wrong one.

Frame clause Window includes When to use it
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW Start of partition through the current row Running totals, cumulative sums, growing aggregates. This is also the default when you have ORDER BY but no explicit frame.
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING Every row in the partition (past + present + future) Required for LAST_VALUE to actually return the partition's final value. Without it the default frame stops at the current row and LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row's value. Also useful for "partition total alongside each row" patterns.
ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW The last N+1 rows ending at the current row Trailing windows: 7-day rolling average (6 PRECEDING), trailing 28-day active count, last-N-events aggregate.
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND N FOLLOWING The next N+1 rows starting at the current row Look-ahead windows: "next 3 events," forward-looking sums, lead aggregates. Mirror image of the trailing window.
ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND N FOLLOWING Centered window of 2N+1 rows around the current row Smoothing time series, symmetric moving averages, "compare to neighbors on both sides."
ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING Just the previous row Equivalent to LAG(). Rarely written this way, but useful for understanding that frame syntax can pluck a single row at any offset.
RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 'N days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW All rows where the ORDER BY value is within N days of the current row's value Date-based rolling windows where input data has missing days. ROWS would count 7 physical rows regardless of dates; RANGE counts the actual 7 calendar days. Postgres only.
(no frame clause) Depends on whether ORDER BY is present With ORDER BY: defaults to RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Without ORDER BY: the entire partition. This is why LAST_VALUE with just ORDER BY silently returns the current row.

ROWS vs RANGE

Mode How it picks rows Diverges from the other when
ROWS By physical row position. ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW takes exactly 3 rows. When the ORDER BY column has duplicate values: ROWS treats each tied row separately; RANGE groups them together. Also when there are gaps in dates: ROWS counts 7 actual rows; RANGE counts the calendar interval.
RANGE By ORDER BY value. RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW means "all rows whose ORDER BY value is within 2 of the current row's value." When ties exist, RANGE pulls in every tied row at the boundary. When dates have gaps, RANGE follows the calendar (missing days don't count as rows but still fall inside the time interval).

Rules of thumb:

  • If the prompt says "last N records," "last N events," or "trailing N rows," use ROWS.
  • If the prompt says "last N days" with missing days in the data, use RANGE (or fill the gaps first with a calendar CTE and then use ROWS).
  • If you're using LAST_VALUE / FIRST_VALUE / NTH_VALUE, always write the frame explicitly. FIRST_VALUE happens to work with the default, but stating the frame both times makes intent visible and prevents the LAST_VALUE trap.
  • If you only have PARTITION BY with no ORDER BY, the frame is the entire partition by default — fine for partition-total patterns but never use this for running aggregates.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Running total / cumulative aggregate 5 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: window_running_total — SUM OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY time) — running aggregate from the start of the partition through the current row. Default frame when ORDER BY is present is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which IS the running total.

Template Running total template

▼

Use when: each row carries the total so far, from the start of its partition.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Use SUM(metric) OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts) — with ORDER BY present, the default frame is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING through current row, which IS the running total.
  2. No frame clause needed unless you want something other than "from the start through now".
  3. Swap SUM for AVG (cumulative average to date) or COUNT (running tally) — same frame.
SELECT t.*,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id
                         ORDER BY ts) AS running_total
FROM tbl t;
-- ORDER BY with no frame = UNBOUNDED PRECEDING .. CURRENT ROW (the running total)

Medium Cumulative Completed Visits by Provider

▼

Running total of completed visits per provider, ordered by completion date, excluding visits that never completed.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • You are analyzing a telehealth platform's visit completion funnel.
  • The visits table records each patient visit with a booking timestamp, the assigned provider, and a completion timestamp (NULL if the visit was never completed).
  • Calculate a running total of completed visits for each provider, ordered chronologically by completion date.
  • For each completed visit, show the provider id, completion date, and the cumulative count of visits that provider has completed up to and including that date.
  • Exclude visits that were never completed (completion_timestamp IS NULL).
  • Order the final result by provider_id, then completion_timestamp.

Schema — visits

ColumnType
visit_idINTEGER PRIMARY KEY
provider_idINTEGER NOT NULL
patient_idINTEGER NOT NULL
booking_timestampTIMESTAMP NOT NULL
completion_timestampTIMESTAMP

Example input — visits

visit_idprovider_idpatient_idbooking_timestampcompletion_timestamp
110150012024-03-01 08:00:002024-03-01 09:15:00
210150022024-03-01 10:00:002024-03-01 11:00:00
310250032024-03-01 09:00:002024-03-01 09:45:00
410150042024-03-02 08:00:00NULL
510250052024-03-02 10:00:002024-03-02 11:30:00
610150062024-03-03 07:00:002024-03-03 08:20:00
710250072024-03-03 09:00:002024-03-03 10:00:00
810350082024-03-01 14:00:00NULL

Expected output

provider_idcompletion_datecumulative_completed
1012024-03-011
1012024-03-012
1012024-03-033
1022024-03-011
1022024-03-022
1022024-03-033

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  WHERE completion_timestamp IS NOT NULL drops the visits that never finished, so they never
  reach the count. (It also means the CASE always evaluates to 1 here -- a plain
  COUNT(*) OVER (...) would give the same result.)

  SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY provider_id ORDER BY completion_timestamp) is the running total.
  PARTITION BY restarts the tally for each provider; the ORDER BY inside OVER is what makes it
  cumulative (the default frame is the start of the partition through the current row), not one
  grand total.

  completion_timestamp::date casts the timestamp down to a date for the output column.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 6 expected rows.
*/

SELECT
    provider_id,
    completion_timestamp::date AS completion_date,   -- show the day, not the full timestamp
    -- running tally per provider: add 1 for each completed visit,
    -- counted from the provider's first completion through the current row
    SUM(CASE WHEN completion_timestamp::date IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
        OVER (PARTITION BY provider_id        -- restart the count for each provider
              ORDER BY completion_timestamp)  -- ORDER BY makes it cumulative (UNBOUNDED PRECEDING .. CURRENT ROW)
        AS cumulative_completed
FROM visits
WHERE completion_timestamp IS NOT NULL        -- drop visits that never completed so they are not counted
ORDER BY 1, 2;                                -- order by provider_id, then completion_date

  • Order the result by gender, then day.

Expected output

Solution Annotated SQL

The query with a comment block explaining the key lines, plus inline notes.

/*
  PARTITION BY gender restarts the running total for each gender; ORDER BY day makes it
  cumulative (each row sums that gender's scores from the first day through the current day).
  With ORDER BY present and no frame clause, the default frame IS the running total

Medium Account Balance

▼

For each account, report the running balance after every transaction date.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • The Transactions table logs deposits and withdrawals per account by day (type is ‘Deposit’ or ‘Withdraw’).
  • For every transaction, show the account, the day, and the running balance after that day — deposits add, withdrawals subtract.
  • Order by account_id, then day.

Schema — Transactions

ColumnType
account_idVARCHAR
dayDATE
typeVARCHAR
amountINT

Example input — Transactions

account_iddaytypeamount
A12024-02-01Deposit100
A12024-02-02Withdraw30
A12024-02-03Deposit50
A22024-02-01Deposit200
A22024-02-02Withdraw250

Expected output

account_iddaybalance
A12024-02-01100
A12024-02-0270
A12024-02-03120
A22024-02-01200
A22024-02-02-50

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with a comment block explaining the key lines, plus inline notes.

/*
  The CASE turns each row into a signed amount (+ deposit, - withdraw), and SUM(...) OVER runs
  that signed amount cumulatively per account, so each row shows the balance after that day's
  transaction. PARTITION BY account_id keeps each account separate; ORDER BY day makes it a
  running balance, not one grand total.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

SELECT
    account_id,
    day,
    SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'Deposit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END)
        OVER (PARTITION BY account_id    -- separate balance per account
              ORDER BY day) AS balance   -- running balance after each day
FROM Transactions
ORDER BY account_id, day;

Medium Last Person to Fit in the Bus

▼

Return the last person who boards before the running total of weights passes 1000.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • The Queue table lists people waiting to board in turn order, each with a weight.
  • People board in turn order until the cumulative weight would exceed 1000.
  • Return the person_name of the last person who fits (cumulative weight still ≤ 1000).

Schema — Queue

ColumnType
person_nameVARCHAR
weightINT
turnINT

Example input — Queue

person_nameweightturn
Alice2501
Bob4002
Carol2003
Dave3004

Expected output

person_name
Carol

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with a comment block explaining the key lines, plus inline notes.

/*
  Inner query: SUM(weight) OVER (ORDER BY turn) is the cumulative boarding weight in queue order.
  Outer query: keep only rows still within the 1000 limit, then the one with the LARGEST
  cumulative weight is the last person who fits -- ORDER BY cumulative_weight DESC LIMIT 1.

  Verified against the example data -- the answer is Carol (cumulative 850; Dave would push it to 1150).
*/

SELECT person_name
FROM (
    SELECT person_name,
           SUM(weight) OVER (ORDER BY turn) AS cumulative_weight  -- running weight in queue order
    FROM Queue
) t
WHERE cumulative_weight <= 1000      -- only people who board before the limit
ORDER BY cumulative_weight DESC      -- the largest one still under the limit ...
LIMIT 1;                             -- ... is the last person to fit
