Per user, a running total of minutes from the start of their history through each session — with a tie breaker on the order column.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • The listening_sessions table records each listening session with the user, episode, start time, and minutes listened.
  • For each session, show the running total of minutes that user has listened from the start of their history through the current session.
  • Order the window by session_start, breaking ties on session_start by session_id (lower first).
  • Return session_id, user_id, episode_id, session_start, minutes_listened, cumulative_minutes ordered by user_id, session_start, session_id.

Schema — listening_sessions

ColumnType
session_idINT PRIMARY KEY
user_idINT
episode_idVARCHAR
session_startTIMESTAMP
minutes_listenedINT

Example input — listening_sessions

session_iduser_idepisode_idsession_startminutes_listened
110E12024-05-01 08:00:0020
210E22024-05-01 08:00:0015
310E32024-05-02 09:00:0010
420E12024-05-01 07:00:0030
520E42024-05-03 10:00:005

Expected output

session_iduser_idepisode_idsession_startminutes_listenedcumulative_minutes
110E12024-05-01 08:00:002020
210E22024-05-01 08:00:001535
310E32024-05-02 09:00:001045
420E12024-05-01 07:00:003030
520E42024-05-03 10:00:00535

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with a comment block explaining the key lines, plus inline notes.

/*
  PARTITION BY user_id gives each user their own running total; ORDER BY session_start, session_id
  makes it cumulative AND breaks ties on session_start using the primary key, so the order is
  deterministic. ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW spells out the running-total
  frame (sum from the partition start through the current row). The outer ORDER BY repeats the
  same tie breaker so the printed row order is deterministic too.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows (note the tie on
  2024-05-01 08:00 for user 10, broken by session_id).
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT
        session_id, user_id, episode_id, session_start, minutes_listened,
        SUM(minutes_listened) OVER (
            PARTITION BY user_id                       -- running total per user
            ORDER BY session_start, session_id         -- cumulative, ties broken by PK
            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ) AS cumulative_minutes
    FROM listening_sessions
)
SELECT session_id, user_id, episode_id, session_start, minutes_listened, cumulative_minutes
FROM base
ORDER BY user_id, session_start, session_id;

Group benchmark compare 2 approaches

▼

nb01 qtype: window_benchmark_compare — AVG / MIN / MAX OVER (PARTITION BY group) with no ORDER BY stamps the whole group's benchmark onto every row; an outer query then compares each row to it. The missing ORDER BY is what separates this from a running average (which is the same function WITH an ORDER BY).

How to pick: no ORDER BY vs explicit full frame

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Whole group window (no ORDER BY) 1 problem

▼

The simplest form: AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY group) with no ORDER BY. The default frame is already the entire partition, so no frame clause is needed.

Template Group benchmark compare template

▼

Use when: each row or entity must be compared to its group's overall average, min, or max.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Compute the benchmark with AVG(metric) OVER (PARTITION BY group_col) — no ORDER BY, so every row in the group gets the same whole group value.
  2. A window function cannot sit in WHERE, so wrap it in a CTE (or subquery), then compare in the outer query.
  3. Pick < (strict, drops ties) or <= (keeps ties) by reading the prompt.
  4. Two grains? If you must first roll rows up per entity (a per entity average) and then compare to a wider group benchmark, compute the per entity aggregate in one step and the group benchmark with a window over the group, then compare.
WITH with_benchmark AS (
    SELECT t.*,
           AVG(metric) OVER (PARTITION BY group_col) AS group_avg   -- no ORDER BY = whole group
    FROM t
)
SELECT *
FROM with_benchmark
WHERE metric < group_avg;          -- strict: ties excluded; use <= to keep them
-- contrast: add ORDER BY -> running average; add ORDER BY + ROWS BETWEEN -> rolling average

Medium Couriers Faster Than Zone Average

▼

Return couriers whose average delivery time is strictly faster than their zone benchmark. Ties are excluded.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • The couriers table lists each courier and their service_zone; deliveries logs each delivery’s time in minutes.
  • Compute each courier’s average delivery time, then the zone benchmark = the average of those courier averages within the zone.
  • Return couriers whose average is strictly faster (lower) than their zone benchmark; exclude ties.
  • Show courier_id, courier_name, service_zone, courier_avg_minutes (2 dp), zone_avg_minutes (2 dp); order by service_zone, then courier_avg_minutes.

Schema — couriers

ColumnType
courier_idINT
courier_nameVARCHAR
service_zoneVARCHAR

Schema — deliveries

ColumnType
delivery_idINT
courier_idINT
delivery_time_minutesINT

Example input — couriers

courier_idcourier_nameservice_zone
1AnaNorth
2BenNorth
3CleoNorth
4DanSouth
5EveSouth

Example input — deliveries

delivery_idcourier_iddelivery_time_minutes
1120
2130
3240
4250
5330
6336
7410
8420
9525
10535

Expected output

courier_idcourier_nameservice_zonecourier_avg_minuteszone_avg_minutes
1AnaNorth25.0034.33
3CleoNorth33.0034.33
4DanSouth15.0022.50

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with a comment block explaining the key lines, plus inline notes.

/*
  Two grains here. First roll deliveries up to ONE average per courier (the GROUP BY in
  per_courier). Then the benchmark is the average of those courier averages within each zone --
  so the AVG window runs over the per-courier rows, NOT the raw deliveries.
  AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY service_zone) with NO ORDER BY stamps the whole zone's benchmark
  onto every courier row; the outer WHERE keeps only couriers strictly below it.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH per_courier AS (
    SELECT c.courier_id, c.courier_name, c.service_zone,
           AVG(d.delivery_time_minutes) AS courier_avg_raw   -- one average per courier
    FROM couriers AS c
    JOIN deliveries AS d USING (courier_id)
    GROUP BY c.courier_id, c.courier_name, c.service_zone
),
benchmarked AS (
    SELECT courier_id, courier_name, service_zone, courier_avg_raw,
           AVG(courier_avg_raw) OVER (PARTITION BY service_zone) AS zone_avg_raw  -- no ORDER BY = whole-zone benchmark
    FROM per_courier
)
SELECT courier_id, courier_name, service_zone,
       ROUND(courier_avg_raw, 2) AS courier_avg_minutes,
       ROUND(zone_avg_raw, 2)    AS zone_avg_minutes
FROM benchmarked
WHERE courier_avg_raw < zone_avg_raw          -- strict: faster than the zone, ties excluded
ORDER BY service_zone, courier_avg_minutes;

Explicit full frame (ROWS UNBOUNDED) 2 problems

▼

The same benchmark written with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. Redundant with no ORDER BY, but required if the window also carries an ORDER BY.

Template Explicit full frame template

▼

Use when: you want the whole group's benchmark but the same window also carries an ORDER BY.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Spell the frame out: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING — the whole partition, past and future.
  2. This is required when the window also has an ORDER BY: with an ORDER BY the default frame stops at the current row, giving a running average instead of the group benchmark.
  3. Wrap in a CTE (a window can't sit in WHERE), then compare in the outer query.
  4. With no ORDER BY the explicit frame is redundant (the default is already the whole partition), but it makes the whole group intent obvious to a reader.
WITH with_benchmark AS (
    SELECT t.*,
           AVG(metric) OVER (
               PARTITION BY group_col
               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
           ) AS group_avg
    FROM t
)
SELECT *
FROM with_benchmark
WHERE metric < group_avg;        -- strict drops ties; use <= to keep them
-- needed when an ORDER BY is also present, else the frame would stop at the current row

  • Return couriers whose average is strictly faster (lower) than their zone benchmark; exclude ties.
  • Show courier_id, courier_name, service_zone, courier_avg_minutes (2 dp), zone_avg_minutes (2 dp); order by service_zone, then courier_avg_minutes.

ColumnType

courier_nameVARCHAR
service_zoneVARCHAR

Schema — deliveries

ColumnType

Example input — couriers

1AnaNorth
2BenNorth

1120

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with a comment block explaining the key lines, plus inline notes.

/*
  Same problem and same answer as the no-ORDER-BY version, but the whole-group frame is spelled
  out: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING covers the entire zone partition.
  With no ORDER BY this explicit frame is redundant (the default is already the whole partition),
  but it becomes REQUIRED the moment the window also carries an ORDER BY -- otherwise the default
  frame stops at the current row and you get a running average instead of the zone benchmark.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH per_courier AS (
    SELECT c.courier_id, c.courier_name, c.service_zone,
           AVG(d.delivery_time_minutes) AS courier_avg_raw

Medium Stories Above Creator's Average View Rate

▼

Return stories whose views beat their creator's own average, with the explicit full frame (the window also carries an ORDER BY).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A photo app wants stories that performed better than their creator's own average view rate.
  • The stories table logs each story's creator and view count (which may be NULL).
  • Return stories whose views are strictly greater than their creator's average views, with story_id, creator_id, views, and the creator's average aliased creator_avg_views (rounded to 2 decimals).
  • Exclude NULL views from both the average and the output. A creator with a single story never appears (it equals the average, not exceeds it).
  • Order by creator_id ascending, then views descending.

Schema — stories

ColumnType
story_idINTEGER PRIMARY KEY
creator_idINTEGER NOT NULL
viewsINTEGER
posted_atTIMESTAMP NOT NULL

Example input — stories

story_idcreator_idviewsposted_at
110112002024-01-15 08:00:00
210115002024-01-16 09:30:00
31019002024-01-17 10:15:00
410224002024-01-15 11:00:00
510218002024-01-16 12:45:00
610230002024-01-17 14:20:00
71035002024-01-15 15:00:00
8104NULL2024-01-16 16:30:00
910411002024-01-17 17:00:00

Expected output

story_idcreator_idviewscreator_avg_views
210115001200.00
610230002400.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  This is a benchmark-compare: every story is decorated with its creator's whole-group average, then
  the outer query keeps stories above it. A window function cannot live in WHERE, so the average is
  computed in a CTE and compared in the outer query.

  Why the explicit frame is required here: the window carries ORDER BY posted_at, and with an ORDER
  BY the default frame stops at the current row -- that would give a running average to date, not the
  creator's overall average. ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING widens the frame
  to the whole partition so AVG sees every story, past and future. (Drop the ORDER BY and the default
  frame is already the whole partition.)

  WHERE views IS NOT NULL up front excludes NULL views from both the average and the output. A creator
  with one story equals their own average, so the strict > drops them (creators 103 and 104). Creator
  101 averages 1200, so only the 1500 story clears it; creator 102 averages 2400, so only the 3000
  story does.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        ROUND(AVG(views) OVER (PARTITION BY creator_id ORDER BY posted_at
             ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING), 2) AS creator_avg_views   -- whole-group average, despite the ORDER BY
    FROM stories
    WHERE views IS NOT NULL          -- NULL views out of both the average and the result
)
SELECT
    story_id,
    creator_id,
    views,
    creator_avg_views
FROM base
WHERE views > creator_avg_views      -- strictly beat the creator's own average
ORDER BY creator_id, views;

LAG / LEAD comparison 3 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: window_lag_lead — LAG(col) / LEAD(col) pulls the previous or next row's value into the current row to compute deltas, growth, gaps, or compare to neighbor. Always handle the NULL at the partition edges explicitly.

Template LAG / LEAD template

▼

Use when: pull the previous or next row's value to compare or subtract.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. LAG(col) OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts) pulls the previous row's value alongside the current row.
  2. The first row in each partition gets NULL from LAG — handle with COALESCE, or with IS DISTINCT FROM when comparing values.
  3. Compute the delta in the outer SELECT: current_col - prev_col.
SELECT t.*,
       LAG(val)  OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY ts) AS prev_val,
       LEAD(val) OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY ts) AS next_val
FROM tbl t;
-- then in an outer query: val - prev_val, or WHERE val > prev_val

Medium Month-over-Month Revenue Growth by Region

▼

For each region, show each month’s revenue, the previous month’s revenue, the change, and the percent change. The first month per region has no previous, so its change columns are NULL.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • The monthly_sales table has one row per region per month with that month’s revenue.
  • For each row show region, month, revenue, prev_revenue (previous month), mom_change (revenue minus previous), and mom_pct (percent change, 1 dp).
  • The first month of each region has no previous month, so its change columns are NULL.
  • Order by region, then month.

Schema — monthly_sales

ColumnType
regionVARCHAR
monthVARCHAR
revenueINT

Example input — monthly_sales

regionmonthrevenue
North2024-011000
North2024-021200
North2024-03900
South2024-01500
South2024-02800

Expected output

regionmonthrevenueprev_revenuemom_changemom_pct
North2024-011000NULLNULLNULL
North2024-021200100020020.0
North2024-039001200-300-25.0
South2024-01500NULLNULLNULL
South2024-0280050030060.0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with a comment block explaining the key lines, plus inline notes.

/*
  LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month) brings the prior month's revenue onto each
  row. Compute it ONCE in a CTE so mom_change and mom_pct both read the same prev_revenue instead of
  repeating the window. The first month of each region has no previous row, so prev_revenue is NULL
  and the change columns come out NULL with no special casing. Use 100.0 (not 100) to force numeric
  division, and PARTITION BY region so LAG never pulls one region's last month onto another's first.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

WITH with_prev AS (
    SELECT region, month, revenue,
           LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue
    FROM monthly_sales
)
SELECT region, month, revenue, prev_revenue,
       revenue - prev_revenue                                    AS mom_change,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - prev_revenue) / prev_revenue, 1) AS mom_pct
FROM with_prev
ORDER BY region, month;

Easy Days Between Consecutive Logins per User

▼

For each login, show how many days since that user’s previous login. The first login per user has no previous, so the gap is NULL.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • The logins table has many rows per user, each a login_date.
  • For each login show user_id, login_date, and days_since_prev = days since that user’s previous login.
  • The first login per user has no previous row, so the gap is NULL.
  • Order by user_id, then login_date.

Schema — logins

ColumnType
user_idINT
login_dateDATE

Example input — logins

user_idlogin_date
12024-06-01
12024-06-04
12024-06-05
22024-06-02

Expected output

user_idlogin_datedays_since_prev
12024-06-01NULL
12024-06-043
12024-06-051
22024-06-02NULL

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with a comment block explaining the key lines, plus inline notes.

/*
  DATE minus DATE returns an integer number of days in Postgres, so
  login_date - LAG(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) is the days since
  that user's previous login. PARTITION BY user_id keeps each user's history separate; the first
  login per user has no previous row, so LAG is NULL and the gap is NULL by design.
  (For a TIMESTAMP column the subtraction yields an interval -- use EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM ...) / 86400.)

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

SELECT user_id,
       login_date,
       login_date - LAG(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS days_since_prev
FROM logins
ORDER BY user_id, login_date;

Medium Detect Subscription Status Changes

▼

Keep only the rows where a customer’s status differs from their previous status — the change points. Use IS DISTINCT FROM so the first row (NULL previous) counts as a change.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • The status_log table has many status rows per customer over time, including repeats of the same status.
  • Return only the rows where status differs from the customer’s previous status (the transition points), with columns customer_id, changed_at, status, prev_status.
  • Each customer’s first row counts as a change (no previous status).
  • Order by customer_id, then changed_at.

Schema — status_log

ColumnType
customer_idINT
changed_atDATE
statusVARCHAR

Example input — status_log

customer_idchanged_atstatus
12024-01-01active
12024-02-01active
12024-03-01paused
12024-04-01active
22024-01-15active
22024-02-15cancelled

Expected output

customer_idchanged_atstatusprev_status
12024-01-01activeNULL
12024-03-01pausedactive
12024-04-01activepaused
22024-01-15activeNULL
22024-02-15cancelledactive

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with a comment block explaining the key lines, plus inline notes.

/*
  LAG(status) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) puts each row's previous status
  beside it (in a CTE, because a window function can't live in WHERE). Keep only rows where
  status IS DISTINCT FROM prev_status -- the NULL-safe "not equal". For each customer's first row
  prev_status is NULL, and 'active' IS DISTINCT FROM NULL is TRUE, so the opening state is kept;
  plain <> would evaluate to NULL there and silently drop it. Repeated same-status rows are dropped.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

WITH with_prev AS (
    SELECT customer_id, changed_at, status,
           LAG(status) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) AS prev_status
    FROM status_log
)
SELECT customer_id, changed_at, status, prev_status
FROM with_prev
WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM prev_status
ORDER BY customer_id, changed_at;

Sliding window aggregate (rolling N days) 7 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: window_sliding — SUM / AVG / COUNT OVER (... ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) gives a trailing window aggregate per row. Use ROWS when the prompt counts rows, RANGE when the prompt counts the date interval and gaps matter.

Template Sliding window template

▼

Use when: a fixed trailing window (last N rows, or last N calendar days).

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Use SUM/AVG/COUNT OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
  2. ROWS counts rows; switch to RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 'N days' PRECEDING when the source has missing days and "N days" should count by calendar.
SELECT t.*,
       AVG(metric) OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id ORDER BY day
                         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_7
FROM tbl t;
-- date-based with missing days:
--   RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW   (Postgres)

Medium Restaurant Growth

▼

For every day from the 7th onward, report the trailing 7-day total revenue and the trailing 7-day average, rounded to 2 decimals.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A restaurant wants to smooth out daily revenue swings by looking at week-long trends.
  • The Customer table records each paid visit with the date and the amount spent. A single day can have several visits.
  • First roll the visits up to one total per day.
  • Then, for every day that has 6 full days before it, report the total revenue over that day plus the previous 6 days, and the average daily revenue over the same 7 days rounded to 2 decimal places.
  • Return visited_on, the 7-day total as amount, and the 7-day average as average_amount, ordered by visited_on.

Schema — Customer

ColumnType
customer_idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
visited_onDATE
amountINTEGER

Example input — Customer

customer_idnamevisited_onamount
1A2024-01-01100
2B2024-01-02110
3C2024-01-0370
4D2024-01-0350
5E2024-01-04130
6F2024-01-05140
7G2024-01-06150
8H2024-01-07160
9I2024-01-08170
10J2024-01-09180

Expected output

visited_onamountaverage_amount
2024-01-07910130.00
2024-01-08980140.00
2024-01-091050150.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Step 1 (daily CTE): roll the visits up to one total per day. Jan 3 has two visits
  (70 + 50), so the GROUP BY collapses them into a single 120 day. Do this FIRST so the
  rolling window counts days, not individual visits.

  Step 2 (rolling CTE): ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is the trailing 7-day
  frame -- today plus the 6 days before it. ROW_NUMBER labels each day in order so the
  outer query can keep only the days that have a full 7-day window behind them.

  Why the window must run BEFORE the filter: a window function sees only the rows that
  survive WHERE. If you filtered out the early days first, the window would have nothing
  to look back on. So compute the rolling sum over every day, THEN drop the first six.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH daily AS (
    SELECT visited_on,
           SUM(amount) AS day_amount        -- one total per day (Jan 3's two visits become 120)
    FROM Customer
    GROUP BY visited_on
),
rolling AS (
    SELECT visited_on,
           SUM(day_amount) OVER (ORDER BY visited_on
                                 ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS amount,          -- trailing 7-day total
           ROUND(AVG(day_amount) OVER (ORDER BY visited_on
                                 ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS average_amount, -- trailing 7-day average
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY visited_on) AS day_number                                -- 1, 2, 3, ... by date
    FROM daily
)
SELECT visited_on, amount, average_amount
FROM rolling
WHERE day_number >= 7          -- keep only days that have a full 7-day window behind them
ORDER BY visited_on;

Medium Rolling Average Steps

▼

Report a 3-day rolling average of steps, but only on rows where a full 3-day window exists.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A fitness app shows each user a 3-day rolling average of their step count to smooth out daily noise.
  • The Steps table records one row per user per day with that day's step count.
  • For each row, average the step count over the current day plus the 2 days before it.
  • Only return rows where the window holds a full 3 days of data, so the first two rows of each user are dropped.
  • Round the average to 2 decimal places and return user_id, steps_date, rolling_average, ordered by user_id, steps_date.

Schema — Steps

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
steps_countINTEGER
steps_dateDATE

Example input — Steps

user_idsteps_countsteps_date
110002024-02-01
120002024-02-02
130002024-02-03
140002024-02-04
25002024-02-01
215002024-02-02

Expected output

user_idsteps_daterolling_average
12024-02-032000.00
12024-02-043000.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY steps_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND
  CURRENT ROW) is the 3-day trailing average. PARTITION BY restarts the window for each
  user so one user's days never bleed into another's.

  QUALIFY filters on the result of a window function the way WHERE filters on a column.
  COUNT(*) over the same 3-row frame tells you how many days are actually in the window;
  keeping only the rows where that count is 3 drops each user's first two rows (their
  windows are still partial). User 2 has only 2 days total, so every one of its windows
  is partial and user 2 never appears.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT user_id, steps_date,
       ROUND(AVG(steps_count) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY steps_date
                                    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS rolling_average  -- 3-day trailing mean
FROM Steps
QUALIFY COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY steps_date
                       ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) = 3   -- keep only full 3-day windows
ORDER BY user_id, steps_date;

Hard Friday Purchases II

▼

Report every Friday in November 2023 with its total spend, showing 0 for Fridays with no sales.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A store reports spending for every Friday in November 2023, including Fridays with no sales at all.
  • The Purchases table records each purchase with a date and an amount. Only Friday purchases count, and a Friday with no purchases must still appear with a total of 0.
  • Build the four Fridays first, then attach the sales, so empty Fridays survive.
  • Also report which week of the month each Friday falls in (week 1 for days 1 to 7, week 2 for days 8 to 14, and so on).
  • Return week_of_month, purchase_date, total_amount, ordered by purchase_date.

Schema — Purchases

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
purchase_dateDATE
amount_spendINTEGER

Example input — Purchases

user_idpurchase_dateamount_spend
12023-11-0350
22023-11-0330
32023-11-06999
12023-11-17100
32023-11-2420

Expected output

week_of_monthpurchase_datetotal_amount
12023-11-0380
22023-11-100
32023-11-17100
42023-11-2420

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Build the skeleton first: generate_series walks every day in November, and the WHERE
  keeps only Fridays (EXTRACT(DOW) returns 0 for Sunday up to 6 for Saturday, so 5 is
  Friday). That gives the four Fridays whether or not any sale happened on them.

  LEFT JOIN the purchases onto the Friday skeleton. A Friday with no matching purchase
  (Nov 10) keeps its row with NULLs on the right side; COALESCE turns the NULL sum into 0.
  A purchase on a non-Friday (Nov 6) never matches a skeleton row, so it is ignored.

  week_of_month: (day of month - 1) / 7, floored, plus 1 puts days 1-7 in week 1, days
  8-14 in week 2, and so on.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH fridays AS (
    SELECT d::date AS purchase_date
    FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-11-01', DATE '2023-11-30', INTERVAL '1 day') AS g(d)
    WHERE EXTRACT(DOW FROM d) = 5            -- 5 = Friday
)
SELECT CAST(FLOOR((EXTRACT(DAY FROM f.purchase_date) - 1) / 7) + 1 AS INT) AS week_of_month,  -- 1..5 within the month
       f.purchase_date,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.amount_spend), 0) AS total_amount        -- empty Fridays become 0, not NULL
FROM fridays f
LEFT JOIN Purchases p ON p.purchase_date = f.purchase_date     -- keep every Friday even with no sale
GROUP BY f.purchase_date
ORDER BY f.purchase_date;

Medium 7-Day Rolling Average Sleep Score

▼

Per user, a 7-day rolling average sleep score, kept only on days where at least 4 of the 7 days have data.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A sleep app shows each user a 7-day rolling average sleep score, but hides days that do not have enough recent data to trust.
  • The sleep_sessions table records one row per user per night with that night's score. Users can skip nights, so the 7 calendar days can hold fewer than 7 rows.
  • For each row, average the score over the current day plus the 6 days before it, rounded to 2 decimals.
  • Only return rows where at least 4 sessions fall inside that 7-day window, and also report how many sessions were in the window.
  • Return user_id, sleep_date, daily_score, rolling_avg_score, days_in_window, ordered by user_id, sleep_date.

Schema — sleep_sessions

ColumnType
session_idINTEGER
user_idINTEGER
sleep_dateDATE
sleep_scoreINTEGER

Example input — sleep_sessions

session_iduser_idsleep_datesleep_score
112024-03-0170
212024-03-0280
312024-03-0390
412024-03-0460
512024-03-05100
622024-03-0150
722024-03-0260
822024-03-0370

Expected output

user_idsleep_datedaily_scorerolling_avg_scoredays_in_window
12024-03-046075.004
12024-03-0510080.005

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The CTE decorates every row with two windowed values over the per-user trailing 7-day
  frame: AVG gives the rolling mean and COUNT gives how many rows actually fell inside that
  frame. ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts rows by position, so skipped
  nights simply mean fewer rows in the frame -- no error, no NULL.

  The outer query then keeps only rows where days_in_window is at least 4. Early rows of a
  user (window size 1, 2, 3) are dropped; the row where the window first reaches 4 survives.
  User 2 never reaches 4 rows, so it never appears.

  The ::numeric cast on AVG lets Postgres' two-argument ROUND(value, digits) work, since it
  needs a numeric input rather than a float.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH sleep_with_window AS (
    SELECT user_id, sleep_date,
           sleep_score AS daily_score,
           ROUND(AVG(sleep_score) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY sleep_date
                 ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)::numeric, 2) AS rolling_avg_score,  -- 7-day trailing mean
           COUNT(sleep_score) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY sleep_date
                 ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS days_in_window                    -- rows actually in the frame
    FROM sleep_sessions
)
SELECT user_id, sleep_date, daily_score, rolling_avg_score, days_in_window
FROM sleep_with_window
WHERE days_in_window >= 4        -- hide days with too little recent data to trust
ORDER BY user_id, sleep_date;

Medium Rolling 7-Day Job Acceptance Rate for Contractors

▼

Per contractor, the acceptance rate over the current offer plus the 6 prior offers (a 7-row trailing window, not 7 days).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A gig marketplace tracks each contractor's recent acceptance rate to spot people who have gone cold.
  • The contractor_offers table records each offer with a date and a true/false flag for whether it was accepted.
  • For each offer, report the fraction of accepted offers over the current offer plus the 6 offers before it, per contractor.
  • The window is counted by rows, not by calendar days, so 7 means exactly 7 offers in sequence. If fewer than 7 offers exist yet, use whatever is there.
  • Round to 2 decimals and return contractor_id, offer_date, rolling_7day_acceptance_rate, ordered by contractor_id, offer_date.

Schema — contractor_offers

ColumnType
contractor_idINTEGER
offer_dateDATE
acceptedBOOLEAN

Example input — contractor_offers

contractor_idoffer_dateaccepted
1012024-04-01true
1012024-04-02false
1012024-04-03true
1022024-04-01false

Expected output

contractor_idoffer_daterolling_7day_acceptance_rate
1012024-04-011.00
1012024-04-020.50
1012024-04-030.67
1022024-04-010.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  CASE WHEN accepted THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END turns the true/false flag into a number, so
  averaging it gives the fraction of accepted offers directly (the mean of 1s and 0s is
  the share of 1s). Use 1.0 / 0.0, not 1 / 0, so the average stays a decimal instead of
  collapsing to integer division.

  ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts the current offer plus the 6 before it
  by row position, so two offers on the same date are still two separate rows (this is the
  ROWS-vs-RANGE distinction the prompt calls out). PARTITION BY restarts the window per
  contractor.

  Partial windows at the start shrink on their own: contractor 101's first offer averages
  1 row (1.00), the second averages 2 rows (1/2 = 0.50), the third averages 3 (2/3 = 0.67).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH offers_with_rate AS (
    SELECT contractor_id, offer_date,
           ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN accepted THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) OVER (
                 PARTITION BY contractor_id ORDER BY offer_date
                 ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)::numeric, 2) AS rolling_7day_acceptance_rate
    FROM contractor_offers
)
SELECT contractor_id, offer_date, rolling_7day_acceptance_rate
FROM offers_with_rate
ORDER BY contractor_id, offer_date;

Medium 7-Day Rolling Acceptance Rate from Daily Aggregates

▼

From a daily counts table, a 7-day rolling acceptance rate as sum of accepts over sum of offers (volume weighted), with a safe divide for zero-offer windows.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A marketplace stores engagement as daily counters: how many offers went out and how many were accepted each day.
  • The daily_job_metrics table has one row per day with offers_sent and offers_accepted.
  • Report a 7-day rolling acceptance rate as the sum of accepts over the sum of offers across the current day plus the 6 days before it, times 100, rounded to 2 decimals.
  • Use sum over sum, not the average of daily rates, so a busy day counts more than a quiet day.
  • If a window holds only zero-offer days, the denominator is 0, so return NULL instead of dividing by zero. Return metric_date, rolling_acceptance_rate, ordered by metric_date.

Schema — daily_job_metrics

ColumnType
metric_dateDATE
offers_sentINTEGER
offers_acceptedINTEGER

Example input — daily_job_metrics

metric_dateoffers_sentoffers_accepted
2024-04-3000
2024-05-0110080
2024-05-02102
2024-05-035025

Expected output

metric_daterolling_acceptance_rate
2024-04-30NULL
2024-05-0180.00
2024-05-0274.55
2024-05-0366.88

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The right rolling rate from daily counters is SUM(accepts) over the window divided by
  SUM(offers) over the window -- NOT the average of each day's rate. Summing the top and
  bottom separately weights each day by its actual volume, so a 1,000-offer day dominates a
  5-offer day. Averaging daily rates would treat both days equally and give a different,
  usually wrong, number.

  The named WINDOW w defines the 7-day trailing frame once and both SUMs reuse it, so the
  numerator and denominator can never drift apart.

  NULLIF(SUM(offers_sent) OVER w, 0) guards the divide: the first row's window holds only a
  zero-offer day, so the denominator is 0, NULLIF turns it into NULL, and the rate becomes
  NULL instead of erroring. Once a real offer day enters the window, the denominator is
  non-zero and the rate computes normally.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT metric_date,
           ROUND(SUM(offers_accepted) OVER w::numeric
                 / NULLIF(SUM(offers_sent) OVER w, 0)        -- safe divide: zero-offer window becomes NULL
                 * 100, 2) AS rolling_acceptance_rate
    FROM daily_job_metrics
    WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY metric_date
                 ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)   -- 7-day trailing frame, defined once
)
SELECT metric_date, rolling_acceptance_rate
FROM base
ORDER BY metric_date;

Hard Find Cumulative Salary of an Employee

▼

Per employee, the salary for the current month plus the two prior months (missing months count as 0), dropping each employee's most recent month.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Finance reports a trailing 3-month salary total for a bonus calculation, but leaves out each employee's latest (unfinished) month.
  • The Employee table has one row per employee per month they were paid. Employees can skip months, so month numbers can have gaps.
  • For each kept month, sum the salary for that month plus the two months before it by month number. A skipped month counts as 0, not as reaching further back.
  • Drop the row for each employee's most recent month.
  • Return id, month, Salary (the 3-month total), ordered by id ascending, then month descending.

Schema — Employee

ColumnType
idINTEGER
monthINTEGER
salaryINTEGER

Example input — Employee

idmonthsalary
1120
1230
1340
2150
2260
2470
2580

Expected output

idmonthSalary
1250
1120
24130
22110
2150

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The gap is the whole trick. RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING reads the ORDER BY value (month)
  as a number, so for month 4 it sums every row whose month is 2, 3, or 4. Employee 2 has
  no month 3, so month 3 simply contributes nothing -- the total is month 2 (60) + month 4
  (70) = 130. ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING would instead grab the two previous ROWS regardless
  of their month number, wrongly pulling month 1 into month 4's window across the gap.

  MAX(month) OVER (PARTITION BY id) tags each employee's most recent month so the outer
  query can drop it with month <> max_month.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

WITH rolled AS (
    SELECT id, month, salary,
           SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY month
                             RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cum_salary,  -- missing months count as 0
           MAX(month) OVER (PARTITION BY id) AS max_month                                -- each employee's latest month
    FROM Employee
)
SELECT id, month, cum_salary AS Salary
FROM rolled
WHERE month <> max_month        -- drop each employee's most recent (unfinished) month
ORDER BY id ASC, month DESC;

FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE 3 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: window_first_last — FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE pull a specific value from the window's frame. LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row unless you spell out ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING — the classic frame trap.

Template FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE template

▼

Use when: copy the first or last row of the whole partition onto every row.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. FIRST_VALUE(col) OVER (...) returns the first row's value within the frame.
  2. LAST_VALUE needs explicit ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING — otherwise the default frame stops at the current row and it silently returns the current value.
SELECT t.*,
       FIRST_VALUE(val) OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY ts
            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS first_val,
       LAST_VALUE(val)  OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY ts
            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_val
FROM tbl t;
-- the explicit frame is required, or LAST_VALUE returns the current row

Medium Change Null Values in a Table to the Previous Value

▼

Fill each NULL drink forward with the most recent non-NULL drink, keeping the original order.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A catalog pipeline records a drink only when it changes, leaving the in-between rows NULL.
  • The CoffeeShop table has an id (the order) and a drink that is NULL on rows where the value was not re-recorded.
  • Replace each NULL with the most recent non-NULL drink above it (a forward fill).
  • Return id and the filled drink, ordered by id.

Schema — CoffeeShop

ColumnType
idINTEGER
drinkVARCHAR

Example input — CoffeeShop

iddrink
1Latte
2NULL
3NULL
4Espresso
5NULL
6Mocha

Expected output

iddrink
1Latte
2Latte
3Latte
4Espresso
5Espresso
6Mocha

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The trick is turning the NULL runs into groups. COUNT(drink) ignores NULLs, so a running
  COUNT over id only bumps up when a real drink appears. Every NULL inherits the count of the
  last real value above it, so all the rows that should share a value end up with the same
  grp_id (Latte rows = 1, Espresso rows = 2, Mocha = 3).

  Inside each grp_id the only non-NULL value is the first row, so FIRST_VALUE(drink) ordered
  by id copies that value down across the NULLs -- a forward fill with no self join.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 6 expected rows.
*/

WITH grp AS (
    SELECT id, drink,
           COUNT(drink) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp_id   -- bumps only on a real drink; NULLs keep the prior count
    FROM CoffeeShop
)
SELECT id,
       FIRST_VALUE(drink) OVER (PARTITION BY grp_id ORDER BY id) AS drink   -- the one real value in each group, copied down
FROM grp
ORDER BY id;

Medium Installment Plan Payment Spread Analysis

▼

Per plan, return the earliest scheduled payment amount and the latest, drilling the LAST_VALUE frame trap.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A buy now pay later service wants to see how each plan's payment schedule is shaped: does it start big and taper, or end with a balloon?
  • The installment_payments table records each scheduled payment with its plan, due date, and amount.
  • For each plan, report the amount of the earliest payment (by due_date) and the amount of the latest payment.
  • Some plans have only one payment, in which case the first and last amounts are the same.
  • Return plan_id, first_payment_amount, last_payment_amount, ordered by plan_id.

Schema — installment_payments

ColumnType
payment_idINTEGER
plan_idINTEGER
due_dateDATE
amountINTEGER
payment_statusVARCHAR

Example input — installment_payments

payment_idplan_iddue_dateamountpayment_status
112024-01-01100paid
212024-02-0150paid
312024-03-0150scheduled
422024-01-15200paid
532024-01-1030paid
632024-02-1030paid
732024-03-10300scheduled

Expected output

plan_idfirst_payment_amountlast_payment_amount
110050
2200200
330300

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE pull the first and last amount within each plan's window ordered
  by due_date. Because every row in a plan gets the SAME first and last value, SELECT DISTINCT
  collapses them to one row per plan.

  The LAST_VALUE frame trap: with no frame, a window's default is "start of partition through
  the current row," so LAST_VALUE would only ever see up to the current row and return the
  CURRENT amount, not the plan's final one. Spelling out ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND
  UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING widens the frame to the whole plan so it can reach the last row.
  FIRST_VALUE works with the default frame, but write the frame on both for symmetry.

  No-frame-trap alternative: skip the window functions and GROUP BY plan_id, picking each side
  with a rank-based conditional aggregate (number rows by due_date ascending and descending,
  then MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 1 ...)). Same answer, no DISTINCT, no frame to remember.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH base AS (
    SELECT plan_id,
           FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY plan_id ORDER BY due_date
                ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS first_payment_amount,
           LAST_VALUE(amount)  OVER (PARTITION BY plan_id ORDER BY due_date
                ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_payment_amount  -- full frame, or this returns the current row
    FROM installment_payments
)
SELECT DISTINCT plan_id, first_payment_amount, last_payment_amount   -- one row per plan
FROM base
ORDER BY plan_id;

Medium First and Last Refill per Patient

▼

Per patient, the medication name from their earliest refill and from their latest refill. Drills the LAST_VALUE frame trap and the DISTINCT-vs-GROUP BY choice.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A 90-day pharmacy adherence program tracks each patient's refills.
  • The refills table records every refill with the patient, the medication name, and the refill date.
  • For each patient, return the medication from their FIRST refill (earliest refill_date) and the medication from their LAST refill (most recent refill_date), using FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE.
  • Some patients have only one refill, in which case the first and last medication are the same.
  • Return patient_id, first_medication, last_medication, ordered by patient_id.

Schema — refills

ColumnType
refill_idSERIAL PRIMARY KEY
patient_idINTEGER NOT NULL
medication_nameVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
refill_dateDATE NOT NULL
days_supplyINTEGER NOT NULL

Example input — refills

refill_idpatient_idmedication_namerefill_datedays_supply
1101Lisinopril 10mg2024-01-1530
2101Metformin 500mg2024-02-2090
3101Atorvastatin 20mg2024-03-1030
4102Levothyroxine 50mcg2024-01-2260
5102Omeprazole 20mg2024-03-1530
6103Amlodipine 5mg2024-02-0190
7104Sertraline 50mg2024-01-1030
8104Sertraline 50mg2024-02-1230

Expected output

patient_idfirst_medicationlast_medication
101Lisinopril 10mgAtorvastatin 20mg
102Levothyroxine 50mcgOmeprazole 20mg
103Amlodipine 5mgAmlodipine 5mg
104Sertraline 50mgSertraline 50mg

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The prompt asks for FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE, so this computes both per patient over the
  window ordered by refill_date. Every row in a patient gets the same first and last value, so
  SELECT DISTINCT collapses them to one row per patient.

  LAST_VALUE frame trap: without a frame, the default window stops at the current row, so
  LAST_VALUE would return the current row's medication, not the patient's most recent one.
  ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING widens it to the whole patient.

  Is DISTINCT the right call? Yes -- it is correct and, at this size, perfectly efficient. The
  only cost is that the window runs on every row and then a dedup pass keeps one per patient.
  If you wanted to avoid DISTINCT you would drop the window functions entirely and GROUP BY
  patient_id, picking each side with a rank-based conditional aggregate:

      WITH ranked AS (
          SELECT patient_id, medication_name,
                 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY refill_date)      AS rn_first,
                 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY refill_date DESC) AS rn_last
          FROM refills
      )
      SELECT patient_id,
             MAX(CASE WHEN rn_first = 1 THEN medication_name END) AS first_medication,
             MAX(CASE WHEN rn_last  = 1 THEN medication_name END) AS last_medication
      FROM ranked GROUP BY patient_id ORDER BY patient_id;

  That makes one row per patient directly (no dedup pass) and sidesteps the LAST_VALUE frame
  trap. Add a tiebreaker like refill_id to the ORDER BY if two refills can share a date.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

SELECT DISTINCT
    patient_id,
    FIRST_VALUE(medication_name) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY refill_date
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS first_medication,
    LAST_VALUE(medication_name)  OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY refill_date
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_medication   -- full frame, or this returns the current row
FROM refills
ORDER BY patient_id;

Sessionization (gap based grouping) 6 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: window_sessionization — Three step recipe: LAG to find the gap to the previous event, CASE flag of 1 when the gap exceeds a threshold (or row starts a new group), then cumulative SUM of the flag produces a session_id. The same shape powers gaps and islands streaks.

Start here Pick your template from the expected output

▼

Look at the columns you must return, then match the shape below. You do not need to memorize anything.

First, one quick question: what starts a new session?

  • A gap since the previous event (the common case) — the templates below work as written.
  • A timeout counted from when the session started — harder, and these templates give the wrong answer. Slow down if you see this.

Then match your expected output to a template. The one question that decides it: is session_id a column in the expected output? (A session belongs to a person, so "one row per session" output always carries the person id too — that person_id + session_id + a number shape is the common one.)

Your expected output columns Open
both a person id and a session_id, plus one numberOne row per session
a person id + one number, no session_idOne row per person
every original event row, with a session_id column added (still has the person id)One row per event

You never need a JOIN. LAG already gives you the previous row. If you are writing a self-join, stop — that is the most common mistake.

One row per session 4 problems

▼

Output has both the person id and a session_id, plus a number about that session (a time span, a count, a total). One row for each session.

Template One row per session

▼

Output = an id + a session_id + one number.

Steps 1-3 tag every row with a session number. The final GROUP BY makes one row per session.

WITH add_previous_time AS (   -- 1. bring each event's previous time onto the row
  SELECT id, ts,
         LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY ts) AS prev_ts
  FROM events
),
flag_new_session AS (         -- 2. put a 1 on the row where a new session starts
  SELECT id, ts,
         CASE WHEN prev_ts IS NULL
                OR ts - prev_ts > INTERVAL '20 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session
  FROM add_previous_time
),
assign_session_id AS (        -- 3. running total of those 1s = the session number
  SELECT id, ts,
         SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY ts) AS session_id
  FROM flag_new_session
)
SELECT id, session_id,
       MAX(ts) - MIN(ts) AS the_number     -- <- put your number here
FROM assign_session_id
GROUP BY id, session_id;
-- add HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2  only if the prompt says "at least N events per session"

Swap in:

  • the number → time span is MAX(ts) - MIN(ts); how many events is COUNT(*); a total is SUM(col).
  • session start / end → MIN(ts) AS session_start and MAX(ts) AS session_end. The group already holds that session's rows, so the smallest time is the start and the largest is the end — no extra window function.
  • "at least N events per session" → add HAVING COUNT(*) >= N.
  • just want the session label on every row? → delete the GROUP BY and select id, ts, session_id.

Medium Group Article Views into Reading Sessions (Sessionization)

▼

Group each user's views into reading sessions where a gap over 30 minutes starts a new session. Drills the LAG → flag → cumulative SUM recipe.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An analytics team measures engagement in reading sessions, not raw views.
  • The article_views table records each view with the user and the timestamp.
  • Group each user's views into sessions where a new session starts whenever the gap to the previous view is over 30 minutes.
  • session_id is sequential per user starting at 1; articles_viewed is the count in the session; session_start is the earliest view time.
  • Return user_id, session_id, articles_viewed, session_start, ordered by user_id, session_id.

Schema — article_views

ColumnType
view_idINTEGER
user_idINTEGER
article_idINTEGER
viewed_atTIMESTAMP

Example input — article_views

view_iduser_idarticle_idviewed_at
11102024-05-01 09:00:00
21112024-05-01 09:10:00
31122024-05-01 11:00:00
42202024-05-01 08:00:00
52212024-05-01 08:20:00

Expected output

user_idsession_idarticles_viewedsession_start
1122024-05-01 09:00:00
1212024-05-01 11:00:00
2122024-05-01 08:00:00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The three step sessionization recipe, no join needed:

  1. LAG brings each view's previous time onto the same row, per user.
  2. A row starts a new session when there is no previous view (first row) OR the gap is over
     30 minutes -- flag those 1, the rest 0.
  3. A running SUM of that flag per user is the session number. The first row's flag is 1, so
     the running total starts at 1 exactly as required.

  Once every row carries a session_id, the rollup is a plain GROUP BY: COUNT(*) is the views
  in the session and MIN(viewed_at) is its start (the group already holds the session's rows,
  so the smallest time is the start -- no extra window function).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH with_prev AS (
    SELECT user_id, viewed_at,
           LAG(viewed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY viewed_at) AS prev_viewed_at   -- 1. previous view's time
    FROM article_views
),
flagged AS (
    SELECT user_id, viewed_at,
           CASE WHEN prev_viewed_at IS NULL
                  OR viewed_at - prev_viewed_at > INTERVAL '30 minutes'
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session_flag                                          -- 2. 1 where a new session starts
    FROM with_prev
),
sessions AS (
    SELECT user_id, viewed_at,
           SUM(new_session_flag) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY viewed_at) AS session_id  -- 3. running total = session number
    FROM flagged
)
SELECT user_id, session_id,
       COUNT(*)       AS articles_viewed,    -- views in the session
       MIN(viewed_at) AS session_start       -- earliest view = start (free from the group)
FROM sessions
GROUP BY user_id, session_id
ORDER BY user_id, session_id;

Medium Workout Session Detection with 20-Minute Gaps

▼

Group each user's exercises into sessions where a gap of 20 or more minutes starts a new one, then report start, end, and count per session.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A fitness app measures engagement in workout sessions, not raw exercise events.
  • The exercise_completions table records each completed exercise with the user, the exercise name, and the completion time.
  • Group each user's exercises into sessions where a gap of 20 or more minutes since the previous exercise starts a new session.
  • The very first exercise per user always starts session 1.
  • Return one row per user per session: user_id, session_id, session_start, session_end, exercises_completed, ordered by user_id, session_id.

Schema — exercise_completions

ColumnType
exercise_idINTEGER
user_idINTEGER
exercise_nameVARCHAR
exercise_completed_atTIMESTAMP

Example input — exercise_completions

exercise_iduser_idexercise_nameexercise_completed_at
11Squat2024-06-01 07:00:00
21Bench2024-06-01 07:10:00
31Deadlift2024-06-01 07:50:00
42Run2024-06-01 18:00:00

Expected output

user_idsession_idsession_startsession_endexercises_completed
112024-06-01 07:00:002024-06-01 07:10:002
122024-06-01 07:50:002024-06-01 07:50:001
212024-06-01 18:00:002024-06-01 18:00:001

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Same three step recipe, with one twist on where session numbering starts.

  Step 1 (flagged): the gap test is current time minus LAG(previous time) >= 20 minutes. On
  the first exercise LAG is NULL, so the comparison is NULL and the CASE falls to 0.

  Step 2 (sessions): the running SUM of the flag therefore starts at 0, so add + 1 to make each
  user's first session 1 instead of 0.

  Step 3: with a stable session_id on every row, start / end / count are a plain GROUP BY:
  MIN and MAX of the timestamp are the session edges (free from the group) and COUNT(*) is the
  number of exercises. Single-exercise sessions get the same start and end.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH flagged AS (
    SELECT user_id, exercise_completed_at,
           CASE WHEN exercise_completed_at
                     - LAG(exercise_completed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY exercise_completed_at)
                     >= INTERVAL '20 minutes'
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session            -- first row's LAG is NULL -> 0
    FROM exercise_completions
),
sessions AS (
    SELECT user_id, exercise_completed_at,
           SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY exercise_completed_at) + 1 AS session_id  -- + 1 so the first session is 1
    FROM flagged
)
SELECT user_id, session_id,
       MIN(exercise_completed_at) AS session_start,     -- first exercise in the session
       MAX(exercise_completed_at) AS session_end,       -- last exercise in the session
       COUNT(*)                   AS exercises_completed
FROM sessions
GROUP BY user_id, session_id
ORDER BY user_id, session_id;

Medium Sessionize Trades by 15-Minute Gaps (start, end, count, volume)

▼

One row per trading session: first and last trade time, trade count, and total volume. Start and end are just MIN / MAX of the group you already have.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A trading app measures activity in sessions, where a new session starts when 15 or more minutes pass since the user's previous trade (a gap over 15 minutes).
  • The trades table records each trade with the user, the timestamp, and the dollar volume.
  • For each session, report the first trade time, the last trade time, the number of trades, and the total volume.
  • A single-trade session has the same start and end time.
  • Return user_id, session_id, session_start, session_end, trades_in_session, total_volume_usd, ordered by user_id, session_start.

Schema — trades

ColumnType
trade_idINTEGER
user_idINTEGER
trade_tsTIMESTAMP
volume_usdINTEGER

Example input — trades

trade_iduser_idtrade_tsvolume_usd
11012024-07-01 10:00:00400
21012024-07-01 10:05:00400
31012024-07-01 10:25:00500
41012024-07-01 10:50:00300

Expected output

user_idsession_idsession_startsession_endtrades_in_sessiontotal_volume_usd
10112024-07-01 10:00:002024-07-01 10:05:002800
10122024-07-01 10:25:002024-07-01 10:25:001500
10132024-07-01 10:50:002024-07-01 10:50:001300

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The standard three step recipe tags each trade with a session_id:

  1. LAG exposes the previous trade's time as its own column (auditable).
  2. Flag a 1 where there is no previous trade OR the gap is over 15 minutes.
  3. A running SUM of the flag is the session number; the first trade is flagged 1, so numbering
     starts at 1.

  The point of this card: once the trades are tagged, the final GROUP BY (user_id, session_id)
  already holds every trade in a session, so the start and end are just MIN / MAX of the
  timestamp -- no FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE needed -- and the count and volume are COUNT / SUM.

  Tiebreak the ordering with trade_id as well as trade_ts so trades at the same instant keep a
  stable order. Single-trade sessions naturally get equal start and end.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH add_prev_time AS (
    SELECT *,
           LAG(trade_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY trade_id, trade_ts) AS prev_ts   -- 1. previous trade's time
    FROM trades
),
flag_new_session AS (
    SELECT *,
           CASE WHEN prev_ts IS NULL
                  OR trade_ts - prev_ts > INTERVAL '15 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session  -- 2. 1 where a session starts
    FROM add_prev_time
),
assign_session AS (
    SELECT *,
           SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY trade_id, trade_ts) AS session_id  -- 3. running total = session number
    FROM flag_new_session
)
SELECT user_id, session_id,
       MIN(trade_ts)   AS session_start,        -- first trade (free from the group)
       MAX(trade_ts)   AS session_end,          -- last trade
       COUNT(trade_id) AS trades_in_session,
       SUM(volume_usd) AS total_volume_usd
FROM assign_session
GROUP BY user_id, session_id
ORDER BY user_id, session_start;

Medium Sleep Session Grouping by Gap

▼

One row per sleep session: start, end, reading count, and average heart rate, split by gaps of 10 minutes or more.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A sleep app records heartbeat readings through the night and groups consecutive readings into sessions.
  • A new session starts whenever this is the user's first reading OR more than 10 minutes have passed since their previous reading (a wake-up or a disconnect).
  • The heartbeat_readings table has one row per reading with the user, timestamp, and heart rate.
  • For each user and session, return session_start, session_end, reading_count, and avg_heart_rate (rounded to 1 decimal), ordered by user_id then session_start.

Schema — heartbeat_readings

ColumnType
reading_idINTEGER PRIMARY KEY
user_idINTEGER NOT NULL
recorded_atTIMESTAMP NOT NULL
heart_rateINTEGER NOT NULL

Example input — heartbeat_readings

reading_iduser_idrecorded_atheart_rate
11012024-01-15 22:05:0068
21012024-01-15 22:07:0065
31012024-01-15 22:09:0063
41012024-01-15 22:25:0072
51012024-01-15 22:27:0070
61022024-01-15 23:10:0058
71022024-01-15 23:12:0060
81022024-01-15 23:30:0055

Expected output

user_idsession_startsession_endreading_countavg_heart_rate
1012024-01-15 22:05:002024-01-15 22:09:00365.3
1012024-01-15 22:25:002024-01-15 22:27:00271.0
1022024-01-15 23:10:002024-01-15 23:12:00259.0
1022024-01-15 23:30:002024-01-15 23:30:00155.0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The standard three step sessionization recipe, then a rollup -- no join needed.

  1. add_prev_time: LAG brings each reading's previous timestamp onto the row, per user.
  2. flag_new_session: a 1 marks a session start -- either the first reading (prev_time IS NULL)
     or a gap over 10 minutes since the previous reading.
  3. add_session_id: a running SUM of those 1s per user turns the flags into a session number.

  Once each reading carries a session_id, the final GROUP BY (user_id, session_id) holds every
  reading in a session, so MIN / MAX of recorded_at are the session edges (free from the group),
  COUNT(*) is the reading count, and ROUND(AVG(heart_rate), 1) is the average. User 101's first
  three readings are within 2 minutes of each other (one session); the 16-minute jump to 22:25
  starts a second.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH add_prev_time AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        LAG(recorded_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY recorded_at) AS prev_time   -- 1. previous reading's time
    FROM heartbeat_readings
),
flag_new_session AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        CASE WHEN prev_time IS NULL OR recorded_at - prev_time > INTERVAL '10 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session   -- 2. 1 where a session starts
    FROM add_prev_time
),
add_session_id AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY recorded_at) AS session_id   -- 3. running total = session number
    FROM flag_new_session
)
SELECT
    user_id,
    MIN(recorded_at) AS session_start,        -- first reading of the session
    MAX(recorded_at) AS session_end,          -- last reading of the session
    COUNT(*) AS reading_count,
    ROUND(AVG(heart_rate), 1) AS avg_heart_rate
FROM add_session_id
GROUP BY user_id, session_id
ORDER BY user_id, session_start;

One row per person 2 problems

▼

Output has only the person id (no session_id) + one number that sums up all their sessions: how many, the longest, or the best.

Template One row per person

▼

Output = an id + one number that sums up all of their sessions.

Same first 3 steps, then group once per session, then once more per person. Two group-bys is the whole trick.

-- Steps 1-3 are the SAME as "One row per session" (they give every row a session_id):
WITH add_previous_time AS (   -- 1. bring each event's previous time onto the row
  SELECT id, ts, metric,
         LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY ts) AS prev_ts
  FROM events
),
flag_new_session AS (         -- 2. put a 1 on the row where a new session starts
  SELECT id, ts, metric,
         CASE WHEN prev_ts IS NULL
                OR ts - prev_ts > INTERVAL '20 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session
  FROM add_previous_time
),
assign_session_id AS (        -- 3. running total of those 1s = the session number
  SELECT id, ts, metric,
         SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY ts) AS session_id
  FROM flag_new_session
),
totals_per_session AS (       -- 4. one row per session, with its total
  SELECT id, session_id, SUM(metric) AS session_total
  FROM assign_session_id
  GROUP BY id, session_id
)
SELECT id,                    -- 5. one row per person
       COUNT(*)           AS number_of_sessions,
       MAX(session_total) AS best_session   -- or MIN / AVG
FROM totals_per_session
GROUP BY id;

Swap in:

  • the number → how many sessions is COUNT(*); longest / best is MAX(...); average is AVG(...).
  • what each session is worth → set it in per_session (e.g. SUM(metric), or MAX(ts) - MIN(ts) for duration).

Hard Longest Winning Streak

▼

Per player, the longest run of consecutive wins. A gaps-and-islands shape: the difference of two row numbers labels each streak.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A sports newsroom reports each player's longest ever win streak.
  • The Matches table records each match with the player, the match day, and the result (Win or Loss).
  • For each player, return the length of their longest run of consecutive wins by match day.
  • A player who never won returns 0.
  • Return player_id, longest_streak, ordered by player_id.

Schema — Matches

ColumnType
player_idINTEGER
match_dayDATE
resultVARCHAR

Example input — Matches

player_idmatch_dayresult
12024-01-01Win
12024-01-02Win
12024-01-03Loss
12024-01-04Win
22024-01-01Loss
22024-01-02Loss
32024-01-01Win
32024-01-02Win
32024-01-03Win

Expected output

player_idlongest_streak
12
20
33

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  This is the gaps-and-islands trick. Number each player's matches overall, then number them
  again within each result. For a run of the same result those two counters move in lockstep,
  so their difference (grp) stays constant across the run and changes when the result changes.
  That grp is a label for each unbroken streak.

  Group by (player_id, result, grp) and COUNT(*) gives the length of every streak. Keep only
  the Win streaks and take the MAX per player.

  Why the LEFT JOIN from a distinct-players list: a player who never won has no Win streak rows
  at all, so a plain join would drop them. Driving off every player and COALESCEing the missing
  MAX to 0 keeps player 2 with a longest_streak of 0.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH runs AS (
    SELECT player_id, match_day, result,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY match_day)
         - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id, result ORDER BY match_day) AS grp  -- constant within a streak
    FROM Matches
)
SELECT m.player_id,
       COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN r.result = 'Win' THEN cnt END), 0) AS longest_streak   -- 0 for players with no win streak
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT player_id FROM Matches) m
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT player_id, result, COUNT(*) AS cnt          -- length of each streak
    FROM runs
    GROUP BY player_id, result, grp
) r USING (player_id)
GROUP BY m.player_id
ORDER BY m.player_id;

Medium Sessionize Player Match Events by 20-Minute Gaps (count + best session)

▼

Per player, the number of sessions and the XP of their best session. Two grains means two GROUP BYs: roll up per session, then per player.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A game measures play in sessions, where a new session starts when more than 20 minutes pass between matches.
  • The match_events table records each match with the player, the completion time, and the XP earned.
  • Assign a session id to each player's matches (a gap over 20 minutes starts a new session), then report each player's session count and the XP total of their best session.
  • A player with a single match is one session of one event.
  • Return player_id, session_count, max_session_xp, ordered by player_id.

Schema — match_events

ColumnType
event_idINTEGER
player_idINTEGER
match_completed_atTIMESTAMP
xp_earnedINTEGER

Example input — match_events

event_idplayer_idmatch_completed_atxp_earned
11012024-08-01 10:00:0050
21012024-08-01 10:15:0075
31012024-08-01 10:50:0060
41012024-08-01 11:05:0080
52022024-08-01 09:00:0090
62022024-08-01 09:45:00100
72022024-08-01 11:30:0070
83032024-08-01 12:00:0040

Expected output

player_idsession_countmax_session_xp
1012140
2023100
303140

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Count of sessions and best session are two different grains, so this needs two GROUP BYs.

  Steps 1-3 are the usual LAG -> flag -> running SUM that tags each match with a session_id.
  The gap test is strictly more than 20 minutes (exactly 20 stays in the same session), and the
  first match per player is flagged 1 explicitly so numbering starts at 1.

  Step 4 (session_totals) rolls each session into one row carrying its total XP -- this is the
  per-session grain.

  The final SELECT then aggregates those per-session rows per player: COUNT(*) is how many
  sessions, and MAX(session_xp) is the best session. Trying to get both in a single GROUP BY
  would mix the two grains and give the wrong count.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH ordered AS (
    SELECT player_id, match_completed_at, xp_earned,
           LAG(match_completed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY match_completed_at) AS prev_completed_at  -- 1
    FROM match_events
),
flagged AS (
    SELECT player_id, match_completed_at, xp_earned,
           CASE WHEN prev_completed_at IS NULL THEN 1
                WHEN match_completed_at - prev_completed_at > INTERVAL '20 minutes' THEN 1
                ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session                                                   -- 2
    FROM ordered
),
sessions AS (
    SELECT player_id, match_completed_at, xp_earned,
           SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY match_completed_at) AS session_id  -- 3
    FROM flagged
),
session_totals AS (
    SELECT player_id, session_id, SUM(xp_earned) AS session_xp                                  -- 4. one row per session
    FROM sessions
    GROUP BY player_id, session_id
)
SELECT player_id,
       COUNT(*)        AS session_count,     -- how many sessions
       MAX(session_xp) AS max_session_xp     -- XP of the best session
FROM session_totals
GROUP BY player_id
ORDER BY player_id;

One row per event template only

▼

Output keeps every original event row (same number of rows as the input), with a session_id column added. The person id is still there. No aggregation — you only label each row.

Template One row per event

▼

Output = every event row + its session_id. No GROUP BY.

Steps 1-2 tag where a session starts; step 3 keeps the running total on every row as the session number. There is no final GROUP BY, so every original row stays.

WITH add_previous_time AS (   -- 1. bring each event's previous time onto the row
  SELECT id, ts,
         LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY ts) AS prev_ts
  FROM events
),
flag_new_session AS (         -- 2. put a 1 on the row where a new session starts
  SELECT id, ts,
         CASE WHEN prev_ts IS NULL
                OR ts - prev_ts > INTERVAL '20 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session
  FROM add_previous_time
)
SELECT id, ts,                -- 3. running total = the session number, kept on every row
       SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY ts) AS session_id
FROM flag_new_session
ORDER BY id, ts;
-- no GROUP BY: every original row stays, now labeled with its session_id

Swap in:

  • need a number per session instead? → add GROUP BY id, session_id and aggregate — that is One row per session.
  • keep extra per-event columns → just list them in the SELECT; they ride along untouched.

Frame clauses (ROWS / RANGE BETWEEN) no problems yet

▼

nb01 qtype: window_frames — Drills the frame clause itself — ROWS vs RANGE, UNBOUNDED PRECEDING vs N PRECEDING, the LAST_VALUE default trap. See the Frame Clause Cheat Sheet inside the Reference container above for the full reference.

Frame Clause Cheat Sheet

The frame clause defines which rows in the partition a window function actually looks at. Every aggregate, FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE / NTH_VALUE, and even some ranking calls respect the frame — so getting the frame right is the difference between a correct answer and a silently wrong one.

Frame clause Window includes When to use it
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW Start of partition through the current row Running totals, cumulative sums, growing aggregates. This is also the default when you have ORDER BY but no explicit frame.
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING Every row in the partition (past + present + future) Required for LAST_VALUE to actually return the partition's final value. Without it the default frame stops at the current row and LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row's value. Also useful for "partition total alongside each row" patterns.
ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW The last N+1 rows ending at the current row Trailing windows: 7-day rolling average (6 PRECEDING), trailing 28-day active count, last-N-events aggregate.
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND N FOLLOWING The next N+1 rows starting at the current row Look-ahead windows: "next 3 events," forward-looking sums, lead aggregates. Mirror image of the trailing window.
ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND N FOLLOWING Centered window of 2N+1 rows around the current row Smoothing time series, symmetric moving averages, "compare to neighbors on both sides."
ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING Just the previous row Equivalent to LAG(). Rarely written this way, but useful for understanding that frame syntax can pluck a single row at any offset.
RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 'N days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW All rows where the ORDER BY value is within N days of the current row's value Date-based rolling windows where input data has missing days. ROWS would count 7 physical rows regardless of dates; RANGE counts the actual 7 calendar days. Postgres only.
(no frame clause) Depends on whether ORDER BY is present With ORDER BY: defaults to RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Without ORDER BY: the entire partition. This is why LAST_VALUE with just ORDER BY silently returns the current row.

ROWS vs RANGE

Mode How it picks rows Diverges from the other when
ROWS By physical row position. ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW takes exactly 3 rows. When the ORDER BY column has duplicate values: ROWS treats each tied row separately; RANGE groups them together. Also when there are gaps in dates: ROWS counts 7 actual rows; RANGE counts the calendar interval.
RANGE By ORDER BY value. RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW means "all rows whose ORDER BY value is within 2 of the current row's value." When ties exist, RANGE pulls in every tied row at the boundary. When dates have gaps, RANGE follows the calendar (missing days don't count as rows but still fall inside the time interval).

Rules of thumb:

  • If the prompt says "last N records," "last N events," or "trailing N rows," use ROWS.
  • If the prompt says "last N days" with missing days in the data, use RANGE (or fill the gaps first with a calendar CTE and then use ROWS).
  • If you're using LAST_VALUE / FIRST_VALUE / NTH_VALUE, always write the frame explicitly. FIRST_VALUE happens to work with the default, but stating the frame both times makes intent visible and prevents the LAST_VALUE trap.
  • If you only have PARTITION BY with no ORDER BY, the frame is the entire partition by default — fine for partition-total patterns but never use this for running aggregates.

Decide ROWS or RANGE?

▼

Both name an explicit frame. The choice is whether the window means a count of rows or a span of ORDER BY values.

Does “the window” mean a fixed number of rows, or a span of ORDER BY values?
A fixed COUNT of rows — “the last 3 rows”, trailing N, centered N, or the whole partition→ROWS BETWEEN A span of VALUES — “the last 7 calendar days”, or all peer rows within a value range→RANGE BETWEEN

The core difference: ROWS counts physical rows, so tied rows are counted separately; RANGE keys on the ORDER BY value, so peers (equal values) share one frame.
