Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Per month, the numerator counts distinct drivers who accepted a ride that month and the denominator
  counts drivers active by month end. The 100.0 forces numeric division so the ratio is not floored; NULLIF
  guards a zero denominator and COALESCE reports 0.00 for months before any driver joined. In month 1, one
  of two active drivers worked = 50 percent.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 12 expected rows.
*/

WITH months AS (SELECT generate_series(1, 12) AS m)
SELECT m.m AS month,
       COALESCE(ROUND(
         100.0 * (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT ar.driver_id)
                  FROM AcceptedRides ar JOIN Rides r ON r.ride_id = ar.ride_id
                  WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM r.requested_at) = 2020 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM r.requested_at) = m.m)
         / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Drivers
                   WHERE join_date < MAKE_DATE(2020, m.m, 1) + INTERVAL '1 month'), 0),
         2), 0.00) AS working_percentage
FROM months m
ORDER BY m.m;

Hard Hopper Company Queries III

▼

Per month 1-10: average ride distance and duration over that month plus the next two.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Leadership reviews a rolling 3-month operational forecast for 2020.
  • Rides has request dates; AcceptedRides has each accepted ride's distance and duration.
  • For each month m = 1..10, return the average average_ride_distance and average_ride_duration over rides requested in months m, m+1, m+2 of 2020 (rounded to 2 decimals; NULL if no rides), ordered by month.
  • Implement the 3-month bucket as a range filter in the join.

Schema — Rides

ColumnType

user_idINTEGER
requested_atDATE

Example input — Rides

ride_iduser_idrequested_at
112020-01-15
222020-02-10
332020-03-20
442020-06-05

Schema — AcceptedRides

ColumnType
ride_idINTEGER

ride_durationINTEGER

Example input — AcceptedRides

ride_iddriver_idride_distanceride_duration
11010010
2820020

Expected output

monthaverage_ride_distanceaverage_ride_duration

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A 10-row calendar; the 3-month bucket is a range filter in the join (months m through m+2). LEFT JOINs
  keep months whose window has no rides (their averages come back NULL). Month 1's window (Jan-Mar) covers
  rides of 100, 200, 300 -> average distance 200.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 10 expected rows.
*/

WITH months AS (SELECT generate_series(1, 10) AS m)
SELECT m.m AS month,
       ROUND(AVG(ar.ride_distance), 2) AS average_ride_distance,
       ROUND(AVG(ar.ride_duration), 2) AS average_ride_duration
FROM months m
LEFT JOIN Rides r
       ON EXTRACT(YEAR FROM r.requested_at) = 2020
      AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM r.requested_at) BETWEEN m.m AND m.m + 2     -- 3-month window
LEFT JOIN AcceptedRides ar ON ar.ride_id = r.ride_id
GROUP BY m.m
ORDER BY m.m;

Medium Bank Account Summary

▼

Final balance per user and whether it went negative.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A P2P payment app shows each wallet its final balance and flags negatives.
  • Users has each account's starting credit; Transactions moves money from a payer to a payee.
  • Return user_id, user_name, final credit (starting credit minus money paid out plus money received), and credit_limit_breached ('Yes' if the final credit is negative, else 'No'), ordered by user id.
  • Normalize debits and credits into one signed column, sum per user, then add the starting credit.

Schema — Users

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
user_nameVARCHAR
creditINTEGER

Example input — Users

user_iduser_namecredit
1Alice3000
2Bob2000
3Carol1000

Schema — Transactions

ColumnType
trans_idINTEGER
paid_byINTEGER
paid_toINTEGER
amountINTEGER
transacted_onDATE

Example input — Transactions

trans_idpaid_bypaid_toamounttransacted_on
11220002020-01-01
22350002020-01-02

Expected output

user_iduser_namecreditcredit_limit_breached
1Alice1000No
2Bob-1000Yes
3Carol6000No

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The flows CTE normalizes each transaction into two signed rows -- a debit for the payer (negative) and a
  credit for the payee (positive). Sum those per user and add their starting credit for the final balance;
  a CASE flags negatives. Bob pays out 5000 against 2000 + 2000 received, landing at -1000.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH flows AS (
    SELECT paid_by AS user_id, -amount AS amt FROM Transactions      -- money out
    UNION ALL
    SELECT paid_to,             amount        FROM Transactions      -- money in
)
SELECT u.user_id, u.user_name,
       u.credit + COALESCE(SUM(f.amt), 0) AS credit,
       CASE WHEN u.credit + COALESCE(SUM(f.amt), 0) < 0 THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END AS credit_limit_breached
FROM Users u
LEFT JOIN flows f ON f.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.user_name, u.credit;

Rate / ratio / percentage 5 problems

▼

Numerator and denominator both come from a join. Build each as a separate CTE (or as SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) in one pass) and divide. Cast at least one side to NUMERIC to avoid integer division; NULLIF the denominator to avoid divide-by-zero.

Rate / percentage per group

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Express numerator and denominator in one pass with SUM(CASE WHEN ...), or build them as two separate CTEs and divide.
  2. Cast at least one side to NUMERIC (or use ::numeric) so the division stays decimal instead of integer.
  3. Wrap the denominator in NULLIF(...., 0) so empty groups produce NULL instead of a divide-by-zero error.
  4. ROUND to the prompt's required decimals; default is 4 in Postgres.
-- one-pass: SUM(CASE) over a single LEFT JOIN
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    ROUND(
      SUM(CASE WHEN b.condition THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)
      / NULLIF(COUNT(b.b_pk), 0)
    , 2) AS rate
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id;
-- NULLIF the denominator so empty groups give NULL, not divide-by-zero.

Medium Confirmation Rate

▼

Per user, the share of confirmation attempts that succeeded, with 0 for users who never confirmed.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An onboarding team measures how many signups finish email or text confirmation.
  • Signups lists each signup; Confirmations logs each attempt with an action of 'confirmed' or 'timeout'.
  • For each signup, return the confirmation rate = confirmed attempts / total attempts, rounded to 2 decimals.
  • A user with no attempts at all should report 0.00, not a blank, ordered by user id.

Schema — Signups

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
time_stampDATE

Example input — Signups

user_idtime_stamp
32020-03-21
72020-01-04
22020-07-29
62020-12-09

Schema — Confirmations

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
time_stampDATE
actionVARCHAR

Example input — Confirmations

user_idtime_stampaction
32021-01-06timeout
32021-07-14timeout
72021-06-12confirmed
72021-06-13confirmed
22021-01-22confirmed
22021-02-28timeout

Expected output

user_idconfirmation_rate
20.5
30.0
60.0
71.0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LEFT JOIN keeps every signup, even one with no confirmation rows. COUNT(CASE...) counts only the
  'confirmed' attempts; COUNT(c.user_id) counts attempts of any kind (NULL from the LEFT JOIN does not
  count). NULLIF guards the divide-by-zero for users with no attempts, and COALESCE turns that NULL into
  0.00. User 7 confirmed twice of two attempts (1.00); user 6 never appears in Confirmations (0.00).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

SELECT s.user_id,
       ROUND(COALESCE(
         COUNT(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1 END) * 1.0   -- confirmed attempts
         / NULLIF(COUNT(c.user_id), 0)                              -- total attempts, guarded
       , 0), 2) AS confirmation_rate
FROM Signups s
LEFT JOIN Confirmations c ON s.user_id = c.user_id
GROUP BY s.user_id
ORDER BY s.user_id;

Medium Game Play Analysis IV

▼

Fraction of players who logged in again the very next day after their first login.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A games team measures day one retention: of all players, what share came back the day after they first showed up.
  • Activity logs one row per player per day they played.
  • Find each player's first login date, then check whether they also logged in exactly one day later.
  • Return that fraction over all players, rounded to 2 decimals.

Schema — Activity

ColumnType
player_idINTEGER
device_idINTEGER
event_dateDATE
games_playedINTEGER

Example input — Activity

player_iddevice_idevent_dategames_played
122016-03-015
122016-03-026
232017-06-251
312016-03-020
342018-07-035

Expected output

fraction
0.33

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  first_login pins each player's earliest date. The LEFT JOIN back to Activity keeps a row only when the
  same player has an event exactly one day after that first date. The fraction is distinct returning
  players over distinct total players. Player 1 first played Mar 1 and returned Mar 2 (counts); players 2
  and 3 never came back the next day. So 1 of 3 = 0.33.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the single expected row.
*/

WITH first_login AS (
    SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_date
    FROM Activity
    GROUP BY player_id
)
SELECT ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT a.player_id)::NUMERIC
             / COUNT(DISTINCT f.player_id), 2) AS fraction
FROM first_login f
LEFT JOIN Activity a
  ON a.player_id = f.player_id
  AND a.event_date = f.first_date + INTERVAL '1 day';   -- came back the next day

Hard Popularity Percentage

▼

Per user, the share of all other users who are their friend, on an undirected graph.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A social product publishes a reach score: what percent of everyone else each user is connected to.
  • Friends has one row per friendship as a pair (user1, user2); friendship is mutual, so the pair is undirected.
  • For each user, return their friend count divided by (total users minus one), as a percentage rounded to 2 decimals, ordered by user.

Schema — Friends

ColumnType
user1INTEGER
user2INTEGER

Example input — Friends

user1user2
21
13
41
15
23
35
34

Expected output

user1percentage_popularity
1100.0
250.0
3100.0
450.0
550.0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Each friendship is stored once but counts both ways, so the first CTE mirrors every pair to make the
  graph undirected. all_users is the distinct set of people. For each user, count distinct friends and
  divide by everyone else (total users minus self). User 1 is connected to all four others (100.00); user
  2 reaches two of four (50.00).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

WITH f AS (
    SELECT user1 AS u, user2 AS v FROM Friends
    UNION                                        -- mirror each pair: undirected
    SELECT user2, user1 FROM Friends
),
all_users AS (SELECT DISTINCT u AS uid FROM f)
SELECT u.uid AS user1,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT f.v)
             / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM all_users) - 1, 0), 2) AS percentage_popularity
FROM all_users u
LEFT JOIN f ON f.u = u.uid
GROUP BY u.uid
ORDER BY u.uid;

Prompt

  • A teacher checks consistency by comparing each student's strongest and weakest assignment.
  • Scores has one row per student with three assignment columns.
  • Return the total of the three scores and the difference between the highest and lowest, ordered by total descending.

Schema — Scores

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The three scores already sit in one row, so no unpivot is needed. GREATEST and LEAST pick the highest
  and lowest of the three across the row, and their difference is the spread. Bob totals 262 with a tight
  9 point spread; Amy totals 249 but swings 31 points.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT student_id, student_name,
       (assignment1 + assignment2 + assignment3) AS total_score,
       GREATEST(assignment1, assignment2, assignment3)
         - LEAST(assignment1, assignment2, assignment3) AS difference_score   -- best minus worst
FROM Scores
ORDER BY total_score DESC;

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A ride platform reports the daily cancellation rate but excludes banned riders and drivers so the number is not polluted.
  • Trips logs each trip with a status and request date; Users flags who is banned.
  • Keep only trips whose rider and driver are both not banned, then for each day in Oct 1 to Oct 3 2013 return the share of trips whose status is not 'completed', rounded to 2 decimals.

Schema — Trips

ColumnType
idINTEGER
client_idINTEGER
driver_idINTEGER
city_idINTEGER
statusVARCHAR
request_atDATE

Example input — Trips

idclient_iddriver_idcity_idstatusrequest_at
11101completed2013-10-01
22111cancelled_by_driver2013-10-01
33126completed2013-10-01
44136cancelled_by_client2013-10-01
51101completed2013-10-02
62116completed2013-10-02
73126completed2013-10-02
821212completed2013-10-03
931012completed2013-10-03
1041312cancelled_by_driver2013-10-03

Schema — Users

ColumnType
users_idINTEGER
bannedVARCHAR
roleVARCHAR

Example input — Users

users_idbannedrole
1Noclient
2Yesclient
3Noclient
4Noclient
10Nodriver
11Nodriver
12Nodriver
13Nodriver

Expected output

DayCancellation Rate
2013-10-010.33
2013-10-020.0
2013-10-030.5

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Joining Trips to Users twice -- once as the rider, once as the driver -- with banned = 'No' in the ON
  acts as a filter: a trip survives only if both parties are clean. The cancellation rate is the average
  of a 0/1 flag for status <> 'completed', which is just cancelled trips over kept trips per day. Trips
  with banned client 2 drop out, leaving Oct 1 at 1/3, Oct 2 at 0/2, Oct 3 at 1/2.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT t.request_at AS "Day",
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN t.status <> 'completed' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS "Cancellation Rate"
FROM Trips t
JOIN Users c ON c.users_id = t.client_id AND c.banned = 'No'   -- rider not banned
JOIN Users d ON d.users_id = t.driver_id AND d.banned = 'No'   -- driver not banned
WHERE t.request_at BETWEEN DATE '2013-10-01' AND DATE '2013-10-03'
GROUP BY t.request_at
ORDER BY t.request_at;

Aggregate + filter (HAVING / conditional CASE) 13 problems

▼

The aggregate is the filter or the filter sits inside the aggregate. HAVING keeps groups whose totals meet a cutoff (bought all products, friends in common ≥ N); SUM(CASE WHEN ...) conditional aggregation counts only the rows that match a predicate per group.

Aggregate + filter (HAVING / conditional CASE)

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. JOIN + GROUP BY the entity.
  2. HAVING filters groups whose AGGREGATE meets a threshold (e.g. bought-all-products = HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products)).
  3. For "sum only the rows matching X per group", use a conditional aggregate: SUM(CASE WHEN tag = 'X' THEN amount ELSE 0 END).
-- HAVING: keep groups whose totals meet a cutoff (e.g. bought all products)
SELECT a.entity_id
FROM entity a
JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT b.product_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products);

-- Conditional CASE: count / sum only qualifying rows per group
SELECT a.entity_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN b.tag = 'X' THEN b.amount ELSE 0 END) AS amount_x
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id;

Prompt

  • A loyalty team finds VIP customers who have bought one of every product.
  • Customer logs each (customer, product) purchase; Product lists the full catalog.
  • Return the customer ids whose distinct product count equals the catalog size, ordered by customer id.

Schema — Customer

ColumnType
customer_idINTEGER
product_keyINTEGER

Example input — Customer

customer_idproduct_key
15

35
36

Schema — Product

ColumnType
product_keyINTEGER

Example input — Product

product_key
5

customer_id
1
3

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  This is relational division: keep a customer only if their distinct product count matches the whole
  catalog. GROUP BY collapses to one row per customer; HAVING compares that count to the scalar catalog
  size. Customers 1 and 3 each bought both products; customer 2 bought only one.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT customer_id
FROM Customer
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_key) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Product)   -- bought the whole catalog
ORDER BY customer_id;

Medium Investments in 2016

▼

Sum one column over policies that share a value on one column but are unique on another.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An insurer totals coverage over a risk pool: policies whose 2015 value is shared with another policy, but whose location is one of a kind.
  • Insurance has each policy's 2015 and 2016 values plus a latitude and longitude.
  • Sum tiv_2016 over policies where tiv_2015 appears on more than one policy AND the (lat, lon) pair appears on exactly one policy, rounded to 2 decimals.

Schema — Insurance

ColumnType
pidINTEGER
tiv_2015INTEGER
tiv_2016INTEGER
latINTEGER
lonINTEGER

Example input — Insurance

pidtiv_2015tiv_2016latlon
11051010
220202020
310302020
410404040

Expected output

tiv_2016
45.0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Two independent group conditions: tiv_2015 must be shared (its group count > 1) and the location must be
  unique (its group count = 1). The cleanest read is two uncorrelated subqueries in WHERE, one grouping on
  tiv_2015, one on (lat, lon). Policy 1 (shared 10, unique location) and policy 4 (shared 10, unique
  location) qualify: 5 + 40 = 45.00. Policy 3 shares its location, policy 2's value is not shared.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the single expected row.
*/

SELECT ROUND(SUM(tiv_2016), 2) AS tiv_2016
FROM Insurance
WHERE tiv_2015 IN (SELECT tiv_2015 FROM Insurance GROUP BY tiv_2015 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1)   -- shared value
  AND (lat, lon) IN (SELECT lat, lon FROM Insurance GROUP BY lat, lon HAVING COUNT(*) = 1);  -- unique spot

Medium Team Scores in Football Tournament

▼

League points per team from match results: win 3, draw 1, loss 0.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A sports site builds a standings table from match results.
  • Teams lists each team; Matches has the host, guest, and goals for each game.
  • Award 3 points for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss, sum per team (including teams with no points), ordered by points then team id.

Schema — Teams

ColumnType
team_idINTEGER
team_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Teams

team_idteam_name
10Leopards
20Falcons
30Bears

Schema — Matches

ColumnType
match_idINTEGER
host_teamINTEGER
guest_teamINTEGER
host_goalsINTEGER
guest_goalsINTEGER

Example input — Matches

match_idhost_teamguest_teamhost_goalsguest_goals
1102030
2301022
3103051
4203011

Expected output

team_idteam_namenum_points
10Leopards7
30Bears2
20Falcons1

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A team appears as host in some rows and guest in others, so normalize both into one (team_id, points)
  stream with UNION ALL, scoring each side with a CASE. LEFT JOIN from Teams keeps teams that never scored,
  and COALESCE turns their NULL sum into 0. Leopards win twice and draw once for 7; Falcons manage one draw.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH scored AS (
    SELECT host_team AS team_id,
           CASE WHEN host_goals > guest_goals THEN 3
                WHEN host_goals = guest_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS pts
    FROM Matches
    UNION ALL
    SELECT guest_team,
           CASE WHEN guest_goals > host_goals THEN 3
                WHEN guest_goals = host_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
    FROM Matches
)
SELECT t.team_id, t.team_name, COALESCE(SUM(s.pts), 0) AS num_points
FROM Teams t
LEFT JOIN scored s ON s.team_id = t.team_id
GROUP BY t.team_id, t.team_name
ORDER BY num_points DESC, t.team_id;

Medium Strong Friendship

▼

Friend pairs who share at least three friends in common.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A community team highlights tightly clustered pairs: two people who are friends and have many mutual friends.
  • Friendship has one row per friendship as a pair; friendship is mutual.
  • Return each friend pair (smaller id first) with three or more common friends, along with that common count.

Schema — Friendship

ColumnType
user1_idINTEGER
user2_idINTEGER

Example input — Friendship

user1_iduser2_id
12
13
23
14
24
15
25

Expected output

user1_iduser2_idcommon_friend
123

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Mirror friendships so the graph is undirected, then walk a triangle: edge a is the pair itself, edge b
  steps from one end to a third person w, edge c confirms w connects back to the other end. Each surviving
  w is a mutual friend, so COUNT over the pair is the common-friend total; HAVING keeps pairs with three or
  more. Users 1 and 2 are friends and both know 3, 4, and 5 -- three in common.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the single expected row.
*/

WITH f AS (
    SELECT user1_id AS u, user2_id AS v FROM Friendship
    UNION ALL
    SELECT user2_id, user1_id FROM Friendship
)
SELECT a.u AS user1_id, a.v AS user2_id, COUNT(*) AS common_friend
FROM f a
JOIN f b ON b.u = a.v AND b.v <> a.u      -- step to a third person
JOIN f c ON c.u = b.v AND c.v = a.u       -- who connects back: a mutual friend
WHERE a.u < a.v
GROUP BY a.u, a.v
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY user1_id, user2_id;

Medium Market Analysis III

▼

Sellers whose first ever sale was an item of their stated favorite brand.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An onboarding report flags sellers whose first sale matched the brand they said they loved.
  • Users has each user's favorite brand; Orders logs sales by seller and date; Items maps items to brands.
  • Rank each seller's orders by date, keep the first, and return sellers whose first item's brand equals their favorite brand, ordered by seller id.

Schema — Users

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
join_dateDATE
favorite_brandVARCHAR

Example input — Users

user_idjoin_datefavorite_brand
12019-01-01Nike
22019-01-01Adidas
32019-01-01Puma

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
order_dateDATE
item_idINTEGER
buyer_idINTEGER
seller_idINTEGER

Example input — Orders

order_idorder_dateitem_idbuyer_idseller_id
12019-08-0110151
22019-08-0510451
32019-08-0210362
42019-08-0310363

Schema — Items

ColumnType
item_idINTEGER

Example input — Items

item_iditem_brand
101Nike
102Adidas
103Puma
104Nike

Expected output

seller_id
1
3

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  ROW_NUMBER over each seller's orders by date marks the first sale (rn = 1). Joining that row to Items
  gives its brand, and the WHERE keeps sellers whose first brand equals their favorite. Seller 1's first
  item is Nike (their favorite); seller 3's is Puma (theirs); seller 2's first is Puma but they favor
  Adidas, so they drop.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT o.seller_id, o.item_id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.seller_id ORDER BY o.order_date) AS rn
    FROM Orders o
)
SELECT u.user_id AS seller_id
FROM Users u
JOIN ranked r ON r.seller_id = u.user_id AND r.rn = 1   -- their first sale
JOIN Items  i ON i.item_id   = r.item_id
WHERE i.item_brand = u.favorite_brand
ORDER BY u.user_id;

Hard Friend Recommendations by Shared Listens

▼

Recommend user pairs who played three or more of the same songs on one day and are not already friends.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A music app recommends new connections: people who listened to at least three of the same songs on the same day, but who are not friends yet.
  • Listens logs each (user, song, day); Friendship lists existing friendships.
  • Return the recommended user pairs (smaller id first).

Schema — Listens

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
song_idINTEGER
dayDATE

Example input — Listens

user_idsong_idday
1102021-03-15
1202021-03-15
1302021-03-15
2102021-03-15
2202021-03-15
2302021-03-15
3102021-03-15
3202021-03-15

Schema — Friendship

ColumnType
user1_idINTEGER
user2_idINTEGER

Example input — Friendship

user1_iduser2_id
13

Expected output

user1_iduser2_id
12

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Self-join Listens on the same song and day with user_id < user_id to pair co-listeners once. Group each
  pair within a day and keep those sharing three or more distinct songs. A NOT EXISTS anti-join against
  Friendship drops pairs who are already friends. Users 1 and 2 share three songs and are not friends;
  user 3 only overlaps on two.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the single expected row.
*/

WITH co AS (
    SELECT a.user_id AS u1, b.user_id AS u2, a.day, a.song_id
    FROM Listens a
    JOIN Listens b ON a.song_id = b.song_id AND a.day = b.day AND a.user_id < b.user_id
),
pairs AS (
    SELECT u1, u2, COUNT(DISTINCT song_id) AS shared
    FROM co
    GROUP BY u1, u2, day
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT song_id) >= 3        -- three shared songs in one day
)
SELECT u1 AS user1_id, u2 AS user2_id
FROM pairs p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM Friendship f
    WHERE (f.user1_id = p.u1 AND f.user2_id = p.u2)
       OR (f.user1_id = p.u2 AND f.user2_id = p.u1)   -- skip existing friends
)
ORDER BY user1_id, user2_id;

Hard Similar Friends by Shared Listens

Existing friend pairs who played three or more of the same songs on a single day.

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A music app marks existing friends as similar when they listened to at least three of the same songs on the same day.
  • Listens logs each (user, song, day); Friendship lists the friendships to check.
  • Return the qualifying friend pairs.

Schema — Listens

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
song_idINTEGER
dayDATE

Example input — Listens

user_idsong_idday
1102021-05-01
1202021-05-01
1302021-05-01
2102021-05-01
2202021-05-01
2302021-05-01

Schema — Friendship

ColumnType
user1_idINTEGER

Example input — Friendship

user1_iduser2_id

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Start from Friendship so only existing pairs are considered, then join each side to Listens and match on
  the same song and day. Grouping per pair per day and requiring three or more distinct shared songs gives
  the similar friends. DISTINCT collapses any pair that qualifies on more than one day. Friends 1 and 2
  share three songs on May 1.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the single expected row.
*/

SELECT DISTINCT f.user1_id, f.user2_id
FROM Friendship f
JOIN Listens a ON a.user_id = f.user1_id
JOIN Listens b ON b.user_id = f.user2_id
              AND a.song_id = b.song_id
              AND a.day = b.day                 -- same song, same day
GROUP BY f.user1_id, f.user2_id, a.day
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.song_id) >= 3
ORDER BY f.user1_id, f.user2_id;

Medium Countries You Can Safely Invest In

▼

Countries whose average call duration beats the global average call duration.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A telecom rates countries by engagement: those whose average call length exceeds the worldwide average.
  • Person has each person's phone number (its first three digits are the country code); Country maps codes to names; Calls logs each call's two parties and duration.
  • A person's calls count whether they were the caller or the callee. Return country names whose average call duration is greater than the global average.

Schema — Person

ColumnType
idINTEGER
nameVARCHAR
phone_numberVARCHAR

Example input — Person

idnamephone_number
1Ana111222333
2Bo222333444
3Cy111999888

Schema — Country

ColumnType
nameVARCHAR
country_codeVARCHAR

Example input — Country

namecountry_code
Xland111
Yland222

Schema — Calls

ColumnType
caller_idINTEGER
callee_idINTEGER
durationINTEGER

Example input — Calls

caller_idcallee_idduration
1230
2340
3150

Expected output

country
Xland

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The country code is the first three digits of the phone number. Each call touches two people, so a
  UNION ALL attributes the duration to both the caller's and the callee's country. Grouping by country and
  comparing its average to the global average in HAVING keeps the strong ones. Xland averages 42.5 against
  a global 40; Yland's 35 falls short.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the single expected row.
*/

WITH lined AS (
    SELECT p.id, SUBSTRING(p.phone_number, 1, 3) AS code FROM Person p
),
durations AS (
    SELECT lined.code, c.duration FROM Calls c JOIN lined ON lined.id = c.caller_id
    UNION ALL
    SELECT lined.code, c.duration FROM Calls c JOIN lined ON lined.id = c.callee_id
)
SELECT co.name AS country
FROM durations d
JOIN Country co ON co.country_code = d.code
GROUP BY co.name
HAVING AVG(d.duration) > (SELECT AVG(duration) FROM Calls)   -- beats the global mean
ORDER BY country;

Hard Page Recommendations II

▼

For each user, pages liked by their friends that they have not liked, with the count of such friends.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A social product recommends pages by how many of your friends like them.
  • Friendship lists mutual friendships; Likes logs which pages each user likes.
  • For each user, return pages liked by their friends that the user has not liked, with the number of friends who liked each, ordered by user, then friend count descending, then page.

Schema — Friendship

ColumnType
user1_idINTEGER
user2_idINTEGER

Example input — Friendship

user1_iduser2_id
12
13

Schema — Likes

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
page_idINTEGER

Example input — Likes

user_idpage_id
250
260
350
370
180

Expected output

user_idpage_idfriends_likes
1502
1601
1701
2801
3801

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Mirror friendships so each user sees all their friends, then join to the friends' likes. A NOT EXISTS
  anti-join removes pages the user already likes, and COUNT(DISTINCT friend) per page is the recommendation
  strength. User 1's friends 2 and 3 both like page 50 (count 2); page 80 is liked only by user 1, so it
  is recommended back to friends 2 and 3.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

WITH friends AS (
    SELECT user1_id AS u, user2_id AS f FROM Friendship
    UNION ALL
    SELECT user2_id, user1_id FROM Friendship
)
SELECT f.u AS user_id, l.page_id, COUNT(DISTINCT f.f) AS friends_likes
FROM friends f
JOIN Likes l ON l.user_id = f.f
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM Likes lk WHERE lk.user_id = f.u AND lk.page_id = l.page_id   -- user has not liked it
)
GROUP BY f.u, l.page_id
ORDER BY f.u, friends_likes DESC, l.page_id;

Hard Viewers Turned Streamers

▼

Users whose first session was as a viewer, with a count of their later streaming sessions.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A video platform studies the viewer to creator funnel: users who started as viewers and later streamed.
  • Sessions logs each session's user, start time, and type ('Viewer' or 'Streamer').
  • Keep users whose earliest session was a Viewer, then count their Streamer sessions, ordered by that count descending then user id descending.

Schema — Sessions

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
session_startTIMESTAMP
session_typeVARCHAR

Example input — Sessions

user_idsession_startsession_type
12021-01-01 10:00:00Viewer
12021-01-02 10:00:00Streamer
12021-01-03 10:00:00Streamer
22021-01-01 10:00:00Streamer
22021-01-02 10:00:00Streamer
32021-01-01 10:00:00Viewer
32021-01-05 10:00:00Streamer

Expected output

user_idsessions_count
12
31

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  ROW_NUMBER per user by start time identifies the very first session; keeping rn = 1 with type 'Viewer'
  selects users who began as viewers. Joining those users back to their 'Streamer' sessions and counting
  gives the conversion volume. User 1 started as a viewer and later streamed twice; user 2 began streaming
  so they are excluded.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH firsts AS (
    SELECT user_id, session_type AS first_type,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY session_start) AS rn
    FROM Sessions
)
SELECT s.user_id, COUNT(*) AS sessions_count
FROM firsts f
JOIN Sessions s ON s.user_id = f.user_id AND s.session_type = 'Streamer'
WHERE f.rn = 1 AND f.first_type = 'Viewer'      -- started out as a viewer
GROUP BY s.user_id
ORDER BY sessions_count DESC, s.user_id DESC;

Hard Market Analysis II

▼

For every seller, flag whether their second ever sale was an item of their favorite brand.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An onboarding analyst checks whether a seller's second sale was their favorite brand, a signal that predicts engagement.
  • Users has each user's favorite brand; Orders logs sales by seller and date; Items maps items to brands.
  • Return every user with 'yes' or 'no' for whether their second order's item brand equals their favorite; sellers with fewer than two orders are 'no', ordered by seller id.

Schema — Users

ColumnType
user_idINTEGER
join_dateDATE
favorite_brandVARCHAR

Example input — Users

user_idjoin_datefavorite_brand
12019-01-01Nike
22019-01-01Adidas
32019-01-01Puma

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
order_dateDATE
item_idINTEGER
buyer_idINTEGER
seller_idINTEGER

Example input — Orders

order_idorder_dateitem_idbuyer_idseller_id
12019-08-0110191
22019-08-0510291
32019-08-0110192
42019-08-0510292
52019-08-0110393

Schema — Items

ColumnType
item_idINTEGER
item_brandVARCHAR

Example input — Items

item_iditem_brand
101Nike
102Adidas
103Puma

Expected output

seller_id2nd_item_fav_brand
1no
2yes
3no

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  ROW_NUMBER per seller by date picks out the second order (rn = 2). LEFT JOINs from Users keep every
  seller, so a seller with fewer than two orders has no matched item and a NULL brand. The CASE compares
  that brand to the favorite, and because NULL never equals the favorite it naturally lands on 'no'. The
  column name starts with a digit, so it is double-quoted. Seller 2's second item is Adidas, their
  favorite; seller 1's second is Adidas but they favor Nike; seller 3 has only one order.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT o.seller_id, o.item_id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.seller_id ORDER BY o.order_date) AS rn
    FROM Orders o
)
SELECT u.user_id AS seller_id,
       CASE WHEN i.item_brand = u.favorite_brand THEN 'yes' ELSE 'no' END AS "2nd_item_fav_brand"
FROM Users u
LEFT JOIN ranked r ON r.seller_id = u.user_id AND r.rn = 2   -- their second sale
LEFT JOIN Items  i ON i.item_id = r.item_id
ORDER BY u.user_id;

Easy Weather Type in Each Country

▼

Label each country Cold, Hot, or Warm from its average November temperature.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A travel site tags each country with a climate label to power destination filters.
  • Countries lists each country; Weather logs daily temperatures.
  • Over November 2019, label a country 'Cold' if its average temperature is 15 or below, 'Hot' if 25 or above, and 'Warm' otherwise, ordered by country id.

Schema — Countries

ColumnType
country_idINTEGER
country_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Countries

country_idcountry_name
1USA
2Peru
3Spain

Schema — Weather

ColumnType
country_idINTEGER
weather_stateINTEGER
dayDATE

Example input — Weather

country_idweather_stateday
152019-11-01
1102019-11-15
2302019-11-02
2282019-11-20
3182019-11-05
3222019-11-25

Expected output

country_nameweather_type
USACold
PeruHot
SpainWarm

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Filter to the November window first, then average each country's temperature and bucket it with a CASE.
  The thresholds are inclusive at the edges (15 and below is Cold, 25 and above is Hot). USA averages 7.5
  (Cold), Peru 29 (Hot), Spain 20 (Warm).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT c.country_name,
       CASE WHEN AVG(w.weather_state) <= 15 THEN 'Cold'
            WHEN AVG(w.weather_state) >= 25 THEN 'Hot'
            ELSE 'Warm' END AS weather_type
FROM Countries c
JOIN Weather w ON w.country_id = c.country_id
WHERE w.day BETWEEN DATE '2019-11-01' AND DATE '2019-11-30'
GROUP BY c.country_id, c.country_name
ORDER BY c.country_id;

Hard Status of Flight Tickets

▼

Label each passenger Confirmed or Waitlist by booking order against the flight's capacity.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An airline issues seats first come first served up to each flight's capacity; the rest are waitlisted.
  • Flights has each flight's capacity; Passengers logs each booking with its time.
  • Within each flight, rank passengers by booking time and label the first capacity of them 'Confirmed' and the rest 'Waitlist', ordered by passenger id.

Schema — Flights

ColumnType
flight_idINTEGER
capacityINTEGER

Example input — Flights

flight_idcapacity
12
21

Schema — Passengers

ColumnType
passenger_idINTEGER
flight_idINTEGER
booking_timeTIMESTAMP

Example input — Passengers

passenger_idflight_idbooking_time
10112021-01-01 09:00:00
10212021-01-01 09:05:00
10312021-01-01 09:10:00
10422021-01-01 08:00:00
10522021-01-01 08:30:00

Expected output

passenger_idStatus
101Confirmed
102Confirmed
103Waitlist
104Confirmed
105Waitlist

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  ROW_NUMBER per flight ordered by booking time gives each passenger their place in line. Joining to the
  flight's capacity, a CASE confirms anyone whose rank is within capacity and waitlists the rest. Flight 1
  seats two, so its third booking is waitlisted; flight 2 seats one, so its second booking is waitlisted.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

SELECT p.passenger_id,
       CASE WHEN rn <= f.capacity THEN 'Confirmed' ELSE 'Waitlist' END AS Status
FROM (
    SELECT passenger_id, flight_id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY flight_id ORDER BY booking_time) AS rn
    FROM Passengers
) p
JOIN Flights f ON f.flight_id = p.flight_id
ORDER BY p.passenger_id;

Date-window / cohort aggregate 3 problems

▼

The grouping key is a date bucket (DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date)) or the data has to be reshaped against a calendar / signup spine before aggregating. Cohort retention and reorder-rate problems all live here. For problems where you must MANUFACTURE missing buckets (e.g. "every week including weeks with zero activity"), see Reshape → Series Generation — that recipe owns the generate_series spine + CROSS JOIN entities + LEFT JOIN actuals pattern.

Date-bucket / cohort aggregate

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date) as the cohort grouping key.
  2. JOIN actions to users on user_id.
  3. SUM(CASE WHEN event_date BETWEEN signup_date AND signup_date + INTERVAL '30 days' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts the in-window events per cohort.
  4. GROUP BY the cohort key and ORDER BY it for a clean time series.
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', a.signup_date) AS cohort_month,
    COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id)          AS cohort_size,
    SUM(CASE WHEN b.event_date BETWEEN a.signup_date
                                   AND a.signup_date + INTERVAL '30 days'
             THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)        AS retained_30d
FROM users a
LEFT JOIN events b ON b.user_id = a.user_id
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', a.signup_date)
ORDER BY cohort_month;

Easy List the Products Ordered in a Period

▼

Products with at least 100 units ordered inside a date window, with their total units.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • An inventory team finds high-demand products in a given month to plan restocking.
  • Products names each product; Orders logs units ordered per product per date.
  • Return product names whose total units ordered in February 2020 reach at least 100, along with that total.

Schema — Products

ColumnType
product_idINTEGER
product_nameVARCHAR
product_categoryVARCHAR

Example input — Products

product_idproduct_nameproduct_category
1Widgettools
2Gadgettools
3Gizmotoys

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
product_idINTEGER
order_dateDATE
unitINTEGER

Example input — Orders

product_idorder_dateunit
12020-02-0560
12020-02-2050
22020-02-1080
32020-01-15200
12020-03-0240

Expected output

product_nameunit
Widget110

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Filter to the February window first with a half-open range (>= Feb 1 and < Mar 1), which avoids any
  end-of-month edge cases. Joining to Products and grouping per product totals its units, and HAVING keeps
  only products that reach 100. Widget orders 60 + 50 = 110 in February; Gadget reaches only 80, and
  Gizmo's 200 units fall in January.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the single expected row.
*/

SELECT p.product_name, SUM(o.unit) AS unit
FROM Products p
INNER JOIN Orders o ON p.product_id = o.product_id
WHERE o.order_date >= DATE '2020-02-01' AND o.order_date < DATE '2020-03-01'   -- February window
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
HAVING SUM(o.unit) >= 100
ORDER BY p.product_name;

Hard Game Play Analysis V

▼

Per install date, the number of installs and the day-one retention rate.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A growth analyst measures day one retention per install cohort.
  • Activity logs one row per player per day they played.
  • Group players by their install date (their first play day). For each install date, return how many players installed and the fraction who also played the very next day, rounded to 2 decimals.

Schema — Activity

ColumnType
player_idINTEGER
device_idINTEGER
event_dateDATE
games_playedINTEGER

Example input — Activity

player_iddevice_idevent_dategames_played
122016-03-015
122016-03-026
232016-03-011
312017-06-250
312017-06-262

Expected output

install_dateinstallsDay1_retention
2016-03-0120.5
2017-06-2511.0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  firsts pins each player's install date as their earliest event. The LEFT JOIN back to Activity matches a
  row only when the same player also played exactly one day later, so a non-NULL match marks a retained
  player. Per install date, COUNT(*) is the cohort size and the average of the retained flag is day one
  retention (the * 1.0 keeps the division decimal). On Mar 1, one of two players returned (0.50); the lone
  Jun 25 installer returned (1.00).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH firsts AS (
    SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS install_date
    FROM Activity
    GROUP BY player_id
)
SELECT f.install_date,
       COUNT(*) AS installs,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN a.player_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0
             / COUNT(*), 2) AS Day1_retention
FROM firsts f
LEFT JOIN Activity a
  ON a.player_id = f.player_id
 AND a.event_date = f.install_date + INTERVAL '1 day'   -- came back the next day
GROUP BY f.install_date
ORDER BY f.install_date;

Medium Monthly Ad Revenue by Cohort Month

▼

Bucket players into signup-month cohorts, then total distinct players and ad revenue per cohort.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A free-to-play game reports ad revenue by signup cohort to see which monthly intake monetizes best.
  • players has each player's signup date; player_sessions logs sessions with ad impressions.
  • Group players into monthly signup cohorts (the first day of their signup month). Per cohort return the count of distinct players and total ad revenue, where each impression is worth $0.02, ordered by cohort month.
  • Every player who signed up that month belongs to the cohort, whether or not they have played a session.

Schema — players

ColumnType
player_idINTEGER
usernameVARCHAR
signup_dateDATE

Example input — players

player_idusernamesignup_date
1ana2021-01-05
2bo2021-01-20
3cy2021-02-03

Schema — player_sessions

ColumnType
session_idINTEGER
player_idINTEGER
session_startTIMESTAMP
ad_impressionsINTEGER

Example input — player_sessions

session_idplayer_idsession_startad_impressions
112021-01-10 10:00:00100
212021-01-12 11:00:0050
332021-02-05 09:00:00200

Expected output

cohort_monthtotal_playerstotal_ad_revenue
2021-01-0123.0
2021-02-0114.0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  DATE_TRUNC snaps each signup to the first of its month, the cohort key. The LEFT JOIN to sessions keeps
  players who never played, so they still count toward the cohort while their NULL revenue is ignored by
  SUM. COUNT(DISTINCT player_id) -- not COUNT(*) -- counts players, since one player has many sessions, and
  the cohort always comes from signup_date, never the session time. January signed up two players earning
  150 impressions (3.00); February's lone player earns 4.00.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

WITH cohort_sessions AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', p.signup_date)::date AS cohort_month,   -- first of signup month
           p.player_id,
           ps.ad_impressions * 0.02 AS ad_revenue
    FROM players AS p
    LEFT JOIN player_sessions AS ps ON ps.player_id = p.player_id
)
SELECT cohort_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT player_id)                   AS total_players,
       COALESCE(SUM(ad_revenue), 0)::numeric(10,2) AS total_ad_revenue
FROM cohort_sessions
GROUP BY cohort_month
ORDER BY cohort_month;

Set membership gate: has ALL of X, none of Y 2 problems

▼

Filter entities whose set of related rows satisfies a membership rule: ALL of a required category set AND NONE of a forbidden category set. The technique is CASE inside an aggregate, used as a HAVING gate (existence flag per category), not as a SELECT projection. Sister leaf to filter by aggregate threshold: same CASE-in-aggregate family, but the test is presence/absence per category, not a numeric cutoff.

Template — set membership gate (HAVING MAX(CASE))

▼

Use when: keep entities that have ALL of some categories and NONE of others ("bought A and B but not C").

What this template does, step by step:

  1. JOIN entity to its category rows, GROUP BY the entity.
  2. One HAVING line per category: MAX(CASE WHEN cat = 'X' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) — = 1 means "has at least one X", = 0 means "never X".
  3. The JOIN means entities with no rows never reach the GROUP, so they drop without extra work.
SELECT a.entity_id, a.name
FROM entity a
JOIN fact f ON f.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.name
HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN f.cat = 'X' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1   -- has X
   AND MAX(CASE WHEN f.cat = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1   -- has Y
   AND MAX(CASE WHEN f.cat = 'Z' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0   -- never Z
ORDER BY a.entity_id;
-- Postgres: BOOL_OR(f.cat = 'X') in place of MAX(CASE...)=1

Easy Customers Who Bought A AND B but NOT C

▼

Customers who bought both required products but never the forbidden one, using a per-category existence flag.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Marketing wants a next best product list: recommend C to customers who already bought A and B but never bought C.
  • Customers names each customer; Orders logs each purchase by product, and a customer can buy the same product on more than one order.
  • Return the customer id and name of those who bought A and B but not C, ordered by customer id.

Schema — Customers

ColumnType
customer_idINTEGER
customer_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Customers

customer_idcustomer_name
1Daniel
2Diana
3Elizabeth
4Jhon

Schema — Orders

ColumnType
order_idINTEGER
customer_idINTEGER
product_nameVARCHAR

Example input — Orders

order_idcustomer_idproduct_name
11A
21B
31D
41C
52A
63A
73B
83D
94C

Expected output

customer_idcustomer_name
3Elizabeth

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  This is a membership test, not arithmetic. For each category build a presence flag with MAX(CASE ...): it
  is 1 if the customer ever bought that product and 0 otherwise, no matter how many times. HAVING then ANDs
  the flags -- A and B must be present (= 1), C must be absent (= 0). The counting trap to avoid: a plain
  SUM of matches would let a customer who bought A three times fake their way past a "= 2" threshold;
  presence flags sidestep that. Only Elizabeth has A and B and lacks C; Daniel also owns C.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the single expected row.
*/

SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM Customers AS c
JOIN Orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name
HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN o.product_name = 'A' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1    -- bought A
   AND MAX(CASE WHEN o.product_name = 'B' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1    -- bought B
   AND MAX(CASE WHEN o.product_name = 'C' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0    -- never bought C
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Medium Prior Auth Coverage Gap Analysis

▼

Per provider, keep those with at least one MRI AND one CT Scan but zero X-Rays. One GROUP BY, a three-part HAVING gate of MAX(CASE...).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Return provider_id and provider_name for providers whose prior-auth requests include at least one MRI AND at least one CT Scan AND zero X-Ray.
  • Providers with no requests at all do not appear. Order by provider_id.

Schema — providers

ColumnType
provider_idINT
provider_nameVARCHAR

Schema — prior_authorizations

ColumnType
auth_idINT
provider_idINT
imaging_modalityVARCHAR

Example input — providers

provider_idprovider_name
101Dr. Alice Chen
102Dr. Bob Martinez
103Dr. Carol Singh
104Dr. David Kim

Example input — prior_authorizations

auth_idprovider_idimaging_modality
1101MRI
2101CT Scan
3102MRI
4102X-Ray
5102CT Scan
6103MRI
7103CT Scan
8103MRI

Expected output

provider_idprovider_name
101Dr. Alice Chen
103Dr. Carol Singh

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  GROUP BY provider, then a three-part HAVING gate over MAX(CASE ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END):
  = 1 means 'has at least one' (MRI, CT Scan), = 0 means 'never' (X-Ray). The JOIN means a
  provider only reaches the GROUP if they have at least one request, so no-request providers
  (104) drop for free. Provider 102 has an X-Ray, so its X-Ray MAX(CASE) = 1, failing the = 0
  test. (BOOL_OR(...) works in place of MAX(CASE)=1 in Postgres.)

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT
    p.provider_id,
    p.provider_name
FROM prior_authorizations AS pa
JOIN providers AS p ON p.provider_id = pa.provider_id
GROUP BY p.provider_id, p.provider_name
HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN pa.imaging_modality = 'MRI'     THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1   -- has an MRI
   AND MAX(CASE WHEN pa.imaging_modality = 'CT Scan' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1   -- has a CT Scan
   AND MAX(CASE WHEN pa.imaging_modality = 'X-Ray'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0   -- never an X-Ray
ORDER BY p.provider_id;

Filtered Join (filter in the JOIN ON) 6 patterns

▼

Keep every entity but count only the qualifying joined rows. A filter on the RIGHT (joined) table rides in the ON; the same filter in WHERE silently turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN and drops the non-matchers.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

LEFT JOIN with a filter in the ON (keep every entity) 2 problems

▼

The "every entity must appear, count only the qualifying rows" shape. A condition on the RIGHT (joined) table — a status, a category, or (the variant here) a date range — rides in the ON so non-matching entities survive with a 0. The same condition in WHERE silently turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN and drops them. This leaf collects problems where that ON-vs-WHERE choice is the whole game; the date-range form below is the one that differs from the plain status / category examples elsewhere. See also the canonical Orders in 2024 per Customer card and the top-of-recipe ON vs WHERE walkthrough.

Medium Weekly Module Completions by Department

▼

Completions per department per week over a fixed window, with every empty (department, week) cell still reading 0.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A weekly onboarding dashboard shows a row for every department every week; a week with zero completions is itself a signal, so it must read 0 rather than vanish.
  • departments names each department; module_completions logs each completion's department and date.
  • Over the four weeks starting Jan 1 2024 (weeks begin Jan 1, 8, 15, 22), report the completion count per (department, week), including empty cells as 0, ordered by department then week.

Schema — departments

ColumnType
department_idINTEGER
department_nameVARCHAR

Example input — departments

department_iddepartment_name
1Engineering
2Sales
3HR

Schema — module_completions

ColumnType
completion_idINTEGER
department_idINTEGER
employee_idINTEGER
module_nameVARCHAR
completion_dateDATE

Example input — module_completions

completion_iddepartment_idemployee_idmodule_namecompletion_date
11101M12024-01-03
21102M22024-01-05
31103M12024-01-10
42201M12024-01-12
52202M22024-01-18
63301M12024-01-25

Expected output

department_nameweek_startcompletions
Engineering2024-01-012
Engineering2024-01-081
Engineering2024-01-150
Engineering2024-01-220
HR2024-01-010
HR2024-01-080
HR2024-01-150
HR2024-01-221
Sales2024-01-010
Sales2024-01-081
Sales2024-01-151
Sales2024-01-220

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Build the skeleton first: generate_series produces the four week starts, and a CROSS JOIN with the
  distinct departments makes every (department, week) cell. The actuals attach with a LEFT JOIN whose ON
  carries BOTH conditions -- same department AND a half-open week window. Keeping the date test in the ON
  (not WHERE) is the whole trick: an empty cell survives with a NULL completion, and COUNT(completion_id)
  -- counting a right-side column, not * -- reports 0. The half-open bounds (>= start and < start + 7 days)
  drop each completion into exactly one week. Engineering's later weeks and most of HR's are empty 0s.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 12 expected rows.
*/

WITH week_spine AS (
    SELECT d.department_name, ws.week_start::date AS week_start
    FROM generate_series(DATE '2024-01-01', DATE '2024-01-28', INTERVAL '1 week') AS ws(week_start)
    CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT department_name FROM departments) AS d
),
modules AS (
    SELECT d.department_name, m.completion_id, m.completion_date
    FROM departments AS d
    JOIN module_completions AS m ON m.department_id = d.department_id
)
SELECT s.department_name, s.week_start,
       COUNT(m.completion_id) AS completions               -- right column: 0 when the cell is empty
FROM week_spine AS s
LEFT JOIN modules AS m
       ON m.department_name = s.department_name             -- same department
      AND m.completion_date >= s.week_start                 -- half-open week window, in the ON
      AND m.completion_date <  s.week_start + INTERVAL '7 days'
GROUP BY s.department_name, s.week_start
ORDER BY s.department_name, s.week_start;

Medium Benefits Enrollment Rates by Department

▼

Per department with a recent hire, count completed first-quarter enrollments, keeping zero-count departments at 0.

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • For departments that made at least one 2024 hire, report how many of their employees completed a benefits enrollment in the first quarter of 2024; a qualifying department with none still shows 0.
  • departments names each department; employees has hire dates; benefit_enrollments logs each enrollment's status and date.
  • Return department name, its count of distinct 2024+ hires, and its count of completed Q1 2024 enrollments, ordered by department name.

Schema — departments

ColumnType
department_idINTEGER
department_nameVARCHAR

Example input — departments

department_iddepartment_name
1Engineering
2Sales
3HR

Schema — employees

ColumnType
employee_idINTEGER
department_idINTEGER
employee_nameVARCHAR
hire_dateDATE

Example input — employees

employee_iddepartment_idemployee_namehire_date
1011Ann2024-02-01
1021Bob2023-01-01
2012Cy2024-03-01
3013Dee2022-05-01

Schema — benefit_enrollments

ColumnType
enrollment_idINTEGER
employee_idINTEGER
enrollment_statusVARCHAR
submitted_dateDATE

Example input — benefit_enrollments

enrollment_idemployee_idenrollment_statussubmitted_date
1101completed2024-02-15
2101completed2023-12-01
3101pending2024-02-20
4201pending2024-03-15

Expected output

department_nameemployee_countcompleted_q1_enrollments
Engineering11
Sales10

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Two filters of different kinds. The hire-date test is an INNER JOIN condition, so only departments with a
  2024+ hire appear at all (HR's lone 2022 hire drops it). The enrollment filters -- completed status AND a
  Q1 date window -- ride in the LEFT JOIN ON, so an employee with no qualifying enrollment still survives
  and COUNT(enrollment_id) lands at 0. COUNT(DISTINCT employee_id) keeps the headcount honest because the
  enrollment join fans one employee into several rows. Engineering has one recent hire with one Q1
  completion; Sales has one recent hire but only a pending enrollment, so 0.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT d.department_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT e.employee_id) AS employee_count,
       COUNT(b.enrollment_id)        AS completed_q1_enrollments
FROM departments AS d
JOIN employees AS e
    ON e.department_id = d.department_id
   AND e.hire_date >= DATE '2024-01-01'              -- INNER: department needs a 2024+ hire
LEFT JOIN benefit_enrollments AS b
    ON b.employee_id = e.employee_id
   AND b.enrollment_status = 'completed'             -- right-side filters in the ON, so an
   AND b.submitted_date >= DATE '2024-01-01'         -- employee with no completed Q1 enrollment
   AND b.submitted_date <  DATE '2024-04-01'         -- still survives with a 0
GROUP BY d.department_name
ORDER BY d.department_name;

The right-side filter is a status or category equality (status = 'resolved'). It rides in the ON so non-matching entities survive with a 0.

  • teams names each team; tickets logs each ticket's team and status.

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
The status filter (status = 'resolved') is on the RIGHT table, so it rides in the ON next to the join key. Beta's only ticket is open and Gamma has none, but the LEFT JOIN keeps both teams and COUNT(t.ticket_id) -- a right-side column, not * -- reports 0. Put status in WHERE and both teams vanish.

SELECT tm.team_id, tm.team_name, COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS resolved_count
FROM teams AS tm

/*

Hard Q1 Training for 2024 Hires

▼

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • For employees hired in 2024, count their training sessions completed in Q1 2024 (Jan 1 to Mar 31). A 2024 hire with no Q1 session must still appear with 0.
  • The hire-date test is about the LEFT (employee) table; the Q1 test is about the RIGHT (session) table.
  • employees lists each hire; sessions logs completed training.
  • Return emp_id, name, q1_sessions, ordered by emp_id.

Schema — employees

ColumnType
emp_idINT
nameVARCHAR
hire_dateDATE

Schema — sessions

ColumnType
session_idINT
emp_idINT
completed_dateDATE

Example input — employees

emp_idnamehire_date
1Ann2024-02-01
2Bob2023-05-01
3Cara2024-06-01

Example input — sessions

session_idemp_idcompleted_date
112024-01-10
212024-05-01
322024-01-15

Expected output

emp_idnameq1_sessions
1Ann1
3Cara0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
Two filters, two clauses. The LEFT-table filter (hired in 2024) removes Bob for real, so it MUST go in WHERE. The RIGHT-table filter (session in Q1) must go in ON so Cara -- a 2024 hire with no Q1 session -- still appears with 0. Swap them and it breaks: a left filter in ON is a no-op (Bob would sneak back), a right filter in WHERE drops Cara. Half-open date ranges throughout.
*/

SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, COUNT(s.session_id) AS q1_sessions
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN sessions AS s
    ON s.emp_id = e.emp_id
   AND s.completed_date >= DATE '2024-01-01'      -- RIGHT filter -> ON
   AND s.completed_date <  DATE '2024-04-01'
WHERE e.hire_date >= DATE '2024-01-01'            -- LEFT filter -> WHERE
  AND e.hire_date <  DATE '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY e.emp_id, e.name
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
The status filter rides in the ON so Ben (only a cancelled order) and Cy (no orders) survive. For a SUM the danger is NULL, not a miscount: with no qualifying row SUM returns NULL, so wrap it in COALESCE(SUM(...), 0). Amy's cancelled $999 never enters because the ON already filtered it out.

SELECT c.cust_id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS completed_spend

/*

Gated Lookup 4 problems

▼

Two tables share an entity key. A flag, threshold, or status in the FIRST table decides whether to compute a per-entity pick (min / max / earliest / latest / first value) from the SECOND table. Non-qualifying entities still appear in the output, usually with NULL or 0.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Walk the questions top to bottom — stop at the first match, tap the green box.

CASE around the aggregate 14 problems

▼

Every entity appears; the gate is a CASE on the picked value, fallback 0 or NULL when it fails.

CASE around the aggregate (back to tree)

▼

Use when: non-qualifiers must appear with NULL / 0, the gate reads only table A, and you're aggregating one B column.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. LEFT JOIN entity A to fact B (so every A row survives even with no B match).
  2. Aggregate B's picked column inside the SELECT: MIN/MAX/COUNT(b.col).
  3. Wrap the aggregate in a CASE WHEN a.gate ... THEN agg ELSE NULL END. CASE runs AFTER the aggregate — only show or hide.
  4. GROUP BY entity A's columns.
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    a.gate_col,
    CASE WHEN a.gate_col >= threshold
         THEN MIN(b.picked_col)
         ELSE NULL END AS picked_value
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.gate_col
ORDER BY a.entity_id;

Prompt

  • Dating app: for each match, return the earliest message time, but only when compatibility_score ≥ 70.
  • If the score is below 70 OR the match has no messages, return NULL.
  • Every match must appear exactly once, ordered by match_id.

Schema — matches

ColumnType

compatibility_scoreINTEGER

Schema — messages

ColumnType

match_idINTEGER
sent_atTIMESTAMP

Example input — matches

match_idcompatibility_score
185
292
355
478
548
688

Example input — messages

message_idmatch_idsent_at
112024-02-01 10:05:00
212024-02-01 10:03:00
322024-02-01 12:00:00
422024-02-01 11:30:00
532024-02-01 10:00:00
642024-02-01 15:00:00

Expected output

match_idcompatibility_scoreearliest_message_time
1852024-02-01 10:03:00
2922024-02-01 11:30:00

4782024-02-01 14:30:00
548NULL
688NULL

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The gate reads matches.compatibility_score (table A), so it belongs in a CASE around the
  aggregate, NOT in WHERE -- a WHERE on the score would drop matches 3 and 5, which the prompt
  needs kept with NULL. Two NULL paths fall out for free: the CASE returns NULL when the gate
  fails, and MIN over an empty group is already NULL when no messages attached (match 6). No
  COALESCE needed. (Equivalent shape: move the gate into the JOIN ON clause.)

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 6 expected rows.
*/

SELECT
    m.match_id,
    m.compatibility_score,
    CASE WHEN m.compatibility_score >= 70      -- gate reads table A only
         THEN MIN(msg.sent_at)                 -- earliest message for this match
         ELSE NULL END AS earliest_message_time
FROM matches m
LEFT JOIN messages msg ON msg.match_id = m.match_id   -- keep every match
GROUP BY m.match_id, m.compatibility_score            -- one row per match
ORDER BY m.match_id;

Medium Squad Invite Cost by Match Completion Gate

Prompt

  • Battle royale: per player, return the cheapest squad-invite cost, but only when completion_rate ≥ 75.
  • Players below the threshold show 0 (a sentinel integer, not NULL).
  • Only players who received at least one invite appear, ordered by player_id.

Schema — players

Schema — squad_invites

player_idINTEGER
coin_costINTEGER

Example input — players

10182.50

10391.25
10445.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Two small choices distinguish this from the plain CASE recipe. (1) FROM is the FACT table
  (squad_invites), so players with no invite drop naturally -- the prompt only wants players with
  at least one offer. (2) The ELSE returns 0, a sentinel value, not NULL -- read the prompt for
  which one it wants. MIN runs first; the gate filters its output afterward.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

SELECT
    s.player_id,
    p.completion_rate,
    CASE WHEN p.completion_rate >= 75    -- gate on table A
         THEN MIN(s.coin_cost)          -- cheapest invite for this player
         ELSE 0 END AS best_invite_cost  -- sentinel 0, not NULL
FROM squad_invites AS s                  -- FROM the fact: drops invite-less players
LEFT JOIN players AS p ON s.player_id = p.player_id
GROUP BY s.player_id, p.completion_rate
ORDER BY s.player_id;

/*

/*

Medium Refill Discount for Adherent Patients

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Refill adherence program: per patient, return their best discount (MAX(offer_amount)).
  • Show it only when adherence_rate ≥ 80; otherwise return 0.
  • A qualifying patient with no offers also returns 0. Order by patient_id.

Schema — patient_adherence

ColumnType
patient_idINTEGER
adherence_rateDECIMAL(5,2)

Schema — refill_offers

ColumnType
offer_idINTEGER
patient_idINTEGER
offer_amountDECIMAL(6,2)

Example input — patient_adherence

patient_idadherence_rate
185.00
270.00
392.00
488.00

Example input — refill_offers

offer_idpatient_idoffer_amount
115.00
218.00
326.00
4410.00

Expected output

patient_idadherence_ratebest_discount
185.008.00
270.000
392.000
488.0010.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Sentinel-0 variant. The per-patient MAX is pre-aggregated, then the gate (adherence_rate) shows
  it or returns 0. Because a qualifying patient with no offers must also read 0 (not NULL), the
  THEN branch wraps the value in COALESCE(..., 0): patient 3 passes the gate but has no offers,
  so COALESCE turns the NULL into 0.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

SELECT
    pa.patient_id,
    pa.adherence_rate,
    CASE WHEN pa.adherence_rate >= 80          -- gate on table A
         THEN COALESCE(ro_max.max_offer, 0)    -- no offers still reads 0, not NULL
         ELSE 0 END AS best_discount           -- sentinel 0 for non-qualifiers
FROM patient_adherence pa
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT patient_id, MAX(offer_amount) AS max_offer
    FROM refill_offers
    GROUP BY patient_id
) ro_max ON pa.patient_id = ro_max.patient_id
ORDER BY pa.patient_id;

ColumnType

brand_nameVARCHAR
avg_ratingDECIMAL(3,1)

Schema — cart_items

ColumnType

brand_idINTEGER

brand_idbrand_nameavg_rating
1Acme4.5
2Bolt3.2

4Dusk4.8

Example input — cart_items

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A CTE computes the per-brand minimum first, which keeps the final SELECT readable. The gate
  (avg_rating, on table A) shows it or returns 0. Brand 4 passes the gate but has no cart items,
  so COALESCE turns the missing minimum into 0.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH brand_min_price AS (
    SELECT brand_id, MIN(offer_price) AS min_price   -- cheapest item per brand
    FROM cart_items
    GROUP BY brand_id
)
SELECT
    b.brand_id,
    b.brand_name,
    CASE WHEN b.avg_rating >= 4.0                 -- gate on table A
         THEN COALESCE(bmp.min_price, 0)          -- no items still reads 0
         ELSE 0 END AS min_offer_price
FROM brands b
LEFT JOIN brand_min_price bmp ON b.brand_id = bmp.brand_id
ORDER BY b.brand_id;

/*
  A CTE computes the cheapest slot per creator. The gate stacks two conditions: quality_score >= 75
  AND min_cpm IS NOT NULL, so a high-quality creator with no slots falls to the ELSE 0.00 branch
  (creator 4). The IS NOT NULL check is what makes the no-slot case land on 0.00 instead of NULL.

FROM creators c

Gate in the JOIN ON 1 problem

▼

The gate (and any row filter on the joined table) goes in the ON so non-qualifiers drop before the aggregate runs.

Gate inside the JOIN ON clause (filter BEFORE aggregating)

▼

Use when: non-qualifiers must still appear AND you need to control which B rows are aggregated (a status / date / category filter on B, an entity gate on A, or both). The ON clause runs BEFORE the GROUP BY, so any condition you stack here decides what the aggregate even sees; non-matching B rows simply do not attach, and the LEFT JOIN keeps the entity row with NULL.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. LEFT JOIN A to B.
  2. Stack ALL filtering conditions (A-gate AND B-row filter, in any order) inside the ON clause with AND.
  3. ON runs BEFORE aggregation — non-matching B rows do not attach, A rows still appear (with NULL from the join).
  4. Aggregate normally; the LEFT JOIN preserves the A grain.
-- Single gate on A
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    a.gate_col,
    MIN(b.picked_col) AS picked_value
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b
       ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
      AND a.gate_col >= threshold
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.gate_col
ORDER BY a.entity_id;

-- Stacked: entity gate on A AND row filter on B
-- (multiple conditions just AND together in ON; the order does not matter)
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    a.gate_col,
    MIN(b.picked_col) AS picked_value
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b
       ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
      AND a.gate_col = 'qualified'
      AND b.row_filter = 'pending'
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.gate_col
ORDER BY a.entity_id;

Medium Reimbursement Cap by Vendor Status (gate on A + filter on B, both in ON)

▼

Lowest pending receipt per vendor, only for active vendors; both the entity gate and the row filter live in the JOIN ON.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Finance ops: per vendor, return the lowest PENDING receipt amount.
  • Only actively certified vendors (certification_status = 'active') get an amount; everyone else still appears with NULL.
  • Two conditions: an entity gate on the vendor (certification_status = 'active') and a row filter on the receipts (reimbursement_status = 'pending'). Order by vendor_id.

Schema — vendors

ColumnType
vendor_idINTEGER
vendor_nameVARCHAR
certification_statusVARCHAR

Schema — receipts

ColumnType
receipt_idINTEGER
vendor_idINTEGER
amountDECIMAL(8,2)
reimbursement_statusVARCHAR

Example input — vendors

vendor_idvendor_namecertification_status
1Office Depotactive
2Staplesactive
3Amazon Businesssuspended
4FedExactive
5UPSsuspended

Example input — receipts

receipt_idvendor_idamountreimbursement_status
1145.00pending
2132.50pending
3178.00approved
42120.00pending
5360.00pending
6490.00approved

Expected output

vendor_idvendor_namemin_pending_amount
1Office Depot32.50
2Staples120.00
3Amazon BusinessNULL
4FedExNULL
5UPSNULL

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Both conditions go in the JOIN ON, not WHERE and not a CASE. The ON clause is the doorman: it
  runs BEFORE the aggregate, so only (active-vendor, pending-receipt) rows attach and MIN never
  sees an approved receipt or a suspended vendor. The LEFT JOIN keeps every vendor, so the three
  NULL paths fall out for free: gate fails (vendors 3, 5) or the B-filter excludes all receipts
  (vendor 4). Why not CASE around MIN? reimbursement_status lives on the many-row receipts side,
  so a CASE would force it into GROUP BY and change the grain to one row per (vendor, status).
  Why not WHERE? a WHERE on reimbursement_status drops the LEFT JOIN's NULL rows and loses
  vendors 4 and 5. No COALESCE: MIN over an empty group is already NULL.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 5 expected rows.
*/

SELECT
    v.vendor_id,
    v.vendor_name,
    MIN(r.amount) AS min_pending_amount
FROM vendors AS v
LEFT JOIN receipts AS r
       ON v.vendor_id = r.vendor_id
      AND r.reimbursement_status = 'pending'   -- B-row filter, in ON
      AND v.certification_status = 'active'     -- A-entity gate, in ON
GROUP BY v.vendor_id, v.vendor_name
ORDER BY v.vendor_id;

WHERE filter template only

▼

Only qualifying entities appear; the gate sits in WHERE, which turns the LEFT JOIN effectively INNER.

WHERE filter (drop non-qualifiers)

▼

Use when: only qualifying entities should appear in the result; the simplest shape.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. JOIN A to B normally (LEFT or INNER, both work since we are about to filter anyway).
  2. WHERE filters out non-qualifying entities — they drop from the result entirely.
  3. GROUP BY the entity columns. This is the simplest shape; use only when the prompt does NOT require non-qualifiers to appear.
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    a.gate_col,
    MIN(b.picked_col) AS picked_value
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
WHERE a.gate_col >= threshold
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.gate_col;

DISTINCT ON (Postgres) template only

▼

Latest / earliest row per entity in one line with DISTINCT ON (group, ...) ORDER BY group, ts.

DISTINCT ON (Postgres only)

▼

Use when: you need the whole row at the pick (text + timestamp + sender), not just an aggregate column. Pair with a WHERE gate when non-qualifiers can drop.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. SELECT DISTINCT ON (entity_id) the columns you want — including the WHOLE row at the pick, not just one aggregated column.
  2. ORDER BY entity_id first, then the pick column (ASC for earliest, DESC for latest).
  3. Returns ONE row per entity. Pair with a WHERE clause for the gate when non-qualifiers can drop.
SELECT DISTINCT ON (b.entity_id)
    b.entity_id, b.picked_col, b.other_col
FROM fact b
JOIN entity a ON a.entity_id = b.entity_id
WHERE a.gate_col >= threshold
ORDER BY b.entity_id, b.picked_col;

ROW_NUMBER + rn = 1 1 problem

▼

Pick the whole row at the min / max (or by an ORDER, not a value): ROW_NUMBER PARTITION BY entity, keep rn = 1.

ROW_NUMBER + rn = 1 (pick by ORDER, not by VALUE)

▼

Use when: the per-entity pick is determined by SORTING on one column (earliest by timestamp, latest by date, top by a ranking metric) but you need to return a DIFFERENT column from that row. Works in any dialect, not just Postgres. This is the case where MIN(value_col) is the wrong move — that returns the smallest value, not the value FROM the row with the smallest sort key.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. CTE: rank fact rows per entity by the sort column with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id ORDER BY sort_col).
  2. LEFT JOIN the CTE on entity_id AND rn = 1 (put rn = 1 in the JOIN ON so the LEFT JOIN keeps entities with no fact rows).
  3. Wrap the picked column in a CASE for the gate, returning NULL when the gate fails.
