  4. This returns the picked column FROM the row at the chosen sort position — not the smallest value of the picked column.
WITH ranked_fact AS (
    SELECT
        f.*,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id
                           ORDER BY sort_col ASC) AS rn
    FROM fact f
)
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    a.gate_col,
    CASE WHEN a.gate_col >= threshold
         THEN rf.picked_col
         ELSE NULL END AS picked_value
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN ranked_fact rf
       ON rf.entity_id = a.entity_id
      AND rf.rn = 1
ORDER BY a.entity_id;
-- Note: the rn = 1 filter goes in the JOIN ON, not in WHERE, so the LEFT JOIN
-- still keeps entities with no fact rows (they get NULL picked_value).

Medium Gig Platform: Approved Worker Earliest Bid

▼

The bid_amount FROM each worker's earliest bid (not the smallest amount); ROW_NUMBER picks the row, a CASE applies the approval gate.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Gig marketplace: per worker, return the bid_amount of their EARLIEST bid by bid_timestamp.
  • Approved workers see the actual amount; pending workers see NULL.
  • Every worker who placed at least one bid appears, ordered by worker_id.

Schema — workers

ColumnType
worker_idINTEGER
worker_nameVARCHAR
approval_statusVARCHAR

Schema — bids

ColumnType
bid_idINTEGER
worker_idINTEGER
bid_amountDECIMAL(8,2)
bid_timestampTIMESTAMP

Example input — workers

worker_idworker_nameapproval_status
1Maraapproved
2Nicopending
3Omarapproved
4Priyaapproved

Example input — bids

bid_idworker_idbid_amountbid_timestamp
1175.002024-01-10 08:00:00
2180.002024-01-10 09:00:00
3265.002024-01-11 07:30:00
4270.002024-01-11 08:00:00
5390.002024-01-12 10:00:00
6455.002024-01-13 11:00:00
7460.002024-01-13 12:00:00

Expected output

worker_idapproval_statusbid_amount
1approved75.00
2pendingNULL
3approved90.00
4approved55.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The pick is determined by SORTING (earliest by timestamp) but returns a DIFFERENT column
  (bid_amount), so MIN(bid_amount) is the wrong move -- that returns the smallest amount, not the
  amount FROM the earliest row. The CTE ranks each worker's bids by bid_timestamp ASC; rn = 1 is
  the earliest row, carrying its own bid_amount. The CASE then applies the approval gate. Since
  rn = 1 already leaves one row per worker, the outer MIN is a harmless no-op. Tip: ORDER BY sets
  the direction (ASC = earliest, DESC = latest); add a tiebreaker like bid_id for ties.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 4 expected rows.
*/

WITH ranked_bids AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY worker_id
                           ORDER BY bid_timestamp ASC) AS rn   -- 1 = earliest bid
    FROM bids
)
SELECT
    w.worker_id,
    w.approval_status,
    CASE WHEN w.approval_status = 'approved'   -- gate on table A
         THEN MIN(b.bid_amount)                -- no-op: rn = 1 left one row
         ELSE NULL END AS bid_amount
FROM workers AS w
LEFT JOIN ranked_bids AS b ON w.worker_id = b.worker_id
WHERE b.rn = 1                                 -- keep only each worker's earliest bid
GROUP BY w.worker_id, w.approval_status
ORDER BY w.worker_id;

Matchup & Leaderboard 1 problem

▼

A table with one row holding BOTH sides of an event (host / guest, A / B, sender / receiver) → per-participant totals, often joined to a dimension so every entity (even those with zero events) shows up.

Signal words: "head-to-head," "matchup," "leaderboard," "points per team," "wins / losses / draws," "goals for / against," "include teams with zero games"

Technique: UNION ALL splits the wide row into one row per participant; score each branch in place with a CASE; GROUP BY the participant; LEFT JOIN a dimension table and COALESCE to 0 to include participants with no events.

Cross-link: The single-table version (no dim join) lives at Pair / Normalize Bidirectional (#1212 Win/Loss is the canonical anchor). For ranking the leaderboard after computing the totals, see Rank & Percentile.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Leaderboard with dim zero-fill 1 problem

▼

nb01 qtype: matchup_unpivot — Self-unpivot the two-sided row with UNION ALL, score each branch with CASE, GROUP BY participant, then LEFT JOIN a dim table so participants with zero events still appear with total = 0.

Soccer points (Win = 3, Tie = 1, Loss = 0) (back to tree)

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. UNION ALL splits the wide event row into one row per side (host_team, then guest_team).
  2. Inside EACH branch, score the side directly with a CASE: 3 if win, 1 if tie, 0 if loss.
  3. CTE aggregates SUM(points) per team.
  4. LEFT JOIN that CTE to the dim teams table + COALESCE 0 so zero-game teams still appear.
WITH per_side AS (
  SELECT host_team AS team,
         CASE WHEN host_goals > guest_goals THEN 3
              WHEN host_goals = guest_goals THEN 1
              ELSE 0 END AS points
  FROM matches
  UNION ALL
  SELECT guest_team,
         CASE WHEN guest_goals > host_goals THEN 3
              WHEN host_goals = guest_goals THEN 1
              ELSE 0 END
  FROM matches
),
totals AS (
  SELECT team, SUM(points) AS points
  FROM per_side
  GROUP BY team
)
SELECT t.team_id, t.team_name, COALESCE(tot.points, 0) AS points
FROM teams t
LEFT JOIN totals tot ON tot.team = t.team_id
ORDER BY points DESC, t.team_id ASC;

Win / loss records only (no ties scored)

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. UNION ALL split: one row per side.
  2. CASE in each branch: 1 for win, 0 otherwise. Repeat for losses with the inverse comparison.
  3. GROUP BY team in the outer query; SUM wins and losses separately.
WITH per_side AS (
  SELECT host_team AS team,
         CASE WHEN host_score > guest_score THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS wins,
         CASE WHEN host_score < guest_score THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS losses
  FROM matches
  UNION ALL
  SELECT guest_team,
         CASE WHEN guest_score > host_score THEN 1 ELSE 0 END,
         CASE WHEN guest_score < host_score THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
  FROM matches
)
SELECT team, SUM(wins) AS wins, SUM(losses) AS losses
FROM per_side
GROUP BY team;

Sum a column for each side (no win / loss logic)

▼

Use when the per-event metric is just a number on each side (inquiries served, kilometres run, calls made).

What this template does, step by step:

  1. UNION ALL: emit (participant_id, metric) for each side of the event.
  2. Drive the final SELECT off the dim participants table.
  3. LEFT JOIN the unpivoted rows so zero-event participants survive.
  4. SUM the metric per participant; COALESCE the SUM to 0.
WITH per_side AS (
  SELECT a_id   AS participant, a_metric AS metric FROM events
  UNION ALL
  SELECT b_id,            b_metric             FROM events
)
SELECT d.participant_id, d.participant_name,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.metric), 0) AS total_metric
FROM dim_participants d
LEFT JOIN per_side p ON p.participant = d.participant_id
GROUP BY d.participant_id, d.participant_name
ORDER BY total_metric DESC, d.participant_id ASC;

Goals for / against / differential per team

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. UNION ALL: emit (team, goals_for, goals_against) for each side — host side gets host_goals as gf and guest_goals as ga; guest side flips them.
  2. GROUP BY team.
  3. SUM both gf and ga; goal differential = SUM(gf) - SUM(ga).
WITH per_side AS (
  SELECT host_team  AS team, host_goals  AS gf, guest_goals AS ga FROM matches
  UNION ALL
  SELECT guest_team,         guest_goals,       host_goals       FROM matches
)
SELECT team,
       SUM(gf) AS goals_for,
       SUM(ga) AS goals_against,
       SUM(gf) - SUM(ga) AS goal_diff
FROM per_side
GROUP BY team;

Medium Saved Search Template Performance Leaderboard

▼

Real-estate platform A/B tests two saved-search templates head-to-head per day and records inquiries per side. Win = 3 points, tie = 1, loss = 0. Total points per template, with templates that never appeared still listed at 0.

Tables: search_templates (template_id, template_name), ab_tests (test_id, template_a_id, template_b_id, inquiries_a, inquiries_b, test_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Matchup & Leaderboard decision tree: Q1 yes (both sides in one row) → Q2 soccer-style (3-1-0) → Q3 yes (every template must appear) → 3-1-0 template.

Real-World Example

A real-estate platform decides which saved-search templates to keep, retire, or scale by ranking them on head-to-head inquiry performance, while making sure newly launched templates that have not yet been tested still show on the leaderboard.

Prompt watch-out: the prompt names tie = 1 and loss = 0 but does NOT spell out the points for a win. The expected output backs it out as win = 3 (template 3 = 1 tie + 2 wins = 7 points). Always reverse-engineer the rule from the expected output when the prompt is ambiguous.

Trace — per-side after UNION ALL, then totals per template:

test_id side template_id inquiries vs. outcome points
101A11510win3
101B21015loss0
102A188tie1
102B388tie1
103A21218loss0
103B31812win3
104A32014win3
104B11420loss0

Totals: template 1 = 3 + 1 + 0 = 4; template 2 = 0 + 0 = 0; template 3 = 1 + 3 + 3 = 7; template 4 never appears in ab_tests so the LEFT JOIN from search_templates picks it up with COALESCE = 0.

▶ 1 UNION ALL self-unpivot + score-in-branch + dim LEFT JOIN
WITH per_side AS ( SELECT template_a_id AS template_id, CASE WHEN inquiries_a > inquiries_b THEN 3 WHEN inquiries_a = inquiries_b THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS points FROM ab_tests UNION ALL SELECT template_b_id AS template_id, CASE WHEN inquiries_b > inquiries_a THEN 3 WHEN inquiries_a = inquiries_b THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS points FROM ab_tests ), totals AS ( SELECT template_id, SUM(points) AS total_points FROM per_side GROUP BY template_id ) SELECT t.template_id, t.template_name, COALESCE(tot.total_points, 0) AS total_points FROM search_templates t LEFT JOIN totals tot ON tot.template_id = t.template_id ORDER BY total_points DESC, t.template_id ASC;

Why this is best: Each UNION ALL branch SELECTs the row's id for that side AND scores that side directly with its own CASE — no goals-for / goals-against swap step. The first CTE produces one row per (test, side) with points. The second CTE collapses to one row per template. The final SELECT drives off search_templates via LEFT JOIN so template 4 (zero events) still appears at 0.

Watch out:

  • UNION ALL, not UNION. UNION dedupes; two tests where a template scored the same number of points would silently collapse into one row.
  • Score inside the branch, not after. Doing UNION ALL first and then a single CASE in an outer query forces you to track which side each row came from, which is what the matchup_unpivot recipe is designed to avoid.
  • Both branches must handle ties. The tie CASE awards 1 to side A AND 1 to side B; if you write the CASE in only one branch and copy-paste blindly into the other, you can miss the tie credit on one side.
  • Drive the final SELECT off the dim, not the totals. If the FROM clause is the totals CTE and you LEFT JOIN the dim, templates with no events are missing from the totals and never appear — an INNER-style result.
  • COALESCE the SUM, not the column inside SUM. SUM over an empty group is NULL; COALESCE(SUM(points), 0) or COALESCE(tot.total_points, 0) after the LEFT JOIN both work. Don't COALESCE the unpivoted points column, that has no NULLs.

Performance: Two scans of ab_tests (one per UNION branch) + one GROUP BY + one LEFT JOIN. Linear in the number of tests.

Rank Within Groups to Select Top-N 16 problems

▼

A table joined to one or more dimensions → the top-N rows per group via window ranking. The 32 problems here belong in Multi-Table because computing the rankable metric REQUIRES a join (e.g. "top customer per region" needs the orders fact + customers / regions dims). For the single-table version (no join needed) and the canonical technique reference, see Rank & Percentile.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Top 1 per group by value (highest / max metric) 7 problems

▼

Single winner per entity by a value column. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC, tiebreak) filter rn = 1. Use ROW_NUMBER when you want EXACTLY one row per group; switch to RANK / DENSE_RANK when ties should share the winner slot.

Medium Department Highest Salary

▼

For each department, return every employee whose salary is the maximum.

Tables: Employee (id, name, salary, departmentId), Department (id, name)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

HR recognition programs publish top earners per department at year-end.

▶ 1 RANK per Partition = 1
SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary FROM ( SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk FROM Employee ) e JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.departmentId WHERE e.rk = 1;

Why this is best: RANK returns all ties at rank 1 (spec-compliant when multiple share the max).

Performance: One window + one join.

Medium Project Employees III

▼

For each project, return the most experienced employee(s).

Tables: Project (project_id, employee_id), Employee (employee_id, name, experience_years)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A staffing plan assigns the senior expert per project to mentor juniors.

▶ 1 RANK per Project
SELECT project_id, employee_id FROM ( SELECT p.project_id, p.employee_id, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.project_id ORDER BY e.experience_years DESC) AS rk FROM Project p JOIN Employee e ON e.employee_id = p.employee_id ) t WHERE rk = 1;

Why this is best: Standard top-N-per-group with RANK.

Performance: One window + one join.

Medium Product Sales Analysis IV

▼

For each user, the product with the highest total spending.

Tables: Sales (sale_id, product_id, user_id, quantity), Product (product_id, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

Personalization uses each user's top-spend product to seed cross-sell bundles.

▶ 1 Per-Pair Spend + RANK
WITH spend AS ( SELECT s.user_id, s.product_id, SUM(s.quantity * p.price) AS amt FROM Sales s JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = s.product_id GROUP BY s.user_id, s.product_id ) SELECT user_id, product_id FROM ( SELECT user_id, product_id, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY amt DESC) AS rk FROM spend ) t WHERE rk = 1;

Why this is best: Standard top-1-per-group on a derived spend metric.

Performance: Aggregate + window.

Hard Generate the Invoice

▼

Return the invoice lines for the order with the highest total price.

Tables: Products (product_id, price), Purchases (invoice_id, product_id, quantity)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

An ERP prints the invoice for the biggest order of the day.

▶ 1 Top-Invoice CTE + Join
WITH totals AS ( SELECT invoice_id, SUM(p.price * pu.quantity) AS total FROM Purchases pu JOIN Products p ON p.product_id = pu.product_id GROUP BY invoice_id ), top_inv AS ( SELECT invoice_id FROM totals ORDER BY total DESC, invoice_id LIMIT 1 ) SELECT pu.product_id, pu.quantity, pu.quantity * p.price AS price FROM Purchases pu JOIN Products p ON p.product_id = pu.product_id JOIN top_inv t ON t.invoice_id = pu.invoice_id;

Why this is best: Identify the top invoice scalar, then return its detail rows.

Performance: Two aggregates + join.

Medium Winning Candidate

▼

Return the candidate with the most votes.

Tables: Candidate (id, name), Vote (id, candidateId)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

An election reporting pipeline calls the winner as soon as all votes are tallied.

▶ 1 Group + Rank 1
SELECT c.name FROM Candidate c JOIN ( SELECT candidateId, COUNT(*) AS votes FROM Vote GROUP BY candidateId ORDER BY votes DESC LIMIT 1 ) t ON t.candidateId = c.id;

Why this is best: Aggregate + ORDER BY + LIMIT gives the top scalar without a window.

Performance: One aggregate.

Hard Tournament Winners

▼

For each group, return the player with the highest total score (ties broken by smallest id).

Tables: Players (player_id, group_id), Matches (match_id, first_player, second_player, first_score, second_score)

View on LeetCode →

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A tournament system crowns a group winner by summing points from every match they played in.

Composite (3 moves): Move 1: normalize-bidirectional (UNION ALL to unstack first/second player). Move 2: group-aggregate (SUM points per player). Move 3: rank-partition (RANK top 1 per group, tiebreaker by smallest player_id).

▶ 1 UNION ALL + Aggregate + RANK per Group
WITH base_matches AS ( SELECT first_player AS player_id, first_score AS points FROM Matches UNION ALL SELECT second_player AS player_id, second_score AS points FROM Matches ), player_points AS ( SELECT player_id, SUM(points) AS total_points FROM base_matches GROUP BY player_id ), base_group AS ( SELECT p.group_id, p.player_id, COALESCE(m.total_points, 0) AS total_points, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.group_id ORDER BY COALESCE(m.total_points, 0) DESC, p.player_id ASC) AS group_rank FROM Players AS p LEFT JOIN player_points AS m ON p.player_id = m.player_id ) SELECT group_id, player_id FROM base_group WHERE group_rank = 1;

Why this is best: Each CTE handles one move. UNION ALL normalizes the bidirectional match data (each player appears once per match). SUM aggregates total points. RANK with LEFT JOIN + COALESCE ensures players with zero matches still appear with 0 points. The tiebreaker (player_id ASC) is baked into the ORDER BY.

Performance: One UNION ALL scan + one aggregate + one window pass.

Key details:

  • LEFT JOIN (not INNER): a player with no matches still gets a row with NULL total, which COALESCE converts to 0
  • RANK vs ROW_NUMBER: either works here because the tiebreaker (player_id) is unique within each group, so no ties survive
  • COALESCE inside ORDER BY: without it, NULL sorts inconsistently across databases and a zero-match player could be ranked first or last

Medium The Most Frequently Ordered Products for Each Customer

▼

For each customer, return the product(s) they ordered most.

Tables: Customers (customer_id, name), Orders (order_id, order_date, customer_id, product_id), Products (product_id, product_name, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

Personalized recommendations use per-customer favorites as a top-tier signal.

▶ 1 Aggregate + RANK
WITH counts AS ( SELECT customer_id, product_id, COUNT(*) AS c, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rk FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id, product_id ) SELECT c.customer_id, c.product_id, p.product_name FROM counts c JOIN Products p ON p.product_id = c.product_id WHERE c.rk = 1;

Why this is best: RANK over grouped counts keeps all tied favorites.

Performance: Aggregate + window + join.

Top 1 per group by date (most recent / earliest) 4 problems

▼

Single winner per entity ordered by a date or timestamp. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts DESC) for most recent, ASC for earliest. Postgres tip: DISTINCT ON (entity) ... ORDER BY entity, ts DESC is the same shape with less ceremony.

Easy Sales Analysis I

▼

Return seller(s) with the highest total sales.

Tables: Product (product_id, product_name, unit_price), Sales (seller_id, product_id, buyer_id, sale_date, quantity, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A sales leaderboard highlights the top-grossing seller(s).

▶ 1 Total per Seller + RANK
SELECT seller_id FROM ( SELECT seller_id, SUM(price) AS total, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(price) DESC) AS rk FROM Sales GROUP BY seller_id ) t WHERE rk = 1;

Why this is best: Aggregate once, then rank the aggregates to handle ties.

Performance: One aggregate + one window.

Product Sales Analysis III (Medium)

▼

Product managers analyze launch-year metrics: which products had strong initial adoption? A product with 50 units sold in year 1 may underperform vs one with 200 units. Early momentum predicts long-term success.

📌
Pattern: Rank First Year per Product

Use RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY year) to identify first year, or use MIN(year). Business: Product analytics finding launch-year performance.

Business Context
Product managers analyze launch-year metrics: which products had strong initial adoption? A product with 50 units sold in year 1 may underperform vs one with 200 units. Early momentum predicts long-term success.
▶ Rank 1: Window Function (RANK) Handles ties naturally
SELECT product_id, year AS first_year, quantity, price FROM ( SELECT product_id, year, quantity, price, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY year) AS year_rank FROM Sales ) t WHERE year_rank = 1;

Performance Analysis: Window function: O(n log n) due to PARTITION sort. RANK() is O(n) once sorted. Memory: O(n) for sort and partition buffer. Filter year_rank = 1 is O(n). No index required but (product_id, year) index helps partition/sort. Result size: <= unique products.

Why Rank 1: RANK() keeps all rows where year matches first year (handles ties). Clean semantics.

▶ Rank 2: Subquery with MIN(year) Simpler aggregation
SELECT s.product_id, s.year AS first_year, s.quantity, s.price FROM Sales s WHERE s.year = ( SELECT MIN(year) FROM Sales s2 WHERE s2.product_id = s.product_id );

Performance Analysis: Correlated subquery runs MIN(year) for EACH row in Sales. Outer scan: O(n). Inner MIN per row: O(n/products) on average. Total: O(n²/products). For 1M rows, 1k products: 1M * 1000 = 1B comparisons. Requires index on product_id to speed inner query to O(log n): O(n log n) total. Window function is still faster: no subquery overhead.

Why Rank 2: More readable but performance degrades without index. Window function avoids repeated subquery execution.

Medium The Most Recent Orders for Each Product

▼

For each product, return the most recent order(s).

Tables: Customers (customer_id, name), Orders (order_id, order_date, customer_id, product_id), Products (product_id, product_name, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A merchandising report shows the latest buyer per SKU to drive a "who recently bought" email.

▶ 1 RANK per Product
SELECT p.product_name, o.product_id, o.customer_id, o.order_id, o.order_date FROM ( SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rk FROM Orders ) o JOIN Products p ON p.product_id = o.product_id WHERE o.rk = 1 ORDER BY p.product_name, o.product_id, o.order_id;

Why this is best: RANK keeps ties on the same date.

Performance: One window + one join.

Easy Sales Analysis II

▼

Buyers who bought S8 but never iPhone.

Tables: Product (product_id, product_name, unit_price), Sales (seller_id, product_id, buyer_id, sale_date, quantity, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

Cross-sell list targets S8 buyers with a next-gen iPhone promo.

▶ 1 Two Flags per Buyer
SELECT buyer_id FROM Sales s JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = s.product_id GROUP BY buyer_id HAVING SUM(p.product_name = 'S8') > 0 AND SUM(p.product_name = 'iPhone') = 0;

Why this is best: Two conditional sums enforce has-S8 and not-iPhone in one pass.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Top N per group (N > 1) 2 problems

▼

More than one winner per group. ROW_NUMBER ≤ N for exactly N rows; RANK ≤ N when ties should share the cutoff; DENSE_RANK ≤ N when you want the top N distinct values. Pick the rank function by tie behavior.

Department Top Three Salaries (Hard)

▼

HR uses this for compensation benchmarking. If IT's top earner is $150k and Sales' is $120k, IT must be specialized. Identifies pay equity issues within departments.

📌
Pattern: DENSE_RANK with JOIN

Use DENSE_RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) <= 3 combined with a JOIN to department names. Business: HR compensation analysis finding top earners per department.

Business Context
HR uses this for compensation benchmarking. If IT's top earner is $150k and Sales' is $120k, IT must be specialized. Identifies pay equity issues within departments.
▶ Rank 1: DENSE_RANK + JOIN Handles ties correctly
SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary FROM ( SELECT id, name, salary, departmentId, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) AS salary_rank FROM Employee ) e JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id WHERE e.salary_rank <= 3 ORDER BY d.name, e.salary DESC, e.name;

Performance Analysis: Window function: O(n log n) for sort per department. DENSE_RANK(): O(n) once sorted. JOIN: hash join on departmentId = O(n + d) where d = departments. Memory: O(n) for partition buffer. Final ORDER BY: O(n log n). Total: O(n log n) dominated by window function sort.

Why Rank 1: DENSE_RANK is correct: two employees with same salary both get rank 2, next different salary gets rank 3. Avoids rank gaps.

▶ Rank 2: ROW_NUMBER + Subquery Requires careful filtering
SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary FROM ( SELECT id, name, salary, departmentId, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS salary_rank FROM Employee ) e JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id WHERE e.salary_rank <= 3 ORDER BY d.name, e.salary DESC;

Performance Analysis: ROW_NUMBER ranks each row uniquely even with same salary. Results in fewer rows returned (at most 3 per dept vs potentially more with DENSE_RANK). Requires tie-breaking with id. Same O(n log n) complexity but potentially better memory cache behavior due to smaller result set. Memory: same O(n).

Why Rank 2: ROW_NUMBER with tie-breaking (id) is incorrect semantically here. Two people with same salary should both be "top 3", but ROW_NUMBER arbitrarily picks one.

Medium The Most Recent Three Orders

▼

Return the most recent three orders per customer, ordered by customer then date desc.

Tables: Customers (customer_id, name), Orders (order_id, order_date, customer_id, cost)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A CS agent view shows each customer's last three orders for fast context.

▶ 1 ROW_NUMBER <= 3
SELECT name AS customer_name, customer_id, order_id, order_date FROM ( SELECT c.name, c.customer_id, o.order_id, o.order_date, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_date DESC) AS rn FROM Orders o JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id ) t WHERE rn <= 3 ORDER BY name, customer_id, order_date DESC;

Why this is best: Top-3 per group using ROW_NUMBER.

Performance: One window + one join.

Nth specific position (exactly N, not top N) no problems yet

▼

Not top-N, just the Nth row per group (the 2nd most recent, the 3rd transaction). ROW_NUMBER = N or RANK = N / DENSE_RANK = N depending on tie semantics. Watch for groups with fewer than N rows — they vanish from the result; LEFT JOIN a dim to keep them.

Special rank patterns (median, threshold from rank, rank deltas, asc/desc exclusion) 4 problems

▼

Patterns where the rank result feeds back into the query — the asc / desc median trick (no PERCENTILE_CONT), a per-group cutoff computed from a rank, comparing ranks across snapshots, and combining a rank with a per-group aggregate threshold.

Medium Find Cutoff Score for Each School

▼

Lowest exam score accepted given a school's capacity, picking the best available cutoff.

Tables: Schools (school_id, capacity), Exam (score, student_count)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

An admissions office picks the top score that fits a given capacity, so the enrollment plan is predictable year over year.

▶ 1 Qualifying Scores + MAX
SELECT s.school_id, COALESCE( (SELECT MAX(e.score) FROM Exam e WHERE e.student_count <= s.capacity), -1 ) AS score FROM Schools s;

Why this is best: Highest score where student count fits capacity is the cutoff; -1 if none qualify.

Performance: One scalar subquery per school.

Medium The Change in Global Rankings

▼

For each team, compute rank change from old to new rankings.

Tables: TeamPoints (team_id, name, points), PointsChange (team_id, points_change)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A sports ranking platform publishes movement (+/-) indicators after each update window.

▶ 1 Two RANKs Joined
WITH combined AS ( SELECT tp.team_id, tp.name, tp.points, tp.points + COALESCE(pc.points_change, 0) AS new_points FROM TeamPoints tp LEFT JOIN PointsChange pc ON pc.team_id = tp.team_id ), ranked AS ( SELECT team_id, name, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, name) AS old_rk, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY new_points DESC, name) AS new_rk FROM combined ) SELECT team_id, name, (old_rk - new_rk) AS rank_diff FROM ranked ORDER BY rank_diff DESC, name;

Why this is best: Two ranks on the same row, then subtract for the delta.

Performance: Two window passes.

Medium Activities Without the Extremes (DENSE_RANK ASC + DESC, exclude both ends)

▼

Activities with NEITHER the maximum NOR the minimum number of participants. Count participants per activity, rank ASC AND DESC, keep rows where neither rank equals 1. The asc/desc rank trick that the leaf's intro names — applied to exclusion rather than median.

Tables: Friends (id, name, activity); Activities (id, name). Each activity in Activities is performed by at least one friend (no zero-participant case in this problem, but the COALESCE makes the shape robust if the prompt changes).

→

Decision Tree Path

Single-table Rank & Percentile would handle the rank, but the count of participants is only available after a JOIN to Friends — so this lives in Multi-Table. Pattern is "rank the result of an aggregate, then filter on the rank from BOTH ends."

Real-World Example

A community board picks "mid-tier" activities for a featured rotation: skip the runaway favorites (everyone already does them) and skip the dead categories (nobody shows up), keep the activities that have steady-but-not-dominant participation.

DENSE_RANK, not ROW_NUMBER — tied extremes must ALL drop

Multiple activities can tie at the max (or at the min). The prompt says "neither the maximum NOR the minimum" — that means EVERY activity tied with the max counts as a max and ALL of them drop. DENSE_RANK gives every tied row the same rank, so the WHERE rn_asc > 1 AND rn_desc > 1 filter excludes the whole tie cluster on each end.

ROW_NUMBER would break ties arbitrarily, so it would silently keep all-but-one of the tied min rows. Wrong.

What this query does, step by step:

  1. Count participants per activity — activity_counts CTE: GROUP BY activity on Friends, COUNT(*) gives the headcount.
  2. Bring the count onto Activities — base CTE: LEFT JOIN Activities to activity_counts; COALESCE the count to 0 in case an activity has no friends (defensive even if the prompt rules it out).
  3. Rank from BOTH ends — same CTE: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY n ASC) identifies the min cluster (all rows tied at the smallest count get rn_asc = 1); DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY n DESC) identifies the max cluster.
  4. Keep rows that are NEITHER end — final SELECT: WHERE rn_asc > 1 AND rn_desc > 1.

Trace — on the example data:

activity n (participants) rn_asc rn_desc kept?
Horse Riding113dropped (min)
Singing222kept
Eating331dropped (max)

Only Singing has neither rank = 1. If two activities had tied at 3 (the max), DENSE_RANK DESC would give both rn_desc = 1 and both would drop — that's the whole point of using DENSE_RANK over ROW_NUMBER.

▶ 1 DENSE_RANK ASC + DENSE_RANK DESC, filter where neither rank = 1
WITH activity_counts AS ( -- 1. Count participants per activity SELECT activity, COUNT(*) AS n FROM Friends GROUP BY activity ), base AS ( -- 2 + 3. Bring count onto the dim, rank from both ends SELECT a.name AS activity, COALESCE(b.n, 0) AS n, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COALESCE(b.n, 0) ASC) AS rn_asc, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COALESCE(b.n, 0) DESC) AS rn_desc FROM Activities AS a LEFT JOIN activity_counts AS b ON b.activity = a.name ) -- 4. Keep rows that are NEITHER the min cluster NOR the max cluster SELECT activity FROM base WHERE rn_asc > 1 AND rn_desc > 1;

Why this is best: One pass over the count CTE, two window passes (one ASC one DESC) on the joined result, one final filter. The asc/desc DENSE_RANK pair is the standard idiom for "filter to non-extremes." Adding a third filter like BETWEEN p10 AND p90 via PERCENT_RANK is a related but heavier shape; here we want exactly the extremes excluded, not a percentile band.

Watch out:

  • DENSE_RANK, not ROW_NUMBER. ROW_NUMBER breaks ties arbitrarily, so if two activities tie at the min, only one would get rn_asc = 1 and the other would be incorrectly kept. RANK works too here, but DENSE_RANK reads as "tied = same rank" without the gap-skipping semantics.
  • Drive the FROM off the dim (Activities), LEFT JOIN to the count. If the prompt allowed zero-participant activities, FROM Friends would silently drop them and they'd never appear in the rank.
  • COALESCE the count, not the rank. Wrap b.n in COALESCE inside the DENSE_RANK's ORDER BY so a zero-participant activity sorts at the bottom of ASC (and top of DESC) instead of being placed by NULL handling.
  • NULLS FIRST/LAST on DESC. If a row's n is NULL (no COALESCE), ORDER BY n DESC puts NULL FIRST in Postgres — a NULL activity would falsely look like the max. COALESCE removes the NULL before the rank, sidestepping the trap.
  • Edge case — all activities tied. If every activity has the SAME participant count, every row gets rn_asc = 1 AND rn_desc = 1, and the result is empty. That matches the prompt's spirit ("neither the max nor the min" — if everyone is both, no one survives).
  • You can't combine the two ranks into one window. A single DENSE_RANK() with an ORDER BY only has one direction. Two separate windows is the canonical move.

Hard Find the Quiet Students in All Exams (per partition DENSE_RANK ASC + DESC, then MIN across the student's exams)

▼

Per exam, rank each student ASC and DESC to identify the lowest and highest scorers for THAT exam. Then for each student, demand that across ALL their exam rows the smallest ASC rank AND the smallest DESC rank are BOTH greater than 1 — meaning they were never the min and never the max in any of their exams. Sibling pattern to Activities Without Extremes: same ASC + DESC DENSE_RANK trick, but partitioned per group and combined with a per entity MIN across rows.

Tables: Student (student_id, student_name), Exam (exam_id, student_id, score). A student can appear in Exam multiple times (once per exam taken). The primary key (exam_id, student_id) means at most one score per student per exam, but a student can take many exams. Students with zero rows in Exam must NOT appear in the output (the "took at least one exam" rule).

→

Decision Tree Path

Rank Within Groups decision tree: Q1 group = per exam → PARTITION BY exam_id. Q2 the rule is "neither extreme" per exam → ASC + DESC DENSE_RANK pair. Q3 must hold across ALL the student's exams → aggregate per student with MIN(rn) > 1 for both ranks. Q4 only students who took at least one exam → INNER JOIN drives off Exam rows; students with zero rows naturally drop out. Cross link: Activities Without Extremes for the whole population version of the ASC + DESC trick.

Real World Example

A school's pastoral team wants to identify steady performers who consistently land in the middle of the pack across all their exams — not the standouts at the top, not the strugglers at the bottom, just kids who quietly do fine. These students are often invisible to teachers focused on the extremes and may benefit from targeted enrichment. The rule "never min and never max in ANY exam they took" is strict by design.

Build order — per partition ranks first, then per student aggregate:

  1. CTE 1 base: for each (exam_id, student_id) row, compute DENSE_RANK PARTITION BY exam_id ORDER BY score ASC AS asc_rnk and DENSE_RANK PARTITION BY exam_id ORDER BY score DESC AS desc_rnk. After this CTE, every row carries the student's rank WITHIN their exam: asc_rnk = 1 means lowest in that exam, desc_rnk = 1 means highest.
  2. JOIN Student on student_id to attach student_name and to drive off the dim.
  3. GROUP BY (student_id, student_name) and apply HAVING MIN(asc_rnk) > 1 AND MIN(desc_rnk) > 1. The MIN across the student's rows is the SMALLEST rank they ever held; demanding it stay above 1 means they NEVER hit rank 1 in EITHER direction in ANY of their exams.
  4. ORDER BY student_id.

Trace — per row ranks for each student on the example data:

student (exam, score, asc_rnk, desc_rnk) MIN(asc_rnk) MIN(desc_rnk) quiet?
1 Daniel(10, 70, 1, 3), (20, 80, 1, 1), (30, 70, 1, 2), (40, 60, 1, 3)11no (was min and was max)
2 Jade(10, 80, 2, 2), (40, 70, 2, 2)22yes
3 Stella(10, 90, 3, 1), (30, 80, 2, 2)21no (was max in exam 10)
4 Jonathan(30, 90, 3, 1), (40, 80, 3, 1)31no (was max in both exams)
5 Will(no exam rows)——no (took no exams, dropped by INNER JOIN)

Only Jade passes the gate. Will took no exams and is naturally excluded by the INNER JOIN against the Exam CTE; no special filter needed.

▶ 1 Per partition DENSE_RANK ASC + DESC, then HAVING MIN per student
WITH base AS ( -- 1. Per exam, rank each student by score in BOTH directions. -- asc_rnk = 1 means lowest in that exam; desc_rnk = 1 means highest. SELECT exam_id, student_id, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY exam_id ORDER BY score ASC) AS asc_rnk, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY exam_id ORDER BY score DESC) AS desc_rnk FROM Exam ) -- 2. Attach student_name (INNER JOIN drops students with zero exam rows). -- 3. A student qualifies only if across ALL their rows the smallest -- asc_rnk AND the smallest desc_rnk are BOTH > 1 (never extreme). SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name FROM base AS b JOIN Student AS s ON s.student_id = b.student_id GROUP BY s.student_id, s.student_name HAVING MIN(b.asc_rnk) > 1 AND MIN(b.desc_rnk) > 1 ORDER BY s.student_id;

Why this is best: The PARTITION BY exam_id makes each exam its own ranking universe so "lowest in this exam" is per exam, not global. The MIN aggregate across the student's rows captures the SMALLEST rank they ever held; demanding it stays above 1 in BOTH directions is the precise translation of "never extreme in ANY exam." INNER JOIN against the dim handles the "took at least one exam" requirement automatically.

Watch out:

  • PARTITION BY exam_id is mandatory. Without it, DENSE_RANK ranks scores across ALL exams together. A student who scored 70 (lowest in their exam, surrounded by 80s and 90s) might have asc_rnk > 1 globally because some OTHER exam had a 60. The per exam ranking is what makes "extreme in THAT exam" mean what the prompt says.
  • Use MIN to enforce "FOR ALL the student's rows." Conditional aggregates that read like English — e.g. BOOL_OR(asc_rnk = 1) — capture "was EVER min" (an EXISTS check). The negation is "was NEVER min" which translates to NOT BOOL_OR(asc_rnk = 1) or equivalently MIN(asc_rnk) > 1. The MIN form reads as "the smallest rank they ever held is still above 1." Do NOT use BOOL_OR(asc_rnk > 1) — that's an EXISTS check ("had at least one row where they weren't the min") and lets students through who were min in some exams and not in others.
  • DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER on ties. If two students tie for lowest in an exam, DENSE_RANK gives them BOTH rank 1, so BOTH are correctly flagged as extreme. ROW_NUMBER would arbitrarily pick one and call only that one extreme; the other would survive the gate incorrectly.
  • RANK works too but DENSE_RANK is cleaner here. Both give tied rows the same rank; the difference is RANK skips ranks after a tie. Since the gate only cares about "is rank > 1," either works, but DENSE_RANK is the standard idiom for "all ties at the top share the same label."
  • INNER JOIN, not LEFT JOIN. Driving from base (which only has students with exam rows) and INNER JOIN to Student automatically excludes students with zero exams. FROM Student LEFT JOIN base would carry through students with zero rows (their MIN over an empty group is NULL, which fails the > 1 check — but you'd be relying on three valued logic instead of structural intent. INNER JOIN is clearer.
  • The naive ASC + DESC trick from Activities Without Extremes is per population, not per partition. Without PARTITION BY this collapses to "the student with the globally lowest score" once, which is not the rule. Always check whether the prompt says "per group" before deciding whether to PARTITION BY.
Reshape Recipes

Four technique families for reshaping data: UNION / UNION ALL (stack independent queries vertically), Conditional Pivot (long rows to wide columns via CASE WHEN inside aggregates), Unpivot via UNION ALL (wide columns back to long rows), and CROSS JOIN / Calendar Skeleton (generate complete combinations then fill with actuals). Each technique opens with a generic template, explanation, and guidance on when to reach for it, followed by nested example problems.

Technique UNION / UNION ALL

▼

Stack rows from two or more independent SELECT statements vertically. UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps all rows.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Stack two separate answers 1 problem

▼

Two unrelated asks that share one output column. Each ask is its own SELECT; UNION ALL keeps both rows and their order.

Template Stack two answers template

▼

Use when: two unrelated asks share one output column.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Write each ask as its own SELECT, each with its own ORDER BY and LIMIT.
  2. Stack them with UNION ALL so both rows survive even if the values match.
  3. Need a guaranteed order? Tag each branch with a literal sort_order and ORDER BY it at the very end.
SELECT name AS result FROM ...      -- first ask
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1
UNION ALL
SELECT title FROM ...                -- second ask
ORDER BY AVG(rating) DESC LIMIT 1;
-- UNION ALL keeps both rows; the output column names come from the first SELECT

Movie Rating (Medium)

▼

Entertainment platforms recognize "Top Reviewer of the Month" and "Movie of the Month" to drive engagement and surface quality content.

Schema: Movies(movie_id, title), Users(user_id, name), MovieRating(movie_id, user_id, rating, created_at)

UNION two queries: (1) User with most ratings (tie: lexicographically smaller name), (2) Movie with highest average rating in Feb 2020 (tie: lexicographically smaller title). Return results column.

Business Context: Platform Recognition Reports

Entertainment platforms recognize "Top Reviewer of the Month" and "Movie of the Month" to drive engagement and surface quality content.

▶ Rank 1: Two Separate Queries UNIONed Clear separation of concerns
-- Top reviewer (most ratings) SELECT u.name AS results FROM Users u INNER JOIN MovieRating mr ON u.user_id = mr.user_id GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, u.name ASC LIMIT 1 UNION ALL -- Top movie in Feb 2020 SELECT m.title AS results FROM Movies m INNER JOIN MovieRating mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id WHERE YEAR(mr.created_at) = 2020 AND MONTH(mr.created_at) = 2 GROUP BY m.movie_id, m.title ORDER BY AVG(mr.rating) DESC, m.title ASC LIMIT 1;

Why this ranks first: Two separate queries are easy to understand and maintain. Each has its own sorting logic. UNION ALL preserves order. No complicated joins or conditionals.

▶ Rank 2: CTEs + Single Query Combines both with CTEs
WITH top_reviewer AS ( SELECT u.name AS results, 1 AS query_order FROM Users u INNER JOIN MovieRating mr ON u.user_id = mr.user_id GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, u.name ASC LIMIT 1 ), top_movie AS ( SELECT m.title AS results, 2 AS query_order FROM Movies m INNER JOIN MovieRating mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM mr.created_at) = 2020 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM mr.created_at) = 2 GROUP BY m.movie_id, m.title ORDER BY AVG(mr.rating) DESC, m.title ASC LIMIT 1 ) SELECT results FROM top_reviewer UNION ALL SELECT results FROM top_movie ORDER BY query_order;

Tradeoff: CTEs add clarity (labeled queries), but increase complexity. Two separate table scans (one per CTE). EXTRACT is more portable than YEAR/MONTH in some databases.

▶ Rank 3: Subqueries in FROM (Complex) Avoid this approach
SELECT * FROM ( SELECT u.name AS results, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY cnt DESC, u.name ASC) AS rn FROM Users u INNER JOIN ( SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM MovieRating GROUP BY user_id ) mr ON u.user_id = mr.user_id ) reviewer WHERE rn = 1 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM ( SELECT m.title AS results, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY avg_rating DESC, m.title ASC) AS rn FROM Movies m INNER JOIN ( SELECT movie_id, AVG(rating) AS avg_rating FROM MovieRating WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2020 AND MONTH(created_at) = 2 GROUP BY movie_id ) mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id ) movie WHERE rn = 1;

Tradeoff: Nested subqueries with window functions are hard to read and debug. Multiple levels of nesting increase query execution overhead. Rank 1 or 2 are clearer.

Separate Queries vs. Combined Logic

Two separate UNION queries (Rank 1) each run their logic independently, then combine. CTEs (Rank 2) materialize both results. Nested subqueries (Rank 3) force multiple scans. For small result sets (LIMIT 1 each), Rank 1 is simplest. For larger result sets, CTEs may cache results better.

Reconcile two one-sided sets 1 problem

▼

Rows that live in one source but not the other. One anti-join per direction, stacked with UNION to drop the overlap.

Template Reconcile sets template

▼

Use when: you need rows that sit in one source but not the other, both directions.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. One anti-join per direction: rows in A missing from B, then rows in B missing from A.
  2. Stack with UNION so any row that somehow lands in both shows once.
  3. NOT IN breaks when the other side can hold NULL; switch to NOT EXISTS if so.
SELECT id FROM a WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM b)
UNION
SELECT id FROM b WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM a)
ORDER BY id;
-- UNION drops duplicates; use NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN if the subquery can return NULL

Easy Employees With Missing Information

▼

Return employee ids present in one source but missing from the other.

Tables: Employees (employee_id, name), Salaries (employee_id, salary)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

An HR audit reconciles two mastered systems and surfaces records missing from either.

▶ 1 Two Anti-Joins via UNION
SELECT employee_id FROM Employees WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Salaries) UNION SELECT employee_id FROM Salaries WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Employees) ORDER BY employee_id;

Why this is best: Each branch finds one-sided rows; UNION combines both.

Performance: Two subqueries. Indexes help.

Hand-build a label set 1 problem

▼

A fixed list of labels that must all appear, even with count 0. UNION ALL manufactures the labels; a join attaches the data.

Template Label set template

▼

Use when: a fixed list of labels must all appear, even the ones with no data.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Type each label as its own one row SELECT, stacked with UNION ALL — this manufactures the complete label set.
  2. CROSS JOIN or LEFT JOIN the data onto the label set so every label survives.
  3. COUNT a column from the data side (not COUNT(*)) so empty labels land at 0.
SELECT c.label, COUNT(t.id) AS n
FROM (
  SELECT 'Low'     AS label UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Average'          UNION ALL
  SELECT 'High'
) c
LEFT JOIN t ON t.value falls in c.label's band
GROUP BY c.label;

Medium Count Salary Categories

▼

Count accounts in three salary categories: Low (<$20k), Average ($20k-$50k), High (>$50k). Result must include all three categories, even with count 0.

Tables: Accounts (account_id, income)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Combined: Cross Join + Count Pattern

Real-World Example

Payroll analytics generates salary band distribution reports for management dashboards. All three categories (Low, Average, High) must appear, even if no accounts fall into a band, to show complete salary structure.

▶ 1 Cross Join with Categories + CASE + COUNT
SELECT c.category, COUNT(CASE WHEN c.category = 'Low Salary' AND income < 20000 THEN 1 WHEN c.category = 'Average Salary' AND income BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000 THEN 1 WHEN c.category = 'High Salary' AND income > 50000 THEN 1 END) AS accounts_count FROM ( SELECT 'Low Salary' AS category UNION ALL SELECT 'Average Salary' UNION ALL SELECT 'High Salary' ) c CROSS JOIN Accounts GROUP BY c.category;

Why this is best: Cross join ensures all three categories exist in result. CASE inside COUNT matches each account to its category, counting only matches. Handles zero-count categories elegantly.

Gotcha: CROSS JOIN multiplies table size (3 × |Accounts|) before filtering. For large tables, suboptimal. See approach #2 for alternative.

Performance: O(n) per category after cross join. Three scans total. Acceptable for small-to-medium Accounts tables.

▶ 2 UNION ALL with Separate Counts
SELECT 'Low Salary' AS category, COUNT(*) AS accounts_count FROM Accounts WHERE income < 20000 UNION ALL SELECT 'Average Salary', COUNT(*) FROM Accounts WHERE income BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000 UNION ALL SELECT 'High Salary', COUNT(*) FROM Accounts WHERE income > 50000;

Why this works: Three separate COUNT queries, one per category. UNION ALL combines results. Guaranteed all three rows in output (even 0 counts). Three full table scans.

Performance: Slower (3 scans) but avoids cross join blow-up. Better for very large Accounts tables. Modern optimizers may merge scans.

▶ 3 Subquery with GROUP BY CASE
WITH categorized AS ( SELECT CASE WHEN income < 20000 THEN 'Low Salary' WHEN income BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000 THEN 'Average Salary' ELSE 'High Salary' END AS category FROM Accounts ) SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS accounts_count FROM categorized GROUP BY category;

Why this works: Single scan to categorize all accounts, then GROUP BY. Missing zero-count categories will be absent from output unless UNION ALL appended.

Performance: Single scan + aggregation. Faster than approach #1 but doesn't guarantee all categories in output.

Technique Pivot (Long to Wide)

▼

Reshape long rows into wide columns using CASE WHEN inside an aggregate function. Use MAX for text values, SUM for numeric values.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Stored category to columns 3 problems

▼

The column key is already a column (continent, month, store). CASE reads it directly. MAX for one value per cell, SUM when the cell adds rows. Sorted easy to hard.

Template Stored category to columns template

▼

Use when: the column key is a value already sitting in a column.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Row key → GROUP BY.
  2. One CASE WHEN col = 'label' THEN value END per output column.
  3. Wrap in MAX for one value per cell (text, a single price), SUM when several rows add into the cell.
SELECT row_key,
       MAX(CASE WHEN category = 'A' THEN value END) AS A,   -- one value per cell: MAX
       MAX(CASE WHEN category = 'B' THEN value END) AS B
FROM source_table
GROUP BY row_key;

Easy Reformat Department Table

▼

Pivot monthly revenue into 12 columns (Jan_Revenue, Feb_Revenue, ...).

Tables: Department (id, revenue, month)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

A finance team builds a side-by-side monthly report from a long-format revenue log.

▶ 1 Conditional MAX Pivot
SELECT id, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Jan' THEN revenue END) AS Jan_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Feb' THEN revenue END) AS Feb_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Mar' THEN revenue END) AS Mar_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Apr' THEN revenue END) AS Apr_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='May' THEN revenue END) AS May_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Jun' THEN revenue END) AS Jun_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Jul' THEN revenue END) AS Jul_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Aug' THEN revenue END) AS Aug_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Sep' THEN revenue END) AS Sep_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Oct' THEN revenue END) AS Oct_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Nov' THEN revenue END) AS Nov_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Dec' THEN revenue END) AS Dec_Revenue FROM Department GROUP BY id;

Why this is best: Twelve conditional MAX expressions pivot the long table into wide format.

Performance: One aggregate pass.

Easy Product’s Price for Each Store

▼

Pivot per-store prices into three columns (store1, store2, store3).

Tables: Products (product_id, store, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

A retailer compares prices across three stores side-by-side per product for markdown decisions.

▶ 1 Conditional MAX per Store
SELECT product_id, MAX(CASE WHEN store = 'store1' THEN price END) AS store1, MAX(CASE WHEN store = 'store2' THEN price END) AS store2, MAX(CASE WHEN store = 'store3' THEN price END) AS store3 FROM Products GROUP BY product_id;

Why this is best: Simple pivot with conditional MAX.

Performance: One aggregate.

Hard Students Report By Geography

▼

Pivot students into three columns (America, Asia, Europe) by continent.

Tables: Student (name, continent)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

An international recruiting team generates a side-by-side roster for regional directors.

▶ 1 Row Number + Conditional MAX
SELECT MAX(CASE WHEN continent = 'America' THEN name END) AS America, MAX(CASE WHEN continent = 'Asia' THEN name END) AS Asia, MAX(CASE WHEN continent = 'Europe' THEN name END) AS Europe FROM ( SELECT name, continent, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY continent ORDER BY name) AS rn FROM Student ) t GROUP BY rn ORDER BY rn;

Why this is best: Assign row numbers within continent, then pivot rows with equal numbers into one reporting row.

Performance: One window + one aggregate.

Computed column key 1 problem

▼

The columns are weekdays or months derived from a date. Compute the key with TO_CHAR / EXTRACT, then CASE on it. Watch the padding trap.

Template Computed column key template

▼

Use when: the columns come from a date or number, not a stored label.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Compute the column key first: TO_CHAR(d,'FMDay') (the FM strips the 9 char padding) or EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM d) for a number.
  2. One CASE branch per target column, matching the computed key.
  3. Add ELSE 0 inside the CASE if the prompt wants zeros instead of NULLs.
SELECT category,
       SUM(CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(d, 'FMDay') = 'Monday'  THEN qty ELSE 0 END) AS Monday,
       SUM(CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(d, 'FMDay') = 'Tuesday' THEN qty ELSE 0 END) AS Tuesday
       -- ... one branch per weekday
FROM t
GROUP BY category;
-- TO_CHAR(d,'Day') pads to 9 chars; the FM prefix removes it

Hard Sales by Day of the Week (multi column pivot × DOW extraction × TO_CHAR padding trap)

▼

Pivot weekly sales per item category across the 7 weekday columns. Two lessons: (a) drive from Items as the dim so categories with zero orders still appear as a row of zeros, and (b) the marquee Postgres trap: TO_CHAR(date, 'Day') returns the day name PADDED with trailing spaces to 9 characters ('Monday   ' not 'Monday'), so the CASE branches silently miss every day except Wednesday. Use TO_CHAR(date, 'FMDay') (fill mode) or TRIM(TO_CHAR(...)).

Tables: Orders (order_id, customer_id, order_date, item_id, quantity), Items (item_id, item_name, item_category). The output schema is a wide table: Category column + 7 day name columns + a 0 for the empty cells.

→

Decision Tree Path

Pivot recipe: fixed set of output columns named in the prompt → multi column pivot via SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE 0 END), one column per target. The category that must appear with all zeros → LEFT JOIN from the dim (Items) to the fact (Orders). The pivot column is derived from a DATE, not a stored column → TO_CHAR(date, 'FMDay') with the FM prefix to strip padding.

Real World Example

Merchandising reads a weekly pattern per SKU to plan weekday specific promos — if Wednesday is the strongest Phone day, marketing buys ad space for Tuesday evening to land at the top of Wednesday's feed. Categories with zero orders this period still appear as a row of zeros so the analyst doesn't mistake "no Glasses sold this week" for "Glasses dropped from the catalog."

Build order — dim drives the LEFT JOIN, CASE pivots the day, SUM aggregates the cell:

  1. Start FROM Items (the dim) so every category appears, including ones with zero orders. LEFT JOIN Orders on item_id; categories with no orders keep one row with all Orders columns NULL.
  2. For each weekday, write a SUM(CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'FMDay') = 'Monday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Monday branch. The ELSE 0 handles two cases at once: rows where the day name doesn't match the column AND rows where o.order_date is NULL (the LEFT JOIN's empty bucket for zero order categories).
  3. GROUP BY i.item_category; ORDER BY i.item_category for deterministic output. SUM over only zeros lands at 0 (not NULL), so no COALESCE is needed around the SUM.

Trace — the TO_CHAR padding trap on the example data:

date TO_CHAR(d, 'Day') TO_CHAR(d, 'FMDay') CASE matches 'Monday' string?
2020-06-01'Monday   ' (9 chars)'Monday' (6 chars)'Day' form: NO. 'FMDay' form: yes
2020-06-03'Wednesday' (9 chars, no padding needed)'Wednesday'Both forms match (the trap LIES when padding happens to be 0)
2020-06-05'Friday   ''Friday''Day' form: NO. 'FMDay' form: yes

Without the FM prefix, only Wednesday (the only 9 char day name) matches the literal in the CASE. Every other column comes back as 0, even on data where the answer should be non zero. This is why your output had 5 for Phone on Wednesday but 0 for everything else.

▶ 1 Single SELECT: Items LEFT JOIN Orders + CASE pivot with FMDay (cleanest)
SELECT i.item_category AS Category, SUM(CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'FMDay') = 'Monday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Monday, SUM(CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'FMDay') = 'Tuesday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Tuesday, SUM(CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'FMDay') = 'Wednesday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Wednesday, SUM(CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'FMDay') = 'Thursday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Thursday, SUM(CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'FMDay') = 'Friday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Friday, SUM(CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'FMDay') = 'Saturday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Saturday, SUM(CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'FMDay') = 'Sunday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Sunday FROM Items AS i LEFT JOIN Orders AS o USING (item_id) GROUP BY i.item_category ORDER BY i.item_category;

Why this is best: Zero CTEs. The LEFT JOIN preserves all categories; the CASE expressions pivot date to day name and check against literal column targets; the ELSE 0 turns "no order on this day" AND "no order at all" into 0 without a separate COALESCE step. One JOIN, one GROUP BY, one pass.

▶ 2 1 CTE form: aggregate to (category, dow) first, then pivot (more readable for complex aggregates)
WITH per_dow AS ( SELECT i.item_category, TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'FMDay') AS dow, SUM(o.quantity)::int AS quantity FROM Orders AS o JOIN Items AS i USING (item_id) GROUP BY i.item_category, TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'FMDay') ) SELECT i.item_category AS Category, SUM(CASE WHEN p.dow = 'Monday' THEN p.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Monday, SUM(CASE WHEN p.dow = 'Tuesday' THEN p.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Tuesday, SUM(CASE WHEN p.dow = 'Wednesday' THEN p.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Wednesday, SUM(CASE WHEN p.dow = 'Thursday' THEN p.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Thursday, SUM(CASE WHEN p.dow = 'Friday' THEN p.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Friday, SUM(CASE WHEN p.dow = 'Saturday' THEN p.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Saturday, SUM(CASE WHEN p.dow = 'Sunday' THEN p.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Sunday FROM (SELECT DISTINCT item_category FROM Items) AS i LEFT JOIN per_dow AS p USING (item_category) GROUP BY i.item_category ORDER BY i.item_category;

Why this is also good: Separates the aggregation step (per category, per day name SUM) from the pivot step (CASE branches into wide columns). Useful when the aggregation is more complex (rate calculations, COUNT DISTINCT, etc.) and you want to compute it once in a CTE rather than repeat it inside every CASE branch.

Watch out — the marquee trap and supporting traps:

  • TO_CHAR(date, 'Day') pads to 9 chars. Postgres formats day and month names with trailing spaces to match the longest member ('Wednesday' = 9 chars, 'September' = 9 chars). Use the FM (fill mode) prefix: TO_CHAR(date, 'FMDay') or TO_CHAR(date, 'FMMonth'). Alternative: TRIM(TO_CHAR(date, 'Day')) — same result, slightly noisier. The padding silently breaks string equality with literals like 'Monday', and the failure mode is "everything is 0 except the days whose names happen to already be 9 chars."
  • Wednesday is the LYING test case. If you debug on a single Wednesday data point, it passes regardless of FM. Always test with at least one Monday or Friday in the sample so the padding asymmetry is visible.
  • Drive the LEFT JOIN from the DIM (Items), not the fact (Orders). FROM Orders o LEFT JOIN Items i drops the T-Shirt category (no Orders rows), and the prompt requires every category to appear. FROM Items LEFT JOIN Orders is the correct direction.
  • ELSE 0 makes COALESCE around SUM redundant. With ELSE 0, every CASE branch returns a number (never NULL), so SUM over the group is the sum of numbers, never NULL. Without ELSE 0 the CASE returns NULL on non matching rows, SUM ignores NULLs, but for a category with NO matching rows at all (T-Shirt) the SUM lands at NULL and you'd need COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) outside. Either is correct; ELSE 0 reads cleaner.
  • Day name literals are case sensitive. TO_CHAR returns title case ('Monday'), not uppercase. CASE WHEN ... = 'monday' matches nothing. If the prompt's output columns are all caps ('MONDAY'), still match on title case in the CASE and ALIAS the column to MONDAY.
  • Alternative DOW representations. EXTRACT(DOW FROM date) returns 0 (Sunday) through 6 (Saturday); EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM date) returns 1 (Monday) through 7 (Sunday). Numeric forms avoid the padding trap entirely. The CASE branches become CASE WHEN EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM o.order_date) = 1 THEN .... Use the numeric form if the prompt doesn't insist on the literal day name string inside the CASE.

Zero-fill the pivot 2 problems

▼

Missing cells must read 0, or every entity must appear even with no rows. Drive from the dim, LEFT JOIN the facts, COALESCE the SUM.

Template Zero-fill pivot template

▼

Use when: missing cells must read 0, or an entity with no rows must still appear.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Drive FROM the dim table so every entity survives; LEFT JOIN the facts.
  2. COALESCE(SUM(CASE ...), 0) turns an all NULL group into 0 (or use ELSE 0 inside the CASE).
  3. Carry the dim's display column through the GROUP BY so it rides next to the row key.
SELECT e.entity_id, e.entity_name,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN f.category = 'A' THEN f.value END), 0) AS A,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN f.category = 'B' THEN f.value END), 0) AS B
FROM dim_entity e
LEFT JOIN facts f USING (entity_id)
GROUP BY e.entity_id, e.entity_name
ORDER BY e.entity_id;

Medium Pivot Trial Adverse Events by Severity (SUM + COALESCE 0)

▼

Pivot a long-format adverse events table into one row per trial with one column per severity level. Demonstrates SUM (multiple rows per category sum together) and the COALESCE 0 default for missing categories.

Tables: trial_adverse_events (trial_id, severity_category, event_count)

Real-World Example

A clinical research platform builds a per-trial safety summary that lists Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical event counts side by side for each trial, fed into the regulatory dashboard.

▶ 1 Conditional SUM with COALESCE 0 Default
SELECT trial_id, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Mild' THEN event_count END), 0) AS mild_events, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Moderate' THEN event_count END), 0) AS moderate_events, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Severe' THEN event_count END), 0) AS severe_events, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Critical' THEN event_count END), 0) AS critical_events FROM trial_adverse_events GROUP BY trial_id ORDER BY trial_id;

Why this is best: SUM (not MAX) is required because a trial can have multiple rows in the same severity (e.g., TRIAL-002 has two Mild rows that must add to 5). The CASE returns NULL on non-matching rows, which SUM skips. COALESCE wraps the whole SUM so an entirely missing category becomes 0 instead of NULL.

Trace through TRIAL-002:

severity_category event_count CASE for Mild CASE for Moderate CASE for Severe CASE for Critical
Mild33NULLNULLNULL
Mild22NULLNULLNULL
Critical1NULLNULLNULL1
SUM—5NULL → 0NULL → 01

SUM over all-NULL columns returns NULL. COALESCE flips that to 0. Output row for TRIAL-002: (TRIAL-002, 5, 0, 0, 1).

Equivalent shorthand using ELSE 0 inside the CASE:

SELECT trial_id, SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Mild' THEN event_count ELSE 0 END) AS mild_events, SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Moderate' THEN event_count ELSE 0 END) AS moderate_events, SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Severe' THEN event_count ELSE 0 END) AS severe_events, SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Critical' THEN event_count ELSE 0 END) AS critical_events FROM trial_adverse_events GROUP BY trial_id ORDER BY trial_id;

Same result. The CASE returns 0 instead of NULL for non-matching rows, so SUM never sees a NULL and the outer COALESCE isn't needed. Either form is fine; pick the one whose intent is clearer for the prompt.

Watch out:

  • Use SUM, not MAX. MAX picks one row per category and silently drops the others. The trial with two Mild rows would report 3, not 5.
  • NULL vs 0 must be in the prompt. If the prompt asks for 0 on missing categories, wrap with COALESCE or use ELSE 0. If it asks for NULL, drop both.
  • Category list is fixed at query time. One CASE expression per target column, hand-written. SQL can't dynamically generate the column names.
  • String literals must match exactly. 'Mild' matches but 'mild' does not (case sensitive in most dialects). Check the prompt's spelling.
  • Don't put severity_category in the GROUP BY. Each trial would split into one row per category and the pivot would never collapse.

Medium Pivot Appointment Types by Provider (LEFT JOIN + SUM pivot)

▼

Enrich the source table with a lookup column (provider_name) before pivoting. The carried-through column rides along in the GROUP BY so it appears next to the row key in the output.

Tables: providers (provider_id, provider_name), appointment_counts (provider_id, appointment_type, count_value)

Real-World Example

A telehealth ops team builds a per-provider visit summary that lists initial consult, follow up, and urgent care counts side by side, joined to the provider's display name for the staffing dashboard.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN Enrich + Conditional SUM Pivot
WITH base AS ( SELECT p.provider_id, p.provider_name, a.appointment_type, a.count_value FROM providers AS p LEFT JOIN appointment_counts AS a USING (provider_id) ) SELECT provider_id, provider_name, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN appointment_type = 'initial_consult' THEN count_value END), 0) AS initial_consult_count, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN appointment_type = 'follow_up' THEN count_value END), 0) AS follow_up_count, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN appointment_type = 'urgent_care' THEN count_value END), 0) AS urgent_care_count FROM base GROUP BY provider_id, provider_name ORDER BY provider_id;

Why this is best: The CTE does the enrich step (LEFT JOIN attaches provider_name to each appointment row) so the pivot step only worries about reshaping. LEFT JOIN keeps providers who have no appointment rows; their CASE expressions all evaluate to NULL, SUM returns NULL, and COALESCE flips it to 0.

Three slots filled (row, column, cell):

Slot Filled by Where it appears
Row keyprovider_idGROUP BY
Column keyappointment_type valuesCASE WHEN inside SUM
Cell valuecount_valueTHEN clause inside CASE
Carry-alongprovider_nameGROUP BY (rides with row key)

Why provider_name is in the GROUP BY: any non-aggregated column in the SELECT list must be in the GROUP BY (Postgres enforces this). Adding it doesn't change the row count because provider_name is functionally dependent on provider_id — one name per id, so the row count stays at one row per provider.

Trace through provider 103 (only urgent_care rows, no initial_consult or follow_up):

appointment_type count_value CASE for initial_consult CASE for follow_up CASE for urgent_care
urgent_care2NULLNULL2
urgent_care1NULLNULL1
SUM—NULL → 0NULL → 03

Output row: (103, Dr. Carol Singh, 0, 0, 3).

Watch out:

  • Use LEFT JOIN, not INNER JOIN, when the lookup table is the “keep all rows” side. If a provider has zero appointment rows, INNER JOIN drops them entirely and the output is missing a provider. The prompt here doesn't have that case in the example data, but real test data often does.
  • Carry the lookup column through the GROUP BY. Dropping provider_name from GROUP BY raises an error in strict dialects (Postgres) or returns one arbitrary value per group in lenient ones (older MySQL). Both are wrong.
  • Don't put appointment_type in the GROUP BY. Each provider would split into one row per type and the pivot wouldn't collapse.
  • USING vs ON: USING (provider_id) works when both tables share the column name and is concise. ON p.provider_id = a.provider_id is more portable and self-documenting. Either is fine.
  • The CTE is optional. You could fold the JOIN into the FROM of the pivot SELECT directly. The CTE just makes the staircase easier to read: enrich first, pivot second.

Signed aggregate (net of opposing categories) 1 problem

▼

Two opposing categories (credit / debit) collapse into one signed net total — SUM(CASE +/-).

Template — signed aggregate (net of opposing categories)

▼

Use when: two opposing categories (credit / debit, in / out) collapse into one net total.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. GROUP BY the entity.
  2. Inside one SUM, add one category and subtract the other with CASE.
  3. The net can be negative; no wide columns needed.
SELECT entity_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'credit' THEN amount ELSE 0 END
         - CASE WHEN type = 'debit'  THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS net
FROM t
GROUP BY entity_id;

Medium Net Delivery Adjustment per Restaurant

▼

Collapse credit and debit rows into one signed net per restaurant with SUM(CASE +/-).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Each adjustment is a credit (positive) or a debit (negative). Compute the net_adjustment per restaurant (credits minus debits; may be negative).
  • Include restaurants with at least one adjustment. Return restaurant_id, net_adjustment, ordered by restaurant_id.

Schema — payout_adjustments

ColumnType
adjustment_idINT
restaurant_idINT
adjustment_typeVARCHAR
amountDECIMAL(10,2)

Example input — payout_adjustments

adjustment_idrestaurant_idadjustment_typeamount
1101credit50.00
2101debit20.00
3102credit100.00
4102credit30.00
5102debit150.00
6103debit25.00
7103debit15.00

Expected output

restaurant_idnet_adjustment
10130.00
102-20.00
103-40.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Opposing categories collapse into ONE signed total: add the amount for credits, subtract it for
  debits, all inside a single SUM over the group. No pivot to wide columns -- the two categories
  net against each other. The result can go negative (restaurants 102, 103).

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 3 expected rows.
*/

SELECT
    restaurant_id,
    SUM(CASE WHEN adjustment_type = 'credit' THEN amount ELSE 0 END
      - CASE WHEN adjustment_type = 'debit'  THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS net_adjustment
FROM payout_adjustments
GROUP BY restaurant_id
ORDER BY restaurant_id;

Set membership: has ALL / NONE 1 problem

▼

Keep entities that have ALL of some categories and NONE of another — HAVING MAX(CASE)=1/=0.

Template — set membership gate (HAVING MAX(CASE))

▼

Use when: keep entities that have ALL of some categories and NONE of others.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. GROUP BY the entity.
  2. One HAVING line per category: MAX(CASE...)=1 means "has", =0 means "never".
  3. Entities with no rows never reach the GROUP, so they drop for free.
SELECT entity_id
FROM t
GROUP BY entity_id
HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN cat = 'X' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1
   AND MAX(CASE WHEN cat = 'Z' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0;
-- Postgres: BOOL_OR(cat='X') in place of MAX(CASE...)=1

Medium Customers Who Bought Bread AND Milk but NOT Soda

▼

Keep customers whose purchases include ALL of some products and NONE of another, via a HAVING gate of MAX(CASE).

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Return customer_id for customers who bought at least one Bread AND at least one Milk AND zero Soda.
  • Order by customer_id.

Schema — purchases

ColumnType
purchase_idINT
customer_idINT
productVARCHAR

Example input — purchases

purchase_idcustomer_idproduct
11Bread
21Milk
32Bread
42Milk
52Soda
63Bread
74Bread
84Milk

Expected output

customer_id
1
4

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  GROUP BY customer, then a HAVING gate of MAX(CASE ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END): = 1 means 'has at
  least one', = 0 means 'never'. Customer 2 has Soda so its Soda MAX(CASE) = 1, failing = 0;
  customer 3 has no Milk. (BOOL_OR works in place of MAX(CASE)=1 in Postgres.)

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT customer_id
FROM purchases
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN product = 'Bread' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1   -- has Bread
   AND MAX(CASE WHEN product = 'Milk'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1   -- has Milk
   AND MAX(CASE WHEN product = 'Soda'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0   -- never Soda
ORDER BY customer_id;

Threshold per category 1 problem

▼

A numeric total per category must clear a bar for every required category — HAVING SUM(CASE)≥N.

Template — threshold per category (HAVING SUM(CASE))

▼

Use when: a numeric total per category must clear a bar for EVERY required category.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. GROUP BY the entity.
  2. One HAVING line per category: SUM(CASE WHEN cat THEN amount ELSE 0 END) >= N.
  3. AND the lines together so all categories must qualify.
SELECT entity_id
FROM t
GROUP BY entity_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN cat = 'A' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) >= N
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN cat = 'B' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) >= N;

Medium Customers Who Spent $100+ in EACH of June and July

▼

A per-category numeric gate: SUM(CASE) per category must clear a threshold for EVERY required category.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Return customer_id for customers whose total spend was at least 100 in June AND at least 100 in July.
  • Order by customer_id.

Schema — orders

ColumnType
order_idINT
customer_idINT
monVARCHAR
amountDECIMAL(10,2)

Example input — orders

order_idcustomer_idmonamount
11June60.00
21June50.00
31July120.00
42June200.00
52July50.00
63June100.00
73July100.00

Expected output

customer_id
1
3

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  GROUP BY customer, then a HAVING gate where each category's SUM(CASE) must clear the threshold:
  SUM the amount for June rows >= 100 AND SUM for July rows >= 100. Customer 2 fails July (only 50).
  Do NOT GROUP BY customer, month with HAVING month='June' AND month='July' -- a single row can't
  be both months; the per-category SUM(CASE) is what makes the AND work.

  Verified against the example data -- output matches the 2 expected rows.
*/

SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN mon = 'June' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) >= 100
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN mon = 'July' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) >= 100
ORDER BY customer_id;

Technique Unpivot (Wide to Long)

▼

Flip wide columns into long rows by writing one SELECT per column and stacking with UNION ALL.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Answer each question — the next one appears, ending on the exact technique to use.

Columns to rows, drop the empties 2 problems

▼

Plain wide to long reshape. One SELECT per column with a literal label; WHERE col IS NOT NULL drops the blanks.

Template Drop the empties template

▼

Use when: you are just reshaping wide to long and blank cells should not appear.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. One SELECT per source column: entity key, a literal label, the column value.
  2. Add WHERE col IS NOT NULL to each branch so empty cells drop out.
  3. Stack with UNION ALL; the output column names come from the first SELECT.
SELECT entity_id, 'col_a' AS label, col_a AS value
FROM t WHERE col_a IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT entity_id, 'col_b', col_b
FROM t WHERE col_b IS NOT NULL;

Easy Rearrange Products Table

▼

Unpivot three price columns into rows (product_id, store, price).

Tables: Products (product_id, store1, store2, store3)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

Analytics normalizes a wide feed into long form for easier downstream aggregation.

▶ 1 UNION ALL with Label Literals
SELECT product_id, 'store1' AS store, store1 AS price FROM Products WHERE store1 IS NOT NULL UNION ALL SELECT product_id, 'store2', store2 FROM Products WHERE store2 IS NOT NULL UNION ALL SELECT product_id, 'store3', store3 FROM Products WHERE store3 IS NOT NULL;

Why this is best: Each SELECT reshapes one column into a labeled row; NULL filter drops missing prices.

Performance: Three scans, one per column.

Example Reverse of #618: Unpivot Students Report Back to (name, continent)

▼

Take the wide result from #618 (America, Asia, Europe columns) and unpivot it back into the original long format (name, continent).

Input (wide): StudentReport (America, Asia, Europe) — the output from #618

Output (long): one row per (name, continent), nulls dropped

Why Reverse a Pivot?

Wide reports are easy to read but hard to aggregate. Analysts often unpivot back to long format before charting, joining to a dimension table, or running a GROUP BY.

Input table (example):
