resolution_time_minutesINT
sla_target_minutesINT

Example input — support_tickets

ticket_idagent_idassigned_dateresolution_time_minutessla_target_minutes
11022024-01-2012060
21022024-02-013060
31022024-03-019060
41022024-01-1020060
51032024-02-0199960

Expected output

breach_rate
66.67

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The whole answer is a single aggregate ratio wrapped in a scalar function. The date guard
  (assigned_date >= p_start_date) drops ticket 4; tickets 1 and 3 breach, 2 does not -> 2/3.
  NULLIF(COUNT(*),0) guards divide-by-zero and COALESCE(...,0.00) returns 0 for an agent with
  no tickets. Verified: the inner query returns 66.67 on the example data.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_agent_breach_rate(
    p_agent_id   INTEGER,
    p_start_date DATE
) RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN (
    SELECT COALESCE(
      ROUND(
        100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN resolution_time_minutes > sla_target_minutes
                         THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)::NUMERIC
              / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0),
        2
      ),
      0.00
    )
    FROM support_tickets
    WHERE agent_id = p_agent_id
      AND assigned_date >= p_start_date
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT calculate_agent_breach_rate(102, '2024-01-15') AS breach_rate;

Easy Calculate Denial Rate by Reviewer

▼

A slimmer scalar rate: percent of a reviewer's reviews that were DENIED, via the AVG(CASE) shortcut.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Write calculate_reviewer_denial_rate(p_reviewer_id INTEGER) RETURNS NUMERIC: the percent of that reviewer's reviews where denial_status = 'DENIED'.
  • Return 0.00 if the reviewer has no reviews. Example call: calculate_reviewer_denial_rate(1).

Schema — diagnosis_reviews

ColumnType
review_idINT
reviewer_idINT
denial_statusVARCHAR

Example input — diagnosis_reviews

review_idreviewer_iddenial_status
11DENIED
21APPROVED
31DENIED
42APPROVED

Expected output

denial_rate
66.67

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  AVG(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100 is the ratio shortcut: the average of a 0/1 flag IS
  the fraction that qualifies. Reviewer 1 has 2 DENIED of 3 -> 66.67. COALESCE returns 0.00 for
  a reviewer with no rows. Verified: the inner query returns 66.67 on the example data.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_reviewer_denial_rate(p_reviewer_id INTEGER)
RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN (
    SELECT COALESCE(
      ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN denial_status = 'DENIED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100, 2),
      0.00
    )
    FROM diagnosis_reviews
    WHERE reviewer_id = p_reviewer_id
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT calculate_reviewer_denial_rate(1) AS denial_rate;

Medium Calculate Average Session Engagement Score (rolling 90 days)

▼

Scalar AVG over a rolling 90-day window. The example uses a fixed cutoff to stay deterministic; the function uses CURRENT_DATE - 90 days.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Write calculate_avg_engagement(p_client_id INTEGER) RETURNS NUMERIC: the average engagement_score across that client's sessions in the past 90 days, or 0.00 if none.
  • Example call: calculate_avg_engagement(1). (Example data below uses a fixed window cutoff so the result is reproducible.)

Schema — therapy_sessions

ColumnType
session_idINT
client_idINT
engagement_scoreDECIMAL(4,2)
session_dateDATE

Example input — therapy_sessions

session_idclient_idengagement_scoresession_date
118.002024-06-01
216.002024-06-15
312.002023-01-01
429.002024-06-10

Expected output

avg_score

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A scalar AVG with a rolling date window. The window keeps only recent sessions (the function uses
  CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'; the example fixes the cutoff so the number is stable), so the
  old 2023 session is excluded and client 1 averages 8 and 6 -> 7.00. COALESCE returns 0.00 when
  the window is empty. Verified: the inner query returns 7.00 on the example data.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_avg_engagement(p_client_id INTEGER)
RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$
BEGIN

    SELECT COALESCE(AVG(engagement_score), 0.00)
      FROM therapy_sessions
     WHERE client_id    = p_client_id
       AND session_date > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'
  );

$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

Medium Calculate Weekly Sleep Goal Adherence Rate (denominator = N exactly)

▼

The denominator is a FIXED 7 nights, not the rows present. Build a 7-day spine, LEFT JOIN logs, count missing nights as failures.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Write calculate_sleep_adherence(p_member_id INTEGER, p_target_week_start DATE) RETURNS NUMERIC: the percent of the 7 consecutive nights starting at the week start where actual_hours_slept ≥ target_hours_per_night.
  • Nights with no log count as failures (denominator is always 7). Example call: calculate_sleep_adherence(1, '2024-01-15').

Schema — members

ColumnType
member_idINT
target_hours_per_nightDECIMAL(3,1)

Schema — sleep_logs

ColumnType
log_idINT
member_idINT
log_dateDATE
actual_hours_sleptDECIMAL(3,1)

Example input — members

member_idtarget_hours_per_night
17.0

Example input — sleep_logs

log_idmember_idlog_dateactual_hours_slept
112024-01-158.0
212024-01-166.0
312024-01-177.5
412024-01-207.0

Expected output

result
42.86

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  The trap: the denominator is exactly 7 nights, not the number of logs. Build a 7-day date spine,
  LEFT JOIN the member's logs, and average a 0/1 hit flag over all 7 rows -- a night with no log
  stays NULL on the join and the CASE makes it a 0 (failure). Here 3 of 7 nights hit -> 42.86.
  Verified: the inner query returns that rate on the example data. (Display uses generate_series;
  DuckDB verify uses range(0,7) for the same 7-day spine.)
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_sleep_adherence(
    p_member_id          INTEGER,
    p_target_week_start  DATE
) RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN (
    WITH dates AS (
      SELECT generate_series(
               p_target_week_start,
               p_target_week_start + 6,
               INTERVAL '1 day'
             )::date AS log_date
    ),
    member_target AS (
      SELECT target_hours_per_night
        FROM members
       WHERE member_id = p_member_id
    )
    SELECT ROUND(
             AVG(
               CASE WHEN sl.actual_hours_slept >= mt.target_hours_per_night
                    THEN 1.0
                    ELSE 0
               END
             ) * 100,
             2
           )
      FROM dates AS d
      LEFT JOIN sleep_logs AS sl
        ON sl.log_date  = d.log_date
       AND sl.member_id = p_member_id
      CROSS JOIN member_target AS mt
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT calculate_sleep_adherence(1, '2024-01-15') AS result;

Medium 30-Day Readmission Rate (LAG previous discharge + scalar rate)

▼

Per department, the percent of admissions that follow the patient's previous discharge from the same department within 30 days. LAG to reach the prior discharge, then a scalar rate.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Write calculate_readmission_rate(p_department_name VARCHAR) RETURNS NUMERIC(5,2). A readmission is an admission to the same department within 30 days of that patient's previous discharge from that department.
  • Return (readmissions / total_admissions) * 100, or 0.00 if none. Example call: calculate_readmission_rate('Cardiology').

Schema — admissions

ColumnType
admission_idINT
patient_idINT
department_nameVARCHAR
admission_dateDATE
discharge_dateDATE

Example input — admissions

admission_idpatient_iddepartment_nameadmission_datedischarge_date
11Cardiology2024-01-012024-01-05
21Cardiology2024-01-202024-01-25
31Cardiology2024-04-012024-04-03
42Cardiology2024-02-012024-02-04

Expected output

readmission_rate
25.0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  LAG pulls each patient's PREVIOUS discharge from the same department onto the current admission;
  it counts as a readmission when this admission is within 30 days of that prior discharge. The
  first admission per patient has a NULL prev (no readmission). Admission 2 (Jan 20) is within 30
  days of discharge Jan 5 -> readmit; admission 3 (Apr) is not. 1 of 4 -> 25.00. Verified.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_readmission_rate(p_department_name VARCHAR)
RETURNS NUMERIC(5,2) AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN (
    WITH base AS (
      SELECT
        a.admission_id,
        a.patient_id,
        a.department_name,
        a.admission_date,
        a.discharge_date,
        LAG(a.discharge_date) OVER (
          PARTITION BY a.patient_id, a.department_name
          ORDER BY a.discharge_date
        ) AS prev_discharge_date
      FROM admissions AS a
      WHERE a.department_name = p_department_name
    ),
    check_readmission AS (
      SELECT
        b.admission_id,
        b.patient_id,
        b.department_name,
        b.admission_date,
        b.discharge_date,
        b.prev_discharge_date,
        CASE
          WHEN b.admission_date <= b.prev_discharge_date + INTERVAL '30 days'
          THEN 1.0
          ELSE 0
        END AS readmitted
      FROM base AS b
    )
    SELECT COALESCE(
             ROUND(AVG(readmitted) * 100, 2),
             0.00
           ) AS readmission_rate
    FROM check_readmission
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT calculate_readmission_rate('Cardiology') AS readmission_rate;

result
33.33

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Filter to the cohort month FIRST (signups 1-3 are January; 4 is excluded), then the rate is the
  share that converted within the window. The gotcha: non-converters (signup 2, NULL; signup 3,
  converted too late) stay in the DENOMINATOR -- only signup 1 converts in time, so 1 of 3 ->
  33.33. A NULL converted_at compares false, so it counts as not converted. Verified.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_conversion_rate(cohort_month DATE, days_window INT)
RETURNS NUMERIC(5, 2) AS $$
BEGIN
    RETURN (
        WITH base AS (
            SELECT
                TO_CHAR(ts.trial_start_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS trial_month,
                TO_CHAR(cohort_month::date, 'YYYY-MM') AS cohort_month,
                CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(ts.trial_start_date, 'YYYY-MM') = TO_CHAR(cohort_month::date, 'YYYY-MM')
                     THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS in_cohort,
                ts.trial_start_date,
                ts.signup_id,
                ts.company_name,
                ts.converted_at,
                ts.trial_start_date::date + days_window AS conversation_deadline
            FROM trial_signups AS ts
        ),
        cohort AS (
            SELECT
                b.trial_month,
                b.cohort_month,
                b.in_cohort,
                b.trial_start_date,
                b.signup_id,
                b.company_name,
                b.converted_at,
                b.conversation_deadline,
                CASE WHEN b.converted_at <= b.conversation_deadline THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END AS converted
            FROM base AS b
            WHERE b.in_cohort = 1
        )
        SELECT COALESCE(
                 ROUND(AVG(converted) * 100, 2),
                 0.00
               )
        FROM cohort
    );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT calculate_conversion_rate('2024-01-01', 14) AS result;

Hard Average Retry Delay (per-day session detect + last-status filter + LEAD within session)

▼

Group attempts into per-day runs, keep only runs that ended failed with 2+ attempts, then average the LEAD gap between consecutive attempts.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Write calculate_avg_retry_delay(p_job_name TEXT) RETURNS NUMERIC: the average delay (minutes) between consecutive retry attempts for runs that ultimately failed.
  • A run = all attempts for the job on one calendar date; only count runs whose LAST attempt was 'failed' AND that had 2+ attempts. Example call: calculate_avg_retry_delay('data_sync').

Schema — job_attempts

ColumnType
attempt_idINT
job_nameVARCHAR
attempted_atTIMESTAMP
attempt_numberINT
statusVARCHAR

Example input — job_attempts

attempt_idjob_nameattempted_atattempt_numberstatus
1data_sync2024-01-01 09:00:001failed
2data_sync2024-01-01 09:10:002failed
3data_sync2024-01-02 09:00:001failed
4data_sync2024-01-02 09:30:002success

Expected output

result
10.00

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Three moves: (1) bucket attempts into per-day runs; (2) keep only runs with 2+ attempts whose LAST
  attempt failed (MAX(status) <> 'success' is the string-max trick that excludes a day ending in
  'success'); (3) LEAD gives the gap to the next attempt within the run, averaged in minutes.
  Jan 1 (two failures) contributes a 10-minute gap; Jan 2 ends in 'success' so it is excluded.
  Average = 10.00. Verified against the example data.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_avg_retry_delay(p_job_name TEXT)
RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$
BEGIN
    RETURN (
        WITH base AS (
            SELECT
                j.attempt_id,
                j.job_name,
                j.attempted_at,
                j.attempted_at::DATE AS attempted_date,
                j.attempt_number,
                j.status,
                SUM(CASE WHEN j.attempt_number = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
                    OVER (PARTITION BY j.job_name ORDER BY j.attempted_at) - 1 AS grp
            FROM job_attempts AS j
            WHERE j.job_name = p_job_name
        ),
        qualifying_days AS (
            SELECT job_name, attempted_date
            FROM base
            GROUP BY job_name, attempted_date
            HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
               AND MAX(status) <> 'success'
        ),
        deltas AS (
            SELECT
                b.attempt_id,
                b.attempted_at,
                b.grp,
                ROUND(
                    EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM
                        LEAD(b.attempted_at) OVER (
                            PARTITION BY b.job_name, b.grp ORDER BY b.attempted_at
                        ) - b.attempted_at
                    ) / 60,
                2) AS min_diff
            FROM base AS b
            JOIN qualifying_days AS q
              ON b.job_name = q.job_name
             AND b.attempted_date = q.attempted_date
        )
        SELECT COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(min_diff), 2), 0.00)
        FROM deltas
    );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT calculate_avg_retry_delay('data_sync') AS result;

Medium Count Invites from Top Squad Leaders (RETURNS scalar + DENSE_RANK gate)

▼

Rank players by wins across the whole population, then return a player's invites sent only if they are top-3 by wins, else 0.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Write count_top_leader_invites(p_player_id INT) RETURNS INT: the number of squad invites that player sent, but only if their win count is in the top 3 (DENSE_RANK) across all players; otherwise 0.
  • Example call: count_top_leader_invites(101).

Schema — match_results

ColumnType
result_idINT
player_idINT
placementINT

Schema — squad_invites

ColumnType
invite_idINT
inviter_player_idINT

Example input — match_results

result_idplayer_idplacement
11011
21011
31011
41021
51032

Example input — squad_invites

invite_idinviter_player_id
1101
2101
3102

Expected output

result
2

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Rank every player by wins with DENSE_RANK across the whole population, count invites sent per
  inviter, LEFT JOIN so a top player who sent none still resolves (COALESCE 0), then gate: return
  the invite count only if rank <= 3, else 0. Player 101 (3 wins) is rank 1 and sent 2 -> 2.
  Verified against the example data.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION count_top_leader_invites(p_player_id INT)
RETURNS INT AS $$
BEGIN
RETURN (
    WITH player_rankings AS (
        -- 1 + 2: wins per player, DENSE_RANK across the whole population
        SELECT
            m.player_id,
            SUM(CASE WHEN placement = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS nbr_wins,
            DENSE_RANK() OVER (
                ORDER BY SUM(CASE WHEN placement = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) DESC
            ) AS rnk
        FROM match_results AS m
        GROUP BY m.player_id
    ),
    total_sent AS (
        -- 3: invites sent per inviter
        SELECT
            inviter_player_id AS player_id,
            COUNT(*) AS invites_sent
        FROM squad_invites
        GROUP BY inviter_player_id
    ),
    base AS (
        -- 4 + 5: combine, COALESCE the missing-sender NULL, cast to INT
        SELECT
            p.player_id,
            p.nbr_wins,
            p.rnk,
            COALESCE(t.invites_sent, 0)::int AS invites_sent
        FROM player_rankings AS p
        LEFT JOIN total_sent AS t USING (player_id)
    )
    -- 6: gate + filter to the input player
    SELECT
        CASE WHEN rnk <= 3 THEN invites_sent ELSE 0 END AS result
    FROM base
    WHERE player_id = p_player_id
);
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT count_top_leader_invites(101) AS result;

RETURNS TABLE 8 problems

▼

Template RETURNS TABLE template (full order)

▼

Use when: the function returns a row set (multiple rows, multiple columns).

The order, top to bottom:

  1. CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION name(args).
  2. RETURNS TABLE ( col type, ... ) — the output columns and types must match the query exactly.
  3. LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$.
  4. BEGIN.
  5. RETURN QUERY ( SELECT ... ); — RETURN QUERY, never RETURN ( ).
  6. END $$;.
  7. Trailing call: SELECT * FROM name(args);.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_name(p_arg INT)
RETURNS TABLE (
    out_id    INT,
    out_total NUMERIC
)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
    RETURN QUERY (
        SELECT id, SUM(metric)
        FROM tbl WHERE key = p_arg
        GROUP BY id
    );
END $$;

-- call with SELECT * FROM:
SELECT * FROM fn_name(123);

Medium Nth Highest Salary (function form)

▼

Anchor problem for the recipe: a function returning the Nth highest DISTINCT salary, or NULL when fewer than N exist.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Write getNthHighestSalary(N INT) RETURNS TABLE(Salary INT): the Nth highest DISTINCT salary, or NULL if fewer than N distinct salaries exist.
  • Example call: SELECT * FROM getNthHighestSalary(2).

Schema — Employee

ColumnType
idINT
salaryINT

Example input — Employee

idsalary
1100
2200
3200
4300

Expected output

Salary
200

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  DENSE_RANK over salary DESC ties equal salaries to one rank, so DISTINCT salary at rank = N is the
  Nth highest. Wrapping the pick in a scalar subquery makes it return NULL (not 'no rows') when
  fewer than N distinct salaries exist. With salaries 300/200/100, rank 2 is 200. Verified.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION getNthHighestSalary(N INT)
RETURNS TABLE (Salary INT) AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY (
    WITH salary_rankings AS (
      SELECT
        e.id,
        e.salary,
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rank
      FROM Employee AS e
    ),
    nth_salary AS (
      SELECT DISTINCT s.salary
      FROM salary_rankings AS s
      WHERE s.rank = N
    )
    SELECT (SELECT n.salary FROM nth_salary AS n)
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT * FROM getNthHighestSalary(2);

Medium Patient Medication Adherence Report (RETURNS TABLE)

▼

Per medication with a refill in the lookback window: refill count, last refill date, and the days-supply from the most recent refill. The example uses a fixed cutoff.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Write get_adherence_report(p_patient_id INTEGER, p_lookback_days INTEGER) RETURNS TABLE(...): per medication with a refill in the window, return medication_name, total_refills, last_refill_date, and days_supply_remaining (from the most recent refill). Order by last_refill_date DESC, medication_name ASC.
  • Example call: SELECT * FROM get_adherence_report(101, 30).

Schema — medications

ColumnType
medication_idINT
medication_nameVARCHAR

Schema — medication_orders

ColumnType
order_idINT
patient_idINT
medication_idINT
order_dateDATE
days_supplyINT

Example input — medications

medication_idmedication_name
1Lisinopril
2Metformin

Example input — medication_orders

order_idpatient_idmedication_idorder_datedays_supply
110112024-06-1030
210112024-06-2530
310122024-06-2060
410122024-04-0160

Expected output

medication_nametotal_refillslast_refill_datedays_supply_remaining
Lisinopril22024-06-2530
Metformin12024-06-2060

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Three CTEs: the patient's orders in the window; per-medication COUNT + MAX(order_date); and DISTINCT
  ON to grab the days_supply from each medication's most recent refill. Lisinopril has 2 refills
  (latest Jun 25), Metformin 1 (Jun 20; its April refill is outside the window). Ordered by last
  refill. Verified. (Display uses CURRENT_DATE - lookback; example uses a fixed cutoff.)
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION get_adherence_report(
    p_patient_id INTEGER,
    p_lookback_days INTEGER
)
RETURNS TABLE (
    medication_name VARCHAR,
    total_refills BIGINT,
    last_refill_date DATE,
    days_supply_remaining INTEGER
) AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY (
    WITH orders_base AS (
        -- this patient's orders within the lookback window
        SELECT
            mo.order_id,
            mo.patient_id,
            m.medication_name,
            mo.order_date,
            mo.days_supply
        FROM medication_orders AS mo
        JOIN medications AS m USING (medication_id)
        WHERE mo.patient_id = p_patient_id
          AND mo.order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - (p_lookback_days || ' days')::INTERVAL
    ),
    aggregates AS (
        -- count refills and find latest refill date per medication
        SELECT
            o.medication_name,
            COUNT(*)        AS total_refills,
            MAX(o.order_date) AS last_refill_date
        FROM orders_base AS o
        GROUP BY o.medication_name
    ),
    latest_refill AS (
        -- one row per medication: days_supply from the most recent refill
        SELECT DISTINCT ON (o.medication_name)
            o.medication_name,
            o.days_supply
        FROM orders_base AS o
        ORDER BY o.medication_name, o.order_date DESC
    )
    SELECT
        a.medication_name::VARCHAR,
        a.total_refills::BIGINT,
        a.last_refill_date::DATE,
        l.days_supply::INTEGER AS days_supply_remaining
    FROM aggregates AS a
    JOIN latest_refill AS l USING (medication_name)
    ORDER BY a.last_refill_date DESC, a.medication_name ASC
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Trailing call so the test harness has rows to evaluate:
SELECT * FROM get_adherence_report(101, 30);

Easy Filter Claims by Denial Category

Return claim rows matching a denial category (case-insensitive) within a date range, ordered. A straight RETURNS TABLE filter.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Write get_claims_by_denial_category(p_denial_category VARCHAR, p_start_date DATE, p_end_date DATE) RETURNS TABLE(...): claims whose denial_category matches (case-insensitive) and whose submission_date is in [start, end], ordered by submission_date then claim_id.
  • Example call: get_claims_by_denial_category('Authorization', '2024-01-01', '2024-12-31').

Schema — claims

ColumnType
claim_idINT
patient_idINT
submission_dateDATE
billed_amountDECIMAL(8,2)
denial_reasonVARCHAR
denial_categoryVARCHAR

Example input — claims

claim_idpatient_idsubmission_datebilled_amountdenial_reasondenial_category
1102024-02-01100.00No auth on fileAuthorization
2112024-03-01200.00Filed lateTimeliness
3122024-05-01150.00Auth missingauthorization
4132023-12-0150.00No authAuthorization

Expected output

claim_idpatient_idsubmission_datebilled_amountdenial_reasondenial_category
1102024-02-01100.00No auth on fileAuthorization
3122024-05-01150.00Auth missingauthorization

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A straight filter wrapped in RETURNS TABLE: LOWER() on both sides makes the category match
  case-insensitive (so 'authorization' matches 'Authorization'), the date range is inclusive, and
  the ORDER BY is deterministic. Claim 4 is out of the window; claim 2 is a different category.
  Claims 1 and 3 remain. Verified against the example data.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION get_claims_by_denial_category(
    p_denial_category VARCHAR,
    p_start_date      DATE,
    p_end_date        DATE
) RETURNS TABLE (
    claim_id        INTEGER,
    patient_id      INTEGER,
    submission_date DATE,
    billed_amount   DECIMAL,
    denial_reason   VARCHAR,
    denial_category VARCHAR
) AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY (
    SELECT c.claim_id,
           c.patient_id,
           c.submission_date,
           c.billed_amount,
           c.denial_reason,
           c.denial_category
      FROM claims AS c
     WHERE LOWER(c.denial_category) = LOWER(p_denial_category)
       AND c.submission_date >= p_start_date
       AND c.submission_date <= p_end_date
     ORDER BY c.submission_date ASC, c.claim_id ASC
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

  • Example call: SELECT * FROM calculate_engagement_scores(1, 10).

Schema — therapists

Example input — therapy_sessions

session_idclient_idtherapist_idsession_dateminutes_attendedhomework_completed

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  One row per session in the window, with the score computed inline. The trick is homework_completed::int
  -- casting a boolean to 0/1 so it can be weighted (x 50) and added to minutes x 10. Jun 25:
  45*10 + 0 = 450; Jun 20: 30*10 + 50 = 350; the January session is outside the window. Verified.
  (Display uses CURRENT_DATE - p_date_range_days; example uses a fixed cutoff.)
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_engagement_scores(
    p_client_id        INTEGER,
    p_date_range_days  INTEGER
) RETURNS TABLE (
    session_date       DATE,
    therapist_name     VARCHAR(100),
    minutes_attended   INTEGER,
    homework_completed BOOLEAN,
    engagement_score   INTEGER
) AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY (
    SELECT ts.session_date,
           t.therapist_name,
           ts.minutes_attended,
           ts.homework_completed,
           (ts.minutes_attended * 10) + (ts.homework_completed::int * 50) AS engagement_score
      FROM therapy_sessions AS ts
      JOIN therapists       AS t USING (therapist_id)
     WHERE ts.client_id    = p_client_id
       AND ts.session_date >= CURRENT_DATE - p_date_range_days
     ORDER BY ts.session_date DESC
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

Medium Loan Stage Duration Analysis (timestamp subtraction + EPOCH extraction)

▼

Per completed stage, the duration in hours (timestamp subtraction via EXTRACT EPOCH), keeping only stages that exited and ran at least p_min_hours.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • Write get_stage_durations(p_application_id INTEGER, p_min_hours NUMERIC) RETURNS TABLE(...): per completed stage, duration_hours rounded to 2 decimals. Exclude stages still open (exited_at IS NULL) and any with duration < p_min_hours. Order by entered_at ASC.
  • Example call: SELECT * FROM get_stage_durations(1001, 10).

Schema — application_stage_history

ColumnType
stage_nameVARCHAR
application_idINT
entered_atTIMESTAMP
exited_atTIMESTAMP

Example input — application_stage_history

stage_nameapplication_identered_atexited_at
Application10012024-01-01 00:00:002024-01-01 12:00:00
Review10012024-01-02 00:00:002024-01-02 05:00:00
Approval10012024-01-03 00:00:00NULL
Funding10012024-01-04 00:00:002024-01-05 00:00:00

Expected output

stage_nameentered_atexited_atduration_hours
Application2024-01-01 00:00:002024-01-01 12:00:0012.0
Funding2024-01-04 00:00:002024-01-05 00:00:0024.0

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  duration_hours = EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (exited_at - entered_at)) / 3600 -- the timestamp difference is
  an interval, EPOCH turns it into seconds, /3600 into hours. Exclude open stages (exited_at NULL,
  the Approval row) and any under the floor (Review's 5h). Application (12h) and Funding (24h)
  remain, ordered by entry. Verified against the example data.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION get_stage_durations(p_application_id INT, p_min_hours NUMERIC)
RETURNS TABLE (stage_name VARCHAR(100), entered_at TIMESTAMP, exited_at TIMESTAMP, duration_hours NUMERIC(10,2)) AS $$
BEGIN
   RETURN QUERY (
     WITH base AS (
       SELECT
          ash.stage_name,
          ash.entered_at,
          ash.exited_at,
          ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ash.exited_at - ash.entered_at)) / 3600, 2) AS duration_hours
       FROM application_stage_history AS ash
       WHERE ash.application_id = p_application_id
         AND ash.exited_at IS NOT NULL
     )
     SELECT b.stage_name, b.entered_at, b.exited_at, b.duration_hours
     FROM base AS b
     WHERE b.duration_hours >= p_min_hours
     ORDER BY b.entered_at ASC
   );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT * FROM get_stage_durations(1001, 10);

Keep goals whose longest streak ≥ p_min_streak_days; order by longest_streak DESC, goal_name ASC.

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  A multi-CTE report: totals (COUNT + AVG over all logged nights), then a gaps-and-islands streak on just
  the met-target nights (date - row_number gives a constant anchor per consecutive run), MAX run =
  longest streak. Here Jan 1-3 meet the target (streak 3), Jan 4 misses, Jan 5 is a streak of 1, so
  longest = 3, which clears the floor. total_nights 5, avg 83.00. Verified against the example data.
*/

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION get_goal_streak_summary(
    p_user_id          INTEGER,
    p_min_streak_days  INTEGER
)
RETURNS TABLE (
    goal_name       VARCHAR(100),
    total_nights    INTEGER,
    avg_score       DECIMAL(5,2),
    longest_streak  INTEGER
)
AS $$
BEGIN
    RETURN QUERY
    WITH joined AS (
        -- 1. Pull the rows: join goals + logs for the user, drop NULL scores
        SELECT
            g.goal_name    AS gname,
            g.target_score AS tgt,
            l.log_date     AS d,
            l.sleep_score  AS s
        FROM sleep_goals AS g
        JOIN sleep_logs  AS l ON l.goal_id = g.goal_id
        WHERE g.user_id = p_user_id
          AND l.sleep_score IS NOT NULL
    ),
    totals AS (
        -- 2. Per goal: COUNT + AVG over every non-NULL logged night
        SELECT
            j.gname,
            COUNT(*)::INTEGER                         AS total_nights,
            ROUND(AVG(j.s)::numeric, 2)::DECIMAL(5,2) AS avg_score
        FROM joined j
        GROUP BY j.gname
    ),
    met AS (
        -- 3 + 4. Filter to met-target rows, compute date - rn anchor
        SELECT
            j.gname,
            j.d - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY j.gname ORDER BY j.d))::INT AS grp
        FROM joined j
        WHERE j.s >= j.tgt
    ),
    runs AS (
        -- 5. Per (goal, grp): COUNT = streak length
        SELECT m.gname, COUNT(*) AS run_len
        FROM met m
        GROUP BY m.gname, m.grp
    ),
    longest AS (
        -- 6. Per goal: MAX run = longest streak
        SELECT r.gname, MAX(r.run_len)::INTEGER AS longest_streak
        FROM runs r
        GROUP BY r.gname
    )
    -- 7. Combine, filter by threshold, order
    SELECT
        t.gname::VARCHAR(100)            AS goal_name,
        t.total_nights                   AS total_nights,
        t.avg_score                      AS avg_score,
        COALESCE(lg.longest_streak, 0)   AS longest_streak
    FROM totals t
    LEFT JOIN longest lg ON lg.gname = t.gname
    WHERE COALESCE(lg.longest_streak, 0) >= p_min_streak_days
    ORDER BY longest_streak DESC, goal_name ASC;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT * FROM get_goal_streak_summary(101, 3);

What you write

Hierarchies, Paths, and Chains 1 problem

▼

Template Recursive CTE template (full order)

▼

Use when: you walk a chain or hierarchy of unknown depth.

The order, top to bottom:

  1. WITH RECURSIVE name AS (.
  2. Anchor query — the starting (seed) rows.
  3. UNION ALL.
  4. Recursive step — join the table back to the CTE name, building one layer per pass.
  5. Close ); the engine repeats until a pass adds no new rows.
  6. Final SELECT from the CTE.
WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
    -- anchor: starting rows
    SELECT id, parent_id, 1 AS depth
    FROM nodes
    WHERE parent_id IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- recursive step: join back to the CTE
    SELECT n.id, n.parent_id, w.depth + 1
    FROM nodes n
    JOIN walk w ON n.parent_id = w.id
)
SELECT * FROM walk ORDER BY depth, id;

Signal words: "from the initial ... through to the final," "trace the chain," "manager / employee," "parent / child," "all ancestors / descendants," "approval path," "depth of the chain."

Technique: WITH RECURSIVE cte AS ( anchor UNION ALL recursive_step ) SELECT ... FROM cte;

Skeleton you'll fill in:

WITH RECURSIVE cte AS (
  -- Anchor: starting row(s)
  SELECT id, parent_id, /* path seed */, 1 AS depth
  FROM t
  WHERE parent_id IS NULL

  UNION ALL

  -- Recursive step: extend the chain
  SELECT t.id, t.parent_id,
         c.path || ',' || t.id, c.depth + 1
  FROM t
  JOIN cte c ON t.parent_id = c.id
)
SELECT * FROM cte
ORDER BY id, depth;

Medium Trace Transaction Approval Chain with Path

▼

Each transaction has an approval chain: the first review is a row with parent_review_id IS NULL, and each subsequent review points back to the prior one. Return every transaction's full reviewer path, depth, and final status.

Tables: transaction_reviews (review_id, transaction_id, parent_review_id, reviewer_id, review_status, reviewed_at)

Prompt: Write a recursive CTE that returns all transactions and their complete approval paths from the initial request through to the final decision. For each transaction, return transaction_id, the full path of reviewer_ids visited (comma-separated, in traversal order), the chain_depth, and the final_status. Start from rows where parent_review_id IS NULL. Order results by transaction_id ascending, then chain_depth descending.

Example input (excerpt):

| review_id | transaction_id | parent_review_id | reviewer_id | review_status |
| --------- | -------------- | ---------------- | ----------- | ------------- |
| 1         | 100            | null             | 501         | pending       |
| 2         | 100            | 1                | 502         | escalated     |
| 3         | 100            | 2                | 503         | approved      |
| 4         | 200            | null             | 504         | flagged       |
| 5         | 200            | 4                | 505         | rejected      |
| 6         | 300            | null             | 506         | approved      |
| 7         | 400            | null             | 507         | pending       |
| 8         | 400            | 7                | 508         | escalated     |

Expected output:

| transaction_id | approval_path | chain_depth | final_status |
| -------------- | ------------- | ----------- | ------------ |
| 100            | 501,502,503   | 3           | approved     |
| 200            | 504,505       | 2           | rejected     |
| 300            | 506           | 1           | approved     |
| 400            | 507,508       | 2           | escalated    |
▶ 1 Recursive CTE + leaf-only filter
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS ( -- Anchor: starting reviews (parent_review_id IS NULL) SELECT review_id, transaction_id, reviewer_id::text AS approval_path, 1 AS chain_depth, review_status AS final_status FROM transaction_reviews WHERE parent_review_id IS NULL UNION ALL -- Recursive step: extend the chain with each child review SELECT t.review_id, t.transaction_id, c.approval_path || ',' || t.reviewer_id, c.chain_depth + 1, t.review_status FROM transaction_reviews t JOIN chain c ON t.parent_review_id = c.review_id ) -- Keep only leaf rows (no further children) SELECT c.transaction_id, c.approval_path, c.chain_depth, c.final_status FROM chain c WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM transaction_reviews t WHERE t.parent_review_id = c.review_id ) ORDER BY c.transaction_id ASC, c.chain_depth DESC;

Pass-by-pass walkthrough:

Pass What it produces
Anchor Picks rows with parent_review_id IS NULL → reviews 1, 4, 6, 7. Each gets path = its own reviewer_id, depth = 1.
Pass 1 Joins the source to the anchor rows. Children of {1, 4, 6, 7} are {2, 5, 8}. Review 6 has no children. Each new row's path is parent's path + new reviewer; depth becomes 2.
Pass 2 Joins the source to pass 1's new rows {2, 5, 8}. Only review 3 (parent 2) matches. Path = 501,502,503; depth = 3.
Pass 3 Joins source to pass 2's new rows {3}. No children → zero rows produced → recursion stops.
Final SELECT Filters the accumulated CTE to rows with no children (the leaves) so only the deepest row per chain survives. Orders by transaction_id, then chain_depth DESC.

Why each piece is there:

  • WITH RECURSIVE: required keyword that lets the CTE reference itself.
  • Anchor's WHERE parent_review_id IS NULL: seeds the chain with each transaction's first review.
  • reviewer_id::text: casts the integer to text so it can be concatenated with commas later.
  • 1 AS chain_depth: starts depth at 1 because the anchor row itself is the first link.
  • JOIN chain c ON t.parent_review_id = c.review_id: walks one step down by matching children to the rows the previous pass added.
  • c.approval_path || ',' || t.reviewer_id: extends the parent's path by appending the new reviewer.
  • WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM transaction_reviews t WHERE t.parent_review_id = c.review_id): keeps only leaf rows so each chain reports only its final state.

Updates, Deletes, and Inserts 22 problems

▼

Reference Scaffolds, DO blocks & when you'll see it

▼

When to reach for a FOR LOOP vs when to skip it

Set-based UPDATEs (no loop) work when every rule's condition can be checked using only columns on the row being updated, and ordering the UPDATEs is enough to keep things consistent. Loyalty points, shipment delays, tiered discounts — all this shape. WHERE priority_level = 'high' AND ... is all the engine needs; it handles "which rows match" in one pass per UPDATE.

Reach for a FOR LOOP when the prompt hands you an event or request log (a queue) AND each event has to read the current state of the target row because an earlier event in the queue may have just changed it. Airline seats, refund queue, cohort enrollment, content watch sessions — two tables (state + queue), and SELECT INTO pulls fresh state into scalars every iteration.

One-question test: "If I ran rule A and rule B in different orders, would I need to look up the latest value of the row in between?" If yes, you need a loop. If no, set-based UPDATEs in the right order are enough.

DML (single UPDATE / DELETE / INSERT)

When to use: the prompt says "write a single UPDATE statement" / "write a DELETE that ..." / "INSERT into archive ...". One statement, often with CASE WHEN for tiered logic, followed by a confirming SELECT.

-- UPDATE shape (tiered with CASE)
UPDATE <target_table>
   SET <col> = CASE
                 WHEN <condition_a> THEN <value_a>
                 WHEN <condition_b> THEN <value_b>
                 ELSE <col>
               END
 WHERE <optional_filter_for_rows_to_touch>;

-- DELETE shape (dedup keeping smallest pk per group)
DELETE FROM <target_table>
 WHERE <pk> NOT IN (
   SELECT MIN(<pk>) FROM <target_table> GROUP BY <group_cols>
 );

-- INSERT shape (archive matching rows with derived columns)
INSERT INTO <archive_table> (<col_list>)
SELECT
    <passthrough_cols>,
    <computed_col_1>  AS <name_1>,
    <computed_col_2>  AS <name_2>,
    CURRENT_TIMESTAMP AS archived_at
FROM <source_table>
WHERE <eligibility_filter>;

-- Trailing confirming SELECT
SELECT * FROM <target_table> ORDER BY <pk>;
UPDATE / DELETE / INSERT (mutating the table) PostgreSQL or MySQL
When you'll see it

Prompt mutates a table directly with conditions; final SELECT confirms the result.

What you write

One or more UPDATE, DELETE, or INSERT statements followed by SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY ...;.

UPDATE target SET col = expr WHERE cond;
SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY id;

DO block — Simple Sequential UPDATEs (set-based, NO loop)

When to use: the prompt gives 2-4 ordered rules where each rule's condition lives entirely on the row being updated and ordering the UPDATEs is enough. Self-test: "Could I rewrite this as a single UPDATE with CASE WHEN?" If yes, set-based.

DO $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE <target_table>
     SET <col> = <value_a>
   WHERE <condition_a>;

  UPDATE <target_table>
     SET <col> = <value_b>
   WHERE <condition_b>;

  UPDATE <target_table>
     SET <other_col> = <col> * <multiplier>
   WHERE <tier_condition>;
END $$;

SELECT * FROM <target_table> ORDER BY <pk>;

DO block — Row-by-Row State Mutation (FOR LOOP, per-iteration state read)

When to use: the prompt hands you a queue/event log AND each event must read the row's CURRENT state because earlier events changed it. Branching on event type AND current state. Self-test: "If I ran rule A and rule B in different orders, would I need to look up the latest value of the row in between?" If yes, FOR LOOP.

DO $$
DECLARE
   r              RECORD;
   current_status INT;
   current_owner  INT;
BEGIN
   FOR r IN
     SELECT * FROM <event_log_table> ORDER BY <sequence_col>
   LOOP
     SELECT <state_col_1>, <state_col_2>
       INTO current_status, current_owner
     FROM <state_table>
     WHERE <state_pk> = r.<event_fk>;

     IF r.<event_type> = <type_a> AND current_status = <precondition_a> THEN
        UPDATE <state_table>
           SET <col> = <new_value>,
               <owner_col> = r.<actor_col>
         WHERE <state_pk> = r.<event_fk>;
     ELSIF r.<event_type> = <type_b> AND current_status IN (<precondition_b1>, <precondition_b2>) THEN
        UPDATE <state_table>
           SET <col> = <reset_value>,
               <owner_col> = NULL
         WHERE <state_pk> = r.<event_fk>;
     END IF;

     -- Optional cleanup: mark this event processed (after END IF, before END LOOP)
     UPDATE <event_log_table>
        SET is_processed = TRUE
      WHERE <event_pk> = r.<event_pk>;
   END LOOP;
END $$;

SELECT * FROM <state_table> ORDER BY <state_pk>;
DO Block (sequential UPDATE) PostgreSQL only
When you'll see it

Prompt says "apply these requests in order" or "after the requests have been performed, return the table." Often involves per-row state checks.

What you write

A DO $$ ... $$; block with a FOR loop and conditional UPDATEs, plus a trailing SELECT.

DO $$
DECLARE r RECORD;
BEGIN
  FOR r IN SELECT * FROM requests
           ORDER BY request_id LOOP
    -- conditional UPDATE
  END LOOP;
END $$;
SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY id;

Single-Statement UPDATE 4 problems

▼

Template Single UPDATE template (full order)

▼

Use when: one set-based UPDATE applies the rules; no procedural body.

The order, top to bottom:

  1. UPDATE tbl.
  2. SET col = ... — a CASE folds several rules into one statement.
  3. WHERE the rows to act on.
  4. Trailing SELECT to confirm the post update state.
UPDATE tbl
SET col = CASE
            WHEN <cond_1> THEN <expr_1>
            WHEN <cond_2> THEN <expr_2>
            ELSE col
          END
WHERE <rows to touch>;

-- confirm:
SELECT * FROM tbl ORDER BY id;

Signal words: "apply a discount tier," "set status based on...," "update column X to ... when ..., otherwise ...," "in a single UPDATE statement."

Technique: UPDATE table SET col = CASE WHEN cond1 THEN expr1 WHEN cond2 THEN expr2 ELSE col END WHERE row_filter; followed by SELECT * FROM table ORDER BY ...;.

Skeleton you'll fill in:

UPDATE target_table
   SET col = CASE
                 WHEN cond_a THEN expr_a
                 WHEN cond_b THEN expr_b
                 ELSE col
             END
 WHERE row_filter;

-- Trailing SELECT so the test scaffold sees output:
SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY key;

Anchor problems — tiered subscription discount (single UPDATE with CASE WHEN tiers), tiered review status updates (multi-column CASE in one SET).

Easy Apply Tiered Discount to Active Subscriptions

▼
  • One UPDATE statement, no DO block.
  • Tiered discount logic encoded as CASE WHEN branches inside SET.
  • Row eligibility (status = 'active') lives in WHERE — ineligible rows stay untouched.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
subscription_idINTprimary key
customer_nameVARCHARpassthrough
box_tierVARCHARpassthrough
monthly_priceDECIMAL(10,2)column being updated
months_subscribedINTdrives the tier
statusVARCHAR'active' rows are eligible; others stay unchanged

Prompt: Update monthly_price on every active subscription based on tenure:

  • months_subscribed in 6–11: 10% off (multiply by 0.90).
  • months_subscribed ≥ 12: 20% off (multiply by 0.80).
  • months_subscribed < 6: no discount.
  • status ≠ 'active': row is not eligible at all (do not touch).
▶ 1 Single UPDATE with CASE WHEN tiers + WHERE eligibility filter
UPDATE active_subscriptions SET monthly_price = CASE WHEN months_subscribed BETWEEN 6 AND 11 THEN monthly_price * 0.90 WHEN months_subscribed >= 12 THEN monthly_price * 0.80 ELSE monthly_price END WHERE status = 'active'; SELECT * FROM active_subscriptions ORDER BY subscription_id;

Why two layers (WHERE and CASE):

  • The WHERE status = 'active' clause decides which rows the UPDATE touches at all. Paused subscriptions never enter the SET evaluation, so monthly_price stays exactly as written in the source.
  • The CASE WHEN inside SET decides what value to assign to rows that DID pass the WHERE. The ELSE monthly_price branch leaves rows in the <6-month bucket unchanged while still being touched by the UPDATE.
  • Mixing them — e.g., putting months_subscribed >= 6 in the WHERE — would still produce the right values for matched rows, but is harder to read and breaks if a future rule needs to TOUCH but not change a row.

Trace through the example data:

id months status price before passes WHERE? CASE branch price after
18active50.00yes6–11 (-10%)45.00
23active30.00yesELSE (no change)30.00
314active75.00yes≥12 (-20%)60.00
46active50.00yes6–11 (-10%)45.00
512active30.00yes≥12 (-20%)24.00
65paused75.00no (paused)not evaluated75.00 (untouched)

Watch out:

  • WHEN months_subscribed BETWEEN 6 AND 11 THEN ... reads cleanly. An equivalent WHEN months_subscribed >= 6 AND months_subscribed < 12 THEN ... works but is wordier.
  • If you write WHEN months_subscribed >= 6 THEN 0.90 * monthly_price WHEN months_subscribed >= 12 THEN 0.80 * monthly_price, the second branch never fires — CASE evaluates top-down. Order branches from most-restrictive first, or use exclusive ranges.
  • Always include ELSE monthly_price. Without ELSE, rows that match no WHEN get NULL.
  • monthly_price is DECIMAL(10,2) — the multiplication rounds to two decimals at write time, which is what the example expects (50.00 × 0.90 = 45.00 exactly).
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM active_subscriptions ORDER BY subscription_id; so the harness has output to verify.

Easy Update Fraud Flags by Risk Score (no WHERE clause)

▼
  • Every row in the table gets evaluated — no row-level eligibility filter, so no WHERE.
  • The CASE WHEN handles ALL the logic: high-risk rows flip to TRUE, low-risk rows flip to FALSE, and middle-risk rows keep whatever flag they had.
  • Useful contrast to the tiered-discount anchor above (which DOES use WHERE for eligibility).

Tables:

Column Type Notes
transaction_idSERIALprimary key
merchant_nameVARCHARpassthrough
amountDECIMAL(10,2)passthrough
risk_scoreINT (0–100)drives the rule
fraud_flagBOOLEANcolumn being updated; middle-risk rows keep the existing value

Prompt: Apply these rules to every row in approvals:

  • risk_score ≥ 80: set fraud_flag = TRUE.
  • risk_score < 50: set fraud_flag = FALSE.
  • risk_score in 50–79: keep the existing fraud_flag.
▶ 1 Single UPDATE with CASE WHEN, no WHERE clause
UPDATE approvals SET fraud_flag = CASE WHEN risk_score >= 80 THEN TRUE WHEN risk_score < 50 THEN FALSE ELSE fraud_flag END; SELECT * FROM approvals ORDER BY transaction_id;

Why no WHERE clause:

  • WHERE is a row-level eligibility filter. It belongs there only when some rows should NOT be touched at all.
  • Here, every row has a rule that applies — even middle-risk rows have a "keep what you have" rule, encoded as ELSE fraud_flag. Touching them and writing back the same value is harmless.
  • Adding WHERE risk_score >= 80 OR risk_score < 50 would also work, but it's redundant: the CASE already routes every row to the correct outcome, and the WHERE just adds noise.
  • Heuristic: if every CASE path produces the right answer (including "leave it alone" via ELSE col), drop the WHERE. If some rows should be ignored entirely, keep the WHERE.

Trace through the example data:

id risk_score flag before CASE branch flag after
115FALSE< 50 → FALSEFALSE
285FALSE≥ 80 → TRUETRUE
355TRUEELSE (50–79)TRUE (kept)
448TRUE< 50 → FALSEFALSE
592TRUE≥ 80 → TRUETRUE
665FALSEELSE (50–79)FALSE (kept)
730FALSE< 50 → FALSEFALSE
880FALSE≥ 80 → TRUETRUE

Watch out:

  • Branch order matters: WHEN risk_score >= 80 must come before WHEN risk_score < 50 only if both could match the same row, which they cannot here. So either order works for this problem — but keep the most-restrictive-first habit so it's safe when ranges might overlap.
  • ELSE fraud_flag is the load-bearing piece. It tells Postgres "for any row not matching a WHEN, write back the column's existing value." Drop ELSE and middle-risk rows get NULL.
  • Boundary check: the rule "keep it" applies to 50–79. risk_score = 80 falls in the ≥ 80 bucket (becomes TRUE). risk_score = 50 is NOT < 50, so it falls into ELSE (kept). Reading the prompt's inclusivity carefully avoids off-by-one mistakes.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM approvals ORDER BY transaction_id; so the harness sees output.

Easy Tag Sleep Logs by Goal Achievement (4-tier ladder)

▼
  • Same shape as the fraud-flag anchor — one bare UPDATE, no WHERE, all logic inside CASE WHEN.
  • Four tiers based on actual_hours as a percentage of target_hours, computed inline as target_hours * N.
  • Demonstrates the actual >= target * 1.1 form (cleaner than actual > target + target * 0.1) and adjacent-range bookkeeping.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
log_idINTprimary key
user_idINTpassthrough
log_dateDATEpassthrough
target_hoursDECIMAL(4,2)user's nightly goal
actual_hoursDECIMAL(4,2)measured for that night
achievement_statusVARCHAR(20)column being updated; one of 'exceeded', 'met', 'partial', 'missed' (starts NULL)

Prompt: Set achievement_status on every row based on the ratio actual_hours / target_hours:

  • actual ≥ 110% of target → 'exceeded'
  • 100% ≤ actual < 110% → 'met'
  • 50% ≤ actual < 100% → 'partial'
  • actual < 50% → 'missed'
▶ 1 Single UPDATE with 4-tier CASE WHEN, top-down ordered ranges
UPDATE sleep_logs SET achievement_status = CASE WHEN actual_hours >= target_hours * 1.1 THEN 'exceeded' WHEN actual_hours >= target_hours THEN 'met' WHEN actual_hours >= target_hours * 0.5 THEN 'partial' ELSE 'missed' END; SELECT * FROM sleep_logs ORDER BY log_id;

Why this is concise:

  • Top-down ordering removes the upper bound. CASE evaluates branches in order. The 'exceeded' branch claims rows at 110%+. The 'met' branch then only sees rows below 110%, so actual_hours >= target_hours is enough — no need to also write AND actual_hours < target_hours * 1.1.
  • Factor the percentage: target_hours + target_hours * 0.1 simplifies to target_hours * 1.1. Same value, less reading.
  • The lowest tier becomes ELSE. Anything that didn't match any earlier branch is below 50% by elimination — no need to write the bound again.
  • Net result: 4 tiers expressed in 4 lines, each with a single comparison.

Trace through the example data:

log_id target actual ratio CASE branch status
18.009.001.125≥ 1.1exceeded
27.507.501.000≥ target (not ≥ 1.1)met
38.006.500.812≥ target * 0.5partial
47.003.000.428ELSEmissed
58.508.000.941≥ target * 0.5partial
66.005.500.917≥ target * 0.5partial

Watch out:

  • Branch order is load-bearing. Flip 'met' above 'exceeded' and a 120% row would land in 'met' (since 120% >= 100% matches first). Always order from most-restrictive to least.
  • The prompt says "≥ 110%" for exceeded and "≥ 100%" for met, both inclusive on the lower end. Use >=, not >, or boundary rows (exactly 110% or 100%) land in the wrong tier.
  • Because every row gets a tier (no row should keep its old status), no WHERE is needed and no ELSE achievement_status fallback is required — the four rules cover every possible value.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM sleep_logs ORDER BY log_id; so the harness sees output.

Medium Apply Tiered Review Status Updates (multi-column CASE in one SET)

▼
  • Two columns updated in ONE statement, each with its own CASE WHEN expression in the SET clause.
  • Both CASEs must use the SAME branch order so each rule's row state is consistent across columns.
  • One CASE applies the multiplier to priority_score; rule 3 has no multiplier so it falls through to ELSE priority_score.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
review_idINTprimary key
icd_codeVARCHARpassthrough
days_since_submissionINTdrives rules 2 and 3
denial_countINTdrives all three rules
review_statusVARCHARcolumn being updated (rule 1, 2, 3)
priority_scoreDECIMAL(10,2)column being updated (rule 1, 2 only; rule 3 leaves unchanged)

Prompt: Apply three rules to every row in code_reviews in a single UPDATE:

  • Rule 1: denial_count ≥ 3 → status = 'escalated', score = score * 1.5
  • Rule 2: denial_count = 2 AND days_since_submission > 14 → status = 'attention_needed', score = score * 1.25
  • Rule 3: denial_count = 1 AND days_since_submission > 30 → status = 'flagged', score unchanged
  • Anything else: both columns unchanged
▶ 1 Single UPDATE with two CASE expressions sharing the same branch order
UPDATE code_reviews SET review_status = CASE WHEN denial_count >= 3 THEN 'escalated' WHEN denial_count = 2 AND days_since_submission > 14 THEN 'attention_needed' WHEN denial_count = 1 AND days_since_submission > 30 THEN 'flagged' ELSE review_status END, priority_score = CASE WHEN denial_count >= 3 THEN priority_score * 1.5 WHEN denial_count = 2 AND days_since_submission > 14 THEN priority_score * 1.25 ELSE priority_score END; SELECT * FROM code_reviews ORDER BY review_id;

Why this is the single-UPDATE shape:

  • One UPDATE, two CASE expressions. The SET clause accepts a comma-separated list of column = expression pairs. Each expression can be its own CASE WHEN.
  • Same branch order in both CASEs. Rule 1 fires before rule 2 in both. If you flipped them in only one column, the row could end up with status from rule 1 but score from rule 2 — an inconsistent row.
  • Rule 3 omits the score branch. The second CASE has only two WHEN clauses; rule 3 rows fall through to ELSE priority_score and keep their score unchanged. Status still flips to 'flagged' via the first CASE.
  • Rules don't overlap, but ELSE is still required. Without ELSE col, rows that match no WHEN get NULL written. Always close both CASEs with the column name as the fallback.

Trace through the example data:

id denial_count days Matching rule new status new score
1010none (ELSE/ELSE)pending (unchanged)50.00 (unchanged)
2220rule 2attention_needed60 * 1.25 = 75.00
335rule 1escalated40 * 1.5 = 60.00
4135rule 3flagged55.00 (rule 3 has no multiplier)
5240rule 2attention_needed70 * 1.25 = 87.50
6112none (12 not > 30)pending (unchanged)45.00 (unchanged)

Watch out:

  • Sequential UPDATEs also produce the right answer here because the WHERE clauses (denial_count = 3 vs 2 vs 1) are disjoint — no row can match two rules. The prompt's "single UPDATE statement" constraint is what forces the CASE form.
  • If rules could overlap, sequential UPDATEs would chain the changes. Rule 1 firing first changes the row state that rule 2 sees, which is rarely what the prompt intends. CASE evaluates every row against the ORIGINAL state, no chaining.
  • Don't drop ELSE col from either CASE. Even though rules cover the rows the prompt cares about, "anything else" still has to land somewhere — and that somewhere is the row's existing value, not NULL.
  • Match the percentage form to the schema. priority_score * 1.5 is unambiguous; priority_score + priority_score * 0.5 is the same value but harder to read. Prefer the multiplier.
  • No WHERE on the UPDATE. Every row needs to be evaluated; rows that match no rule are protected by the ELSE branches in both CASEs.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM code_reviews ORDER BY review_id; so the harness sees output.

Single-Statement DELETE 5 problems

▼

Signal words: "remove duplicates," "keep only the smallest/largest id per group," "delete orphaned rows," "prune rows older than ...," "deduplicate," "purge."

Technique: DELETE FROM target WHERE pk NOT IN (SELECT MIN(pk) FROM target GROUP BY group_cols); for deduplication, or DELETE FROM target WHERE fk NOT IN (SELECT pk FROM parent); for orphan removal.

Medium Delete High-Churn Client Trade Alerts

▼

Delete rows that meet a plain-column rule AND a per-group volume rule found with a GROUP BY ... HAVING subquery.

Problem Case study & test data

▼

The prompt, schema, example input, and expected output — the same view you get in the practice notebook.

Prompt

  • A robo-advisor wants to clear out noisy alerts: remove the 'pending' alerts that belong to high-volume clients (5 or more total alerts).
  • trade_alerts has one row per alert with its client, type, status, and date.
  • Write a single DELETE that removes only the 'pending' rows whose client_id has 5 or more alerts in the table, then return the remaining rows ordered by client_id, alert_id.

Schema — trade_alerts

ColumnType
alert_idINTEGER (PK)
client_idINTEGER
alert_typeVARCHAR
statusVARCHAR
created_atDATE

Example input — trade_alerts

alert_idclient_idalert_typestatuscreated_at
1101rebalancepending2024-01-15
2101rebalancecompleted2024-01-16
3101driftpending2024-01-17
4101rebalancepending2024-01-18
5101tax_losscompleted2024-01-19
6101driftpending2024-01-20
7202rebalancepending2024-01-15
8202driftpending2024-01-16
9303rebalancecompleted2024-01-17

Expected output

alert_idclient_idalert_typestatuscreated_at
2101rebalancecompleted2024-01-16
5101tax_losscompleted2024-01-19
7202rebalancepending2024-01-15
8202driftpending2024-01-16
9303rebalancecompleted2024-01-17

Solution Annotated SQL

▼

The query with inline comments on the lines that do the work.

/*
  Two conditions joined by AND. The plain one (status = 'pending') filters columns on the row itself. The
  volume one is a group test: a subquery lists the clients whose total alert count is 5 or more, and
  client_id IN (...) keeps only rows belonging to them. The subquery is evaluated against the table as it
  stands before the delete, so the counts are not affected mid-statement. Client 101 has 6 alerts, so its 4
  pending rows go; clients 202 (2 alerts) and 303 (1) are untouched.

  Verified against the example data -- 5 rows remain.
*/

DELETE FROM trade_alerts
WHERE status = 'pending'                                   -- the plain row condition
  AND client_id IN (                                       -- the per-client volume condition
      SELECT client_id
      FROM trade_alerts
      GROUP BY client_id
      HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5                                 -- clients with 5+ total alerts
  );

SELECT * FROM trade_alerts ORDER BY client_id, alert_id;   -- trailing read so the harness sees output

Duplicate rows 2 problems

▼

Keep one row per group, delete the rest. The subquery returns the ids to KEEP.

Template Duplicate rows template

▼

Use when: Keep one row per group, delete the rest. The subquery returns the ids to KEEP.

DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE pk NOT IN (
     SELECT MIN(pk)
       FROM target_table
      GROUP BY group_col_1, group_col_2
 );

End with a trailing SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY pk; so the harness sees output.

Easy Remove Duplicate Article Views by User

▼
  • Classic dedupe: keep one row per (article_id, user_id) group — the one with the smallest view_id.
  • Subquery returns the IDs to KEEP; outer DELETE removes everything else.
  • The first instinct — matching (article_id, user_id) NOT IN (...) — trips on a column-shape mismatch. The fix is to filter on the primary key.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
view_idINTprimary key, monotonic; smallest = earliest
article_idINTfirst part of the dedupe key
user_idINTsecond part of the dedupe key
viewed_atTIMESTAMPpassthrough; not used in the rule
session_idVARCHAR(50)passthrough

Prompt: Remove duplicate views — rows that share the same (article_id, user_id) as another row. Keep only the row with the smallest view_id per group.

▶ 1 DELETE WHERE pk NOT IN (SELECT MIN(pk) ... GROUP BY group_cols)
DELETE FROM article_views WHERE view_id NOT IN ( SELECT MIN(view_id) FROM article_views GROUP BY article_id, user_id ); SELECT * FROM article_views ORDER BY view_id;

How to read the WHERE clause: "Delete every row whose view_id is NOT the minimum within its (article_id, user_id) group." The subquery first computes the minimum view_id per group (the rows to KEEP), then the outer DELETE removes everything else.

The mismatch you'll trip on first:

  • Writing WHERE (article_id, user_id) NOT IN (SELECT MIN(view_id) FROM ... GROUP BY article_id, user_id) errors with "subquery has too few columns."
  • The left side has 2 columns (the tuple), the right side returns 1 column (MIN(view_id)). Postgres can't compare a 2-tuple to a scalar.
  • The fix is to think about it differently: the subquery already gives you the IDs of rows to KEEP. Filter the outer DELETE by view_id, not by the tuple.

Trace through the example data:

view_id article user group MIN of group verdict
11015(101, 5)1keep
21015(101, 5)1delete (2 ≠ 1)
31015(101, 5)1delete (3 ≠ 1)
41025(102, 5)4keep
51017(101, 7)5keep
61017(101, 7)5delete (6 ≠ 5)
71038(103, 8)7keep
81038(103, 8)7delete (8 ≠ 7)

Final state: 4 rows survive (1, 4, 5, 7). Four duplicates (2, 3, 6, 8) get deleted.

Watch out:

  • Subquery shape rule: WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM ...) compares one column to one column. WHERE (x1, x2) NOT IN (SELECT y FROM ...) needs a 2-column subquery (SELECT y1, y2 FROM ...). For dedup, use single-column on both sides — the primary key.
  • NOT IN with NULLs is silent. If view_id can be NULL (it can't here because it's a primary key), one NULL in the subquery makes NOT IN evaluate to UNKNOWN for every row and DELETE keeps everything. Use NOT EXISTS when the column is nullable.
  • MIN vs MAX: the prompt says "smallest view_id," so use MIN. For "keep most recent," swap to MAX. The structure stays the same.
  • MySQL caveat: MySQL forbids reading from the same table you're deleting in a subquery. Wrap with another SELECT layer (WHERE view_id IN (SELECT view_id FROM (SELECT MIN(view_id) ...) AS sub)) or use a CTE. Postgres has no such restriction.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM article_views ORDER BY view_id; so the harness sees the surviving rows.

Easy Remove Duplicate Kit Shipments by Patient

▼

Keep only the earliest shipment for each patient and kit type, deleting all later duplicates.

Tables: kit_shipments (shipment_id, patient_id, kit_type, shipped_date, tracking_number), test_results (result_id, shipment_id, result_status, released_date)

Real-World Example

A diagnostic kit platform hit a sync bug that shipped some patients the same kit type twice. The cleanup keeps the first shipment per patient and kit type and removes the rest.

▶ 1 Keep MIN(shipment_id) per (patient_id, kit_type), delete the rest
Working solution (Trinidad, 2026-06-16):
DELETE FROM kit_shipments WHERE shipment_id NOT IN ( SELECT MIN(shipment_id) FROM kit_shipments GROUP BY patient_id, kit_type ); SELECT * FROM kit_shipments ORDER BY shipment_id;

The subquery returns the rows to keep (the smallest shipment_id in each patient and kit type group); everything else is deleted. The trailing SELECT lets the harness see the remaining rows.

Watch out:

  • NOT IN is safe here because shipment_id is the primary key, so MIN(shipment_id) is never NULL. If the keep column could be NULL, NOT IN would drop every row and you would switch to a positive WHERE or NOT EXISTS.
  • Smallest id is the earliest shipment only because ids are assigned in shipment order. If that were not true, you would keep MIN(shipped_date) instead.
  • Group by both keys. Grouping by patient_id alone would collapse different kit types into one group and keep only one shipment per patient.

Orphan rows template only

▼

A foreign key has no matching parent row anymore.

Template Orphan rows template

▼

Use when: A foreign key has no matching parent row anymore.

DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE fk NOT IN (
     SELECT pk FROM parent_table
      WHERE pk IS NOT NULL
 );

End with a trailing SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY pk; so the harness sees output.

Cross table template only

▼

Delete rows where a related row in another table meets a condition.

Template Cross table template

▼

Use when: Delete rows where a related row in another table meets a condition.

DELETE FROM target_table t
 USING other_table o
 WHERE t.fk = o.id
   AND o.status = 'expired';

End with a trailing SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY pk; so the harness sees output.

▼

Delete rows older than N days. Older means a smaller date, so use <.

Template Time-based pruning template

▼

Use when: Delete rows older than N days. Older means a smaller date, so use <.

DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE created_at < CURRENT_DATE - 90;

End with a trailing SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY pk; so the harness sees output.

Two-condition (group + row) 1 problem

▼

The group must qualify AND the individual row must qualify. Two separate filters in the WHERE.

Template Two-condition (group + row) template

▼

Use when: The group must qualify AND the individual row must qualify. Two separate filters in the WHERE.

DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE group_id IN (
     SELECT group_id
       FROM target_table
      GROUP BY group_id
     HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
 )
   AND row_status = 'pending';
