Medium Remove Obsolete Milestone Records After Final Delivery

▼
  • Two-condition DELETE: a row is removed only if its shipment qualifies AND the row itself isn't exempt.
  • Distinct from the dedup pattern — here the qualification rule is on the SHIPMENT (does it have a delivered milestone?), not on the milestone row.
  • The first instinct — "keep MAX(milestone_id) of the delivered ones" — over-deletes shipments that have NO delivered milestone yet, because none of their IDs land in the keep-set.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
milestone_idSERIALprimary key
shipment_idINTgroups milestones by shipment
milestone_statusVARCHAR(50)'picked_up' | 'in_transit' | 'out_for_delivery' | 'delivered'
milestone_timestampTIMESTAMPpassthrough
location_codeVARCHAR(20)passthrough

Prompt: Delete obsolete milestone records.

  • A shipment is "completed" once it has a 'delivered' milestone.
  • For completed shipments, all earlier milestones become obsolete — delete them.
  • Keep the 'delivered' milestone itself (it's the survivor).
  • Shipments that have NO delivered milestone yet are still in flight — do NOT touch any of their rows.
▶ 1 Two-condition WHERE: shipment-level eligibility AND row-level exemption
DELETE FROM shipment_milestones WHERE shipment_id IN ( SELECT shipment_id FROM shipment_milestones WHERE milestone_status = 'delivered' ) AND milestone_status <> 'delivered'; SELECT * FROM shipment_milestones ORDER BY shipment_id, milestone_timestamp;

How to read the WHERE clause:

  • Subquery (shipment-level eligibility): "list every shipment_id that has at least one delivered milestone." This is the set of completed shipments.
  • First AND-clause: the row's shipment must be in that set. Anything else is an in-flight shipment and gets skipped entirely.
  • Second AND-clause: within those completed shipments, only delete the milestones that are NOT the delivered one.
  • Net effect: delete rows belonging to a completed shipment, but spare the delivered milestone itself.

Trace through the example data:

milestone_id shipment_id status shipment in keep-set? status = delivered? verdict
1100picked_upyes (100 has delivered)nodelete
2100in_transityesnodelete
3100out_for_deliveryyesnodelete
4100deliveredyesYES (exempt)keep
5200picked_upno (in-flight)—keep
6200in_transitno—keep
7300picked_upyes (300 has delivered)nodelete
8300deliveredyesYES (exempt)keep

Survivors: 4 (delivered for ship 100), 5 and 6 (ship 200 still in flight), 8 (delivered for ship 300). Four rows deleted.

Watch out:

  • Group-eligibility vs row-eligibility. When a rule reads "for groups satisfying X, delete rows satisfying Y," the WHERE has TWO conditions: one finds the eligible groups (subquery), one filters within them. Mixing them into a single NOT IN MAX shortcut works for dedup but breaks here.
  • The exemption uses milestone_status <> 'delivered' rather than milestone_id NOT IN (delivered ids). Both work, but the string compare is easier to read and avoids a second subquery.
  • NOT IN with NULLs caveat applies to the subquery. If shipment_id could be NULL on some rows (it can't here, NOT NULL constraint), you'd need NOT EXISTS instead.
  • The trailing SELECT orders by shipment_id, milestone_timestamp to match the prompt; matching the harness's expected sort key is part of correctness.

NULL-safe positive WHERE 1 problem

▼

When the keep set might contain NULL, NOT IN breaks. Write the WHERE for the rows to DELETE, not the inverse.

Template NULL-safe positive WHERE template

▼

Use when: When the keep set might contain NULL, NOT IN breaks. Write the WHERE for the rows to DELETE, not the inverse.

-- Avoid: WHERE pk NOT IN (SELECT keep_pk FROM ...)
DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE duration < 180
    OR quality_flag IS NULL;

End with a trailing SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY pk; so the harness sees output.

Easy Remove Incomplete Sleep Sessions (positive WHERE vs NOT IN + NULL handling)

▼
  • Two-condition DELETE where one rule fires on a numeric threshold and the other on NULL.
  • Demonstrates why writing the WHERE as a positive delete (rows-to-act-on) beats inverting through NOT IN.
  • Walks through how NULL behaves in a WHERE clause: NULL comparisons evaluate to NULL, and WHERE only fires on TRUE.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
session_idINTprimary key
user_idINTpassthrough
session_dateDATEpassthrough
duration_minutesINTnumeric threshold column; can be NULL
quality_scoreINT 1-10NULL-trigger column

Prompt: Remove sleep sessions where duration_minutes < 180 OR quality_score IS NULL. Write a single DELETE statement, then a confirming SELECT * FROM sleep_sessions ORDER BY session_id;.

▶ 1 Positive DELETE (writes WHERE for rows to delete, not rows to keep)
DELETE FROM sleep_sessions WHERE duration_minutes < 180 OR quality_score IS NULL; SELECT * FROM sleep_sessions ORDER BY session_id;

How NULL behaves in a WHERE clause (the rule that drives this whole problem):

  • SQL has three possible answers to a comparison: TRUE, FALSE, and NULL.
  • NULL means "unknown." Any comparison involving NULL gives NULL: NULL < 180 is NULL, NULL = 7 is NULL, even NULL = NULL is NULL.
  • The only operator that gives a real TRUE/FALSE answer for NULL is IS NULL (or IS NOT NULL).
  • WHERE only fires on TRUE. Both FALSE and NULL are treated the same: the row stays untouched.
  • So in a DELETE, a NULL-valued comparison means the row is NOT deleted — even though the comparison didn't strictly say "false."

Why "write the WHERE for rows to delete" wins over "invert through NOT IN": three sample rows show how each approach behaves. Session 14 (duration=120, quality=7) and session 16 (duration=200, quality=NULL) should be DELETED. Session 18 (duration=NULL, quality=7) should be KEPT.

Approach 1: Positive DELETE — WHERE duration < 180 OR quality IS NULL

session_id duration quality first check first result second check second result combined OR DELETE fires? action correct?
141207120 < 180TRUE7 IS NULLFALSETRUEYESDELETEDYES
16200NULL200 < 180FALSENULL IS NULLTRUETRUEYESDELETEDYES
18NULL7NULL < 180NULL7 IS NULLFALSENULLNOKEPTYES

Approach 2: NOT IN with AND keep set — keep set = quality IS NOT NULL AND duration >= 180

session_id duration quality first check first result second check second result combined AND in keep set? NOT IN deletes? action correct?
1412077 IS NOT NULLTRUE120 >= 180FALSEFALSENOYESDELETEDYES
16200NULLNULL IS NOT NULLFALSE200 >= 180TRUEFALSENOYESDELETEDYES
18NULL77 IS NOT NULLTRUENULL >= 180NULLNULLNOYESDELETEDNO

Approach 3: NOT IN with OR keep set — keep set = quality IS NOT NULL OR duration >= 180

session_id duration quality first check first result second check second result combined OR in keep set? NOT IN deletes? action correct?
1412077 IS NOT NULLTRUE120 >= 180FALSETRUEYESNOKEPTNO
16200NULLNULL IS NOT NULLFALSE200 >= 180TRUETRUEYESNOKEPTNO
18NULL77 IS NOT NULLTRUENULL >= 180NULLTRUEYESNOKEPTYES

The takeaway: Approach 1 has YES all the way down. Approach 2 fails on session 18 (the NULL-duration row). Approach 3 fails on sessions 14 and 16 (the regular delete rows). Neither AND nor OR in the inverted keep set covers every case — only the positive DELETE handles NULLs cleanly without you having to think about how three-valued logic propagates through inversion.

Watch out:

  • Rule of thumb: express WHERE clauses as the condition for the rows you want to ACT on, not as the inverse of the rows you want to keep. It's almost always shorter and almost always handles NULLs correctly.
  • If you really need the inverted form, coalesce NULLs to a sentinel that passes the threshold: WHERE quality_score IS NOT NULL AND COALESCE(duration_minutes, 999) >= 180. The COALESCE(NULL, 999) turns NULL into 999, which passes >= 180, so the NULL-duration row stays in the keep set. Awkward but correct.
  • Tuple comparison with NULL is also broken. (col1, col2) <> (NULL, NULL) evaluates to NULL because any equality with NULL is NULL. Always use col1 IS NOT NULL AND col2 IS NOT NULL when you want to filter for both columns being populated.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM sleep_sessions ORDER BY session_id; so the harness sees the post-delete snapshot.

Single-Statement INSERT 2 problems

▼

Template Single INSERT template (full order)

▼

Use when: you add rows, often copied from another table.

The order, top to bottom:

  1. INSERT INTO tbl (cols) — always name the target columns.
  2. A SELECT (or VALUES) supplying the rows.
  3. WHERE filter on the source.
  4. Trailing SELECT to confirm.
INSERT INTO archive_tbl (id, col_a, col_b)
SELECT id, col_a, col_b
FROM tbl
WHERE <rows to copy>;

-- confirm:
SELECT * FROM archive_tbl ORDER BY id;

Signal words: "archive applications into ...," "copy qualifying rows to ...," "seed the target table from ...," "insert all rows where ...," "do not duplicate existing rows."

Technique: INSERT INTO target_table (col1, col2, ...) SELECT expr1, expr2, ... FROM source WHERE cond AND key NOT IN (SELECT key FROM target_table); followed by SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY ...;.

Skeleton you'll fill in:

INSERT INTO target_table (col_a, col_b, computed_col, literal_col)
SELECT s.col_a,
       s.col_b,
       expr_using_source_columns AS computed_col,
       'literal value'           AS literal_col
  FROM source_table AS s
 WHERE eligibility_predicate
   AND s.key NOT IN (SELECT key FROM target_table WHERE key IS NOT NULL);

-- Trailing SELECT so the test scaffold sees output:
SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY key;

Anchor problems — archive approved loan applications (INSERT ... SELECT with computed columns, literals, and an anti-join against existing target rows), archive failed job runs with retry context (compute an aggregate from the FULL source table, then attach it to a filtered subset of the same table).

Medium Archive Approved Loan Applications into History

▼
  • One bare INSERT INTO ... SELECT statement copies qualifying rows from loan_applications into application_history.
  • Three transformations: computed days_to_approval, literal 'funded', and the run-time archive_date.
  • NOT IN anti-join against application_history keeps already-archived rows from being inserted twice.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
loan_applications
(source)		application_idINTprimary key, used for anti-join
applicant_nameVARCHARpassthrough
submission_dateDATEpassthrough; subtracted from approval_date
approval_dateDATEsubtracted from submission_date for days_to_approval
funded_dateDATEeligibility filter; NOT NULL means funded
loan_amountDECIMAL(10,2)passthrough
statusVARCHAReligibility filter; must equal 'approved'
application_history
(target)		application_idINTprimary key
applicant_nameVARCHARcopied from source
submission_dateDATEcopied from source
approval_dateDATEcopied from source
funded_dateDATEcopied from source
loan_amountDECIMAL(10,2)copied from source
days_to_approvalINTcomputed: approval_date - submission_date
archive_dateDATEruntime: CURRENT_DATE
archive_reasonVARCHAR(50)literal: 'funded'

Prompt: Insert qualifying rows from loan_applications into application_history:

  • Eligibility: status = 'approved' AND funded_date IS NOT NULL.
  • Skip rows whose application_id already exists in application_history.
  • Compute days_to_approval = approval_date - submission_date.
  • Set archive_date to the current date.
  • Set archive_reason to the literal 'funded'.
▶ 1 INSERT INTO ... SELECT with computed columns, literals, and a NOT IN anti-join
INSERT INTO application_history ( application_id, applicant_name, submission_date, approval_date, funded_date, loan_amount, days_to_approval, archive_date, archive_reason ) SELECT la.application_id, la.applicant_name, la.submission_date, la.approval_date, la.funded_date, la.loan_amount, la.approval_date - la.submission_date AS days_to_approval, CURRENT_DATE AS archive_date, 'funded' AS archive_reason FROM loan_applications AS la WHERE la.status = 'approved' AND la.funded_date IS NOT NULL AND la.application_id NOT IN ( SELECT application_id FROM application_history ); SELECT * FROM application_history ORDER BY application_id;

How the four pieces map to the prompt:

  • Eligibility filter — WHERE status = 'approved' AND funded_date IS NOT NULL drops rows that aren't ready to archive.
  • Anti-join — application_id NOT IN (SELECT application_id FROM application_history) protects against duplicate-key conflicts when the script runs more than once.
  • Computed column — la.approval_date - la.submission_date AS days_to_approval calculates inline. The alias matches the target column name.
  • Literal and runtime values — 'funded' is a hardcoded string, CURRENT_DATE is evaluated at INSERT time. Both get aliases so the column list lines up.

Trace through the example data:

app_id status funded_date already in history? inserted?
101approved2024-01-15noyes
102approved2024-01-20YESno (anti-join skips)
103approvedNULLnono (not funded)
104pendingNULLnono (not approved)
105approved2024-01-28noyes

Two rows inserted (101, 105). Row 102 is skipped by the anti-join. Final state: 3 rows in application_history — the original 102 plus the two new ones.

Watch out:

  • NOT IN with NULLs is the silent killer. If application_history.application_id ever contains NULL, NOT IN evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row and the INSERT inserts nothing. Either guard with WHERE application_id IS NOT NULL in the subquery, or rewrite as NOT EXISTS: AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM application_history h WHERE h.application_id = la.application_id).
  • Column lists line up by position, not by name. The order of expressions in the SELECT must match the order of columns in INSERT INTO target (...). Aliases inside SELECT are documentation; they do not steer the mapping.
  • CURRENT_DATE evaluates at INSERT time, so re-running the script tomorrow would write a different archive_date. That's usually the desired behavior for an archive timestamp.
  • approval_date - submission_date in Postgres returns an INTEGER number of days. If either operand is TIMESTAMP, you'd get an INTERVAL instead and have to extract days; sticking to DATE columns keeps the math simple.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM application_history ORDER BY application_id; so the harness sees the post-insert state.

Medium Archive Failed Job Runs with Retry Context (aggregate from full table, attach to filtered subset)

▼
  • INSERT INTO ... SELECT where each archived row needs a per-group aggregate computed across the FULL source table (not just the filtered subset).
  • Trap: filtering to status = 'failed' BEFORE the aggregate makes the retry count blind to the successful retries.
  • Two ranked solutions: window function with FILTER (single CTE, single scan), and the more portable GROUP BY + JOIN form.

Tables: job_runs (run_id, job_id, attempt_number, status, started_at, duration_seconds), failed_runs_archive (same columns plus total_retries)

Real-World Example

A workflow automation platform archives every failed job run for compliance reporting. Each archived row carries a total_retries field that counts how many times the job was retried across ALL statuses (including successful retries) so investigators can see if a failure eventually resolved.

Prompt: INSERT into failed_runs_archive one row per failed job run. Each row includes the original columns plus total_retries = count of rows in job_runs for that job_id where attempt_number > 1 (across all statuses, not just failed).

▶ 1 Window function with FILTER, then filter the result (single CTE, single scan)
INSERT INTO failed_runs_archive ( run_id, job_id, attempt_number, status, started_at, duration_seconds, total_retries ) WITH retry_counts AS ( SELECT run_id, job_id, attempt_number, status, started_at, duration_seconds, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE attempt_number > 1) OVER (PARTITION BY job_id) AS total_retries FROM job_runs ) SELECT run_id, job_id, attempt_number, status, started_at, duration_seconds, total_retries FROM retry_counts WHERE status = 'failed' ORDER BY run_id; SELECT * FROM failed_runs_archive ORDER BY run_id;

Why this is best: One CTE, one scan of job_runs, no JOIN. The window function attaches the per-job_id retry count to every row, then the outer WHERE filters down to the failed ones.

Key insight: WHERE applies BEFORE window functions

If you filter where? What the window sees Correct?
Inside the CTE (same level as the window)Only failed rowsNo — misses successful retries that should count
In an outer SELECT AFTER the CTEAll rowsYes — retry count is computed across every row of the job

Trace through job 104 (the tricky one):

run_id job_id attempt_number status total_retries (window) Passes WHERE failed?
51041failed1 (sees run 6's attempt 2)yes — inserted
61042success1 (sees itself)no — filtered out

Run 5 gets archived with total_retries = 1. The retry that produced the count was run 6 — a SUCCESS that's invisible if you filter to failed before the window.

FILTER vs CASE WHEN inside SUM:

Form Notes
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE attempt_number > 1)SQL:2003 standard; cleanest read. Postgres + modern engines support it.
SUM(CASE WHEN attempt_number > 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)Portable to older engines (MySQL < 8, SQLite); reads as conditional counting.
▶ 2 Two-CTE GROUP BY + LEFT JOIN (more portable)
INSERT INTO failed_runs_archive ( run_id, job_id, attempt_number, status, started_at, duration_seconds, total_retries ) WITH retry_counts AS ( SELECT job_id, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE attempt_number > 1) AS total_retries FROM job_runs GROUP BY job_id ) SELECT jr.run_id, jr.job_id, jr.attempt_number, jr.status, jr.started_at, jr.duration_seconds, COALESCE(rc.total_retries, 0) AS total_retries FROM job_runs AS jr LEFT JOIN retry_counts AS rc USING (job_id) WHERE jr.status = 'failed' ORDER BY jr.run_id; SELECT * FROM failed_runs_archive ORDER BY run_id;

Why pick this over Rank 1: If the engine doesn't support window FILTER (older MySQL, some legacy environments), this form falls back on portable SQL while keeping the same logic. retry_counts is built from the FULL job_runs table (no status filter), so it includes successful retries; the final SELECT then filters to failed rows.

Trade-off vs Rank 1:

Aspect Rank 1 (window) Rank 2 (GROUP BY + JOIN)
CTEs11 (just retry_counts)
JoinsnoneLEFT JOIN
Passes over job_runs1 scan with partitioned window2 scans + hash join
PortabilityModern engines onlyAny engine that supports CTEs

Watch out (applies to both ranks):

  • Filter location matters. Compute the aggregate from the FULL source table; filter to the archive's subset only after. If you filter first, the aggregate sees a shrunken denominator.
  • "Retries" means attempt_number > 1, not "failed attempts". A success that was a second attempt still counts. Read the parenthetical in the prompt carefully.
  • One archived row per failed run, but they share the per-job count. Job 102 has two failed runs (attempts 1 and 2); both archived rows carry the same total_retries = 1 because there's only one row with attempt_number > 1 in the entire job 102 history.
  • Column lists line up by position. The order of expressions in the SELECT must match the INSERT's column list. Aliases are documentation; they don't steer the mapping.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM failed_runs_archive ORDER BY run_id; so the harness sees the post-insert state.

Simple Sequential UPDATEs 4 problems

▼

Template Simple Sequential template (full order)

▼

Use when: every rule checks only columns on the row being updated; the order of the UPDATEs is the logic.

The order, top to bottom:

  1. DO $$ — open the block.
  2. BEGIN — start the body. No DECLARE (there are no variables).
  3. The UPDATE statements, written in the order the rules apply.
  4. END $$; — close the block.
  5. A trailing SELECT — a DO block returns nothing, so add it to see the result.
DO $$
BEGIN
    -- rule 1 runs first
    UPDATE tbl SET col = <expr_1> WHERE <condition_1>;

    -- rule 2 sees the table AFTER rule 1
    UPDATE tbl SET col = <expr_2> WHERE <condition_2>;
END $$;

-- a DO block returns nothing, so add a trailing SELECT to see the result
SELECT * FROM tbl ORDER BY id;

Signal words: "apply these adjustments in order," "after step N, ...," "round to two decimals at the end," "for every row in the table, do X then Y then Z."

Technique: DO $$ BEGIN UPDATE ... ; UPDATE ... ; UPDATE ... ; END $$; SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY ...;

Skeleton you'll fill in:

DO $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE target_table SET col_a = expr_a WHERE rule_1_predicate;
  UPDATE target_table SET col_b = expr_b WHERE rule_2_predicate AND guard_predicate;
  UPDATE target_table SET col_c = expr_c WHERE rule_3_predicate AND guard_predicate;
END $$;

-- Trailing SELECT so the test scaffold sees output:
SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY key;

Anchor problems — tiered discounts (chained percentage UPDATEs), driver shifts (rule chain on independent guard columns), loyalty points (set-based with guard predicates, plus a per-row variant for when guards are not enough).

Easy Sequential Price Updates with Tiered Discounts

▼

A simpler DO block anchor: apply a fixed sequence of UPDATE statements to the same table without any per-row loop. Useful for problems where the rule order matters but each rule is a single set-based UPDATE.

Tables: products (id, category, base_price, final_price)

Prompt: Apply the following rules in sequence, then return the updated table.

  1. Set final_price = base_price for all rows.
  2. Apply a 10% discount (multiply final_price by 0.90) to all Electronics products.
  3. Apply an additional 5% discount (multiply final_price by 0.95) to all products where final_price > 100 after the previous step.
  4. Round all final_price values to 2 decimal places.
▶ 1 DO block with set-based UPDATEs (no per-row loop)
DO $$ BEGIN UPDATE products SET final_price = base_price; UPDATE products SET final_price = final_price * 0.90 WHERE category = 'Electronics'; UPDATE products SET final_price = final_price * 0.95 WHERE final_price > 100; UPDATE products SET final_price = ROUND(final_price, 2); END $$; SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY id;

Why this is best: Each rule is a single set-based UPDATE inside the DO block, applied in the exact order written. Postgres treats the four UPDATEs as one procedural unit, so each rule sees the result of the previous one. The trailing SELECT gives the test harness its output.

Differences from the airline seats pattern:

  • No DECLARE needed — there are no variables.
  • No FOR ... LOOP — every UPDATE is set-based.
  • No IF / ELSIF — conditions live in WHERE clauses on each UPDATE.
  • This is the right shape when the prompt is "apply N rules in order to one table," not "iterate through a list of requests."

Watch out:

  • "Where final_price > 100 after the previous step" means the comparison runs against the value sitting in final_price at that moment, not the original base_price.
  • If the column is DECIMAL(10,2), intermediate rounding can flip strict > comparisons. Test borderline values.
  • Don't forget the trailing ; after END $$.

Easy Apply Driver Shift Performance Adjustments

▼

Same set-based shape as tiered discounts, applied to a ride-share payout table. Three sequential UPDATEs, each one reading the value left behind by the previous rule.

Tables: driver_shifts (shift_id, driver_name, hours_worked, completed_trips, acceptance_rate, base_payout)

Prompt: Apply the following rules to driver_shifts in order, then return the updated table sorted by shift_id.

  1. If completed_trips >= 15, multiply base_payout by 1.20 (a 20% bonus).
  2. After step 1, if acceptance_rate < 0.75, multiply base_payout by 0.85 (a 15% penalty).
  3. After step 2, if hours_worked > 10, add a flat $25 bonus to base_payout.
▶ 1 Three set-based UPDATEs in a DO block
DO $$ BEGIN UPDATE driver_shifts SET base_payout = base_payout * 1.20 WHERE completed_trips >= 15; UPDATE driver_shifts SET base_payout = base_payout * 0.85 WHERE acceptance_rate < 0.75; UPDATE driver_shifts SET base_payout = base_payout + 25 WHERE hours_worked > 10; END $$; SELECT * FROM driver_shifts ORDER BY shift_id;

Why this is best: Every rule is a single set-based UPDATE that filters on a column the prior rule did not change (completed_trips, acceptance_rate, hours_worked). So the order of UPDATEs only affects the cumulative base_payout, not which rows match. No DECLARE, no FOR LOOP, no IF.

Watch out:

  • base_payout is DECIMAL(10,2). Two multiplicative UPDATEs in a row can introduce penny-level rounding. Test borderline values if the prompt depends on a strict > or < comparison against payout.
  • If a future variant adds a rule that filters on base_payout itself, the set-based shape still works — just remember the filter sees the value after prior UPDATEs, not the original.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, and a trailing SELECT so the harness has output.

Medium Loyalty Points Sequential Tier Adjustment

▼

Three rules where each rule's filter depends on a column an earlier rule just changed (tier). Solvable with set-based UPDATEs only if you add a guard so a row that already moved up does not get reclassified.

Tables: member_accounts (member_id, member_name, current_points, tier)

Prompt: Apply the following rules to member_accounts in order, then return the table sorted by member_id.

  1. If current_points >= 5000, set tier = 'platinum' and deduct 500 points.
  2. After step 1, if current_points >= 2000 AND tier <> 'platinum', set tier = 'gold' and deduct 200 points.
  3. After step 2, if current_points < 500 AND tier <> 'bronze', set tier = 'bronze' and add 100 points.
▶ 1 Set-based UPDATEs with guard predicates
DO $$ BEGIN UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'platinum', current_points = current_points - 500 WHERE current_points >= 5000; UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'gold', current_points = current_points - 200 WHERE current_points >= 2000 AND tier <> 'platinum'; UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'bronze', current_points = current_points + 100 WHERE current_points < 500 AND tier <> 'bronze'; END $$; SELECT * FROM member_accounts ORDER BY member_id;

Why the guards matter: The platinum UPDATE drops points by 500. Without tier <> 'platinum' on rule 2, a member that just became platinum at 5300 points would land at 4800 and re-match the gold rule (current_points >= 2000), demoting them. The guard pins each row to the highest tier it qualified for in this pass.

Watch out:

  • Reading "set tier to X if current_points satisfies condition" without a tier guard is the trap. Always ask: could a row that already mutated still match a later rule's WHERE?
  • The bronze rule uses current_points < 500. After the gold UPDATE, a row that started at 2400 now sits at 2200 — it does not match. But a row that started at 600 with no tier change drops nowhere from rule 1 or 2 and stays eligible for rule 3.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM member_accounts ORDER BY member_id; after END $$; so the harness sees output.
▶ 2 Per-row FOR LOOP with IF blocks (when guards are not enough)
DO $$ DECLARE rec RECORD; curr_points INT; curr_tier VARCHAR(20); BEGIN FOR rec IN SELECT member_id FROM member_accounts ORDER BY member_id LOOP SELECT current_points, tier INTO curr_points, curr_tier FROM member_accounts WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; IF curr_points >= 5000 THEN UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'platinum', current_points = current_points - 500 WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; END IF; SELECT current_points, tier INTO curr_points, curr_tier FROM member_accounts WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; IF curr_points >= 2000 AND curr_tier <> 'platinum' THEN UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'gold', current_points = current_points - 200 WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; END IF; SELECT current_points, tier INTO curr_points, curr_tier FROM member_accounts WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; IF curr_points < 500 AND curr_tier <> 'bronze' THEN UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'bronze', current_points = current_points + 100 WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM member_accounts ORDER BY member_id;

When you actually need this: If the prompt says "process rows in a specific order and the result for row N depends on what just happened to row M," the loop is required. The set-based version above only works because each row's three rules read and write that row's own columns. A loop is also the right fall back if you cannot construct a clean guard predicate.

How to spot the loop case: The prompt names a specific iteration order ("for each member, in order"), or one row's outcome would change another row's eligibility. If neither holds, prefer the set-based version — it is shorter and ships fewer round trips between the procedural body and the table.

Easy Update Delayed Shipment Priority Levels

▼

Two set-based UPDATEs that promote rows up a priority ladder for delayed shipments. Order of UPDATEs matters — the higher-tier promotion runs first so freshly-promoted rows do not get double-promoted. Includes the current_date reserved-keyword trap.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
shipment_idINTprimary key
tracking_numberVARCHARpassthrough
scheduled_delivery_dateDATEdelay reference point
actual_delivery_dateDATENULL means undelivered (shipment can be delayed)
priority_levelVARCHAR'standard' | 'high' | 'critical'

Prompt: Assume the current date is '2024-01-15'. A shipment is "delayed" when actual_delivery_date IS NULL AND the current date is more than 2 days past scheduled_delivery_date. For every delayed shipment:

  • If priority is 'high', promote it to 'critical'.
  • If priority is 'standard', promote it to 'high'.
  • 'critical' stays 'critical'.
▶ 1 Two set-based UPDATEs in a DO block, highest tier first
DO $$ DECLARE v_today DATE := '2024-01-15'; BEGIN -- Promote 'high' to 'critical' FIRST. This must run before the standard-to-high -- UPDATE, otherwise rows that just became 'high' would get double-promoted. UPDATE shipments SET priority_level = 'critical' WHERE priority_level = 'high' AND actual_delivery_date IS NULL AND v_today > scheduled_delivery_date + INTERVAL '2 days'; -- Promote 'standard' to 'high' second. The first UPDATE has already finished, -- so the rows that just became 'critical' are NOT in the 'standard' set. UPDATE shipments SET priority_level = 'high' WHERE priority_level = 'standard' AND actual_delivery_date IS NULL AND v_today > scheduled_delivery_date + INTERVAL '2 days'; END $$; SELECT * FROM shipments ORDER BY shipment_id;

Why no FOR LOOP is needed: Both rules check columns that live on the row being updated (priority_level, actual_delivery_date, scheduled_delivery_date). Promoting one row never affects whether a different row qualifies. So set-based UPDATEs in the right order are enough — passes the "one-question test" at the top of this topic.

Why order matters:

  • Run standard → high first and a delayed standard shipment becomes high. Then the second UPDATE (high → critical) sees it and double-promotes it to critical. Wrong.
  • Run high → critical first. The freshly-critical rows are no longer 'high'. The second UPDATE only sees the original standards and promotes them to high. Correct.
  • Same shape as the loyalty points anchor: when a chain of UPDATEs walks rows up a tier ladder, do the topmost promotion first or use a guard predicate.

Two traps that look right but break this problem:

  • Naming a variable current_date. current_date is a reserved keyword in Postgres that returns today's actual date. A local variable with the same name is silently ignored — the engine substitutes the keyword. Comparisons like "today (2026) > scheduled (2024) + 2 days" then evaluate as TRUE for everything, and rows that should not have been delayed get promoted anyway. Rename to something unambiguous like v_today.
  • Reading "more than 2 days past" as >=. "More than" is strict >. A shipment scheduled exactly 2 days ago does NOT qualify. Using >= would silently flip a row that should stay unchanged.

Trace through the example data (today = 2024-01-15):

id priority before delivered? scheduled days late delayed? priority after
1highno2024-01-105yescritical
2standardno2024-01-123yeshigh
3standardyes (2024-01-14)2024-01-14—no (delivered)standard
4criticalno2024-01-114yescritical (no rule)
5highno2024-01-132no (not > 2)high (unchanged)
6standardno2024-01-087yeshigh

Watch out:

  • Use a v_ prefix (or any non-keyword name) for variables. Postgres has many reserved words: current_date, current_time, current_user, session_user, localtime, localtimestamp, etc.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM shipments ORDER BY shipment_id; after END $$; so the harness has output to compare.
  • Even though the prompt asks for a DO block, no DECLARE-of-record + FOR LOOP is required. Reach for the loop only when the topic-level decision rule says you must.

Row-by-Row State Mutation 7 problems

▼

Template Row-by-Row template (full order: DO / DECLARE / BEGIN / FOR LOOP)

▼

Use when: each event must read the row's current state because an earlier event may have changed it.

The order, top to bottom:

  1. DO $$ — open the block.
  2. DECLARE — the record variable and any scratch variables, before BEGIN.
  3. BEGIN — start the body.
  4. FOR r IN SELECT ... ORDER BY ... LOOP — walk the queue in order.
  5. SELECT ... INTO — pull the target's current state into a variable.
  6. IF / ELSIF / END IF — branch on state or event type.
  7. UPDATE — mutate the target row.
  8. END LOOP; then END $$; — close the loop, then the block.
  9. A trailing SELECT — to see the result.
DO $$
DECLARE
    r RECORD;               -- holds one queue row at a time
    current_status INT;     -- scratch var for the target's fresh state
BEGIN
    FOR r IN
        SELECT * FROM queue ORDER BY id          -- walk the queue in order
    LOOP
        -- read the target's CURRENT state (an earlier iteration may have changed it)
        SELECT status INTO current_status
        FROM target
        WHERE id = r.target_id;

        IF current_status = 0 THEN
            UPDATE target SET status = 1 WHERE id = r.target_id;
        ELSIF current_status = 1 THEN
            UPDATE target SET status = 2 WHERE id = r.target_id;
        END IF;
    END LOOP;
END $$;

-- a DO block returns nothing, so add a trailing SELECT to see the result
SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY id;

Signal words: "return the table after the requests have been performed," "apply these updates in order," "process each request from lowest id," "if the seat is free / reserved by this person, then..."

Technique: DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; ... BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM requests ORDER BY id LOOP ... IF ... THEN UPDATE ... END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM table ORDER BY ...;

Skeleton you'll fill in:

DO $$
DECLARE
  r RECORD;
  current_state INT;
BEGIN
  FOR r IN SELECT * FROM requests ORDER BY request_id LOOP
    SELECT col INTO current_state
    FROM target_table
    WHERE key = r.key;

    IF some_condition_using_r_and_current_state THEN
      UPDATE target_table
      SET col = new_value
      WHERE key = r.key;
    END IF;
  END LOOP;
END $$;

-- Trailing SELECT so the test scaffold sees output:
SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY key;

Anchor problems — airline seats (queue + seat state), refund queue (queue + line state with amount guard), cohort enrollment (queue + two-column state guard), readmission severity (history lookup with self-gating downstream rules), content watch session (four-state FSM with viewer guard and progress cap).

Medium Airline Seats: apply reserve / purchase requests in order

▼

Anchor problem for the DO block recipe. Apply requests from lowest request_id upward. A reserve succeeds only if the seat is free; a purchase succeeds if the seat is free or already reserved by that same person.

Tables:

  • seats(seat_no, status, person_id) — status: 0 free, 1 reserved, 2 purchased.
  • requests(request_id, request, seat_no, person_id) — request: 1 reserve, 2 purchase.
▶ 1 DO block + FOR loop + IF / ELSIF + trailing SELECT
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; current_status INT; current_owner INT; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM requests ORDER BY request_id LOOP SELECT status, person_id INTO current_status, current_owner FROM seats WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; IF r.request = 1 AND current_status = 0 THEN UPDATE seats SET status = 1, person_id = r.person_id WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; ELSIF r.request = 2 AND (current_status = 0 OR (current_status = 1 AND current_owner = r.person_id)) THEN UPDATE seats SET status = 2, person_id = r.person_id WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM seats ORDER BY seat_no;

Line-by-line walkthrough:

Line What it does
DO $$ Opens an anonymous procedural block. Postgres treats everything between the dollar quotes as a single PL/pgSQL routine.
DECLARE Starts the variable declaration section. All variables used in the body must be declared here before BEGIN.
r RECORD; Declares r as a generic row type that will hold one request row at a time during the loop.
current_status INT;
current_owner INT;		 Two scalar variables that will hold the seat's current state (read fresh each iteration).
BEGIN Marks the start of the procedural body. Logic runs from here until END.
FOR r IN SELECT * FROM requests ORDER BY request_id LOOP Iterates through every request, one row at a time, in request_id order. The current request is bound to r on each pass.
SELECT status, person_id INTO current_status, current_owner FROM seats WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; Reads the seat's current status and owner into the scalar variables. Done fresh each iteration so any update from a prior iteration is reflected.
IF r.request = 1 AND current_status = 0 THEN Reserve branch: only fires when the request is "reserve" (1) and the seat is currently free (0).
UPDATE seats SET status = 1, person_id = r.person_id WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; Marks the seat reserved (status 1) and records the requester as the owner.
ELSIF r.request = 2 AND (current_status = 0 OR (current_status = 1 AND current_owner = r.person_id)) THEN Purchase branch: fires when the request is "purchase" (2) and the seat is either free, or already reserved by the same person making this request.
UPDATE seats SET status = 2, person_id = r.person_id WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; Marks the seat purchased (status 2) and records the buyer as the owner.
END IF; Closes the IF/ELSIF block. Requests that match neither branch are silently ignored, which is what the prompt requires.
END LOOP; Closes the FOR loop. Returns to the next request until requests are exhausted.
END $$; Closes the procedural body and the DO block. The mutations to seats are now committed.
SELECT * FROM seats ORDER BY seat_no; Trailing SELECT so the test harness has output to compare against the expected table. Without this line the Return Value column is empty and the test fails.

Medium Process Refund Requests in Queue Order

▼

Same shape as airline seats: a state table plus a request queue, processed one request at a time in request_id order. The current row's status is read fresh each iteration so a state change from an earlier request affects whether a later request fires.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
refund_stateorder_line_idINTprimary key
statusVARCHAR(20)'none' | 'pending' | 'approved'
refundable_amountDECIMAL(10,2)decreases as approvals consume it
refund_requestsrequest_idINTprimary key, queue order
request_typeINT1 = initiate, 2 = approve, 3 = cancel
order_line_idINTFK into refund_state
customer_idINTpayload
requested_amountDECIMAL(10,2)amount to deduct on approve

Prompt: Iterate refund_requests in request_id order. For each request, read the current state of the referenced line and apply the matching rule.

  • If request_type = 1 AND current status = 'none': set status = 'pending'.
  • If request_type = 2 AND current status = 'pending' AND refundable_amount >= requested_amount: set status = 'approved' and subtract requested_amount from refundable_amount.
  • If request_type = 3 AND current status = 'pending': reset to 'none'.
  • Anything else is a no-op.
▶ 1 FOR loop + SELECT INTO + IF / ELSIF, mirroring airline seats
DO $$ DECLARE rec RECORD; cur_status VARCHAR(20); cur_refundable DECIMAL(10,2); BEGIN FOR rec IN SELECT * FROM refund_requests ORDER BY request_id LOOP SELECT status, refundable_amount INTO cur_status, cur_refundable FROM refund_state WHERE order_line_id = rec.order_line_id; IF rec.request_type = 1 AND cur_status = 'none' THEN UPDATE refund_state SET status = 'pending' WHERE order_line_id = rec.order_line_id; ELSIF rec.request_type = 2 AND cur_status = 'pending' AND cur_refundable >= rec.requested_amount THEN UPDATE refund_state SET status = 'approved', refundable_amount = refundable_amount - rec.requested_amount WHERE order_line_id = rec.order_line_id; ELSIF rec.request_type = 3 AND cur_status = 'pending' THEN UPDATE refund_state SET status = 'none' WHERE order_line_id = rec.order_line_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM refund_state ORDER BY order_line_id;

Why this is best: The FOR loop walks the queue strictly in request_id order. The SELECT INTO reads the current state freshly each iteration so the prior iteration's UPDATE is visible. Each IF / ELSIF branch checks both the request type and the current state, so a request that does not match any condition is silently a no-op — exactly the behavior the prompt requires.

Why a set-based UPDATE chain fails here:

  • Request 1 marks line 101 'pending'. Request 2 then approves it — this only works if request 1 already ran. A set-based UPDATE refund_state SET status='approved' WHERE ... can't see the intermediate 'pending' state because all UPDATEs would run against the original snapshot.
  • Request 4 (cancel on line 102) only fires if line 102 is currently 'pending', which it became from request 3. The order matters.
  • Request 6 (initiate on line 104) is a no-op because line 104 is already 'approved'. A set-based UPDATE with no state guard would wrongly reset it to 'pending'.

Trace through the example data:

request_id type line state read action resulting state
11 (initiate)101none, $50set 'pending'pending, $50
22 (approve)101pending, $50approve, $50 ≥ $50approved, $0
31 (initiate)102none, $100set 'pending'pending, $100
43 (cancel)102pending, $100reset to 'none'none, $100
52 (approve)103pending, $75approve, $75 ≥ $75approved, $0
61 (initiate)104approved, $0no match (status ≠ 'none')unchanged

Watch out:

  • refundable_amount is DECIMAL(10,2). The strict >= comparison can flip on borderline values if you pre-rounded the input. Trust the column's stored value, not a computed approximation.
  • Re-read state with SELECT INTO at the top of every iteration. Reading once before the loop and reusing the variables would miss the mutations made by earlier requests in the same run.
  • An UPDATE inside an IF branch must filter by WHERE order_line_id = rec.order_line_id; — not a global UPDATE.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, then a trailing SELECT * FROM refund_state ORDER BY order_line_id; so the harness sees output.

Medium Patient Cohort Enrollment DO Block Processor

▼

Same queue + state shape as airline seats and refund queue. The twist: the DISCHARGE rule guards on TWO state columns, so the iteration must read both enrollment_status and program_id fresh each pass.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
cohort_enrollmentspatient_idINTprimary key
enrollment_statusVARCHAR(20)'ACTIVE' | 'INACTIVE'
program_idINTNULL when INACTIVE
cohort_enrollment_requestsrequest_idINTprimary key, queue order
patient_idINTFK into cohort_enrollments
request_typeVARCHAR(20)'ENROLL' | 'TRANSFER' | 'DISCHARGE'
program_idINTtarget program for ENROLL/TRANSFER, must-match key for DISCHARGE

Prompt: Iterate cohort_enrollment_requests in request_id order. For each request, read the patient's current enrollment_status and program_id from cohort_enrollments, then apply the matching rule.

  • ENROLL AND current status is 'INACTIVE': set status to 'ACTIVE' and copy program_id from the request.
  • TRANSFER AND current status is 'ACTIVE': overwrite program_id with the request's value (status stays ACTIVE).
  • DISCHARGE AND current status is 'ACTIVE' AND current program_id equals the request's program_id: set status to 'INACTIVE' and clear program_id to NULL.
  • Anything else is a no-op.
▶ 1 FOR loop + per-iteration SELECT INTO + three-branch IF / ELSIF
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; current_status VARCHAR(20); current_program INT; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM cohort_enrollment_requests ORDER BY request_id LOOP SELECT enrollment_status, program_id INTO current_status, current_program FROM cohort_enrollments WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id; IF r.request_type = 'ENROLL' AND current_status = 'INACTIVE' THEN UPDATE cohort_enrollments SET enrollment_status = 'ACTIVE', program_id = r.program_id WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id; ELSIF r.request_type = 'TRANSFER' AND current_status = 'ACTIVE' THEN UPDATE cohort_enrollments SET program_id = r.program_id WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id; ELSIF r.request_type = 'DISCHARGE' AND current_status = 'ACTIVE' AND current_program = r.program_id THEN UPDATE cohort_enrollments SET enrollment_status = 'INACTIVE', program_id = NULL WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM cohort_enrollments ORDER BY patient_id;

Why this is best: Three branches, three guards. The DISCHARGE branch is the load-bearing one — it requires that the request's program_id matches the row's CURRENT program_id, not the original. So if a TRANSFER changed the program earlier in the queue, a later DISCHARGE that names the old program is correctly skipped.

Why a set-based UPDATE chain fails here:

  • A patient can be ENROLLED, then TRANSFERRED, then DISCHARGED in the same run. Each step depends on the prior step's mutation being visible.
  • A second ENROLL on a patient who is already ACTIVE must be a no-op. A set-based UPDATE without the current_status = 'INACTIVE' guard would clobber the existing program.
  • A DISCHARGE that names the wrong program (because a TRANSFER moved them) must be silently skipped. Only a fresh per-iteration read can catch that.

Watch out:

  • Two scalars in DECLARE, not one. Both current_status and current_program need to be re-read every iteration because either can change.
  • SELECT INTO requires the column order in the target list to match the variable order. Mixing them swaps the values silently.
  • The DISCHARGE branch's current_program = r.program_id guard will fail unexpectedly if current_program is NULL (NULL never equals anything). That is fine here because the status guard already excludes INACTIVE rows where program is NULL, but if the prompt allowed ACTIVE-with-NULL-program rows you'd need IS NOT DISTINCT FROM instead.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, then a trailing SELECT * FROM cohort_enrollments ORDER BY patient_id; so the harness sees output.

Medium Sequential Readmission Severity Update via DO Block

▼

One table only, but each iteration must look up the patient's prior discharge before applying the rules. Mixes a guarded UPDATE inside an IF with two self-gating UPDATEs whose WHERE clauses do the conditional work outside the IF.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
admission_idINTprimary key
patient_idINTgroups admissions across time
patient_ageINTused by rule 3
admission_dateDATEFOR loop sort key
discharge_dateDATENULL while still admitted
severity_scoreINTmutated by rules 1 and 3
high_riskBOOLEANflipped by rule 2

Prompt: Iterate patient_admissions in chronological order (admission_date, then admission_id). For each admission, apply these rules in order:

  • If the patient was discharged from a prior admission within 30 days of the current admission_date, increase severity_score by 10.
  • After rule 1, if severity_score > 75, set high_risk = TRUE.
  • After rule 2, if high_risk is TRUE AND patient_age > 65, increase severity_score by an additional 5.
  • "After rule N" means temporally after — rules 2 and 3 still run even if rule 1 did not fire.
▶ 1 FOR loop + history lookup + IF for rule 1, self-gating UPDATEs for rules 2 and 3
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; prior_discharge DATE; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM patient_admissions ORDER BY admission_date, admission_id LOOP -- History lookup: most recent discharge for this patient before the current admission. SELECT MAX(discharge_date) INTO prior_discharge FROM patient_admissions WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id AND admission_date < r.admission_date; -- Rule 1: guarded by IF because the 30-day window only applies when prior_discharge exists. IF r.admission_date - prior_discharge <= 30 THEN UPDATE patient_admissions SET severity_score = severity_score + 10 WHERE admission_id = r.admission_id; END IF; -- Rule 2: self-gates via WHERE; runs every iteration regardless of rule 1. UPDATE patient_admissions SET high_risk = TRUE WHERE admission_id = r.admission_id AND severity_score > 75; -- Rule 3: self-gates via WHERE; runs every iteration regardless of rules 1 and 2. UPDATE patient_admissions SET severity_score = severity_score + 5 WHERE admission_id = r.admission_id AND high_risk = TRUE AND patient_age > 65; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM patient_admissions ORDER BY admission_id;

Why two shapes in the same loop body:

  • Rule 1's condition (a 30-day gap from a prior discharge) is data the row itself does not carry — you have to look it up. The result lives in a scalar variable, so the gate is a procedural IF.
  • Rules 2 and 3's conditions (severity_score > 75, high_risk = TRUE AND patient_age > 65) live entirely on the row being updated. The WHERE clause already filters them out when the condition fails, so no IF is needed.
  • Putting rules 2 and 3 inside the IF would silently drop them for any admission with no prior discharge — the test fails on those rows because high_risk never flips.

Trace through admission 5 (patient 101, age 72, severity 68, prior discharge 2024-01-30, current admission 2024-02-10):

Step What runs Row state after
Ahistory lookupprior_discharge = 2024-01-30
BIF gap 11 days ≤ 30 → rule 1 fires (+10)severity 78, high_risk FALSE
Crule 2 UPDATE; WHERE severity > 75 matchesseverity 78, high_risk TRUE
Drule 3 UPDATE; WHERE high_risk AND age > 65 matches (age 72)severity 83, high_risk TRUE

Trace through admission 6 (patient 103, age 58, severity 80, no prior admission):

Step What runs Row state after
Ahistory lookupprior_discharge = NULL
BIF NULL ≤ 30 → NULL, branch skippedseverity 80, high_risk FALSE
Crule 2 UPDATE; WHERE severity > 75 matchesseverity 80, high_risk TRUE
Drule 3 UPDATE; high_risk TRUE but age 58 — no matchseverity 80, high_risk TRUE

Watch out:

  • "After applying rule N" is a temporal phrase, not a conditional one. Rules 2 and 3 still run even when rule 1 did not.
  • A window function like LAG(discharge_date) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ...) cannot sit inside a procedural IF condition. Use a separate SELECT MAX(discharge_date) INTO prior_discharge ... WHERE admission_date < r.admission_date first.
  • NULL minus a date is NULL, and IF NULL <= 30 evaluates as false, so admissions with no prior discharge correctly skip rule 1 with no extra IS NOT NULL guard.
  • Order the FOR loop by admission_date, admission_id. Sorting by admission_id alone happens to be equivalent for this dataset but the prompt asks for chronological order.
  • Each UPDATE filters by admission_id = r.admission_id to scope to the row currently being processed. Skip that scope and rules 2 and 3 will fire on every row in the table on every loop iteration.

Medium Content Watch Session Queue Processing

▼

Classic finite-state-machine queue: idle → watching → paused → watching → idle. Four event types, each guarded by current state and viewer ownership. The FINISH branch also accumulates a delta with a hard cap.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
content_itemsitem_idINTprimary key
viewer_idINTNULL when idle
watch_statusINT0=idle, 1=watching, 2=paused
completion_pctINT0–100, accumulated by FINISH
watch_eventsevent_idSERIALprimary key, queue order
item_idINTFK into content_items
viewer_idINTwho fired the event
event_typeINT1=START, 2=PAUSE, 3=RESUME, 4=FINISH
progress_deltaINTadded to completion_pct on FINISH

Prompt: Iterate watch_events in event_id order. For each event, read the item's current watch_status and viewer_id, then apply the matching transition.

  • START (1) AND status = 0: set status to 1, assign viewer_id from the event.
  • PAUSE (2) AND status = 1 AND current viewer matches event viewer: set status to 2.
  • RESUME (3) AND status = 2 AND current viewer matches: set status to 1.
  • FINISH (4) AND status = 1 AND current viewer matches: add progress_delta to completion_pct (cap at 100), set status to 0, clear viewer_id.
  • Anything else is a no-op.
▶ 1 FOR loop in event_id order + four IF / ELSIF transitions + LEAST cap
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; current_status INT; current_viewer INT; current_completion_pct INT; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM watch_events ORDER BY event_id LOOP SELECT watch_status, viewer_id, completion_pct INTO current_status, current_viewer, current_completion_pct FROM content_items WHERE item_id = r.item_id; IF r.event_type = 1 AND current_status = 0 THEN UPDATE content_items SET watch_status = 1, viewer_id = r.viewer_id WHERE item_id = r.item_id; ELSIF r.event_type = 2 AND current_status = 1 AND current_viewer = r.viewer_id THEN UPDATE content_items SET watch_status = 2 WHERE item_id = r.item_id; ELSIF r.event_type = 3 AND current_status = 2 AND current_viewer = r.viewer_id THEN UPDATE content_items SET watch_status = 1 WHERE item_id = r.item_id; ELSIF r.event_type = 4 AND current_status = 1 AND current_viewer = r.viewer_id THEN UPDATE content_items SET watch_status = 0, completion_pct = LEAST(completion_pct + r.progress_delta, 100), viewer_id = NULL WHERE item_id = r.item_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM content_items ORDER BY item_id;

Why this is best: Four state transitions, four guarded branches. The viewer guard (current_viewer = r.viewer_id) prevents user B from pausing or finishing user A's session. The LEAST(completion_pct + r.progress_delta, 100) caps cumulative progress so a delta that overshoots saturates instead of overflowing.

Two traps that look right but break this problem:

  • Wrong sort key in the FOR loop. Ordering by item_id instead of event_id processes events grouped by item, in undefined order within an item. A FINISH that fires before its START in that ordering becomes a no-op (status still 0), then the START runs and leaves the row as "watching" forever. Always order by the queue's monotonic key.
  • Procedural IF inside an UPDATE's SET clause. Trying to write SET completion_pct = IF current_completion_pct < 100 THEN ... END IF raises a syntax error. SET only accepts column = expression pairs — use CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END as the expression, or use LEAST(...) for a cap.

Watch out:

  • The PAUSE, RESUME, and FINISH branches do NOT need to overwrite viewer_id; the current viewer stays the same. Only START assigns it; only FINISH clears it.
  • If the viewer guard is omitted on FINISH, a different viewer's FINISH event would close someone else's session and credit progress to the wrong row. The guard is part of correctness, not just defensiveness.
  • An empty UPDATE ... SET watch_status = 1 with no other columns is fine. PostgreSQL does not require you to list every changing column.
  • Reading three scalars in one SELECT INTO is one round trip per iteration; the column order in the SELECT list must match the variable order or values get swapped silently.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, then a trailing SELECT * FROM content_items ORDER BY item_id; so the harness sees output.

Medium Sequential Medication Dose Adjustments

▼

Priority-ordered queue with three operation types — increase and decrease compose multiplicatively, while set overrides whatever the prior operations produced. Adjustments are flagged processed inside the loop. No SELECT INTO needed because each branch is a plain UPDATE that re-reads the row's current value.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
medication_ordersorder_idINTprimary key, target of adjustments
patient_idINTunused by mutation
medication_nameVARCHAR(100)unused by mutation
current_daily_doseDECIMAL(10,2)value mutated each iteration
dose_unitVARCHAR(20)passthrough
pending_adjustmentsadjustment_idINTprimary key
order_idINTFK into medication_orders
operation_typeVARCHAR(20)'increase' / 'decrease' / 'set'
adjustment_factorDECIMAL(10,2)multiplier, divisor, or replacement value
adjustment_priorityINTloop ORDER BY column — lowest first
is_processedBOOLEANflipped to TRUE inside the loop

Prompt: Iterate pending_adjustments in adjustment_priority order (lowest first). For each row, apply the operation to the matching medication_orders.current_daily_dose:

  • 'increase': multiply current_daily_dose by adjustment_factor.
  • 'decrease': divide current_daily_dose by adjustment_factor.
  • 'set': replace current_daily_dose with adjustment_factor.

After applying the operation, mark that adjustment is_processed = TRUE. Trailing SELECT * FROM medication_orders ORDER BY order_id;.

▶ 1 FOR LOOP ordered by priority + branchy UPDATE + mark-processed inside loop
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM pending_adjustments ORDER BY adjustment_priority LOOP IF r.operation_type = 'increase' THEN UPDATE medication_orders SET current_daily_dose = current_daily_dose * r.adjustment_factor WHERE order_id = r.order_id; ELSIF r.operation_type = 'decrease' THEN UPDATE medication_orders SET current_daily_dose = current_daily_dose / r.adjustment_factor WHERE order_id = r.order_id; ELSIF r.operation_type = 'set' THEN UPDATE medication_orders SET current_daily_dose = r.adjustment_factor WHERE order_id = r.order_id; END IF; UPDATE pending_adjustments SET is_processed = TRUE WHERE adjustment_id = r.adjustment_id; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM medication_orders ORDER BY order_id;

Three patterns this anchor adds to the Row-by-Row State Mutation recipe:

  • ORDER BY the priority column, not the surrogate id. The prompt explicitly orders by adjustment_priority, not adjustment_id. On example data the two columns happen to be aligned, so iterating by adjustment_id still passes — but on test data with reshuffled priorities, a 'set' ordered last by priority but middle by id would land in the wrong slot and the final dose would be wrong. Always order by the column the prompt names.
  • FOR LOOP without SELECT INTO. Earlier anchors (airline seats, content watch) capture state into scalar variables because each branch GUARDS on the row's current state. Here every branch is a plain UPDATE with no state guard — the only thing that varies per branch is which arithmetic to apply. UPDATE implicitly re-reads the row each time, so the prior iteration's effect is already visible without a manual SELECT col INTO var step.
  • Mark-processed UPDATE belongs after END IF, not inside a branch. Putting the cleanup UPDATE inside the 'set' branch only marks 'set' rows; putting it before END LOOP; but after END IF; marks every row regardless of which branch fired. The WHERE adjustment_id = r.adjustment_id filter targets only the current iteration's row — without it, every iteration would mark every adjustment, which works on the final state but is wasteful and obscures intent.

Trace through the example data (4 orders, 4 adjustments):

priority order_id op factor dose before dose after
11 (Metformin)increase1.501000.001500.00
22 (Lisinopril)decrease2.0010.005.00
31 (Metformin)set2000.001500.002000.00 (override)
43 (Atorvastatin)increase2.0020.0040.00

Final doses: Metformin 2000.00, Lisinopril 5.00, Atorvastatin 40.00, Levothyroxine 50.00 (no adjustment).

Watch out:

  • 'set' must come AFTER 'increase' and 'decrease' to override. The priority field encodes the intended order. If priority 3 is a 'set' and priority 1–2 are 'increase'/'decrease', the multiplicative ops fire first and the 'set' overwrites them. Reordering would silently change the answer.
  • The mark-processed UPDATE without WHERE is the easy bug. UPDATE pending_adjustments SET is_processed = TRUE with no WHERE sets every row in the table to TRUE on every iteration — the final state is correct, but if the harness checks pending_adjustments per iteration (or if a future requirement adds a partial-failure rollback), the bug surfaces. Always anchor the cleanup UPDATE to WHERE adjustment_id = r.adjustment_id.
  • DECIMAL(10,2) rounds intermediate values. Each UPDATE's result is stored back into a DECIMAL(10,2) column, so values are rounded to 2 decimals between iterations. A sequence like increase * 1.333 then decrease / 1.333 won't return to the original because the intermediate is rounded; the prompt should be designed so this rounding doesn't matter.
  • No-op when order_id doesn't match. If a pending_adjustments.order_id points to a non-existent order, the UPDATE ... WHERE order_id = r.order_id updates zero rows and silently moves on. That's correct behavior here, but worth noting if the prompt expects an error in that case.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, then SELECT * FROM medication_orders ORDER BY order_id; so the harness sees the post-mutation snapshot.

Medium Apply Sequential No-Show Penalties (compounding state mutation)

▼
  • FOR LOOP iterating an event log (appointments) to mutate state in a parent table (patients).
  • Each iteration's contribution depends on the patient's CURRENT penalty_points value, so the increment compounds (doubles plus 1) instead of staying linear.
  • Demonstrates the linear vs compounding distinction: same surface prompt language, very different math.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
patientspatient_idINTprimary key, target of mutation
patient_nameVARCHAR(100)passthrough
penalty_pointsINT DEFAULT 0value mutated on each no-show; pre-existing values count as the patient's "starting state"
appointmentsappointment_idINTprimary key
patient_idINTFK into patients
scheduled_atTIMESTAMPloop ORDER BY column — chronological
statusVARCHAR(20)'completed' / 'no_show' / etc.; only 'no_show' triggers mutation

Prompt: Iterate appointments in scheduled_at order. For each row where status = 'no_show', increment that patient's penalty_points using the rule that each no-show contributes (prior penalty + 1) — meaning the patient's current penalty_points value is treated as the running prior count. Trailing SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id;.

▶ 1 FOR LOOP + IF status filter + compounding UPDATE (2x+1)
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM appointments ORDER BY scheduled_at LOOP IF r.status = 'no_show' THEN UPDATE patients SET penalty_points = 2 * penalty_points + 1 WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id;

Why 2 * penalty_points + 1 matches the expected output:

  • The rule says "increment by (prior count + 1)." If you treat the patient's current penalty_points as the prior count: new = old + (old + 1) = 2 * old + 1.
  • Algebraically equivalent forms: penalty_points + (penalty_points + 1), 2 * penalty_points + 1, (2 * penalty_points) + 1. All three give the same answer.
  • Since the rule reads the column as part of the increment, you don't need a SELECT INTO variable — the UPDATE itself reads the current value and writes the new one in one statement.

Linear vs compounding (the trap):

Approach Formula Bob's path (start 1, 2 no-shows) Final
Linear (external counter)new = old + counter (counter starts at 0, increments by 1)1 → 1+1=2 → 2+2=44 (wrong)
Linear (counter from existing penalty)new = old + counter (counter starts at existing penalty)1 → 1+2=3 → 3+3=66 (still wrong)
Compounding (current value as count)new = 2 * old + 11 → 2(1)+1=3 → 2(3)+1=77 (correct)

Trace through the example data (scheduled_at order):

appointment_id patient_id status patient before UPDATE fires? patient after
1011 AlicecompletedAlice 0noAlice 0
1022 Bobno_showBob 1yesBob 2(1)+1 = 3
1031 Aliceno_showAlice 0yesAlice 2(0)+1 = 1
1043 CarolcompletedCarol 0noCarol 0
1051 Aliceno_showAlice 1yesAlice 2(1)+1 = 3
1062 Bobno_showBob 3yesBob 2(3)+1 = 7

Final: Alice 3, Bob 7, Carol 0.

Linear vs compounding cheatsheet:

  • Linear formula: new = old + k. Add a fixed amount each step. After n steps: start + n*k.
  • Compounding formula (pure): new = old * r. Multiply by a fixed ratio each step. After n steps: start * r^n.
  • Compounding with offset: new = old * r + k. The no-show formula uses r=2, k=1 → new = 2 * old + 1.
  • Spotting compounding in a prompt: if the rule's contribution refers to the CURRENT value of the column you're updating (not a fixed amount, not an external counter), it compounds. Words like "double," "based on current," "depends on existing value" — compounding signal. Words like "add 1 each time," "add a fixed bonus" — linear signal.
  • Snowball memory device: linear adds the same scoop of snow each step; compounding rolls a snowball downhill that picks up more snow because it's already bigger.

Watch out:

  • Status string typo silently no-ops everything. IF r.status = 'now_show' (with a stray 'w') never matches, so no UPDATE fires and the patients table comes back unchanged. Match the literal in the data exactly: 'no_show'.
  • The UPDATE doesn't need SELECT INTO here. Because the new value is a function of the column itself (2 * penalty_points + 1), Postgres reads the current row value as part of the UPDATE expression. Capturing into a variable first is harmless but unnecessary; the FOR LOOP exists only to enforce chronological order on the appointments side.
  • Existing penalty_points values matter. A patient who starts at 0 follows 0 → 1 → 3 → 7 → 15. A patient who starts at 1 (like Bob, who already had 1 prior no-show before the example data) follows 1 → 3 → 7. The compounding rule means starting state heavily affects the final result, unlike linear addition.
  • Pre-filtering the FOR LOOP to only no-show rows is also valid. FOR r IN SELECT * FROM appointments WHERE status = 'no_show' ORDER BY scheduled_at LOOP avoids the IF check inside. Either form works; the IF version is closer to the prompt's "iterate all appointments" wording.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, then SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id; so the harness sees the post-mutation snapshot.

Editorial note — why the prompt language was confusing: the prompt phrasing "first no-show adds 1, second adds 2, third adds 3" sounds linear (counter-based), but the answer key uses a compounding rule that treats the patient's current penalty_points as the running "prior count." Those two interpretations only match for a patient starting at 0 — for any non-zero starting value, they diverge. When a problem mixes "increment by N" framing with a column whose value compounds, the math depends on which interpretation the answer key picked, and the prompt has to be explicit about that.

Hard Process Story View Events in Order (DO block, derived column update trap)

▼

FOR loop over an event log in chronological order; each event reads the current state, checks preconditions, and conditionally updates the target row. The marquee lesson: inside a single UPDATE statement, the RIGHT side of every SET expression reads the OLD row values, so a tier flip that depends on the just incremented total_views silently uses the stale BEFORE the update value.

Tables: stories (story_id, creator_id, status, total_views, tier) holds the current state; story_events (event_id, event_type, story_id, requester_id, view_count) is the chronological event log. Event types: 1 = view_burst (+view_count, may flip tier to 'viral' at 1000+), 2 = archive_request (gated on requester = creator), 3 = reactivate_request (gated on requester = creator + resets tier to 'standard'). Failed preconditions are no ops.

ⓘ INFO — Conditional SET on a derived value inside a single UPDATE

When one SET expression depends on the NEW value of another column being assigned in the SAME UPDATE, naming the column on the right side reads its OLD value, not its just assigned NEW value. Postgres evaluates ALL right side expressions against the BEFORE the update row, then applies all SET assignments simultaneously.

The pattern that DOES NOT work:

UPDATE stories
SET total_views = c_total_views + r.view_count,
    tier = CASE WHEN total_views >= 1000 THEN 'viral' ELSE tier END
WHERE story_id = r.story_id;

The total_views in the CASE is the OLD column value (e.g. 800), NOT the new c_total_views + r.view_count (e.g. 1050). The tier never flips to 'viral'.

Three fixes, pick the one that fits your style:

  1. Replicate the expression in the CASE (least typing, reads cleanly when the expression is short):
    tier = CASE WHEN c_total_views + r.view_count >= 1000 THEN 'viral' ELSE tier END
  2. Compute the new value into a local variable BEFORE the UPDATE (cleanest when the expression repeats more than once or is complex):
    new_total := c_total_views + r.view_count;
    UPDATE stories SET total_views = new_total,
        tier = CASE WHEN new_total >= 1000 THEN 'viral' ELSE tier END
    WHERE story_id = r.story_id;
  3. Two sequential UPDATEs (each statement sees the prior one's writes): set total_views in the first UPDATE, then read it via SELECT and set tier in a second UPDATE. More verbose but eliminates the trap entirely.

The same trap applies to any column derived SET (price = base * 1.1 followed by tax = price * 0.08), any UPSERT with conditional ON CONFLICT logic, and any trigger function that references NEW.col where col was set earlier in the same statement.

→

Decision Tree Path

Events arrive in an order AND must see prior writes → FOR loop over story_events ORDER BY event_id. Each event reads state → SELECT ... INTO local variables. Conditional updates with derived columns → either replicate the expression in the CASE OR compute into a local variable first (see INFO callout above). No op on failed preconditions → gate the UPDATE behind IF; do nothing in the ELSE.

Real World Example

A photo sharing app has stories that accumulate views from a stream of events. The tier ('standard' → 'viral') drives ranking in the feed. Events arrive out of order from the analytics pipeline but must be processed in event_id order so the same view burst followed by an archive request lands the story in the correct final state. The processor runs nightly to reconcile the day's events.

Build order — loop, read, gate, update with derived value safely:

  1. FOR loop driven by SELECT * FROM story_events ORDER BY event_id — the ORDER BY is mandatory so dependent events see prior writes.
  2. Inside the loop, SELECT status, creator_id, total_views INTO local_vars FROM stories WHERE story_id = r.story_id to read the current state for this iteration. Subsequent iterations naturally see prior UPDATEs because each iteration re reads.
  3. Branch on r.event_type with IF / ELSIF: each branch checks its preconditions against the local variables, then either UPDATEs or does nothing.
  4. For event_type 1 (view_burst): the tier flip depends on the NEW total_views. Replicate the expression in the CASE: tier = CASE WHEN c_total_views + r.view_count >= 1000 THEN 'viral' ELSE tier END. ALTERNATIVE: compute new_total := c_total_views + r.view_count; at the top of the branch and use new_total in both the SET and the CASE.
  5. For event_type 2 (archive): straightforward UPDATE if both preconditions pass.
  6. For event_type 3 (reactivate): UPDATE both status and tier; tier reset to 'standard' is a literal, no derived value trap.
▶ 1 FOR loop + SELECT INTO + IF / ELSIF branches + CASE with replicated expression
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; c_status VARCHAR(20); c_creator_id INT; c_total_views INT; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM story_events ORDER BY event_id LOOP -- Re read state every iteration so prior UPDATEs are visible. SELECT status, creator_id, total_views INTO c_status, c_creator_id, c_total_views FROM stories WHERE story_id = r.story_id; IF r.event_type = 1 AND c_status = 'active' THEN UPDATE stories SET total_views = c_total_views + r.view_count, -- Derived value trap: replicate the expression in the CASE. -- Naming `total_views` here would read the OLD 800, NOT the new 1050. tier = CASE WHEN c_total_views + r.view_count >= 1000 THEN 'viral' ELSE tier END WHERE story_id = r.story_id; ELSIF r.event_type = 2 AND c_status = 'active' AND c_creator_id = r.requester_id THEN UPDATE stories SET status = 'archived' WHERE story_id = r.story_id; ELSIF r.event_type = 3 AND c_status = 'archived' AND c_creator_id = r.requester_id THEN UPDATE stories SET status = 'active', tier = 'standard' WHERE story_id = r.story_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM stories ORDER BY story_id;
▶ 2 Compute the new value into a local variable (cleaner when the expression is complex or repeated)
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; c_status VARCHAR(20); c_creator_id INT; c_total_views INT; new_total INT; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM story_events ORDER BY event_id LOOP SELECT status, creator_id, total_views INTO c_status, c_creator_id, c_total_views FROM stories WHERE story_id = r.story_id; IF r.event_type = 1 AND c_status = 'active' THEN new_total := c_total_views + r.view_count; -- compute once UPDATE stories SET total_views = new_total, tier = CASE WHEN new_total >= 1000 THEN 'viral' ELSE tier END WHERE story_id = r.story_id; ELSIF r.event_type = 2 AND c_status = 'active' AND c_creator_id = r.requester_id THEN UPDATE stories SET status = 'archived' WHERE story_id = r.story_id; ELSIF r.event_type = 3 AND c_status = 'archived' AND c_creator_id = r.requester_id THEN UPDATE stories SET status = 'active', tier = 'standard' WHERE story_id = r.story_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM stories ORDER BY story_id;

Why this is also good: The new value lives in a named variable so both the SET total_views and the CASE read it consistently. Easier to read for future you when the derived expression grows beyond a simple addition.

Watch out:

  • ORDER BY event_id in the FOR loop is mandatory. Without it, Postgres returns rows in physical / arbitrary order; events that depend on prior state (archive_request gated on active status) will see the wrong current state and silently no op.
  • Read state inside the loop, NOT outside. Hoisting the SELECT INTO outside the loop would freeze the state to whatever it was before iteration 1; subsequent events would see stale data. Each iteration must re read.
  • ELSIF preconditions are checked TOP DOWN. If event_type 1 also passes the precondition check for type 2 by coincidence, the type 1 branch fires and type 2 doesn't even get evaluated. This is the desired behavior; mention it because some procedural languages re evaluate every branch.
  • The trailing SELECT must be OUTSIDE the DO block. A SELECT inside a DO block does nothing visible; PL/pgSQL doesn't return rows from a DO. The graded output comes from a separate SELECT statement AFTER the DO $$ ... $$;.
  • Failed preconditions are silent no ops, not errors. The prompt says "if preconditions fail, do nothing." Do NOT raise an exception or log a warning — just let the IF branch be false and continue the loop. Tests will fail loudly if you raise on every no op event.

Window Function Edges reference

▼

Reference Shape & when you'll see it

▼
Window Function Edge Cases PostgreSQL or MySQL 8+
When you'll see it

A normal-looking window problem where the choice between ROWS / RANGE or RANK / DENSE_RANK / ROW_NUMBER materially changes the answer.

What you write

A SELECT with a carefully chosen window frame.

... OVER (
  PARTITION BY group_col
  ORDER BY ts
  ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING
       AND CURRENT ROW
)

Reference Window Function Edges

▼

The two window-function distinctions that flip answers: ROWS vs RANGE, and RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER.

ROWS BETWEEN vs RANGE BETWEEN

What it does
ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE counts by ORDER BY value. They diverge when ORDER BY values repeat or have gaps.
When to reach for it
Time-series with missing dates: use RANGE for "last 7 days" so missing days still count. Use ROWS for "last 7 records" regardless of date.
SUM(amt) OVER (
  ORDER BY d
  RANGE BETWEEN
    INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING
    AND CURRENT ROW
)

RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER

What it does
RANK skips numbers after ties (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2); ROW_NUMBER never ties (1, 2, 3) and the tiebreak depends on ORDER BY.
When to reach for it
"Nth distinct" use DENSE_RANK; "exactly one winner per group" use ROW_NUMBER with a tiebreak; "Olympic-style ranking" use RANK.
DENSE_RANK() OVER (
  PARTITION BY dept
  ORDER BY salary DESC
)
